The book offers English readers a broad, early survey of Jewish mystical and legal writing. It serves as a door into texts once known only to scholars.
28407-the-plant-lore-garden-craft-of-sha:
Henry N. Ellacombe, vicar of Bitton and a fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, wrote The Plant-Lore and Garden-Craft of Shakespeare from a double love of Shakespeare and gardening. Reviewers praised it as the fullest book on its subject, drawn from Saxon and early English herbals as well as the plays.

Ellacombe traces every plant Shakespeare names, explaining its garden use, its folklore, and its meaning in the passage where it appears. The book suits gardeners who love poetry and Shakespeare readers who love gardens, and it remains a readable store of out-of-the-way knowledge about Elizabethan plants.
28548-gipsy-life-being-an-account-of-our:
George Smith of Coalville published Gipsy Life in London in 1880, as an account of British Gypsies and their children, with suggestions for their improvement. Smith dedicates the work to Parliament, asking not for ethnology but for attention to neglected roadside lives.

Part one rambles through Gipsydom, covering origins, travels, Acts of Parliament, and Gypsies of Notting Hill, with illustrations from the Illustrated London News and the Graphic. Later parts describe the start of Smith's crusade. He asks above all that the schoolmaster reach the children, and that vans and movable homes come under the sanitary inspector's eye.
28552-twinkle-and-chubbins-their-astonis:
Laura Bancroft's Twinkle and Chubbins, copyrighted in 1911 and illustrated by Maginal Wright Enright, sends a farmer's little girl into Nature-Fairyland. Twinkle's father sets a steel trap for a woodchuck eating his clover, and Twinkle creeps to the hole to watch for the animal.

Instead of catching the woodchuck, Twinkle is drawn into his world, where Mr. Woodchuck captures a girl, scolds, argues, and takes her before a judge. Later adventures bring Bandit Jim Crow, Prairie-Dog Town, Prince Mud-Turtle, Twinkle's enchantment, and Sugar-Loaf Mountain. Bancroft writes a charming animal fantasy for young children.
28576-cutting-it-out-how-to-get-on-the-w:
Samuel G. Blythe's Cutting It Out, published in Chicago in 1912, tells how its author got on the waterwagon and stayed there. Blythe insists at once that his book is not a temperance lecture, tract, warning, or admonition, but a plain tale of a personal adventure that wound up rather satisfactorily.

Blythe drank as hundreds of thousands of men drank, attended to his business, kept his health, and provided for his family, and he never thought his drinking immoral. He quit because he wanted to, not because he had to, taking no vow and signing no pledge. Chapters cover why, how, what, and when he quit, and life after quitting, in a frank and humorous voice.
2861-the-sleuth-of-st-james-s-square:
Melville Davisson Post wrote The Sleuth of St. James's Square as a set of detective stories linked by a great investigator and his cases. The contents run from the thing on the hearth, marked by a woman's bare footprint, to the lost lady and the cambered foot. Later cases add the man in the green hat, American horses, spread rails, and a pumpkin coach. Each case turns on a small physical clue read with care.

Post's detective works by reason and by homely detail, as when a father tests a quill pen and writes a dozen formal words about contests in court. The stories favor quiet deduction over chase and violence. The collection appeals to readers who enjoy classic puzzle mysteries in an Edwardian London setting.
28645-lost-in-the-future:
John Victor Peterson's Lost in the Future asks what might follow if people ever passed the speed of light. A narrator and Harry Albrecht fly a shuttleship from their stellatomic, orbiting from pole to pole, two thousand miles over the second planet of Alpha Centauri. A week earlier they made man's first trip through hyperspace, and now they attempt to land first on a peopled world of another sun.

Their receivers pick up no signals, and their radarscopes show no blips from the atmosphere ships crowding the airways. At the airport, people in bizarre dress show no curiosity at the strangers. Readers get a compact puzzle of first contact, where the visitors pass unseen.
2870-washington-square:
Henry James published Washington Square in 1881, setting it in the New York of the first half of the nineteenth century. Dr. Sloper, a respected physician, guards his plain and wealthy daughter Catherine against Morris Townsend, a handsome suitor the doctor believes is after her fortune. Morris swears his affection is pure and disinterested, and the doctor takes note while refusing to believe him.

The novel turns on Catherine's slow growth from obedience to judgment, as her father's cold certainty meets her steady love. James keeps the action within drawing rooms and family talks, letting small speeches carry large stakes. It stands as one of his most accessible novels, sharp about money, pride, and a father's power.
29076-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this third volume of Critical Miscellanies, opening with his essay On Popular Culture, published by Macmillan in 1904. The essay began as an address at Birmingham town hall on October 5, 1876, when Morley presided over the Midland Institute. Its contents run from provincial centers and French classes to a short course of general history, the value of evidence, and popular culture and academic organization.

Morley argues that general knowledge need not be superficial, and that a sound notion of evidence matters more than textbook logic. He opens with a French philosopher who nearly wept before an eager, well-taught youth at an examination. Readers get a Victorian liberal's case for adult education, earnest and eloquent, from a statesman who believed study should reach beyond the university.
29229-andre:
William Dunlap wrote this play about Major John Andre, performed by the Old American Company in New York on March 30, 1798. Dunlap, called the father of the American theatre, lived from 1766 to 1839, and his life preserves much of what we know about the early American stage. As a boy with a Loyalist father, he frequented the playhouse of the Red Coats.

The volume adds authentic documents to the play, including letters to Miss Seward and the Cow Chace poem. Dunlap's Andre treats the British officer's fate with sympathy and ceremony. Readers get a founding work of American drama, important for its subject, its documents, and its author's central place in theatre history.
29244-chronicles-of-border-warfare:
Alexander Scott Withers wrote this history of the settlement of northwestern Virginia and its Indian wars and massacres, edited and annotated by Reuben Gold Thwaites. The text here is a 1971 reprint of the 1895 edition, which expands Withers's original 1831 edition. A memoir of Withers by Lyman Copeland Draper opens the volume.

Withers tells how white settlers pushed into the region, built forts, and fought wars that shaped the frontier. Thwaites's notes add sources and corrections to the older narrative. Readers get a classic, if one-sided, frontier history, valuable for its firsthand material and for showing how nineteenth-century Americans remembered the border wars.
29284-an-encore:
Margaret Deland published this Old Chester story in New York and London in 1907 with Harper and Brothers, copyrighted in 1904 and 1907, illustrated by Alice Barber Stephens. In Old Chester, Deland writes, being romantic ranked just one shade below putting on airs in blame. Captain Alfred Price, through all his seventy years, never put on airs, but certainly had something to answer for in romance.

The frontispiece shows the moment Alfred Price fell for Miss Letty Morris. Later illustrations bring the captain and Cyrus afraid of Gussie, and Dr. Lavender beginning to speak. Readers get a gentle late-life love story from Deland's Old Chester world, where an old captain's heart gets an encore and a village watches with affection.
29370-portuguese-architecture:
Walter Crum Watson published this illustrated study of Portuguese architecture in London in 1908 with Archibald Constable and Company. Watson dedicates the book, in Portuguese, to dear relatives and friends who welcomed him in Portugal. His chapters move from early buildings in the north and south through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries to the Battle of Aljubarrota.

Later chapters treat Batalha and the deliverance of Portugal, with sections on painting in Portugal and church plate. Watson writes as a traveler-scholar, attentive to stone, carving, and history. Readers get a detailed early survey of Portugal's buildings, useful for travelers and for students of a national architecture too often overshadowed by Spain.
29426-things-as-they-are:
Set as mission work in southern India, this book gives a plain, first-hand account of life, caste, and faith in old India, as seen by workers on the ground. Its opening picture shows an old man who tells the reader, you think you know us, but you know nothing at all about us. Closed doors, carved temples, and the three-skein cord mark a world where only a Brahman may enter, understand, or touch.

Letters from missionaries in many parts of India, received within weeks of the book's first printing, confirmed its picture. The account stresses that in old India, caste alone counted for anything, even when a prince gives his weight in gold to Brahmans. Readers of mission history and Indian society will find a frank, vivid record of a vanished social order.
29453-traffic-in-souls-a-novel-of-crime-:
Eustace Hale Ball's 1914 novel grew from Walter MacNamara's photo-play of the same name. Its scenes draw on real vice reports of the day, among them the Rockefeller inquiry and District Attorney Whitman's white-slave report. Set in New York, it follows young women lured into a vice ring and the people who fight to free them. Pictures from the film stand beside the text.

Night courts, gangsters, purity leagues, and poisoned needles crowd chapters that move fast and moralize hard. Ball means the book to expose a trade and to stir reform, not merely to thrill. Readers today will find a frank, if dated, window on Progressive-era fears about city vice and the crusade to end it.
29466-lords-of-the-stratosphere:
Arthur J. Burks's complete novelette, printed in Astounding Stories in March 1933, lifts the great buildings of New York high into the air by a ray from a source no telescope could locate. Eleven chapters run from the take-off through ghostly columns, strange levitation, and frantic scheming, into the void, stratosphere currents, and an invisible globe. Cataclysmic hunger, a scheme described, and a rescue close the tale.

Burks writes at pulp speed, with Tema and Jeter examining a strange ship for clues. The tale's wonder lies in its scale: a city raised to the sky by unseen power. Fans of early science fiction will enjoy a bold, breathless yarn of height, hunger, and daring in the upper air.
29504-what-s-he-doing-in-there:
Fritz Leiber's short tale asks its title question with comic dread. Earth's first Martian visitor, fresh from an orbit-parked rocket, has learned English from radio and television and sought out a cultural anthropologist before any government. The Professor congratulates him on his wisdom, when the Martian stands, grows anxious, and asks, hesitantly, where is it? His long mouth curves upward, which, he has explained, is his smile when it curls down.

Leiber turns the first-contact story into a joke about manners, bodies, and the most private of human rooms. The Martian stepped into a place no Martian had entered, and the tale asks whether he would return, or stay gone for good. Readers get a witty, humane tale that finds alien wonder in the most ordinary of earthly needs.
29577-mayflower-flor-de-mayo-a-tale-of-t:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez's Mayflower, or Flor de Mayo, translated from the Spanish by Arthur Livingston and printed in New York in 1921 by E. P. Dutton, tells a tale of the Valencian seashore. Its chapters open in the widow's tavern, follow Sina Tona's family and a family enterprise, and bring Mary and Jesus to meet. Two women quarrel, smugglers work the coast, and alarm spreads along the shore.

Blasco Ibanez writes of poor fisher folk for whom wind from a certain quarter means tragedy at sea. The novel blends love, labor, and smuggling with the color of Valencia. Readers of Spanish fiction in translation will find a vivid, storm-tossed tale of the sea and the shore folk who live by it.
29647-the-eighteenth-century-in-english-:
Issued in the Langham Series of art monographs, edited by Selwyn Brinton, this illustrated volume treats the eighteenth century in English caricature. Its opening notes that the word caricature resists precise definition, tracing it to the Italian caricare, to load or charge. The book follows English caricature through its great age, when artists loaded portraits with meaning, mockery, and political bite.

Pictures and commentary show how print shops turned politicians, fops, and kings into figures of fun and fear. The series sets the volume beside monographs on Bartolozzi, Japanese color prints, and Montmartre. Students of art and satire will find a learned, well-illustrated guide to an age when a drawing could wound.
29921-storyology-essays-in-folk-lore-sea:
Benjamin Taylor published Storyology in London in 1900, with Elliot Stock. His preface speaks to the general reader, not the expert folklorist or the case-hardened mythologist. The ordinary person who likes to read about what he has no time to study is his audience. Some of the papers had run in a once popular magazine, now defunct, which Taylor notes long survived the ordeal of printing them.

Fourteen chapters follow: Storyology itself, then The Magic Wand, The Magic Mirror, and The Magic Moon. The Devil's Candle leads to the sea and its legends, Mother Carey and her chickens, and Davy Jones's Locker. Flowers of fancy, rosemary for remembrance, herb of grace, and the romance of a vegetable close the plant lore. Taylor claims no great originality, only one or two new ideas, told with charm.
30044-the-carnivore:
G. A. Morris wrote The Carnivore, with pictures by Burchard. Its headnote asks why the visitors were apologetic: it was not their fault that they came to Earth much too late. The narrator wakes to beings standing round his bed in air suits, their heads covered by globes like upturned fishbowls. The scene feels like a masquerade, yet the masks are their faces, and the narrator argues with them as people.

They remind him of Ronny, a small, round, eager medical student he once knew, a pacifist who read his poetry aloud at ill-timed moments and stuttered when he talked too fast. They are all fright and gentleness. The narrator is not the only survivor, but he is the first found, the least damaged, and the one chosen to represent the human race.
30072-angelot-a-story-of-the-first-empir:
Eleanor C. Price wrote Angelot, a story of the First Empire, printed in New York in 1902 by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company. Price had already written The Heiress of the Forest. Twenty-six chapters carry the tale, opening in the depths of old France, where owls hoot in the daytime and a general cries, Je suis le General Bim-Bam-Boum.

La Belle Helene takes an evening walk, Mademoiselle Moineau sleeps, and Monsieur Joseph meets many annoyances. Common sense fights and triumphs, Angelot refuses what has not been offered, and Monsieur Urbain smokes a cigar. The prefect's dog snaps at the general, Monsieur Simon shows himself a little too clever, and Henriette reads history to some purpose. Two soldiers come home from Spain, Angelot climbs a tree, and a dance with General Ratoneau leads toward Angelot's kept tryst.
3015-the-man-made-world-or-our-androcent:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote Our Androcentric Culture, or The Man-Made World, as a feminist analysis of a society shaped by men. Chapters take up humanness, the man-made family, health and beauty, and men and art. Masculine literature, games, ethics, education, fashion, law, crime, politics, industry, and a human world beyond follow. Gilman begins, inoffensively, with sheep.

The sheep, familiar from religious imagery and painters' stock, introduces her argument that male dominance distorts even familiar things. A later chapter notes that games remain vital to human life, yet in a two-sex society where one sex dictates terms, play is divided with great inequality. The book remains a foundational feminist text, clear, systematic, and still provocative.
30227-eighteenth-century-essays-on-shake:
D. Nichol Smith edits nine eighteenth-century essays and prefaces on Shakespeare, published at Glasgow in 1903 by MacLehose and Sons. His preface states the aim: to give an account of Shakespeare's reputation in the century, and to challenge the common view that the age did not give him his due. Rowe's life of Shakespeare from 1709 opens the set, followed by Dennis on genius and writings in 1711.

Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, and Warburton supply editors' prefaces from 1725 to 1747, while Johnson's famous preface of 1765 anchors the middle. Farmer writes on Shakespeare's learning in 1767, and Morgann closes with an essay on Falstaff in 1777. Notes and an index support the texts, making the book a compact course in how the eighteenth century read its greatest playwright.
30244-the-land-of-the-miamis-an-account-:
Elmore Barce tells how the North-West was secured from the end of the Revolution until 1812, in a Fowler, Indiana, volume from the Benton Review Shop in 1922. A picture of General Harrison's house at Vincennes fronts the book, and photos and maps by Lieutenant Don Heaton support the text. Barce, a member of state and national bar associations and the Indiana State Historical Society, dedicates the work to his wife, Carrie May Barce.

Chapters survey the early Northwest Indian wars, the country north of the Ohio as Virginia gave it, and the beaver trade that made furs a prize worth fighting for. Prairie and buffalo, the Wabash and Maumee as chief lines of contact, and the seven tribes who opposed settlement, centered on Kekionga, follow. The book suits readers who want a local, detailed account of the Miami country in its contested years.
30248-crayon-portraiture:
J. A. Barhydt gives complete instructions for making crayon portraits on crayon paper and on platinum, silver, and bromide enlargements, with directions for transparent liquid water colors and for making French crystals. Baker and Taylor published the revised and enlarged New York edition, under copyrights of 1886 and 1892, with pictures throughout. A front illustration shows a free-hand crayon on Steinbach paper, stipple in the face and broken line in the background.

Barhydt, author of the Appleton's Annual Cyclopedia article on the subject in 1890, writes for photographers and amateur artists. His preface promises that a studio experience of twenty-four years stands behind the lessons, including new free-hand crayon work. The book suits readers who want period photographic craft, step by step, from enlargement to finished color portrait.
30249-ways-of-nature:
John Burroughs meditates on ways of nature in a Houghton Mifflin volume from Boston and New York, published in October 1905, with a bird in sight as frontispiece. Chapters treat bird songs, nature with closed doors, the wit of a duck, factors in animal life, and animal communication. Devious paths follow, with the questions of what animals know and whether they think and reflect. A pinch of salt, the literary treatment of nature, and a beaver's reason follow.

Reading the book of nature closes the main run, before gathered notes on training wild animals, an astonished porcupine, birds and strings, mimicry, colors of fruits, instinct, the robin, and the crow. Burroughs opens amused by letters from Californian schoolchildren asking him questions, and answers in the plain, observant voice that made him America's best-loved nature writer. The book suits readers who watch birds and beasts closely.
30298-the-magnificent-adventure-being-th:
Emerson Hough tells the story of the world's greatest exploration and the romance of a very gallant gentleman, in a novel illustrated by Arthur I. Keller and published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1916. Mother and son open, with Meriwether and Theodosia, Mr. Burr and Mr. Merry, and president and secretary following, before a pell-mell and its consequences and a great conspiracy. Colonel Burr and his daughter, a parting, and Mr. Thomas Jefferson lead to the threshold of the west.

The taming of Patrick Gass and Captain William Clark follow, under three flags. Part 2 moves under one flag through a mysterious letter, the day's work, and the crossroads of the west. An appeal, a choice of way, the mountains, trail's end, a summons, and an abyss carry the expedition onward, toward guests of a nation. Hough, author of The Covered Wagon, writes exploration as both history and romance.
30354-the-broom-squire:
S. Baring-Gould tells The Broom-Squire, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York and London under copyrights of 1895 and 1896. Baring-Gould, author of Mehalah, Court Royal, The Gaverocks, Noemi, and Eve, opens at the sign of the Ship, with wandering souls, a punch-bowl, and a girl without a roof. Mehetabel follows, only a charity girl, and then Bideabout, a net, and a surname at last.

Unexpected turns, home, not paradise, and Iver, again Iver, carry the tale through dreams and realities, back again, and gone, to Thor's stone, a shot, and an ironstone hammer. An apparition, a secret, poison, a threat, and a herald of strife lead to a bequest, surprises, Markham, a picture, the only chance, a sleeping draught, and a menaced life. Baring-Gould writes Devon folk life with strong, old-fashioned colour.
30417-the-bright-face-of-danger-being-an:
Robert Neilson Stephens tells The Bright Face of Danger, an account of some adventures of Henri de Launay, son of the Sieur de la Tournoire. Freely translated into modern English, it was published in Boston by L. C. Page and Company in April 1904, illustrated by H. C. Edwards. Stephens, author of An Enemy to the King, Philip Winwood, and The Mystery of Murray Davenport, notes the tale is, in a distant way, a sequel to An Enemy to the King. It may be read alone.

Monsieur Henri de Launay sets out on a journey, with a young man who went singing. Where the lady was, who the lady was, the chateau de Lavardin, and what the peril was follow. Strange disappearances, Mathilde, the winding stairs, more than mere pity, the rat-hole and the water-jug, and the rope ladder carry the adventure onward.
30505-jane-shore:
Nicholas Rowe writes Jane Shore, a tragedy in five acts, correctly given as performed at the Theatres Royal, with remarks, printed in London by D. S. Maurice. Remarks note that Rowe seldom moves pity or terror, yet often elevates sentiments, delights the ear, and improves the understanding.

The tragedy, always acted with great applause, proves Rowe's power in domestic scenes and private distress. Its emotional peaks come when Alicia parts from Hastings, when Jane Shore meets Alicia, and in the final catastrophe. Rowe nearly follows the history of the misguided and unhappy fair one, turning her story into an appeal to pity.
30585-a-diplomatic-adventure:
S. Weir Mitchell writes A Diplomatic Adventure, published in New York in April 1906 by the Century Company, with an illustration of a woman in an agony of alarm. Mitchell opens by noting that no history of a nation's greater years can include its minor incidents, though some may have swayed events.

He was himself an actor in one such lesser incident, as second secretary to the American legation in France during the summer of 1862. He may overestimate its ultimate importance, he admits, since Mr. Adams, minister at St. James, seems to have left it unrecorded. Mitchell tells a first-person tale of diplomacy, danger, and small deeds with large ripples.
30750-the-sex-worship-and-symbolism-of-p:
Sanger Brown II, a doctor and assistant physician at Bloomingdale Hospital, wrote this 1916 study with an introduction by James H. Leuba. Brown argues that psychiatry can learn from related studies of how minds grow, in the individual and in the race, and that early peoples show motives that still matter for mental life. His book is an interpretation, not a field report, and it speaks in the language of early twentieth-century psychiatry.

Four chapters move from simple sex worship through symbolism to sun myths, mysteries, and later forms of worship, closing with interpretations, references, and an index. Brown reads old rites and symbols as signs of deep human drives. Modern readers should treat its theories as dated and its terms as of their time, while still seeing how early students tried to join anthropology and the study of the mind.
30763-am-i-still-there:
James R. Hall wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Analog in September 1963, about a man named Lee and the question in its title. Lee has had a medical check every six months of his adult life. He now feels dull pains that seem to move through his brain, as if a part of his head were cut off from him. Doctors tell him he is fit for surgery, and that the operation should end the pain, as it has before.

The tale turns on identity: if parts of a brain can be changed or replaced, what still makes Lee himself? Hall frames that puzzle in plain hospital scenes, with charts, machines, and a final talk with a chief of post-operative adjustment. Readers get a short, sharp story that asks what the word I means when the body and mind can be remade piece by piece.
30823-memoirs-of-life-and-literature:
W. H. Mallock wrote these memoirs of life and literature, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1920. Mallock, known for novels and for books on belief and democracy, looks back over a long life among writers, churchmen, and society folk. His chapters run from family roots in Devon through Oxford, Torquay society, and a wide circle of friends.

Early chapters recall the Mallocks of Cockington, the rural poor of Devon, and a private tutor, before turning to Byron's grandson, Lord Houghton, and dandies of the old school. At Oxford he meets Browning, Swinburne, and Ruskin, and later chapters follow his own writing and thought. It is a rich, opinionated memoir for readers who enjoy Victorian literary life from the inside.
30975-soil-culture-containing-a-comprehe:
J. H. Walden wrote this 1858 guide to soil culture, published by Robert Sears in New York and entered for copyright in 1857. Its full title promises a comprehensive view of agriculture, horticulture, pomology, domestic animals, rural economy, and agricultural literature, with numerous engravings. Walden dedicates the volume to the practical cultivators of the soil, whom he calls the true lords of the manor.

His prefatory note recalls the saying that he who makes two blades of grass grow where one grew before is a benefactor of his race. It adds that one who teaches millions how it is done is no less so. The last half century, Walden says, brought more knowledge of soil work through experiment and writing than all previous history. It is a solid mid-nineteenth-century manual for farmers, gardeners, and students of rural life.
30982-an-introduction-to-shakespeare:
H. N. MacCracken, F. E. Pierce, and W. H. Durham wrote this introduction to Shakespeare. They were of the department of English literature in the Sheffield Scientific School of Yale University. It was published by the Macmillan Company in New York in 1925, with copyright in 1910 and many reprintings in between. Its frontispiece shows the title page of the First Folio, the first collected edition of Shakespeare's plays, from the copy in the New York Public Library.

Eight chapters run from an outline of Shakespeare's life and English drama before Shakespeare through the Elizabethan theater and Elizabethan London. They continue with Shakespeare's nondramatic works, the sequence of his plays, his development as a dramatist, and the chief sources of his plays. It is a clear, scholarly textbook introduction, built for students meeting Shakespeare whole for the first time.
3109-fashions-in-literature:
This posthumous set gathers Warner's essays on reading and writing. An introduction recalls that readers had known him for thirty years and more. Since My Summer in a Garden, it says, his name alone had been introduction enough. His fame had mellowed into memory by the time these pieces were collected.

Clarity of mind and lucidity of style marked his work, joined to sincerity and urbanity. The essays weigh literary fashion: what lasts, what merely passes, and how taste forms around new books. They give a working critic's view of American letters at the turn of the century, in prose free of the jargon it gently mocks.
31090-inspiration-and-interpretation-sev:
The Reverend John William Burgon, fellow of Oriel College and select preacher, preached these seven sermons before the University of Oxford in 1861 as an answer to Essays and Reviews. Dedicated to William Sewell of Exeter College, the volume defends the integrity of Christian truth against what Burgon saw as unscrupulous assaults in that controversial collection.

Burgon's preface explains that the first sermon grew from advice he had already given students face to face. The series builds into a sustained Oxford defense of biblical inspiration and interpretation. For readers of Victorian religion, the book captures the high-church counterattack in the sharpest years of the Essays and Reviews storm.
31151-the-english-novel-in-the-time-of-s:
Jusserand's study of the English novel in Shakespeare's age traces fiction from its remote origins through old historical romances and the Norman Conquest's effect on English minds. It also covers Caxton's printing press with its share for fiction. The Renaissance chapters follow the Italian invasion of England, Erasmus's judgments, and the wider awakening of learning.

Later chapters take up Lyly's Euphues, a book for women, with its foreign-born euphuism and courtly talk. They go on to Lyly's heirs Greene, Breton, and Lodge, Sidney's life and works, and the merry books that kept readers healthy. The book remains a learned, readable guide to how the novel grew up beside Shakespeare's stage.
31174-the-planet-with-no-nightmare:
Jim Harmon's science fiction story follows a survey team bound for the planetoids of Yancy-6, months by jump drive from the nearest Earth star, visited four times in three generations. Tension eases as the ship lands. The crew steps out under a black sky crowded with a fiery belt of minor planets. Most of them are large enough to hold air, though no one knows why some do not.

Among the crew are Ekstrohm, hiding a secret night problem from his shipmates, the bulky Ryan, and the sharp-eyed Nogol. Their puzzle soon becomes the planet's creatures, which die with strange ease and yet seem not to die at all. The story turns exploration into quiet horror, asking what a world without nightmares might cost.
31555-under-the-liberty-tree-a-story-of-:
James Otis's Under the Liberty Tree, a story of the Boston Massacre, belongs to his Stories of American History series, published by Estes and Lauriat. The series also offered The Boys of 1745 at the Capture of Louisbourg and An Island Refuge: Casco Bay in 1676. It also offered Neal the Miller: A Son of Liberty and Ezra Jordan's Escape from the Massacre at Fort Loyall. Each volume, cloth bound, sold for seventy-five cents.

Otis writes American history as adventure for young readers, with the Boston Massacre as its dramatic center. Under the liberty tree itself, colonists gathered, plotted, and protested, and Otis's young heroes learn what liberty cost. Readers of historical fiction for children will find a straightforward, patriotic tale, where history arrives through boys caught in great events.
31588-the-house-from-nowhere:
Arthur G. Stangland's time-travel story opens on the morning of July 24, 2052, with Philon Miller at breakfast. On his closed-circuit industrial television screen glows the Food Preparation Center menu, and he punches the button for orange juice, coffee, ham, and eggs. His last night's visitors are still on his mind, and they had made matters appear justifiable.

The visitors are the MacDonalds, new neighbors who offer a bit too much, as the story's tagline puts it, because they are anachronistic. A presidential election campaign is going badly, and its chairman Rakoff worries over his poll quota. Stangland's tale plays the paradoxes of time travel against ordinary domestic life.
31729-the-apple-the-kansas-apple-the-big:
The Apple, the Kansas Apple, the Big Red Apple, was compiled and revised by the Kansas State Horticultural Society, with William H. Barnes as secretary, and printed at Topeka in 1898. Its full title calls the apple the luscious, red-cheeked first love of the farmer's boy and the healthful, hearty heart of the darling dumpling. The book covers what the apple is, how to grow it, its commercial and economic importance, and how to use it.

The society's volume joins pomology to farm economics, teaching growers to plant, tend, and sell the Kansas apple. It is a practical book of its place and time, when the apple was a crop, a food, and a source of pride.
31828-vocal-expression-a-class-book-of-v:
Katherine Jewell Everts's Vocal Expression, a class-book of voice training and interpretation published by Harper and Brothers in 1911, is organized as studies for speakers and readers aloud. Part one covers vocal interpretation, from establishing a conscious purpose and vitality in thinking to humor, imagination, and dramatic instinct.

Each study pairs discussion with material for practice, from direct appeal in prose and verse to lyric poetry, fairy story, fable, short story, and monologue. Part two studies pause and the vocal vocabulary. Readers get a practical elocution textbook for classrooms, still useful for anyone learning to read aloud with sense and feeling.
31870-frances-of-the-ranges-or-the-old-r:
Amy Bell Marlowe's 1915 girls' novel Frances of the Ranges, or The Old Ranchman's Treasure, published by Grosset and Dunlap, opens on a short-grassed plain at sunset. A single rider, Frances on her pinto Molly, pulls in at the report of a bird gun. She hears the snarl of a mountain lion from a deep coulie ahead.

Chapters follow an adventure in the coulie, an old Spanish chest, a shadow in the court, a stampede, and surprising news, as Frances acts for herself on the range. Readers get a wholesome western adventure for young readers, with a sixteen-year-old heroine in olive green, divided skirts, and a broad-brimmed hat, riding to meet danger.
32101-the-crimson-gardenia-and-other-tal:
Rex Beach's collection, published by Harper and Brothers in April 1916, gathers eleven tales of adventure under the title story's name. Beach, known for The Spoilers and Heart of the Sunset, draws on magazine work from Cosmopolitan, the Metropolitan, and other periodicals, with copyrights running from 1906 to 1916. The contents list runs from The Crimson Gardenia and Rope's End through Inocencio and The Wag-Lady to The Stampede, McGill, and The Brand.

The title story opens in festival style, with a royal yacht anchored amid cannon fire, a king going ashore, and a city bright with bunting and whistles. Other illustrations hint at wider ground: a son rising from his father's body as soldiers of the republic charge, and a gunman warned to take his hand off his weapon. Readers get brisk, outdoor adventure fiction, mixing romance, revolt, and frontier incident in the popular magazine manner.
32183-folk-lore-of-shakespeare:
The Reverend T. F. Thiselton Dyer's Folk-Lore of Shakespeare, published in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1884, collects the folk-lore in Shakespeare's plays. Dyer, author of British Popular Customs, Past and Present, argues in his preface that the value of Shakespeare's plays for the social life of the Elizabethan age can hardly be overstated. Shakespeare, he writes, possessed a rich treasury of varied knowledge, much of it picked up almost intuitively.

The plays, Dyer notes, are embellished with illustrations descriptive of the period. Apart from copious references to manners and customs, Shakespeare shows wide knowledge of technical subjects and close knowledge of the folk-lore of earlier days. The following pages collect and group those subjects as far as arrangement permits. Readers get a Victorian reference work, mining the plays for the beliefs, customs, and lore of Shakespeare's England.
32672-direct-wire:
Clee Garson tells of Mort Robbins and Mike Harrigan, two small-time gambling men who ran a cigar store and then closed it to join the armed forces. Both had talked loudly against the Axis, yet both had also nursed excuses, from Mike's supposed ulcer to Mort's asthma, to stay out of uniform.

Their enlistment turns out to be voluntary, and a stranger mystery follows: calls arrive on a phone that bypasses the exchange. A voice on the line wants only Hitler and Mussolini, for a boss too busy for lesser folk, and the tale turns on who is calling, and why. The pair are comic figures, not heroes. Their story asks what fear and greed will do to ordinary men.
3269-the-autobiography-of-mark-rutherfor:
Mark Rutherford's autobiography arrives edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott, at least in the book's own frame. The 1913 Hodder and Stoughton edition gives the chapters in order: childhood, preparation, and Water Lane, then Edward Gibbon Mardon, Miss Arbour, and Ellen and Mary. Emancipation closes the arc the contents reveal.

Rutherford's story is one of religious doubt and slow liberation. A dissenting upbringing, a ministry tried and left, and friendships that widen the mind carry the narrative. Doubt and slow liberation carry the narrative to its emancipation, without a sermon in sight.
32754-one-way-ticket-to-nowhere:
Leroy Yerxa tells of Jeff Blake, a space serviceman who comes home to Hope on a stormy night. Old Holly O'Toole greets him with trouble: Jeff's identical twin Wade plans to marry Dauna Ferrell, and Wade stands deep in a plot over the Mono rail line.

Soon a whole Mono train vanishes like a ghost in the night, and Jeff must find where it went. Forty or fifty captives ride its cars toward a fate planned by Grudge Harror and his gang. With O'Toole at his side, Jeff fights through couplings, cabs, and a swim at Loon Lake to break the plot and free the train.
32769-the-last-generation-a-story-of-the:
James Elroy Flecker tells a story of the future, published by the New Age Press in London in 1908. Seven chapters run from Birmingham Town Hall and a proclamation through a mutual extermination club and the episode of a baby. They end with the Florentine League, the outside world, and the last men.

The narrator wakes on a tall electric standard above a quiet, orderly crowd. Every man carries a rifle, before a Town Hall festooned with red flags. A black-bearded man with green eyes addresses his army: civilization will be destroyed by the weapons of her own making, and they march on London. Later the narrator finds a sad, enchanted garden, a Grecian temple library, and Fiore di Fiamma singing songs that gave up all hope of fame.
32842-london-impressions-etchings-and-pi:
William Hyde's etchings and pictures in photogravure pair with essays by Alice Meynell in a Westminster volume from Archibald Constable and Company, dated 1898. Full-page plates show Westminster Abbey, the Clock Tower, St. Paul's at dawn, Waterloo Bridge, and a night scene in Bermondsey. Plates in the text add a cheap market, a coffee stall, and rain, smoke, and traffic.

Meynell's essays include The London Sunday, A Pilgrim, The Effect of London, and The Climate of Smoke. The London Sunday essay finds the day poorly grasped even by Londoners who know it well, passed out of doors in summer sunshine. Other essays treat the trees, Chelsea Reach, the spring, and the roads, which Meynell reads as signs of perpetual explosion from a center. The volume joins image and essay in one impression of the city.
3290-valerius-terminus-of-the-interpreta:
Francis Bacon's Valerius Terminus survives only in fragments, and this volume gathers them. A preface by Robert Leslie Ellis explains the state of the text. The pieces first appeared in Stephens's Letters and Remains in 1734. They hold detached passages and an epitome of twelve chapters of the first book of Bacon's proposed work on the interpretation of nature.

The detached passages give the first, sixth, and eighth chapters whole, with parts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and ninth. Readers meet Bacon planning his great instauration: a new method for reading nature, against scholastic habit. The fragments suit students of science's history, showing a system still forming, in notes rather than in finished argument.
32907-you-too-can-be-a-millionaire:
Noel Loomis's story, from IF Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1952, imagines a world where money has lost its worth, yet no one dares go broke. Mark Renner runs through streets of broken shop windows, hiding in a jewelry store behind iron grating, while life has become a frantic scramble for points. The system that replaced cash is confusing to him, and dangerous to misunderstand.

The tale's turn comes when a figure called Point-Plus-Pearlie explains the new rules, and the title's promise starts to sound like a trap. Loomis uses satire rather than hardware, poking at economies that reward gaming the score instead of doing useful work. It is a short, wry story about wealth, status, and what a million means when the counting itself has changed.
33005-an-outline-of-russian-literature:
The Hon. Maurice Baring's Outline of Russian Literature offers a short, clear guide to a literature many English readers then knew only by name. It was first printed in 1914-15 for the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. It opens with the origins of Russian writing, moves into the new age of Pushkin. It continues through the great nineteenth-century writers, giving each period its shape and its leading figures. Baring, author of books on Russia and its people, writes from first-hand knowledge.

The outline is meant for general readers, not specialists, and it keeps biography, history, and criticism in balance. It explains why Russian fiction, poetry, and drama took the forms they did, and what English readers should look for first. As an entry point it still works: brief, readable, and confident, it maps a vast field without drowning the newcomer in detail.
33062-a-short-history-of-french-literatu:
George Saintsbury's Short History of French Literature, in a fourth edition from the Clarendon Press in 1892, attempts what its author believed was new in English. The attempt is a succinct history compiled from examining French literature itself, not merely from previous accounts of it. Saintsbury warns that his method changes across the book, because early French literature is largely anonymous. Its authors were shaped more by prevalent styles and forms than by individual genius.

The history therefore treats forms, schools, and periods as well as authors, moving from medieval song and romance through the classical age to modern writing. Saintsbury writes with the confidence of a critic who knew French letters deeply, and his judgments, though dated, remain lively. For students, the book is still a useful short survey, clear about its method and generous in its range.
33356-the-vagabond-in-literature:
Arthur Rickett's study, published in London in 1906, traces the vagabond in literature, from wanderers who lived aloof on hill and valley to modern tramps of the road. With six portraits, it opens with talk on Waterloo Bridge and a last sight of George Borrow, whose Children of the Open Air gives the book its key image. Rickett writes of writers who loved sun, wind, and the sweet reproof of storms.

The study suits readers who love the open road in books, from Hazlitt to Borrow and beyond. Its tone is learned yet warm, and its portraits add a visual thread. For students of literary history, The Vagabond in Literature offers a thoughtful tour of a figure who has haunted English writing: the wanderer who will not settle.
33445-naval-warfare:
James R. Thursfield's Naval Warfare, in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature, gives a short, clear account of war at sea. Thursfield, an honorary fellow of Jesus College, Oxford, writes for general readers who want the principles of naval strategy, tactics, and history without a long treatise. The manual was printed by Cambridge University Press, with offices from London to Bombay.

The book's strength is its concise, lucid style, moving from sail to steam and from blockade to battle in a few chapters. Its tone is scholarly yet plain, suited to students and officers alike. For readers of military history, Naval Warfare remains a handy, thoughtful introduction to how navies fight and why sea power matters.
33447-the-pencil-of-nature:
H. Fox Talbot's Pencil of Nature, published in London in 1844, is the first book illustrated with photographs, and a founding text of the art. Talbot's plates show part of Queen's College, Oxford, the boulevards of Paris, articles of china and glass, a bust of Patroclus, an open door, a leaf, a library scene, and a haystack. His text gives a brief history of his invention.

The book's fame rests on its plates, which proved that light itself could draw, and on Talbot's modest, clear prose. Its value for photographers and historians is immense, as the first proof that pictures could be printed like books. For all who love photography, The Pencil of Nature is a treasure: the art's birth, in its maker's own words and images.
33525-stories-from-tagore:
Stories from Tagore, published by Macmillan in 1918, gathers ten short stories by the Bengali writer in English translation. The contents include The Cabuliwallah, The Home-Coming, Once There Was a King, The Child's Return, Master Mashai, Subha, The Postmaster, The Castaway, The Son of Rashmani, and The Babus of Nayanjore.

The opening story shows a talkative five-year-old, Mini, befriending a fruit seller from Kabul, and the rest range from village schoolmasters and postmasters to returning children and decaying landlord families. Tagore's stories are tender, ironic, and attentive to caste, family duty, and the inner lives of women and children. The collection is an inviting introduction to one of India's great storytellers.
33556-the-fortunes-of-glencore:
Charles James Lever presents a novel of character rather than incident, as his preface plainly states. The story of Glencore turns on family fortune, social standing, and the motives that drive people in well-bred society. Lever watches how pride, affection, ambition, and disappointment shape choices that look small from outside but matter greatly to those who make them.

The narrative moves through drawing rooms and country houses, tracing how a family's position rises and falls with decisions made years earlier. Its interest lies in close observation of manners and feeling, and in the slow untangling of why people act against their own interests. Readers who enjoy social portraiture will find the book's pleasures in its people, not in sudden plot turns.
33589-architecture:
Mrs. Arthur Bell offers a short, illustrated survey of architecture for general readers, defining the art as building that fully fulfills its purpose while bearing the impress of a genuine style. From the humblest cottage to the most dignified temple or palace, she argues, any structure combining practical utility with beauty of design and execution belongs to architecture. Suitability of material and harmony with surroundings give a building vitality.

Eleven chapters move from Egyptian, Asiatic, and early American work through Greek, Roman, early Christian, Byzantine and Saracenic, Romanesque, Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman, Gothic in Europe and Britain. An introduction distinguishes the two main styles, trabeated and arcuated. The book is a clear first guide to reading buildings across history.
33684-on-the-trail-of-deserters-a-phenom:
Captain Robert Goldthwaite Carter of the United States Army recounts a record capture of deserters in this 1920 Washington pamphlet. The year 1871, full of incidents for the Fourth Cavalry and its new colonel, Ranald S. Mackenzie, yielded a capture of ten deserters. Carter believes no earlier capture in the Military Department of Texas, and perhaps in no American military department at all, had matched it. Carter, who lived the experience closely, tells of terrible exposure and unavoidable hardship.

The Fourth Cavalry, doing about three-fourths of the army's active work in subduing Native tribes and opening the frontier to settlement, suffered desertions despite high morale and near-perfect discipline. Carter asks whether Mackenzie was a martinet, and answers through the story itself. The pamphlet preserves a vivid frontier memoir of pursuit, endurance, and military justice.
33739-cuba-its-past-present-and-future:
A. D. Hall surveys Cuba, its past, present, and future, in this 1898 Street and Smith volume, published in the year of the Spanish-American War. Opening with Columbus, who called Cuba the goodliest land eye ever saw, Hall traces discovery and early history, the British occupation, and early struggles for liberty. He also traces the Ten Years' War, the Virginius affair, Cuban heroes and tactics, and Weyler's harsh rule.

Later chapters treat the crime of the century, two methods of warfare, America's charity and Spain's diplomacy, the last days of peace, and the island's topography and resources. Written from a strongly pro-Cuban, anti-Spanish standpoint, the book is a vivid contemporary account of the island's fight for independence and a useful source on American opinion in 1898.
33926-dick-hamilton-s-cadet-days-or-the-:
Howard R. Garis wrote this second Dick Hamilton tale, published in 1910 by Grosset and Dunlap. Dick, a young millionaire, came into his fortune by meeting terms in his mother's will, and more tasks his mother planned still lay ahead. One was to gain a good military training, and this volume sends him to a leading military school.

At Kentfield Academy, Dick meets chums, drills, and the handicap of his wealth: classmates may doubt a rich boy's grit. Garis writes for boys in a brisk, friendly voice. The book offers a cheerful school story with drill, friendship, and fair play.
33969-new-hire:
Dave Dryfoos wrote this short science tale, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in September 1953. Boswell W. Budge, called Bozzy, wakes on February 30, 2054, the most important morning of his life, roused not by his electronic awakener but by his children. Sophie, Howard, and baby Ralph crowd his bed with kisses, demands, and egg on his face.

The tale plays Bozzy's lazy rule, never do tomorrow what can wait past forty, against a day that will not wait. Dryfoos writes with brisk humor about family life in a wired future. The story is a light, funny look at a man, a morning, and a job that must be faced.
34076-fox-trapping-a-book-of-instruction:
A. R. Harding edited this book of instruction on fox trapping, published at Columbus, Ohio, in 1906. It tells how to trap, snare, poison, and shoot foxes, with chapters on general information, baits and scents, foxes and odor, and the chaff method. Traps and hints, land sets, snow sets, and sets for red and grey fox follow.

Wire and twine snares, a Tennessee trapper's method, many good methods, and fox ranches round out the book, with pictures of catches and skins. Harding writes for working trappers in plain terms. The book preserves the fox trapper's craft of its age.
34139-real-gold-a-story-of-adventure:
George Manville Fenn's adventure Real Gold follows two boys, Cyril and Perry, with their father, a colonel, on a journey along a Pacific coast where Spanish is spoken. The boys start by fishing from a boat, then join a trek inland.

Nights by the fire, talks with local Indians, and the slow work of learning a new tongue fill the road. The party presses on in search of the gold of the title. Fenn writes for young readers, mixing outdoor detail with the perils and puzzles of a strange land.
34240-nevermore:
Nevermore is a novel by Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms, printed at London in 1892. It opens in a quarrel between father and son. The son swears he will leave the country rather than be bullied for doing what scores of other fellows have done. The father answers that in their family gambling debts and shady dealings with turf-robbers are forbidden luxuries.

No gift of foresight is needed to read sullen defiance on one side and wounded family pride on the other. The young man is Mervyn Trevanion of Wychwood, head of one of the oldest families in Cornwall, and plainly the son of Launcelot Trevanion. Both men are strong and sinewy, dark, and marked by gentle nurture and assured place. Boldrewood, famed for tales of the Australian bush, here sets a story of debt and disgrace in an old Cornish house.
34370-ephemera-critica-or-plain-truths-a:
Ephemera Critica is a book of literary essays by John Churton Collins, in a fourth edition printed at New York in 1902. Dutton and Constable issued it. Its subtitle promises plain truths about current literature. A note to the second edition regrets an injustice done to Jusserand over a manuscript.

The contents open with the present functions of criticism. Three chapters treat English literature at the universities, and three more our literary guides. Log-rolling and education, the gentle art of self-advertisement, and literary iconoclasm take their turns. Collins argues a paradox: the more widely education spreads, the greater the danger to art and letters. Skilled work, he says, depends on standards the crowd may lower.
34373-the-priestly-vocation-a-series-of-:
The Priestly Vocation is a book of fourteen conferences addressed to the secular clergy. Its full title names the audience directly: priests working in parishes rather than in religious orders. The head of this text is filled with publishers' lists of Catholic books. They place the volume in the Westminster Library, a series of manuals for Catholic priests and students.

Those lists show the company the book keeps. Lives of Bishop Challoner stand beside histories of the Catholic revival in England. Works on emancipation and on the restored hierarchy of 1850 stand near them. The series was edited by Bernard Ward, bishop of Brentwood. A manual of conferences on the priestly calling belongs to the working shelf of the clergy: talks meant to be read, pondered, and used in the care of souls.
34376-our-domestic-birds-elementary-less:
Our Domestic Birds, subtitled Elementary Lessons in Aviculture, is a school textbook by John Robinson. Ginn and Company published it in Boston in 1913. Photographs illustrate it throughout, beginning with Houdan chicks under a barred Plymouth Rock mother.

The first chapter places birds in the animal kingdom and in domestication, and asks what wild birds mean to civilization. The second treats the characters and habits that fit birds for use. It covers the structure and colour of feathers, the wing's mechanism, scratching and swimming, digestion, and the hatching of eggs. Later chapters divide the species and trace the races of fowls, Italian, English, French, Spanish and Asiatic. The hen-fever period of fancy breeding gets its due. Robinson, a poultry authority, wrote the standard school text on the barnyard.
34728-betty-lee-sophomore:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote Betty Lee, Sophomore, for the World Syndicate in 1931. The Cleveland and New York house holds the rights from that year. Chapter one, called Gypsy, opens in talk between Betty and Kathryn. Betty cries that Kathryn is awfully pretty, and not to console her. Kathryn was hurt by a tale that Peggy called her plain.

Betty does not believe Peggy ever said it, and says so roundly. Contents promise Carolyn's arrival, a great surprise, and Betty meeting a countess. Betty does her best for Lucia, and joins a breakfast hike of the girls' athletic group. Halloween surprises, games with the juniors, and the sorority question fill the year. Class championship games, a party with a real date, and the countess entertaining close the tale. Grove gives a schoolgirl's second year in warm, brisk chapters.
34797-the-man-from-archangel-and-other-t:
Doran at New York issued this gathering of Conan Doyle's fiction, its copyrights running from 1894 to 1919. The tales sort themselves under two banners. Tales of adventure open the book: the debut of Bimbashi Joyce in the Sudan, the surgeon of Gaster Fell, borrowed scenes, and the title story of the man from Archangel. A motor mystery and a sealed room close that half.

Tales of medical life fill the second half, and they are the doctor speaking. A physiologist's wife, a student's first operation, the curse of Eve, and the doctors of Hoyland show the surgery and the sickroom as he knew them. The opening tale sets the scene on Egypt's frontier, where the Mahdist tide had ebbed and left horrors behind the blue hills of Dongola. Doyle before and beside Holmes is on show: soldier tales, sea tales, and the profession he left for the pen.
34930-thomas-moore:
Stephen Gwynn wrote this life of Thomas Moore for the English Men of Letters line, and Macmillan printed it in London in 1905. Moore was the Irish poet whose songs made him famed across Europe. Gwynn opens by noting how swift fame can fade once the man himself is gone.

Seven chapters carry Moore from boyhood and early poems to his last years. Lalla Rookh, his great eastern tale in verse, takes a chapter of its own. Other parts treat his marriage, his years abroad, and his work as a life writer and debater. Gwynn closes with a plain summing up, and notes that Scott and Byron alone outshone Moore on the Continent in his day.
35109-shakespeare-in-the-theatre:
Shakespeare in the Theatre is a book of essays by William Poel, founder and director of the Elizabethan Stage Society. Sidgwick and Jackson published it in London in 1913. The papers are reprinted from journals, the National Review, the Westminster Review, and others among them. Poel collected them for readers who cared about stage reform in the playing of Shakespeare.

The first part treats the stage of Shakespeare: the Elizabethan playhouse, the plays, and the players. Poel had spent years staging the plays as he believed their own age staged them, with bare platforms and swift, unbroken action. Against the heavy scenery and cut texts of the Victorian theatre he argued for the conditions of the Globe. The book is a reformer's brief, written by the man who did the work on real stages.
35208-on-canada-s-frontier-sketches-of-h:
On Canada's Frontier is a book of sketches of history, sport, and adventure in western Canada, by Julian Ralph. Harper published it at New York in 1892. Ralph dedicates it to the people of Canada, in thanks for the extreme friendliness he met on many long journeys in their west. The contents open with titled pioneers and chartering a nation.

A famous missionary, Antoine's moose yard, and big fishing follow. A skin for a skin, talking musquash, and Canada's El Dorado fill the later chapters. One sketch paints the plains of Assiniboia, just north of North Dakota. There the plains reach away in an almost level, unbroken brown ocean of grass, he writes. Strange phases of settlement and human endeavour appeared there. Ralph was an American newspaper man who roamed the dominion. His book mixes fur traders, Indians, missionaries, and new settlers into a lively portrait of the frontier west.
35232-a-letter-to-american-workingmen-fr:
N. Lenin wrote this letter to the working men of America, printed at New York in December 1918. It comes from the Socialist Soviet Republic of Russia, as the title page states. The letter is dated from Moscow, 20 August 1918. A short head note tells how it came to the West. A Russian man of the red camp, who had a hand in the revolt of 1905 and had lived long in America, gave his word to bear the letter west.

Lenin took the chance with joy, the note says. The work folk of America who rise against the rule of wealth of their own land have a great task at this hour, in his view. The letter opens with a look at the past of that land. The tale of new America, he says, starts with one of the few true wars of freedom.
35342-the-romance-of-a-poor-young-man-a-:
The Romance of a Poor Young Man is a drama adapted from the French of Octave Feuillet by Pierrepont Edwards and Lester Wallack. Samuel French published it as number 225 of the Standard Drama acting edition, entered in 1859. The edition adds costume notes, the cast, entrances and exits, stage positions, and the whole of the stage business.

Wallack himself played Manuel, the Marquis de Champcey. Around him stand Desmarets, once of the French army, and a man of the world named Bevannes. Gaspar Laroque, an aged former captain of a privateer, stands there too, with his daughter Marguerite. The first act is set in Paris, the rest in Brittany. Tableau one opens in a simply furnished room, where Madame Vauberger, once Manuel's nurse and now his lodging house keeper, is at work. She searches his writing desk and finds his purse empty, not one solitary sous left.
35488-the-road-to-paris-a-story-of-adven:
Robert Neilson Stephens wrote this story of adventure, published in Boston in 1898. The contents open with a lodge in the wilderness and run through Bunker Hill, the march through Maine with Arnold's army, and a stay within the walls of Quebec. Later chapters cross to London, then to France, with an elopement from a diligence and a chapter on the favor of a prince.

An Dumas epigraph from The Viscount of Bragelonne sets the mood: the lonely swordsman retaking the road to Paris. The introduction recalls the riflemen who marched through the Maine wilderness to attack Quebec. Readers get a fast, romantic tale of the old wars.
35749-the-adventures-of-fleet-foot-and-h:
The Adventures of Fleet Foot and Her Fawns is a nature story for children and their elders by Allen Chaffee. It was published at Springfield, Massachusetts, in nineteen twenty, as its copyright page states. Chaffee's other animal tales, including Twinkly Eyes and a black bear book, are listed in the front matter. The book is dedicated to a dear friend named Polly.

Fleet Foot is a deer, and her spotted fawns stand at the centre of the tale. Chapter heads promise a foxy trick, a visit to a valley farm, and a round up. A son of the wild enters the story later. True to nature in its billing, the book teaches woodland life through one deer family.
35777-governor-winthrop-s-return-to-bost:
Washington Warren wrote this poem for church and club readings in Boston in 1882. The book came out in 1883 in just three hundred copies. It fancies Governor John Winthrop back in Boston as a spirit. Warren calls the piece an interview with a great character.

Winthrop statue in Scollay Square sets the opening scene at night. The governor speaks on First Church, wealth, and old Boston ways. He recalls the stocks, the Thursday Lecture, and John Harvard. Warren ends with praise of Winthrop life and lasting worth to the city. Warren signed the piece with his full name, G. Washington Warren.
35898-the-seven-lamps-of-architecture:
John Ruskin wrote The Seven Lamps of Architecture, here bound with his lectures on building and painting. The notes grew, Ruskin says, while he worked on the third volume of Modern Painters. He once thought to give them a fuller form.

Seven chapters name the lamps: sacrifice, truth, power, and beauty. Life, memory, and obedience complete the set. Plates show tracery from Giotto's tower at Florence and work at Rouen, Caen, and Venice. Lectures on Turner and the Pre-Raphaelites follow in the same volume. Ruskin held that plain expansion would lessen the use of the notes.
35933-a-month-in-yorkshire:
Walter White wrote a travel book on Yorkshire, issued in a fourth edition in 1861. White had written a Londoner's walk to the Land's End and other travel books. A foreword answers critics of the first editions. White says he was pelted with attacks for a talk reported from a villager at Burnsall, in chapter twenty two.

He replies that he set down less than was spoken and named no town. His claim that the town was not in Yorkshire was treated as no defence. Two gentlemen from Leeds later took up the county's cause. The book records a month of walking, talk, and observation across Yorkshire towns and dales.
35987-the-radio-boys-search-for-the-inca:
The Radio Boys Search for the Inca Treasure is a boys roam tale by Gerald Breckenridge. A Burt house of New York brought it out in nineteen twenty two. The set gear in the front cut matches an army field kit in most ways. Jack Hampton leans on a coast ship rail and calls the land rich in tale. Vast mounts, vast streams, vast wilds, and free tribes fill his speech.

Part names run from off for gold through a tale of old in rank. Feast day, charmed city, and wire in a friar house fill next parts. A send post built and the trip off mark the start of the hunt. Inca hands, mount in, and jail in the high keep crowd mid parts. Raymi feast, a kind prince, and wire as past link fill late parts.
36005-my-treasure:
My Treasure is a children's gift book edited by Thomas W Handford, who signs himself Elmo. Belford, Clarke and Company of Chicago and New York published it in 1888, from copyright of 1887. Its frontispiece shows Jumbo broken loose, and nearly every piece carries a picture.

Short stories and verses crowd the contents. A Reckless Ride, the fishing-boat Nancy, the shark, and Brave Hal supply the adventure. Bell and her pet dog, the three kittens, the pet rabbit, and Polly and her dead bird supply the animals. Children misbehave and mend: the disobedient mouse, Frankie minds mamma, Dolly knits then hides. The gypsy camp, a little hand-organ man, and Rose and the little beggar widen the world a little. Poems on cowslips, the robin, the blacksmith, and May Day are mixed through, all of it sized for young readers.
36068-poems-of-james-mcintyre:
Poems of James McIntyre is a verse collection printed at Ingersoll, Ontario, at the office of the Chronicle in 1889. McIntyre had registered the book in 1884. The title page carries his own couplet: Fair Canada is our theme, land of rich cheese, milk and cream.

In a note to the public, McIntyre says friends urged him to issue this larger volume after a first little work. It adds about a hundred new pieces, among them dairy odes and patriotic songs written in the past year. The poems praise Canada and the nationalities that form the young Dominion. The book also prints kind letters and verses sent to the author by readers. It is small-town Canadian print at its most earnest.
36152-a-new-atmosphere:
New Atmosphere is a book of essays by Gail Hamilton of Massachusetts. Hamilton also wrote Country Living and Country Thinking and Gala Days. Fields, Osgood of Boston issued this seventh edition in 1870. Entry dates the work to 1864 under Ticknor and Fields. The first essay opens on air: a spoiled atmosphere kills growth.

One may be wise, learned, rich, and beautiful, she argues there. If the air he breathes is saturated with fever, nothing avails him. The subtile malaria creeps into his inmost frame against all defences. It looks out from his languid eye and droops in his step. Hamilton turns that figure on the moral air of American life.
36538-playing-with-fire:
Amelia Barr wrote Playing with Fire, a novel set in Glasgow, with art by Howard Heath, held in 1914 by Appleton. Barr had won readers with The Bow of Orange Ribbon and tales of Dutch New York. Here the lead house is that of a minister, and a motto at the front warns that truth, like water, goes stale when it stands still.

Twelve parts bring in Lord Richard Cramer, a son named Donald who takes his own way, and a girl named Marion who must choose her path. Faith, love, pride, and a great lure test the whole house. A hard lesson for Macrae and a dream scene deepen the tale before its close on love as law fulfilled.
36544-pope-his-descent-and-family-connec:
Pope, His Descent and Family Connections, by Joseph Hunter, is a tract on the ancestry of the poet Alexander Pope. Smith published it at London in 1857. Hunter says it enlarges the main part of an account he plans for a book of new facts on poets from Chaucer to Pope. A line from Shakespeare stands at its head: ancestry, whose grace chalks successors their way.

Two persons of noble birth, Hunter begins, thought themselves insulted in Pope's imitation of Horace. They answered with elaborate attacks, seeking out all that could offend him. Their jibes at his birth galled the poet more than anything, Hunter writes. Pope then lived in high society, and it mattered to him not to be thought meanly bred. Hunter, a famed digger in records, weighs facts and guesses about the Pope family.
36609-the-immortal-lure:
Cale Young Rice, author of A Night in Avignon and Yolanda of Cyprus, published this book of verse dramas with Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City in February 1911. Four plays make the volume: Giorgione, Arduin, O-Ume's Gods, and the title piece, The Immortal Lure. A motto of infinite passion and pain heads the book.

Giorgione opens the collection in the painter's work-room on the edge of the Venetian lagoon, with Bellini, Titian, and the poet Aretino among its characters. The young painter, anguished on his couch, swears that the portrait of the woman he adored shall be carried through the streets by ribald hands as a public thing, to her shame. Bellini, who reared him as his own son, warns that deeds of wounded pride and love fall back upon the doer, but Giorgione answers that he cares not.
36643-a-tour-throughout-south-wales-and-:
Barber's Tour Throughout South Wales and Monmouthshire was printed by Nichols at London in 1803. It carries a map and twenty views engraved from the author's drawings, and surveys the scenery, antiquities, history, manners, and trade of southern Wales. His advertisement explains the plan: most tours follow one route, but he gathered the best accounts of places he could not visit, so one volume covers the whole country. The introduction sketches Welsh history and ancient buildings; the chapters sail from Bristol to Swansea and work west through the castles.

Contents promise Swansea and Oystermouth, Arthur's Stone, Kidwelly and Caermarthen castles, Tenby, Pembroke, Milford Haven, and the cathedral and palace ruins at Saint David's. The dedication, dated February 15, 1803, goes to Richard Brinsley Sheridan, member of Parliament. Barber was a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, and the transcriber worked from the 1803 Nichols edition.
37048-a-caution-to-the-directors-of-the-:
A Caution to the Directors of the East-India Company was printed in London in 1767 for George Kearsly. The pamphlet warns the directors against making the midsummer dividend of five per cent without due heed to a late act of Parliament and a by-law of their own. A quote from a famed speech, urging repeal of a law absolutely and at once, heads the title page.

The writer opens by saying never was caution more needed since the company was founded. Great gains in India, he argues, have drawn the envy of countrymen and rival powers, while a swollen dividend alarms holders of other funds. Quarrels among the proprietors invite Parliament to strike at the company's charter. The tract is a sharp shot in the great East India debate.
37187-ulster-folklore:
Ulster Folklore, a study by Elizabeth Andrews, was published by Elliot Stock of London in 1913, with fourteen illustrations. Photographs by R Welch show harvest knots, souterrains, and crosses of rush and straw. Andrews gathered her matter from the country people of Down and other parts of the north of Ireland. A harvest knot stands at the front.

The first chapter treats fairies and their dwelling places. At Ballynahinch she was told the fairies had been blown away by a great storm fifty years before. A day at Maghera, the lore of raths and souterrains, and traditions of dwarf races follow. Folklore from Donegal, giants and dwarfs, and a life of the Reverend William Hamilton close the book. The plates give the underground passages and old forts their due.
37207-winona-of-the-camp-fire:
Margaret Widdemer wrote Winona of the Camp Fire, for Burt at New York. Rights were held in 1915 by Lippincott, by whose leave Burt printed it. Widdemer had written Winona of Camp Karonya and Winona's War Farm. Chapter one opens in the den of Winnie Merriam's house. Five girls sit round a wood fire in the big stone fireplace.

They have toasted marshmallows past the point of pleasure, the tale says. Helen Bryan has fed all hers to the dog Puppums for ten minutes. Winnie is fourteen, but her slim height makes her seem a year older. Big blue eyes and a quick smile make people call her pretty. A plate shows the girls descending in a body on Adelaide's tent. The poor old pup will look more pathetic tomorrow, Winnie jokes. Widdemer gives camp life, friendship, and fun for girls.
37271-the-ranch-girls-and-their-heart-s-:
The Ranch Girls and Their Heart's Desire, by Margaret Vandercook, is a girls' novel in the Ranch Girls series, published in Philadelphia in 1920. Wilson V Chambers drew the pictures.

The story returns to the old Rainbow ranch. The first chapter opens at twilight on the prairie, where a man and woman ride slowly over sand, clover, and roses. The talk turns on Jack living at the ranch again, like a hurt bird coming home to the nest. Later chapters bring Jean, Olive, and Frieda, a tea party, and then a jump of a year. A maiden speech, proposals, and a decision lead into an election campaign. The final chapter, The Heart's Desire, resolves the fight. Ranch life and a young woman's bid for public office drive the tale.
37309-violins-and-violin-makers-biograph:
Violins and Violin Makers, by Joseph Pearce, was published at London in 1866 by Longman and Company. The book is a biographical dictionary of the great Italian artists, their followers and imitators, to the present time, with essays on subjects connected with the violin. Its makers are arranged in alphabetical order.

The preface notes that the violin, though small and of trifling original cost, has commanded most extraordinary prices. To tell by outward marks and tone which instrument will be of value is a hard acquirement. The book means to assist the amateur and collector in that pursuit. Essays follow on Cremona, the Amati family, the Cremona varnish, and Guarnerius. Bow makers, great players and their instruments, and the repairs of instruments complete the little work.
37342-medieval-english-literature:
W P Ker surveys the early literature of England in a short volume of the Home University Library. Oxford University Press first issued it in 1912. This printing was reset in 1945 and reprinted in 1948.

Ker starts with a warning. Little Anglo-Saxon writing has come down to us. What survives rests chiefly in four manuscript books, saved by chance. One poem, Waldere, is known from two scraps found in a book binding at Copenhagen. Chapters move from the Anglo-Saxon age to the Middle English years. Romances, songs, ballads, and comic verse each get a place. Allegory, sermons, and histories follow. Chaucer closes the book. Ker writes with a scholar's range and a storyteller's ease, made for the general reader.
37513-spencer-s-philosophy-of-science-th:
Spencer's Philosophy of Science is the Herbert Spencer Lecture delivered by C Lloyd Morgan at the Museum on 7 November 1913. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published it the same year, priced at two shillings. Morgan opens not with Spencer but with his own boyhood reading.

Near the close of 1870, still in his teens, he read Tyndall on the scientific use of the imagination. Tyndall's great sentence fired him: mind itself was once latent in a fiery cloud. A friend of his father's answered with a grave smile. Had the notion been stripped too naked, the old man asked. He sent the boy back to Sartor Resartus and its philosophy of clothes. Morgan's lecture grows from that caution. It asks what Spencer's system of evolution really claims, and how much of it exact science can own.
37514-jemima-placid-or-the-advantage-of-:
Jemima Placid is a tale for the young on the gain of good temper. The book came out in London in a fresh form in 1819. Its full name adds that good nature pays in the long run. Small home scenes show the point by deeds, not by rules.

The first words take on the claim that youth is a glad age. The writer holds that the woes of the young are real to them. A small slight can fill the whole sky of a child's mind. Ill temper makes each let-down cut twice as deep, he shows. To yield with grace when one must is the wise path here. A walk in a park and a meal with friends start the tale. Two girls who fret at a wait show the flaw the book cures.
37603-the-history-of-the-nineteenth-cent:
The History of the Nineteenth Century in Caricature is a past of the jest draw by Arthur Bartlett Maurice and Frederic Taber Cooper. It came out with rights in nineteen three and a London form the next year. A score of drawn plates fill it. The book stands in four parts, from the age of the great French chief to the end of the age.

Parts trace the start of the state jest draw, its first great hands, and the chief as first head and as crowned head. The bait of a pear shaped king, the start of a famed jest sheet, and the year of revolt take parts. Wars of the age, the rise of the draw in the United States, and the men of the day close the book. A front note holds the state draw a child of new times.
37675-arteriosclerosis-and-hypertension-:
Arteriosclerosis and Hypertension, with chapters on blood pressure, is a medical book by Louis Warfield, a doctor trained at Johns Hopkins. He had been a professor of clinical medicine and chief physician to a county hospital at Milwaukee. An erratum at the front corrects a picture: the gauge shown is not the maker's named in the text but another firm's. That firm's instrument is carefully made, the note allows, though the author has not used it himself.

Hardening of the arteries and high pressure of the blood were rising themes of the medicine of his day. A book joining the two, with the new craft of measuring blood pressure by cuff and gauge, served doctors meeting both in daily practice. Warfield writes as a clinician for clinicians, from hospital ground.
377-kansas-women-in-literature:
Nettie Garmer Barker profiles Kansas women writers in this early survey, opening with a verse praising the state and its daughters. Each short sketch gives a life, a list of works, and a taste of the writer's voice. Teachers, poets, novelists, and lecturers appear side by side, many born in Kansas and some adopted by it.

Barker stresses work done in schools, papers, and homes, not only in books. Her sketches show how Kansas women wrote through farm life, town life, and public service. The volume now serves as a first map of a state literary scene that later histories often passed over.
37703-about-the-holy-bible-a-lecture:
