About the Holy Bible is a lecture by Robert Ingersoll, the famed American orator and sceptic, dated 1894. A single line heads the text: in the nature of things, there can be no evidence to establish the claim of inspiration. That sentence is the whole argument in brief.

Ingersoll opens by granting the faith of his opponents its full force. Millions, he says, take the Bible as the inspired word of God, their staff and guide, the fountain of law, justice, and mercy. They credit it with the liberty and civilization of the world. They remember heaven, he charges, but forget the dungeon of eternal pain. The first section, on the origin of the Bible, begins with the wandering families from whom its story grew. The lecture is a set piece of nineteenth-century freethought.
37756-the-byzantine-empire:
The Byzantine Empire, by Charles Oman, fellow of All Souls College at Oxford, tells the story of the East-Roman Empire from the founding of Constantinople in 328 to its fall. This third edition appeared from Fisher Unwin in London and Putnam in New York in 1902. Chapters run through the fight with the Goths, Justinian and his conquests, the coming of the Slavs and Saracens, and the Iconoclast emperors.

Oman writes against Gibbon, whose verdict on the Byzantines as vicious weaklings had stood for generations. Following Finlay and Bury, he credits the empire with holding back the Saracen and keeping the lamp of learning alight through the Dark Ages. His short history helped English readers take Byzantium seriously as a great civilization in its own right.
3778-the-interdependence-of-literature:
Georgina Pell Curtis sketches a subject no schoolman had treated alone, the way the literatures of all ages and peoples borrow from one another. She opens with De Quincey's split between the literature of knowledge, which teaches like a rudder, and the literature of power, which moves like an oar or a sail. Chapters then range from Babylonian and early Hebrew writing through Sanskrit, Persian, Egyptian, Greek, and Roman letters to heroic poetry, Scandinavian, Slavonic, and Gothic tales.

Later sections follow chivalry, romance, drama, and the Arabian, Spanish, Portuguese, and French traditions, with German mysteries giving way to opera and then to Goethe. Curtis writes in narrative style rather than as a textbook. Students of comparative letters will find a lively outline, meant to wake interest for a larger history still to come.
37795-the-world-s-best-books-a-key-to-th:
Frank Parsons made this guide to the best books of the world for Little, Brown of Boston. The third edition, revised and enlarged, came out in 1893. Parsons calls it a key to the treasures of literature, and its plan was his own.

Crawford and Richardson helped him, with criticism, checking, and the gathering of the appendix. Parsons thanks them in his preface to this edition. The public and the critics met the book with a warmer welcome than he dared hope, he writes. Such guides served a keen age: readers with scant time wanted the great books sorted, weighed, and mapped by a hand they could trust.
37842-small-horses-in-warfare:
Small Horses in Warfare is a study by Sir Walter Gilbey, printed at London in 1900 with pictures. Gilbey writes from Elsenham Hall in Essex in May 1900, in the midst of the war in South Africa. The campaign there, he argues, has proved the need for a mounted force like that of the Boers, quick in movement and hard in the field.

The contents survey small horses in past wars and far lands: the Crimea, the Cape, the Soudan, India, Morocco, and Texas. Burnaby's ride to Khiva gets a chapter of its own. Gilbey holds that small horses show staying power, hardiness, and freedom from high feeding, and that England holds foundation stock to breed her own supply rather than buy abroad.
37865-studies-in-medi-val-life-and-liter:
Edward Tompkins McLaughlin, a Yale teacher of rhetoric, wrote essays on medieval life and letters, printed in 1894. The book opens with a life of the author, born in Sharon, Connecticut, in 1860. Essays treat the medieval feeling for nature and the memoirs of Ulrich von Liechtenstein. Others cover Neidhart von Reuenthal and his Bavarian peasants.

Later essays take up Meier Helmbrecht, a German farmer of the thirteenth century, and childhood in medieval books. One essay is devoted to a medieval woman. An appendix closes the volume. The set gives general readers a clear path into German medieval writing and the daily life behind it.
37939-liquid-drops-and-globules-their-fo:
Liquid Drops and Globules is a book of three lectures on physics by Charles Darling, a lecturer at the City and Guilds technical college in London. The lectures were delivered to popular audiences and printed by Spon with forty-three illustrations. Darling had written practical treatises on pyrometry and on heat for engineers. This small book turns the same hand to a prettier subject.

Its theme is the drop: how drops and globules form, and how they move. A raindrop, a bead of mercury, and a bubble obey rules that the lecture room can show with simple gear. Surface tension, the skin that holds a drop round, does the work. Such popular lectures carried the laboratory to general audiences in the age before wireless. Darling's drops make a fine case: a whole hidden force seen in a bead of water.
38008-mated-from-the-morgue-a-tale-of-th:
John Augustus O'Shea, a special correspondent, wrote this tale of the Second Empire, published in London in 1889. In his apology he claims one merit: the study of manners was made on the spot, not from the shelves of the British Museum.

The contents run from a houseless dog and a crush at the morgue through the song-bird's nest and an old Bonapartist's story, ending on the fifth of May 1870. The scene is the Latin Quarter in the spring of 1866, cold and damp under deceitful blossoms. O'Shea calls the quarter the land of frolic and genius, of vaulting ambition and limp money-bags. Readers get Parisian bohemia in the empire's last years.
38022-nature-and-culture:
Harvey Rice published Nature and Culture in eighteen seventy-five, then brought out a second edition in eighteen eighty-nine. Rice wrote from Cleveland, Ohio, and made a few changes and adds for the new issue. The book gathers essays on nature, learning, and public life.

Nature and Her Lessons opens the set, on how nature shows herself in her works. Later essays treat the schooling of the masses and the sphere of woman. Aim High and America and Her Future urge ambition and hope. A life of the Reverend Joseph Badger and a piece on a mission monument close the book.
38061-white-fire:
White Fire is a novel by John Oxenham, issued at Toronto in 1905. Copp Clark published it with sixteen pictures. A verse on the title page gives the theme. White fire is a great enthusiasm, it says. Such fire is the mightiest force in the world. The book is dedicated to James Chalmers. He was the famed missionary of New Guinea. Great Heart is his name in the verses.

Chalmers died a martyr in that island field. The novel's chapters open with a Miss Inquisitive. The Man and his man follow in the list. A leap year and a sudden wide horizon stir the tale. Arms and the man bring war into it. The flaming sword marks a late crisis. Oxenham wrote tales of faith and hard coasts.
38105-shakespeare-a-lecture:
Robert Ingersoll lectured on Shakespeare. Shakespeare, an intellectual ocean, whose waves touched all the shores of thought, the head line runs. William Shakespeare was the greatest genius of our world, Ingersoll begins. He left to us the richest legacy of all the dead, the treasures of the rarest soul that ever lived.

He was the greatest man that ever touched this grain of sand and tears we call the world, he cries. Take from our world what the men and women of genius have given, and all the niches would be empty and all the walls naked. Shakespeare is too great a theme, he owns. I feel as though grasping a globe so large that the hand obtains no hold. Ingersoll's golden voice praises the golden tongue.
38183-from-the-thames-to-the-tiber-or-my:
From the Thames to the Tiber is a travel book by Wardle, printed at Nottingham in 1909. Wardle also wrote a life of General Gordon. The full title promises his visit to Paris, Rome, Florence, Venice, Milan, and Switzerland. Illustrations and a portrait of the author dress the volume.

The first chapter leaves London's teeming millions from Victoria Station for Newhaven. New friends on the boat, a landing at Dieppe, and a run through Rouen with its cathedral bring the party to Paris. The Louvre, Notre Dame, the Pantheon, and the Champs-Élysées fill the Paris chapters. Dijon and Chambéry lead on to Italy, the Quirinal, and Nero's house at Rome. Wardle writes the cheerful, church-going record of an English traveller on the classic tour, prices, hotels, and all.
38231-arguments-before-the-committee-on-:
Arguments Before the Committee on Patents is a printed record of House hearings held in May 1906. The subject is a bill to amend the copyright title of the Revised Statutes. The Government Printing Office in Washington issued the volume, which lists the committee's members and chairman.

The chairman was Frank Currier of New Hampshire. Fourteen members are named, from states across the Union. The record opens with proceedings of May 2 and continues on May 3, 1906. Speakers address the committee on how the copyright law should change. A telegram about the bill is read into the record at the start. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg, and it preserves the hearing as a primary source on copyright reform.
38276-the-cruise-of-the-snowbird-a-story:
The Cruise of the Snowbird is a boys' adventure novel by Gordon Stables. Hodder and Stoughton published it at London; this edition is dated 1882. Its subtitle promises a story of Arctic adventure. Chapter one introduces the young chief of Arrandoon. Allan McGregor stands with a gun on a winter mountainside. His deer hound lies at his feet in the empty glen. A rising storm drives snow through the withered bracken.

Glentroom's summer braes and heather give way to a leaden frozen lake. Allan is the young laird, heir to a few thousand sheep and acres of heather. His father died sword in hand with his regiment in Afghanistan two years before. A widowed mother and a sister keep the ancient castle. The title's cruise carries Allan from that Highland glen to the Arctic. Stables wrote sea and polar adventure for boys by the shelf.
38921-the-romance-of-a-great-store:
The Romance of a Great Store is a history of Macy's by Edward Hungerford. McBride of New York brought the illustrated book out in 1922. Vernon Howe Bailey drew the pictures of the great New York store. Hungerford gives the book to the men and women of the Macy family. Their fidelity and enthusiasm upbuilt a lasting institution, he tells them.

Chapters divide into yesterday, today, and tomorrow of the store's life. The ancestral beginnings of Macy's and the New York of 1858 open it. Fourteenth Street days and the coming of the Straus brothers follow. The store treks uptown in the fifth chapter of the yesterday part. A day in a great store and its organization fill the today part. Buying, displaying, and distributing goods get chapters of their own there. Nantucket's old families, Coffins and Macys among them, open the tale.
39185-across-the-cameroons-a-story-of-wa:
Captain Charles Gilson wrote a story of war and adventure printed in London and Glasgow in 1916, with pictures by Arch Webb. Gilson had written A Motor Scout in Flanders. Down, cried the guide, for your life, cries the cover picture. Late on a September afternoon in 1913, two boys returned to Friar's Court by way of the woods, guns under their arms and an Irish water spaniel at heel.

Captain von Hardenberg, a sunstone, false evidence, and a pursuit into the bush open the tale. A captive, a shot from the clouds, buried alive, and a valley of the shadow follow. The last cartridge, the conquest of a colony, caves, a white madman, and a race for life fill a boys war tale of Africa.
39284-curiosities-of-puritan-nomenclatur:
Curiosities of Puritan Nomenclature is a study of odd Puritan Christian names by Charles Bardsley, printed at London in 1880. Bardsley also wrote a standard work on English surnames, and he gives this book to his fellow members of the Harleian Society. A line from King Henry the Eighth heads the volume: the times and titles now are altered strangely.

In his preface Bardsley scolds writers who denied that the Puritans gave their children eccentric names at the font. Their error, he says, was to look only at the Commonwealth years, when the custom was already in decay. Clergymen across England sent him extracts from their registers, and the book sorts the strange names those records hold.
39333-curiosities-of-human-nature:
The author of Peter Parley's Tales wrote Curiosities of Human Nature, printed at Boston by J E Hickman. The contents promise curious lives in a long list. Child prodigies lead the set: Zerah Colburn, Baratiere, Gassendi, Pascal, Grotius, and Newton. Magliabechi and the Admirable Crichton stand among the learned wonders.

Colburn's life opens the book, born at Cabot, Vermont, on September 1, 1804, the sixth child of poor parents. He seemed the most backward of the children till age six, when his astonishing powers drew all eyes. Later lives treat Mozart, Ethan Allen, Davy Crockett, Daniel Boone, and Robin Hood. Impostors, misers, giants, dwarfs, and the Siamese twins fill the back of the list.
39374-the-curse-of-carne-s-hold-a-tale-o:
Henty's tale of adventure opens with a puzzle of place. Carne's Hold, in the valley of the Dare above the village of Carnesford, shows no sign of a curse. Cursed houses, Henty says, usually sit low and damp among trees, with rank vegetation and lichens. This one stands high on a hill slope in the sunshine. Its walls are a medley of styles, for the old fortified house was battered by Essex bombardiers and burned, and each owner since has built to his own fancy.

The contents promise the curse's working out: how it began, Margaret Carne, two quarrels, a terrible discovery, and an inquest. Ruth Powlett confesses late in the book. There is enlistment, an outbreak, fighting in the Amatolas, and a wagon-train attack, before the fire at Carne's Hold and the clearing at last. Henty mixes an English mystery with a colonial war, his double engine.
39577-the-broncho-rider-boys-with-the-te:
The Broncho Rider Boys with the Texas Rangers is a boys' western by Frank Fowler, issued in 1915. Its subtitle promises the capture of the smugglers on the Rio Grande. Fowler had already sent his boys to Keystone Ranch, to Arizona, along the border, and on the Wyoming trail. A plate shows Adrian stepping toward a broken door, his Marlin rifle grasped firm.

The first chapter is a mule hunt in the chaparral. Crack goes Broncho Billie's revolver, and a silver dollar tossed in the air spins into the yellow waters of the Rio Grande. Such marksmanship opens a tale of Rangers, smugglers, and the border country. The Broncho Rider Boys were among the most popular of the cheap series heroes, and this volume puts them in uniform beside the Rangers themselves.
39622-the-church-in-politics-americans-b:
The Church in Politics, subtitled Americans Beware, is a lecture by M M Mangasarian. He delivered it before the Independent Religious Society at Orchestra Hall, Chicago. The lecture answers President Roosevelt's letter on religion in politics. Roosevelt looked forward to a Catholic president someday. He called refusing a Catholic one's vote mere bigotry. Protestant bodies, Mangasarian notes, protested the pronouncement.

Mangasarian argues the opposite from the Constitution itself. The document, he says, never mentions God at all. It is a downright secular instrument aimed at the rights of man. The church's supreme end is God, not man. Between the two stands an irreconcilable difference. A sincere Christian, Catholic, or believing Jew therefore cannot honestly take the presidency. The United Presbyterians, about a million strong, refuse even to vote. Mangasarian calls them consistent and courageous. Churchmen who accept office, he charges, must stultify themselves or belittle their church.
39712-goblin-tales-of-lancashire:
James Bowker gathered these goblin and fairy tales of Lancashire folk lore. Sonnenschein printed the book in London with Gliddon drawings. Bowker gives the book to the Marquis of Hartington in thanks. A Spenser line on finding Faery land by signs heads the work.

Tales bear names like The Skriker, The Fairy Spade, and The Spectral Cat. The Fairy Funeral, Satan Supper, and The Demon of the Oak follow. Bowker traces such beliefs to Celtic and Norse forebears of the county. An appendix of comparative notes closes the lore rich volume.
40168-the-old-adam-a-story-of-adventure:
Arnold Bennett wrote this novel, printed by George H Doran of New York with a 1913 copyright. Bennett was known for The Old Wives' Tale and How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day. The tale opens on Edward Henry Machin, coming home to Bleakridge at six minutes to six. He has just made three hundred and forty-one pounds by two phone calls to his Manchester stockbrokers, on rubber shares.

Yet he does not feel jolly, and the lack stings him. It is the autumn of the great gambling year, 1910. Chapters move through a dog-bite, a bank-note, a doorway into the theatrical world, and Lord and Lady Woldo. A first night and a woman named Isabel wait in the second part. Bennett watches a rich man hunt for a feeling money cannot buy.
40355-nooks-and-corners-of-shropshire:
Thornhill Timmins wrote Nooks and Corners of Shropshire, published by Elliot Stock in London in 1899. Timmins drew the numerous illustrations himself and supplied a map. He had already written matching volumes on Herefordshire and Pembrokeshire. The book takes readers by road through one English county, town by town and ruin by ruin, in search of its quiet corners.

Shrewsbury opens the tour, with Butcher Row, the old market house, and houses in Wyle Cop. Routes run to Pitchford Hall and its house in a tree, to Stokesay Castle, and round Ludlow. Wenlock Edge, Wroxeter, and the Wrekin fill another chapter. Tong and Boscobel, Bridgnorth, and the Welsh border close the circuit. Timmins mixes history with scenery: a chalice here, a font there, an old bridge on a Roman road. The book serves walkers and local readers who wanted their county's past gathered into one illustrated guide.
40375-the-london-venture:
Michael Arlen published The London Venture with the Doran Company of New York in 1920, with drawings by Michel Sevier. A short apologia at the front explains his pen name: he was born Dikran Kouyoumdjian, a name his English acquaintances could not say twice running the same way.

The narrator looks back from the library of a country house at his months in London, and at how he complained while he was there. He recalls abusing the artificial necessity of living, the monotonous routine of politeness, and streets full of bowler hats and cinema posters. Now, away from it, he finds he cannot imagine being pleased to return, or sorry to have left. Arlen's other books of the moment, The Green Hat among them, made his name in that polished, weary manner.
40441-a-day-with-william-shakespeare:
Maurice Clare spends an imagined day with the playwright in A Day with William Shakespeare, from Hodder and Stoughton. The volume belongs to a series that gives the same treatment to Tennyson, Browning, Burns, Byron, Shelley, Scott, and others. A painting of Romeo and Juliet by W Hatherill fronts the book, with Juliet's bud-of-love lines above it.

The day begins early on a bright June morning in 1599, in the Silver Street house of Christopher Mountjoy, the wig-maker. Shakespeare, the family's lodger, is thirty-five, handsomely made, with light hazel eyes and auburn hair. Clare walks him through one full day.
40493-the-king-of-diamonds-a-tale-of-mys:
Louis Tracy wrote The King of Diamonds, a tale of mystery and risk held in 1904 at New York. Tracy had writ The Wings of the Morning and The Pillar of Light. Twenty two chapters carry the tale. A front line says swift acts beat a century of soft talk.

The tale opens at Number Three, Johnson's Mews, with a sick mother. A doctor tells her son there is no hope now. The boy says they are alone in the world and hard up. A strange stone, a rich man named Isaacstein, and a court scene build the plot. Gains, loss, a face from the past, and a rescue fill the late chapters. Old scores are paid at the end.
40613-arguments-before-the-committee-on-:
Congress printed the arguments heard on June 6 through 9, 1906, by the House Committee on Patents sitting with the Senate committee, on a bill to amend and consolidate the copyright acts. Frank D Currier of New Hampshire chaired the House committee. Solomon R Dresser of Pennsylvania and Joseph M Dixon of Montana sat among its members. The Government Printing Office at Washington issued the hearings.

Publishers, authors, and manufacturers argued over the bill that became the Copyright Act of 1909. Mechanical music, photographs, and lectures were contested ground. The transcript preserves the lobby in its own words. Such hearings are primary sources for American copyright history.
40670-makers-of-modern-agriculture:
Makers of Modern Agriculture, a set of five lives by William Macdonald, was published by Macmillan in 1913. Macdonald edited the Agricultural Journal of the Union of South Africa. A portrait of Jethro Tull stands at the front. A line from Carlyle, that great men are profitable company, sets the tone.

The lives follow the men who changed farming in Britain and America. Jethro Tull is cast as founder of the principles of dry farming. Coke of Norfolk and Arthur Young stand for the age of improvement on the land. John Sinclair carries the story into Scotland and public service. Cyrus H McCormick closes the set with the reaper and the machine age on the farm.
40846-voltaire:
A critical biography of Voltaire by John Morley. Macmillan published the London edition in 1886. Morley treats Voltaire's name as a force in itself. He calls Voltairism the Renaissance of the eighteenth century. Its power, he argues, came from sincerity, penetration, and courage. Voltaire lacked all intellectual cowardice. He also lacked worldly indifference to truth and justice.

A first chapter sets the movement against Catholicism, Calvinism, and the age of Louis the Fourteenth. Descartes and Bayle prepared the ground, on Morley's telling. A second chapter weighs the English influences on the young writer. His birth, the Regency circle, and a famous insult fill its pages. Morley's study became a standard English account of the French thinker.
40874-wenderholme-a-story-of-lancashire-:
Wenderholme, by Philip Gilbert Hamerton, is a story of Lancashire and Yorkshire life. Roberts Brothers issued this author edition at Boston in 1876 in full. A letter to an old lady in Yorkshire opens the American printing here. She recalls halls undisturbed before mills and railways changed the north country.

Hamerton says a London publisher talk shaped the book odd fate in advance. Short novels did not pay; long ones were the safer investment then. So art yielded to trade, and the tale grew to three volumes long. Valleys filled with towns and fields with villas in her long lifetime. Vanishing contrasts of northern life are the story true subject.
40968-desire-no-more:
Desire No More, a story by Algis Budrys with illustrations by Milton Luros, opens with a blurb that states its hero's whole life. He had but one ambition, one desire: to pilot the first manned rocket to the moon, and he had prepared himself as no man had ever prepared before. A Chaucer line gives the title.

The scene then cuts to a quiet parlour. A small young man tells his father he has a trade already: he is a rocket pilot. Howard Isherwood laughs until the Sunday paper slides off his lap, and shouts after the boy as he bolts for a bus. Martin Isherwood, rocket pilot, weight a hundred and two pounds and under five feet tall, had come of age at seventeen.
41062-the-final-figure:
Final Figure is a science fiction novelet by Sam Merwin the younger, drawn from Dynamic Science Fiction of January 1954. Paul Orban supplied the pictures for the magazine printing of the tale. Its hook is a puzzle about a man named MacReedy and his gift. He designs new weapons and builds models of them before the armed forces have them.

A general in plain clothes visits the firm Models and Miniatures to see the work. What he finds raises a hard question for the men who guard new arms. Is MacReedy a wild talent, a prophet, or a risk no service can afford? His final figure, shown with a mobile rocket launcher, forces the issue.
41094-eastern-nights-and-flights-a-recor:
Captain Alan Bott wrote a record of oriental adventure printed at Garden City, New York, in 1919. A photograph shows Bott in Constantinople while he was a prisoner, signed in the name of Fritz Richter, first lieutenant in the German flying corps. While escaping, the false signature convinced a Turkish gendarme that he was a German officer in mufti. A prologue through the looking glass opens the book.

Pain, purgatory, and a plan, and the flight that failed follow. Nazareth and the Christian charity of a Jew, Damascus and the second failure, and the Berlin Bagdad railway fill the road. Cuthbert, Alfonso, and a mud village, in the shadow of the black rock, and Constantinople and how to become mad come next. Theodore the Greek, John Willie the Bosnian, and David Lloyd George's rogues fill the middle. Sofia and Salonika close a flying man's great escape.
41115-solomon-and-solomonic-literature:
Moncure Conway wrote a study of King Solomon and the books linked to his name. The work came out in Chicago and London in 1899. Conway looks at tales of the king in myth and in the Bible. He treats the old texts with care and doubt.

Chapters cover the famed choice of the king, his wives, and his fall. Later parts take up Proverbs, the Song of Songs, and the book called Koheleth. Conway also tracks how the fame of Solomon shaped views of Jesus. Readers get a broad, plain guide to a rich old theme.
41176-the-great-airship-a-tale-of-advent:
The Great Airship, a tale of adventure by Brereton, was published in London and Glasgow by Blackie and Son. Brereton wrote many boys' war and scout tales, from On the Field of Waterloo to A Hero of Panama. Drawings are by Padday. The story turns on the fame of the Zeppelin and a bold new British airship.

Contents name Andrew Provost, midshipman Dicky Hamshaw, and a sportsman named Carl Reitberg. The crew flies toward Adrianople and a besieged city, then to the northwest frontier for a brush with Pathan fighters. Record high flying, rescues, and fights fill the later chapters. The book sells speed, daring, and new flight tech to young readers of its day.
41213-the-secrets-of-a-kuttite-an-authen:
The Secrets of a Kuttite, by Captain Mousley, tells an authentic story of Kut. John Lane published it at London and New York in 1922. A plate shows Ctesiphon, where the wounded were gathered at the height of battle. Its subtitle promises adventures in captivity and Stamboul intrigue in the war.

A poem called The Trek stands at the front of the memoir in verse. No pause, no rest, forward the column pushes across the stern plain, it runs. Thirst darts at the brain and the great heat crushes the spirit of the men. The ruthless Turk urges them on beside his impatient horse in that march. British prisoners after the fall of Kut tell a hard road in this book.
41366-the-flying-boat-a-story-of-adventu:
The Flying Boat is a story of adventure and misadventure by Herbert Strang, printed at London in 1912. Dugdale drew the pictures. Twenty-two chapters carry the tale from Enter Mister Ting to Mister Ting Explains. A picture at the front shows Mister Ting astonishing the school.

The tale opens at Cheltonia school as term draws to its close. Every boy, from senior prefect to smallest fourth former, is out practising for the sports. Big fellows of the sixth try the high jump in friendly rivalry. Then the action moves up country, to river pirates and a swamp discovery. Su Fing holds a prisoner, and Reinhardt shows his colours. Strang mixes school life with Far Eastern adventure.
41391-constantinople-the-story-of-the-ol:
Constantinople is a city history in a series of stories of the great capitals. Its subtitle calls the city the old capital of the empire. An illustration shows the interior of Saint Sophia, with the Sultan's pew and the stairs to the pulpit. A verse woven into the front matter gives the church its own voice: Most Holy Wisdom chose me for her home.

The book tells the city's long story from Byzantium to the Ottoman capital. Mosque and palace, siege and sultan, fill its chapters. The transcriber's notes to this edition worry over small spellings in Greek words and place names, a sign of the text's dense antiquarian texture. The volume is a turn-of-the-century guide for the thinking traveller: part chronicle, part companion for walking the streets between Saint Sophia and the Golden Horn.
41495-russia-its-people-and-its-literatu:
Emilia Pardo Bazán wrote Russia: Its People and Its Literature, here in Fanny Hale Gardiner's English translation. McClurg of Chicago published the translation in 1901. Pardo Bazán was a Spanish writer of wealth and standing. Her survey treats the Russian people and their books together.

The translator's preface sketches the author's life. Books were nearly her only pleasure as a lonely child in Galicia. She read widely by fourteen but was kept from the French romantics. Forbidden fruit tasted sweetest when she finally got Dumas, Sand, and Hugo. Marriage at sixteen took her to Madrid, where reading lapsed. Exile with her father taught her French, English, and Italian. She then read those literatures and German philosophy deeply.
41642-the-court-of-cacus-or-the-story-of:
Alexander Leighton tells the story of Burke and Hare in The Court of Cacus. Leighton also wrote tales of Scottish life and custom. The book came out in 1861.

In his preface Leighton defends the telling of dark deeds. He calls the crimes a series of tragedies with no match in their depth. He holds that such facts will be known, one way or the other. So he pairs the knowledge that kills with the knowledge that cures. The book aims to warn as much as to thrill. Readers get a grave account of guilt, trial and shame. The tale is set in Edinburgh, where the crimes took place.
41719-white-fire:
White Fire, by Roy Snell, came out in Chicago in 1922 as a mystery story for boys. Chapter one is called The Beginning of a Mystery. Johnny Thompson works in a great plant that turns out cars and planes. A notch in a metal casting before him turns dull red, then bright red, then white hot. Yet his torch is off and the oxygen drum stands empty.

Johnny tests the spot with a drop of water and hears it hiss. The metal yields to his hammer like wax to a seal. Chapter heads promise traps, flights, a desert race, and flying knives. Found chests and a race in mid air come near the end. The tale mixes shop work, flight, and a puzzle no tool can explain.
41912-a-survivor-s-recollections-of-the-:
Matilda J Sager Delaney recalled the Whitman massacre as one who lived through it. The Esther Reed Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution backed the book at Spokane in 1920. A front note calls her account vivid and of great weight for Northwest history. Her portrait stands at the front of the slim volume.

Born in 1839 near St Joseph, Missouri, she crossed the plains in 1844. Her father Henry Sager caught the Oregon fever that spring, she writes. Seven Sager children made the trail after one was born on the road. Readers gain a pioneer's own words on loss, faith, and survival.
42019-motor-boat-boys-river-chase-or-six:
Louis Arundel wrote this Motor Boat Boys tale, copyrighted by Donohue at Chicago in 1914. A plate shows a sharp report and a flash of flame at the front. Ready for the start opens the contents, and the cruise begun follows in the second chapter.

Buster captures a fish, a mystery looms up and the first camp fire fill the early list. A startling interruption, a treasure cache and Jack playing scout carry the six chums onward. The man with the blue moon sweater, a river pirate and a moonlight chase close a river adventure for boys of the gasoline age.
42074-the-spirit-lake-massacre:
The Spirit Lake Massacre, by Thomas Teakle, was published at Iowa City in nineteen eighteen. The publisher was the State Historical Society of Iowa. The subject is the killing of white settlers near Lake Okoboji and Spirit Lake in March eighteen fifty-seven. A band under the leader Inkpaduta carried out the attack.

Teakle argues the attack was the climax of a long contest over settlement in northern Iowa. It pushed state and federal power to drive the Sioux toward the Missouri River. Settlement then rushed in, and the Indian question for Iowa was settled. The editor notes that the familiar name is kept, though most of the tragedy happened on Lake Okoboji's borders. The study rests on primary materials where possible. It also takes new positions on causes and incidents, which makes it a standard state history of the event.
4211-the-treasure:
A novel called The Treasure follows Owen Sargent, Sandy Salisbury, and Mrs. Salisbury in the town of River Falls. Owen's constant visits would have filled Mrs. Salisbury's heart with wild maternal hope, had Owen and Sandy been a few years older.

As it is, with Sandy barely nineteen and Owen not quite twenty-two, their friendship gives her more tantalizing discomfort than satisfaction. Owen is a dear boy, queer but fine, and Sandy the prettiest girl in town. Readers who enjoy gentle domestic fiction will find a quiet story of youth and watching mothers.
42205-studies-on-the-legend-of-the-holy-:
The Folk-Lore Society prints a scholarly study of the Grail legend as its twenty-third publication, dated 1888. Andrew Lang and Edward B Tylor stand among the society's vice-presidents. The Earl of Strafford presides.

The study asks where the Grail story came from and how its parts joined. Special weight falls on the old versions and their homelands. One quoted question runs in German: which people did the tale of Parzival's youth belong to, and which tradition, written or spoken, bound it to the Grail saga? The author weighs claims people by people. Celtic material stands near the centre of the argument. The book lists the author's earlier paper on the Aryan expulsion and return formula among the Celts. Such society volumes built folklore into a science.
4256-stammering-its-cause-and-cure:
Benjamin Nathaniel Bogue wrote this book from experience. He had been a chronic stammerer for almost twenty years. He then devised the Bogue Unit Method and founded the Bogue Institute for Stammerers. The first part tells his own life as a stammerer.

It covers early attempts at a cure and the hunt for work. It covers failures that taught him what helped. Later parts define stuttering and stammering and discuss their causes. They discuss effects on mind and body, and set out his method for setting the tongue free. The book speaks directly to sufferers and their families, mixing memoir with practical instruction.
42688-the-red-lure:
Roy Snell wrote The Red Lure, published by Reilly and Lee in Chicago in 1926 as one of its Mystery Stories for Boys. The hero, Johnny Thompson, opens the tale bent over the black waters of a jungle river. A white gleam on the surface warns him to dive an instant before danger strikes.

An alligator nearly takes him as he scrambles ashore. Chapters promise a jaguar, mysterious sounds, and a party lost in the jungle. A hidden city, forgotten tribes, and century-old caverns lie ahead. A character called Pant sets a trap and springs it, and a Spanish girl reappears. The book closes with the battle of Rio Hondo. Snell writes swift boys' adventure in an exotic setting.
42710-bizarre:
Bizarre is a book of humorous pieces by Lawton Mackall of New York. Lieber and Lewis published it in the year 1922 for light readers. Stout drew twenty six drawings for the volume's comic sketches. Mackall also wrote Scrambled Eggs in the same vein of wit. He dedicates Bizarre to his favourite poet, Virginia Woods Mackall.

Thanks go to Life, Judge, The Century, and The Quill for pieces reused. The New York Times and Literary Review stand thanked there too. What Nots heads the contents with unsolicited personal adornments in fun. Shelf culture, portable pigeonholes, simile, and the art of packing follow. Snowy bosoms, the care of the husband, and indoor farming ensue.
42887-cheshire:
Cheshire is a county history by Charles E Kelsey, published at Oxford in nineteen eleven in the Oxford County Histories series. Ten maps and forty nine illustrations appear in the book. Contents open with the position and natural features of the county. The making of Cheshire takes two chapters before its early inhabitants appear.

Romans in Cheshire then fill two chapters of the contents in turn. Roads, salt, cheese, and old towns are the county's classic matter in such a survey. Kelsey writes for schools and general readers who want one county whole, from geology to modern life. The Clarendon Press form gives the book a sober, lasting shape.
42978-the-sea-shore: Furneaux takes young collectors to the coast in The Sea Shore, a handbook in the Out Door World series from Longmans. The series list shows the book with eight coloured plates and more than three hundred pictures in the text. A rock pool fronts the volume as its first plate. Shore life, from rock pool to open beach, is the book's whole field.
43098-selected-works-of-voltairine-de-cl:
Selected Works of Voltairine de Cleyre is a gathering of the poems and essays of an American anarchist writer. It was edited by Alexander Berkman and published in New York in 1914 by the Mother Earth Publishing Association. Hippolyte Havel wrote the sketch of her life at the front. The poems come first. Their names show her themes: The Burial of My Past Self, The Freethinker's Plea, Written in Red. A grave poem stands for the men hanged after Haymarket.

The essays fill the great bulk of the book. The Dominant Idea opens the run. Anarchism and Anarchism and American Traditions state her creed. Crime and Punishment, Direct Action, and The Paris Commune take up its practice. In Defense of Emma Goldman stands for her loyalty to a friend. The book is the chief store of de Cleyre's work, made by her own movement just after her death.
43117-maud-florence-nellie-or-don-t-care:
Maud Florence Nellie is a girls tale by Coleridge with cuts by Staniland. A church set house of London brought the book out in its day. Florrie Whittaker, age fifteen, dresses for Sunday school in part one. Cream lace and bands crown her new warm months hat in that scene. Full brown hair in frizz rings frames her plump rose face.

Her sire keeps the gate lodge of the great town grave yard of Rapley. Rows of grave stones were the play ground of her youth with her kin. Grave rites and bell tolls were day sounds that left them gay. She counts her self among the best dressed girls of her class. Sun road to town frames her strut in the first part scene.
43124-the-flaming-sword-in-serbia-and-el:
The Flaming Sword in Serbia and Elsewhere is a war book by Stobart. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London in 1916. Its frontispiece shows the author on horseback in the Serbian retreat. That retreat ran from October to December 1915.

Stobart dedicates the book to Alexander, Crown Prince of Serbia. She praises the courage with which he and his nation held to freedom. A reader's guide maps the five parts of her account. The first covers hospital work in Bulgaria, Belgium, France, and Serbia. The second turns to roadside tent dispensary work in Serbia itself. The third is a diary of the great Serbian retreat. The last parts weigh the war work of women and the Serbian character. They close with reflections on the evils of war itself.
43148-an-english-squire:
C R Coleridge wrote An English Squire, issued at London by Sampson Low and partners with no year on the title page shown here. A front note owns that the lead man, Alvar Lester, was not her own invention. A friend proposed the man in talks with her. He came from a Spanish home, she says.

Coleridge says she did no more than turn him into an English squire. Part One is named Home Life. Chapter One treats the Lesters of Oakby. Mr Gerald Lester heads a family of good blood at Oakby Hall in Westmoreland. The Yorkshire line crosses his land. Heather moors, fells, and rich valleys wrap the house. Oakby was dear to its owner, the tale stresses. Kin and kind, in the words of Hamlet, frame the home tale.
43218-the-boy-patrol-around-the-council-:
Edward S Ellis wrote a Boy Patrol adventure in 1913, drawn by Edwin J Prittie. Scouts of the Stag, Blazing Arrow, and Eagle patrols camp on Gosling Lake in southern Maine. Jack Crandall falls from a tall pine while looking into a bird's nest. His friends Gerald Hume and Arthur Mitchell carry him on a litter to the clubhouse.

A man named Spellman paddles across in a canoe and sets the broken limb. Chapters ahead promise a council of war, an unwelcome guest, and a match of wits. One chapter tells the true story of a famous sea serpent. Ellis mixes camp craft with mystery and peril.
43221-the-ceramic-art-a-compendium-of-th:
The Ceramic Art, a compendium of the history and manufacture of pottery and porcelain by Jennie Young, was published in 1878. Harper and Brothers issued it at New York with 464 illustrations. A line from Horace on wet clay stands as the motto of the work. The preface states the aim of the author in plain terms.

She seeks to answer, as tersely and clearly as she can, the chief questions on pottery and porcelain. Recent research is brought to bear on problems of the science of ceramics that lack answers. The literature of the field is vast, as she warns her readers at the start. Collectors, makers, and students of craft all form the audience for such a handbook.
43707-finger-ring-lore:
William Jones wrote a lore book on finger rings through the ages. The book came out in London in 1877. Jones was a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. Many plates show rings of note. He gave the book to his wife with a ring pledge plate.

Jones first meant to write on ring omens alone, he says. Old books gave him far more: tales, facts, and odd bits. Rings mark vows, rank, grief, and faith in his store. Cut gems and fine gold work show the art of old hands. He ties small facts to great points of creed and use. Ring lovers get a deep, warm store of lore.
43711-a-history-of-chinese-literature:
A History of Chinese Literature is a survey by Herbert Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge and late consul at Ningpo. Appleton printed the book, first copyrighted in 1901. Its contents divide the vast field by dynasty. Book the First covers the feudal period, from 600 to 200 before Christ.

Legendary ages, early civilisation, and the origin of writing open the account. Confucius and the Five Classics follow, then the Four Books and Mencius. Poetry, inscriptions, and Taoism with its Tao Tê Ching close the first book. The Han dynasty brings the First Emperor and the burning of the books, then history, lexicography, and Buddhism. Giles begins from the beginning of all things, nicely calculated, he notes, by Chinese chronologers. His history was for decades the English reader's one road into Chinese letters.
43735-the-oxford-reformers-john-colet-er:
The Oxford Reformers, by Frederic Seebohm, tells of the fellow work of Colet, Erasmus, and More. Longmans published the history at London, New York, and Bombay. A Latin line from Colet stands as a motto on the title page. It bids the reader listen with patience while truth is struck from clashing flints.

Seebohm also wrote on the English village community and the tribal system in Wales. His era of the Protestant revolution belongs to the same shelf of studies. John Colet at Oxford, Erasmus the wandering scholar, and Thomas More form a linked trio here. Their shared push for cleaner learning and faith before the Reformation is the theme. Students of Tudor England meet three friends who tried to reform the church from within.
43838-the-pearl-of-the-andes-a-tale-of-l:
Gustave Aimard wrote The Pearl of the Andes, a tale of love and adventure, issued in New York by the John W Lovell Company in eighteen eighty four. Percy B St John revised and edited the text. Aimard had earlier written The Adventurers, Trail Hunter, and Pirates of the Prairies. Forty four chapters carry the story.

Chapter one opens in the cabildo. Don Tadeo comes back to his senses after Dona Rosario's escape with the help of Curumilla, the book recalls. An Indian's love, a countermine, and the passage of the defile fill the early action. Later chapters bring a human sacrifice, the King of Darkness, and the battle of Conderkanki. Captivity, an ultimatum, and a hurricane raise the close. Adventure readers get a South American romance of pursuit, war, and escape in the Andes.
43910-the-danes-in-lancashire-and-yorksh:
The Danes in Lancashire and Yorkshire was written by Partington. Sherratt and Hughes published it in 1909. London and Manchester share the imprint. A front plate shows Canute. The preface is dated at Bury, October 1909. Danes and Norsemen, the last invaders before the Normans, are the subject. Their adventures, crafts, beliefs, and character fill the book. Traces in language and law show what they left behind. Contents open with invasion and conquest. Settlements, place-names, and family names follow. Stone crosses, runes, and memorials get chapters of their own.

Literature, mythology, and superstitions close the list. Partington thanks the writers who fed his work. Collingwood on Scandinavian Britain is named among them. Articles by John Just of Bury first set him on the trail.
43937-finding-the-lost-treasure:
Helen Persons wrote this girls' novel, published by Saalfield in 1933. It opens in Nova Scotia, where Desiré finds an old paper covered with figures and carries it to her brother Jack, who is gazing across St Mary's Bay.

Jack explains: their dying father showed him the paper days before his death. It is a memorandum handed down in the family for generations, its writer and meaning lost, but each father warned his eldest son to keep it carefully, for it was valuable. The mortgage on the farm is news to Desiré. The contents promise a pie social, a blue-covered book, the old Godet house, and a final chapter of bare figures. Readers get a Maritime treasure hunt.
44072-the-seat-of-empire:
The Seat of Empire is a travel book on the American north west by Charles Carleton Coffin. Fields, Osgood published it at Boston in 1870. A Seward speech at Saint Paul in 1860 fronts the book as a motto. Seward believed the last seat of government on the continent would stand there. He spoke at the head of navigation on the Mississippi River. The contents open with a journey from Chicago to Minneapolis. Cutting loose from care and a map of the north west begin it.

A Fourth of July dance on a steamboat enlivens the first chapter. Up the Mississippi, Winona, Saint Paul, and Minneapolis follow. The Father of Waters in harness ends that chapter's heads. Coffin dedicates the book to a Vermont governor of the war years. The book sells the north west as America's future seat.
44101-the-holy-roman-empire:
Holy Roman Empire, by James Bryce, traces the Empire as a system. Macmillan of London issued the third edition, revised, in eighteen seventy one. Bryce was a fellow of Oriel College and Oxford civil law professor. A list of emperors and popes in date order fronts the treatise.

Bryce says his aim is the Empire itself, not a tale of its lands. Yet the growth and decay of imperial power need events to be clear. So the book weds the theory of the Empire to political history. Germany from the ninth century and medieval Italy fill the narrative side. The Empire grew from beliefs and traditions now almost wholly passed away.
44268-the-americans-as-they-are:
The Americans As They Are describes a tour through the valley of the Mississippi. The author of Austria As It Is wrote it, unnamed. Hurst, Chance and Company published it at London in 1828. The advertisement owns that the tour was meant for 1827 and was delayed. The American, it says, is prone to exaggeration about his own country. English travellers, on the contrary, undervalue brother Jonathan and his land.

The author claims neither side. He has twice seen the countries he describes, he says. Truth and practical observation are his chief points, and he claims no literary merit. Whether his statements are correct, the reader must judge and experience confirm. The preface begins half a century back from his tour. The book belongs to the great run of European tours of the young republic.
44369-pals-young-australians-in-sport-an:
Pals: Young Australians in Sport and Adventure, by Joseph Bowes, was printed in London in 1910. James Glass issued the book with eight full-page coloured plates by John Macfarlane. The frontispiece shows Yellow Billy passing a whip thong round a brute's neck.

The contents promise bushrangers twice over, a great match, and a big flood on the waters. A forest monarch falls, a tree hides a secret, and a rescue follows. Christmas fun, a bush ride, and a dingo raid fill the holiday stretch. An emu fights a dingo to a finish, and wild horses draw a brumby hunt. The Warrigal's strategy is broken by Yellow Billy in turn. A day's shoot, a corroboree, and a camp by the sea lead to the gold diggings. Bullion and a bushranger close the tale.
44487-captured-at-tripoli-a-tale-of-adve:
Captured at Tripoli, subtitled A Tale of Adventure, is a boys' novel by Percy Westerman. Blackie and Son published it in London, Glasgow and Bombay, at two shillings and sixpence in cloth. Charles Sheldon illustrated the book, and the Schoolmaster is quoted in front calling it an ideal gift-book or prize for a youthful book-lover.

The chapters promise a modern war story with an old romance inside it. The heroes go off to the seat of war, come under fire, and are taken prisoners. A sheikh's salt, a sandstorm and an escape follow, then a fight in the desert, a mirage, and a medieval city. A knightly Sir Jehan appears before the Moslem host closes in, and the tale ends with a dash for a gun and a struggle at the breach. The opening shows troops of the 89th Regiment filing through a guarded gateway at Naples.
44502-every-day-science-volume-6-the-con:
Henry Smith Williams, assisted by Edward Williams, wrote this sixth volume of Every-Day Science, subtitled The Conquest of Nature. The Goodhue Company published it at New York and London in 1909, copyrighted in 1910. A frontispiece shows a primitive use of the animal machine still in vogue in many European countries.

The first chapter, Man and Nature, surveys man's use of nature's gifts from clothing and heated dwellings and the early taming of animals through gunpowder to steam and electricity. It ends with the decline of drudgery. How Work Is Done treats the lever as Archimedes conceived it, wheels and pulleys, inclined planes, derricks, and friction. The Animal Machine compares muscle to machinery and takes horse-power as the standard of the world's work. Later chapters give the work of air and water, from Ctesibius's fire engine to the windmill, water-wheel, and turbine.
44603-chats-on-cottage-and-farmhouse-fur:
Chats on Cottage and Farmhouse Furniture is a collector's guide by Arthur Hayden, in the Books for Collectors series. Hayden also wrote the companion volume, Chats on Old Furniture, illustrated by seventy two full-page plates. The series, in large crown octavo with coloured frontispieces, covered English china, old prints, costume, lace and miniatures for the Edwardian collector.

The companion's contents, printed here, show the method. They march through styles, from the Renaissance on the Continent and in England, through Jacobean and Queen Anne work. Chippendale follows, then Adam, Hepplewhite and Sheraton, with hints to collectors at the end. The cottage volume applies the same approach to humbler pieces. Its author notes that works on old English furniture have grown fast in ten years. Latterly the subject has been treated from every side, historic and practical alike.
44867-the-discovery-of-the-future:
Wells wrote The Discovery of the Future, printed in New York in 1913. The piece was a talk given at the Royal Institution. It opens by parting two kinds of mind, told apart chiefly by their stance toward time. The first kind, the type of most living people, scarcely thinks of the future at all. To it the future is a blank nothing, on which the present will presently write events.

The second kind, a rarer modern type, thinks constantly of things to come. From the first view, Wells says, our life is simply to reap the fruits of the past. From the second, our life is to make ready the future. He calls the first the legal or yielding type, shaped by the lawyer's trade of leaning on what is already laid down. The second he calls the law-making, shaping type.
44975-a-history-of-roman-literature:
Harold Fowler, a professor at Western Reserve University, wrote A History of Roman Literature for the Twentieth Century Text-Books series. Appleton published it in 1903. A bust of Augustus in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts serves as frontispiece. The book surveys Latin writing from its beginnings to the fifth century, in twenty-one chapters meant for students.

Early chapters treat Roman tragedy and comedy, then the prose of the Scipionic circle and the satirist Lucilius. Lucretius and Catullus follow, then Cicero at the centre of the republic's letters. Virgil, Horace, and Ovid anchor the Augustan chapters. Later chapters move through the silver age, Suetonius, and the early Christian writers, ending with the pagan literature of the third century and a conclusion. A bibliography and a chronological table close the volume. Fowler gives students a single clear road through a thousand years of Latin authors.
45002-harmonies-of-political-economy-tra:
Frederic Bastiat's Harmonies of Political Economy, in Patrick James Stirling's translation from the third French edition, is kept in its second edition. Oliver and Boyd printed it at Edinburgh, with Simpkin, Marshall in London. Stirling, who wrote The Philosophy of Trade, also supplied a notice of the life and writings of the author.

The translator's preface tells the work's sad state. The first ten chapters were all that appeared in Bastiat's lifetime, or had his finishing touch. He meant to recast the book and widen it from the principles of political economy into social philosophy. On his last journey to Italy he left his friends Fontenay and Paillottet a list of the new chapters in order. To them, in his last moments, he entrusted the manuscripts, and they arranged the continuation without altering the text.
45069-lincoln-in-caricature:
Rufus Rockwell Wilson made this book, Lincoln in Caricature, printed for private distribution in 1903 with thirty-two plates. Wilson had written Washington: The Capital City before it. He opens by calling Lincoln's treatment in cartoons a phase of his career that has lacked fair study. Lincoln, he says, was the most bitterly assailed and savagely cartooned public man of his time.

Cartoons in London Punch from 1861 to 1865 show British feeling toward the Union and its president. Vanity Fair, Frank Leslie's paper, and Harper's Weekly supply more of the plates. Wilson sets the plates in time order, with such comment as makes their point clear. He calls them human documents that catch the hopes and fears of the North.
45099-the-rise-of-the-russian-empire:
The Rise of the Russian Empire is a history by Munro, published in London by Grant Richards in 1900. The title page carries a French saying: that no one can know Russia of to-day who does not climb higher into her past. Two maps and a long list of works used open the book.

The sources named are the great histories of Russia in several tongues. Karamzin and Solov'ev stand first. Rambaud's history in English and the chronicle of Nestor in French follow. Works on the Mongols and on the Golden Horde are listed as well. The text itself opens with the land. Russia, Munro says, holds a rich mix of tribes and peoples. Yet one sameness of plain and climate runs through the greater part of its huge extent.
45124-great-facts-a-popular-history-and-:
Frederick Bakewell, who wrote a manual of electricity, made this plain history of the age's great inventions. Appleton printed Great Facts at New York in 1860, with many engravings. The Great Eastern steamship, launched in 1858, fronts the book.

Bakewell says in his preface that the comforts and gains of new devices stir a wish to know their birth. Made things, he holds, count for more in daily life than the bare science under them. A man who stops at pure rules, he warns, is like a traveller who never looks at the land. The book traces how the century's best thoughts were turned into tools, ships, and wires for all men's use.
45146-the-radio-boys-under-the-sea-or-th:
J W Duffield wrote a Radio Boys adventure published by Donohue at Chicago and New York. The series list shows the boys in the secret service, cast away on an iceberg. In the flying service they are held for ransom by Mexican bandits. In the Thousand Islands they follow a Yankee Canadian wireless trail. Under the sea, they hunt sunken treasure.

A picture caption announces that the volcano wakes. The Radio Boys were one of several syndicate series riding the wireless craze. Their sets worked in boats, planes, and diving gear. Duffield's name covers house writers producing volumes to order. Treasure under the sea gave the radio a salvage plot.
4515-the-golden-snare:
James Oliver Curwood sets this northern tale among the forests and rivers far north of the settled lands, where trappers, traders, and wild animals live close together. Bram Johnson, a huge man raised in that hard country, stands at the centre of the story. The book traces his family back three generations, showing how the north shaped his temper, his strength, and his way of dealing with other people.

When a young woman and a rival enter Bram's lonely world, pity and menace mix in everything he does. Curwood follows hunts, traps, flights, and confrontations through snow and timber country. Readers get a fast-moving adventure about a man who is both pitiable and dangerous, and about the claims of love and loyalty in a place with little law.
45187-the-household-of-sir-thomas-more:
This historical tale of Sir Thomas More's Chelsea household was printed at London by John Nimmo in 1899. The Reverend Hutton of Saint John's College, Oxford, wrote the introduction. Twenty-five illustrations by John Jellicoe and Herbert Railton fill the book. Its decorated title page borrows Margaret More's Latin motto, saying the little book was begun by Margaret, aged fifteen, at Chelsea.

The story shows More at home among his family rather than at court, with Erasmus visiting among the peacocks, children Jack and Cecy at play, and Margaret up a tree. More reads Wynkyn de Worde, receives the Cardinal's procession, and sits down to rest and talk with his household. The author's other tales, named at the front, include The Old Chelsea Bun-Shop and Cherry and Violet, a tale of the Great Plague.
45249-the-history-of-signboards-from-the:
Jacob Larwood and John Camden Hotten compiled The History of Signboards, here in its twelfth impression from Chatto and Windus of London in 1908, with one hundred illustrations. Their preface calls the subject a by-way of history that earlier writers had left alone.

Signs, they explain, were once indispensable: when few could read or write, the painted board named the house, and many street names still come from an old inn sign. House numbering ended the need, and the boards lingered as ornament and advertisement. The hard part of the work was sorting thousands of single and double signs into classes. The authors gather famous signs, absurd combinations, and popular humour from Addison's day to their own.
45293-what-was-the-religion-of-shakespea:
What Was the Religion of Shakespeare, by Mangasarian, is a lecture given in Chicago in 1907. He spoke before the Independent Religious Society at Orchestra Hall on a Sunday morning. A line from Schiller on toleration and wide knowledge stands as a motto. Mangasarian calls himself a mortal seeking knowledge in a second motto.

His method is to watch how often set views and phrases recur across the works of Shakespeare. Stress and steady preference for such views can reveal a philosophy, he argues. The plays are not a treatise on theology or a manual of thought, he grants. Readers must thus read between the lines to find the man behind the work. A great mind cannot hide or fake its earnest convictions for long, in his view.
45306-an-american-hobo-in-europe-a-true-:
An American Hobo in Europe is a true narrative by Windy Bill, printed at San Francisco with copyright in 1907. Its subtitle promises the adventures of a poor American at home and in the old country. Fifteen chapters run from Frisco to Scotland. Glasgow takes up much of the book's second half.

The tale opens with little Billy, the author's pal on the road. The two had been on the bum together a long while. They prospected for gold in Utah, Nevada, and California, and never quarreled. Walking the railroad between Ogden and Salt Lake City, they meet two Mormon girls. Windy Bill tells the whole tramp's life plainly, as one of the road's own men.
45321-serbian-folk-lore:
Madame Mijatovich Englished Serbian Folk-Lore from the Serbian in a second edition printed in London in 1899. Denton wrote an introduction. Contents open with that introduction, then the tales: the bear's son, the wonderful kiosk, and the snake's gift, the speech of animals. The golden apple-tree and the nine peahens follow. Papalluga, or the golden slipper, comes next.

The golden-fleeced ram, the wise girl, and good deeds are never lost stand among the tales. The wicked stepmother, bird girl, and Sir Peppercorn appear as well. Bash-Chalek, or true steel, and the golden-haired twins fill later pages. The introduction holds that the worth of folk-lore has only of late years been frankly owned. Such tales, passed down among peasants and youth, serve the historian and the student of peoples, it says, beyond their moment's pleasure.
45353-a-history-of-american-literature:
Percy Boynton, a teacher at the University of Chicago, published A History of American Literature in 1919. Boynton had already written on composition and on London in English writing, and he edited a volume of American poetry. His history runs from the colonial period to the drama and poetry of his own day in twenty-nine chapters.

Early chapters cover the seventeenth century, the earliest verse, Jonathan Edwards, Benjamin Franklin, and the farmer-writer named in the chapter on Crevecoeur. Middle chapters take up Irving, Cooper, Bryant, Poe, and the Transcendentalists, with full chapters for Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, and Whitman. Later pages turn west to Mark Twain and close with the rise of fiction under William Dean Howells. Charts of dates help readers place each writer. The book gives students a clear map of how American writing grew over three centuries.
45496-insect-architecture:
Insect Architecture is a natural history book by James Rennie. A new and much enlarged edition was prepared by the Reverend Wood, author of Homes Without Hands. Bell and Daldy published the edition at London in 1869, with near two hundred pictures. In his preface Wood explains that he added many fresh examples, drawn in most cases from real specimens.

The chapters sort insect building by trade and method. Mason wasps and mason bees come first, then mining bees and carpenter bees. Long chapters treat the hive bee, its wax, its glue, and the building of the cell. Later parts cover leaf rolling caterpillars, caddis worms, and the ant lion. Wood notes that most figured specimens rest in the British Museum or his own cabinet. He left Rennie's text untouched apart from his bracketed additions.
45498-history-of-the-union-jack-and-flag:
Barlow Cumberland wrote a history of the Union Jack and the flags of the empire, in a third edition printed at Toronto in 1909. Nine coloured plates and many illustrations fill the book. Cumberland gives the story to the flag itself, with much respect, as one of its sons. First plates show the crosses of Saint George, Saint Andrew, and Saint Patrick.

The history grew from a paper meant to inform his boys, Cumberland says. He wanted them to know how the flag grew into its form, and how its colours trace the constitutional development of the British realm. A search for more facts ran wide. New chapters tell of the Jacks in the thirteen American colonies and in the United States, plus the proper proportions of the flag.
45809-a-glossary-of-words-used-in-the-co:
A Glossary of Words Used in the County of Wiltshire, by George Edward Dartnell and Edward Hungerford Goddard, was published in London in 1893 for the English Dialect Society. Oxford printed the book. The glossary proper runs to 186 pages, with addenda, specimens of dialect in verse and tale, a bibliography, and old word-lists in appendices.

The first entry is the letter word A itself: he or she, as a pronoun. A second A names a harrow or drag, perhaps from an old English word for the tool. The note says the term still lingered in Somerset and Wiltshire thirty years before, but is now disused. A-drag, a heavy drag for harrowing turnips, is still used in south Wiltshire. The book saves a county speech that farming change was already thinning.
45961-south-america-observations-and-imp:
South America: Observations and Impressions, by James Bryce, author of The Holy Roman Empire and The American Commonwealth. It appears here in a new edition corrected and revised, published by Macmillan at New York in 1914. Bryce dedicates the book to his friends of the English Alpine Club.

A note to the revised edition, dated February 1913, records that many corrections have been made. The contents open with the Isthmus of Panama: the route from Colon to Culebra, the view from Ancon hill, the San Blas Indians, and the English raiders Drake and Morgan. The canal chapters cover the Gatun locks and lake, the great cutting at Culebra, administration and sanitation in the Canal Zone, and the French failure ascribed primarily to disease. A second chapter turns to the coast of Peru, its cold Antarctic current, aridity, and barrenness.
46002-motor-tours-in-yorkshire:
Mrs Rodolph Stawell wrote motor tours in Yorkshire, with photos by R de S Stawell. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book from New York and London. She had written Motor Tours in Wales for the same house. Four tours fill the book, from the Dales to York and the south.

Plates show Fountains Abbey, Bolton Priory, Whitby Abbey, and York Minster. The Dales tour runs 240 miles in all, with notes on roads and hills. Buttertubs Pass is steep in parts, the guide warns, and Richmond has hard climbs. Early motorists gain routes, sights, and road lore for a rich county.
4612-the-altar-fire:
Arthur Christopher Benson published The Altar Fire in 1907, with a Latin epigraph on fire falling from the Lord and devouring the burnt offering. His preface warns that the book may truly be felt as morbid, since it deliberately pictures a diseased spirit. Yet a pathological treatise on cancer or paralysis, he argues, is not necessarily morbid, and bodily ailments are now rightly seen as natural phenomena, not hidden away in attics and bedrooms.

Benson extends that plea to the heart and soul: suffering there is still treated as unreal, imaginary, or hypochondriacal, and thought curable by a little resolution and cheerful society. By foolish, secretive reticence, he says, much is lost. Readers get a serious Edwardian study of a troubled mind and spirit, written with candour about faith, illness, and inner life, and best read slowly, without expecting a light tale.
46148-the-child-in-the-midst-a-comparati:
The Child in the Midst is a study of child welfare across the globe by Mary Labaree. Its full title adds the match of lands of the faith and lands past it. A church group for the joint study of far missions put the book out. Rights date the work to January of the year nineteen fourteen.

A front print shows the shop at Nazareth where Christ learned a trade. The front note says this is a book about the young, not for the young. Facts on schools, work, health, and homes are set land by land. The aim is to spur prayer, work, and gifts for the worlds poor youth. The book was the fourteenth text in its study set for church groups.
46207-a-vision-of-venus-or-a-midsummer-n:
A Vision of Venus, or A Midsummer Nights Nightmare is a jest play by Harry Pleon. It is in two acts and eight scenes and was first played at a stage house of the east end in March of eighteen ninety-three. Its full name calls it a droll piece of odd kind, in part past a famed tale of a tint wife of stone. Pleon him self played its lead on that stage.

That lead is a hair man and scent man who, past some hid power, is loved and dogged past the love dame of old. A crime desk man, a jolly chap, two rob men, an old man, and a dress wife fill the cast. The live wife of stone claims the hair man in one scene and sits in his shop in the next. The play runs past an hour and a part.
46338-a-medley-of-weather-lore:
Wright collects old sayings in A Medley of Weather Lore, printed at Bournemouth in 1913. The book runs month by month, from January to December, with an index at the end. A verse from The Shepherd's Legacy of 1670 stands at the front.

January shows the form. The old Cornish name is Mis-jenver, cold air month, and the jewel is the garnet. Rhymes tie gay New Year weather to wintry months to come. Scots lore gives each wind its gift: south for heat, west for milk and fish, north for cold. Warwickshire men bow nine times to the first new moon for luck. Farm folk get a year of such signs.
46375-the-phantom-treasure:
The Phantom Treasure is a girls school tale by Harriet Pyne Grove. The Saalfield house of Akron and New York brought it out in nineteen twenty eight. Janet, a school girl, learns of a box come for her at the school desk. Her mate Allie May brings the word on April first, which breeds doubt. Janet has had no box in her life save shop goods, she says.

A front plate shows Janet on a drop down ledge with ease. Her chum Lina shares her room and her late light rule slips. Verse drill in class, with a strict miss to ape, fills the first talk. Janet hopes the box holds a grand cake with rich goods in it. Allie May swears the news is no April jest that day.
46501-some-zulu-customs-and-folk-lore:
L H Samuelson, writing under the name Nomleti, described Zulu customs and folk lore in a London volume. Footnotes signed ED come from Miss Werner's paper in the Journal of the African Society. A Zulu wedding opens the contents. The bridegroom must compose a song a month ahead and teach it to the young men of the neighborhood.

His sisters and their friends join the singing and dancing, beating time with their feet. Chapters treat twins, departed spirits, and sacrifices to spirits. The death of a chief, the annual feast, and the doctoring of an army follow. Rain doctors, eclipses, and praying for the corn appear. A tale tells how death came into the world.
46582-clutterbuck-s-treasure:
Fred Whishaw wrote an adventure novel published at London in 1910, named for an old miser's treasure. A front picture shows a third shot whizzing past the heroes' hiding place. Chapter one is a cowardly attack. The narrator's father died and left him penniless, and friends told him his failure to find work was his own fault.

He lacked grit, they said, in energy, perseverance, or pluck. The great prize is offered in chapter three, and the narrator enters for the race. Treachery, ghosts, and rats in a trap follow. A night with a lion and a bad elephant mark the African chapters. Forty three chapters end with all over but the shouting.
46633-the-characters-of-jean-de-la-bruye:
Henri van Laun translated The Characters of Jean de La Bruyère into English, in an edition published by Nimmo in London in 1885. Only five hundred copies were printed, three hundred for England and two hundred for America. Twenty-four etchings illustrate the volume, with portraits of Montaigne and Descartes among them. An introduction and a life of the author stand before the text.

La Bruyère's chapters take society piece by piece. He writes of works of the mind, of personal merit, of women, and of the affections. The town, the court, and the great each get a chapter. Later chapters treat the sovereign and the state, mankind in general, fashion, and freethinkers. His book, first published under Louis the Fourteenth, drew sharp portraits of the types around him. Van Laun's rendering made the French classic available to English readers in a fine illustrated form.
46641-tent-work-in-palestine-a-record-of:
Claude Reignier Conder wrote Tent Work in Palestine, a record of finds and risk, in a new edition at London in 1887. Conder led the survey party for the Palestine Exploration Fund. J W Whymper drew the pictures. The book is given to the Prince of Wales with his leave.

A front note traces the Survey of Western Palestine from 1872. Captain Stewart began it and fell ill at once. Conder took charge and came in the summer of that year. By October 1875 he had mapped four thousand seven hundred square miles. Lieutenant Kitchener did the last one thousand three hundred in 1877. The book tells of tent life, finds, and hard trips in that work.
46790-a-history-of-bohemian-literature:
Count Lutzow wrote A History of Bohemian Literature, in English. Heinemann at London put it out first in 1899. A new edition followed in 1907 from the same house. The book stands in a series of short literary histories. Gosse edited that series of the world's literatures for Heinemann.

Lutzow sat in Bohemia's royal society of sciences, the title says. He sat in the Bohemian academy as well in those years. Comparing great literature with a small country's might be attempted, it opens. If such comparison were possible at all, the preface muses. A small and little-known country is his subject throughout the book. Greek, French, Italian, and Spanish volumes stand in the series list. Japanese, Sanskrit, Hungarian, and Russian histories stand there also. Lutzow gives English readers a whole literature they lacked.
46850-the-motor-boys-on-the-wing-or-seek:
The Motor Boys on the Wing, or Seeking the Airship Treasure, is a boys' tale by Clarence Young. He was the hand of two more sets of boys' tales, named on the title leaf. The book was put out at New York in nineteen twelve. It stands in a set of tales of boys and their road craft. The set list at the front names twelve books of that set in all.

The first books of that set take the boys past land, past a south land, and past the plains. Afloat, on two great seas, and in strange wa ters fill the mid run. In the clouds, past the great hills, and past the sea stand in the late run. This book is the last of the set list.
46852-the-hills-of-desire:
Richard Aumerle Maher wrote The Hills of Desire, a novel copyrighted by Macmillan in 1919 and reprinted in 1925. Maher had earlier written The Shepherd of the North. The book opens in dialect, with an Irishman named Casey trying to count the men at a picnic and losing the fifth.

Jimmie Wardwell, who is typing Casey's count, leaps up when the lodging-house keeper Augusta announces that the boarders cannot stand it. He kisses her in jest and cries to arms against the boarders. The narrator owns that Augusta is somewhat incredible and hard to make understood. Maher builds a boarding-house comedy of talk, work, and longing, in which small people chase the hills of desire.
46872-the-putnam-hall-rivals-or-fun-and-:
The Putnam Hall Rivals is a school story by Arthur Winfield, printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1906. Its subtitle promises fun and sport afloat and ashore. Winfield also wrote the Putnam Hall Cadets and the Rover Boys series. Putnam Hall stands on a beautiful lake in the upper part of New York State.

As at all boarding academies, there are many keen rivalries, in the classroom, at the gymnasium, and on the athletic field. The chapters open out on the ice, with a game of snap-the-whip. The bully of the school, a dose of snow and icicles, and a doctored cake follow. A boathouse fire puts the boys under suspicion. Boat races, target practice, a mad dog, and a cave fill the middle of the fun.
46879-the-miner-s-friend-or-an-engine-to:
Thomas Savery wrote The Miner's Friend, an engine to raise water by fire. S Crouch printed it at London in 1702. A reprint came in 1827 from W Clowes. Savery signs himself a gentleman. A Seneca line heads his title in Latin. Content with others' finds marks a sluggish wit, it says.

Savery showed a small model to the king, he opens. Hampton Court hosted that trial of the engine. The king showed seeming satisfaction at its power. A patent and act of parliament followed that grace. The engine now stands complete and in practice, he says. Repeated success and applause attend its work. Miners will gain most from its fire-raised water. Other uses stand listed in the treatise too. Objections made against it get their answers there. The first practical steam engine's own manual argues with skeptics in the age of Queen Anne.
46978-dig-here:
Gladys Allen wrote this mystery tale for young readers, and Goldsmith of Chicago printed it in 1937. Dig Here is the cry of the title and of chapter eighteen, near the tale's heart. A treasure and its unveiling close the list of chapters.

Aunt Cal opens the tale, then Fishers Haven and Craven House set the scene. Prisoners, a piece of paper, and a scalp lock raise the pitch. Daisy June and the Blue Emerald, a missing Circe, and tracks in the dust crowd the middle. The Rescue, a closed door, and an escape mark the late turns. Eve and Sandy, with roommate Hattie May Lewis, drive the talk in the first scene, in bright schoolgirl style.
47053-domestic-folk-lore:
Domestic Folk-Lore is a handbook of popular traditions by Thiselton Dyer, author of British Popular Customs and English Folk-Lore. Cassell, Petter, Galpin published it in London, Paris, and New York. Dyer's preface first explains the word folk-lore itself. For the term in its present sense, covering popular traditions, proverbial sayings, superstitions, and customs, we are indebted to Thoms, the editor of Notes and Queries. He suggested it in the Athenaeum of August 22, 1846.

The study's object, Dyer says, is to collect, classify, and preserve survivals of popular belief, and trace them to their source. The task grows urgent. School-boards and railways are fast sweeping away every vestige of the old beliefs and customs of social and domestic life. A passage preserved in the copy turns to nursery tales.
47059-meteorology-the-science-of-the-atm:
