Charles Fitzhugh Talman wrote Meteorology, the science of the atmosphere, as volume one of the Popular Science Library published by Collier in New York in 1922. Garrett Serviss edited the set. A remarkable tornado photograph, painted over for the book, opens the volume: the photographer stood too close to fit the whole funnel into his camera. Talman chaired a committee of the American Meteorological Society.

Nineteen chapters survey the air. Talman begins with the anatomy and resources of the atmosphere, then treats it as a highway. Dust and smoke, weather instruments, and cloudland follow. Winds and storms, atmospheric electricity, and optics take up the middle. Later chapters specialise: weather maps and forecasts, and the meteorology of farming, commerce, the sea, and flight. The book gave general readers of 1922 a full, plain account of the young science that forecast their weather.
47061-mr-incoul-s-misadventure:
Mr Incoul's Misadventure is a novel by Edgar Saltus. Benjamin and Bell published it in New York in 1887. Saltus was known for bleak philosophy books. Reviewers quoted in front call him a scientific pessimist. A verse from Deuteronomy stands as the motto. Thine eye shall not pity, it reads.

The first chapter introduces Harmon Incoul. His wife has died, and his world expects no second marriage. The bereavement was known to be bitter. He is childless and proverbially rich. Nothing keeps him in New York. Yet travel promises little change, the narrator muses. A man abroad is like an invalid turning in bed. Eighteen chapters follow. Biarritz, Spain, and a Paris house host the misadventure.
47105-notes-and-queries-for-worcestershi:
John Noake compiled Notes and Queries for Worcestershire, printed in London in 1856 at five shillings. Noake had written The Rambler. He gives the book, by leave, to John Goodwin, twice mayor of Worcester, under patrons including the Dean of Worcester and Earl Beauchamp. A verse at the front bids the reader sit by the fire and hear tales of ages long ago.

A preface calls the book another small instalment toward the history of Worcestershire. The usual stuff of history books, Noake writes, is pedigrees, charters, battles, sieges, and lists of manors. Such things are but the dry bones, the frame of history. The spirit of the past must be called up from papers and old tales, by care and comparison. Older writers have heaped up great masses on the county, he grants. Yet what do we know of the manners, hopes, and daily life of our forebears?
47364-rustic-speech-and-folk-lore:
Elizabeth Mary Wright wrote this study of country speech and old custom for Oxford University Press. Humphrey Milford printed Rustic Speech and Folk-Lore in London in 1913. Wright, a keen ear for dialect, treats both the words men use and the tales they keep.

Dialect speakers open the book, with the decay of pure dialect and tales of Yorkshire folk. A rich stock of words comes next: names for a fool, the runt of a litter, a foxglove, or a stream. Wright shows how fine shades of sense live in small word shifts, hard to match in standard English. Lists of works she used close the study, a rich mine for speech lovers.
47439-the-new-glutton-or-epicure:
The New Glutton or Epicure, published at New York in 1906, is Horace Fletcher's book of economic nutrition. Fletcher's earlier works include a primer of our own nutrition and The New Menticulture. His system taught eaters to chew food to liquid and eat only what the body truly wants. The book runs to three hundred and forty-four pages.

Fletcher thanks the friends who pushed his inquiry at hard moments. William James of Harvard quoted Menticulture with approval in his lectures on religious experience. Helpers studied the diet habits of peoples in the Balkan Peninsula, Turkey and along the Dalmatian Coast. Their reports fed the primer. The tone stays earnest and hopeful: right eating, Fletcher holds, is a reform any person can practice.
4746-kennedy-square:
F. Hopkinson Smith opens Kennedy Square with an author's preface on the place in the late fifties. Rough stone seats stood among birds, trees, and blossom, while vine-heavy bowers drooped over earth tracks edged with boxwood. Tall magnolias scented the enclosure, and roses clambering over a decaying fence vanished and reappeared between its bars.

Youngsters laughed on shaded paths, playing with hoops and balls while old Black mammies in pale aprons and bright headscarves watched. Quiet nooks sheltered lovers talking together, weary travellers taking rest, and elderly men absorbed in books for long stretches. Beyond the turf edge and a shaky wooden barrier, a bumpy walkway lay dappled with shade and flecked with green mould. In summer a melon seller halted his cart beside it, and in winter Moses stopped his own cart there. Readers get a nostalgic Baltimore novel of an old square and its people.
47842-queen-moo-s-talisman-the-fall-of-t:
Queen Moo Talisman, the fall of the Maya empire, is a romance by Alice Dixon Le Plongeon. Peter Eckler published the book at New York, entered for copyright in June 1902. Le Plongeon is named as author of Here and There in Yucatan on the title page. 

Queen Moo is the Maya queen of the Le Plongeon reconstruction of that lost world in their books. Alice and her husband Augustus spent years among the ruins of Yucatan in their explorations. Their theories of a Maya Atlantis and of queens who ruled it were famous and disputed in their day. This novel dresses those theories as a tale of the empire fall. It is at once an adventure story and a creed, written by a believer who had camped in the temples she peoples with her court.
48100-the-sabbath-school-index-pointing-:
The Sabbath-School Index, by Pardee, was published in Philadelphia in 1868. The full title promises the history and progress of Sunday schools, with approved modes of instruction, examples in picture and object teaching, and the use of the blackboard. Infant classes, teachers' meetings, conventions, and institutes all come under its scope.

Pardee says his earlier manual, The Sunday-School Worker Assisted, was so well received that calls came from many parts of the land and many church groups for a fuller work. Teachers who once had to buy a dozen English and American books for details could now find them in one. The index is a practical handbook for pastors, superintendents, and teachers who ran the vast Sunday-school movement.
48117-the-heir-to-grand-pre:
John Frederic Herbin wrote a tale of Grand-Pre in Nova Scotia, printed at Wolfville and Toronto in 1907. Herbin had written a history of Grand-Pre and a book called The Marshlands. The tale opens with what the tide brought. A young man lies on a cabin roof in the shadow of a still mainsail and smokes at ease.

Dulse, a precious stocking, salmon, and amethyst mark the early chapters. Marie, an adoption, and a blue vein of mystery follow. Evangeline returns, and Gabriel returns too, in names that recall the famed Acadian exile tale. Tide marshes, dyke lands, and village love shape a quiet Canadian romance rooted in place and memory.
48123-echoes-of-old-lancashire:
William E A Axon gathered echoes of old Lancashire life and lore. William Andrews and Company issued the book in London in 1899. Five hundred copies were printed, and the copy shown is Number 228. The book is given to the Earl of Crawford of Haigh.

Tales treat a Lancashire plot, De Quincey's highwayman, and county folk past a hundred years. Kufic coins, giants, and the first book printed in Manchester fill the gleanings. Axon aims at byways of local lore, not the grand tale of mills. Local readers gain quaint, warm scraps of a county changing fast.
48299-the-story-of-a-hare:
John Tregarthen wrote The Story of a Hare, first published in 1912 and reprinted in 1915 by Hearst's International Library in New York. Tregarthen also wrote life stories of a fox and an otter. His hare lives on the Cornish heights near Land's End, among four wild hills above a treeless tableland. The first chapter covers the hare's early troubles.

The contents promise a hard life. Chapters treat the hare's education and independence, a chase by polecats, and a delusive refuge. The great winter, peril of death, and the fiends of the wild follow. Man appears late under a chapter title in French suggesting that man amuses himself. Tregarthen drew a sketch map of the scene and filled the book with pictures of the country around Sennen and Mount's Bay. The story follows one animal through the dangers of a Cornish year.
48355-legends-and-satires-from-medi-val-:
Martha Hale Shackford, who taught English literature at Wellesley College, edited Legends and Satires from Medieval Literature for Ginn and Company in 1913. Fra Angelico's Last Judgment gives the frontispiece, a view of Paradise. Notes at the back back up each piece.

The book is sorted by kind. A proem treats man's body and soul, made, it says, of four elements, with the eyes as his sun and moon. Debates follow, with Phillis and Flora pleading love's cause, then a vision of Saint Patrick's Purgatory and the lives of Saint Brandon and Saint Margaret. A bestiary, a lapidary of stones, and sharp satires fill the rest: the Land of Cockaygne, Sir Penny, and the lay of Sir Orfeo at the end.
48515-psycho-vox-or-the-emerson-system-o:
Charles Wesley Emerson wrote this book on the care of the voice, in a print of 1923. He was the man who set up the Emerson College of Oratory at Boston. The list of parts gives the plan of his way. The voice is the tale-bearer of the man by kind, the first head says. Then come the parts that make the voice, that give it strength, and that give it its ring.

More heads treat of the tie of the right use of the voice to health, and to the state of the nerves. Pitch and ring, ways to train the voice, drills, beat, and the kind of the voice fill the rest of the list.
48561-berkshire:
Monckton wrote Berkshire, a volume in the Cambridge County Geographies, in 1911. Cambridge University Press made the book, with maps, diagrams, and pictures. Contents open with the meaning of county and shire, and the traits of the ground. Size, shape, boundaries, surface, watershed, and rivers follow in order. Geology and soil, natural history, and climate and rainfall take their turns.

People, farming, industries, and minerals lead into the history of the shire. Antiquities are split into prehistoric finds and Roman and Saxon finds. Architecture is treated in churches, religious houses, castles, and homes in four parts. Roads, rule, schools, the forest, and a roll of honour fill the close. Plates show Windsor Castle, the Ridgeway, and the Thames at Pangbourne. The book gives a whole county in one neat school tome.
48603-we-and-our-neighbors-or-the-record:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote We and Our Neighbors, a novel dated eighteen seventy-five and a sequel to My Wife and I. Stowe was known worldwide for Uncle Tom's Cabin. The front picture shows two sisters peering at new folk across the street.

Who can have taken the Ferguses' house, one brisk old lady asks through the blinds. Chapters follow the street's folk through calls, letters, and small storms in teapots. Aunt Maria rouses tempests, clears her conscience, and frees her mind in turn. A dinner on washing day and a mistress without a maid show daily life. Faith and neighbourhood manners carry the tale.
48612-psychological-warfare:
Psychological Warfare, by Paul Linebarger of the School of Advanced International Studies, reached its second edition in the nineteen-fifties. Linebarger defines his subject by what it is not. It runs before, during and after war, and no laws of war govern it. It cannot be mapped by terrain, order of battle or named engagements.

The book falls into four parts. History and definition come first, with chapters on both world wars. Analysis, intelligence and the estimate of the situation follow. Planning and operations, for civilians and against troops, make the third part. The last part faces the cold war and seven small wars. Charts of famous leaflets, from Bunker Hill to Anzio, fill the illustration list.
48976-once-upon-a-time-in-delaware:
Katharine Pyle wrote Once Upon a Time in Delaware, edited by Emily P Bissell with drawings by Ethel Pennewill Brown, for the Delaware Society of the Colonial Dames of America in 1911. A letter to Delaware children heads the book. The society calls the tales true stories writ just for them. A map of Delaware faces the title.

The tales tell how brave men and women crossed the ocean to a wild land. They made farms, towns, and a state among Native tribes, the letter says. Delaware is one of the first thirteen colonies, it notes. Young citizens must one day uphold its honor, the society urges. An editor's note says the book is for school and home use. Points in dispute are smoothed for young readers, it owns.
48986-around-the-camp-fire:
Around the Camp-Fire, by Charles Roberts with pictures by Charles Copeland, was copyrighted in 1896 and published in New York by Crowell. A front plate shows the camp on Beardsley Brook. Nine chapters of camp tales range over the Squatook country. A panther at the parsonage and bear against birch-bark open the set. A fight with the hounds of the sea, and a bull and a leaping-pole, follow.

Later chapters bring an idyl of lost camp, peril among pearls, Labrador wolves, and a mad stallion. A bull moose, a wreck in a boom-house, and being tracked by a panther fill the middle. The last camp-fire closes with Indian devils and a bruin's boxing match. Roberts, the Canadian poet-naturalist, tells hunting and woodcraft tales as fireside yarns, half memoir and half invention, from the New Brunswick woods he knew well.
49022-a-year-at-the-shore:
Year at the Shore is a seaside natural history by Philip Henry Gosse. Strahan published it in London in the year 1865 for shore lovers. Thirty six illustrations by the author print in colours throughout it. Contents sort the shore by months, from January through the year. January opens with the advance of waves upon a beach.

Foam, shingle voices, climbing the cliff, and assault of the sea follow. Gulls, a cavernous recess, and a rock pool fill that first month. A purple spotted top shell shows its tentacles, eyes, and progression. Dog whelks, a twisted cone, and a cowry crowd the January pages. Gosse watches pools and cliffs through all the seasons in turn.
49128-curiosities-of-street-literature:
Curiosities of Street Literature gathers the cheap print sold in London streets, reprinted word for word from the originals. Its title page lists cocks or catchpennies, street drolleries, squibs, and comic tales in prose and verse. Broadsides on the royal family, political litanies, dialogues, and catechisms fill the heap. Dying speeches and confessions of criminals stand among them.

A front plate shows a long song seller crying three yards a penny for the newest songs. One sample ballad tells of a cruel murder in verses meant to make the blood run cold. The edition was small, only two hundred and fifty copies, notes show. Such street papers were the news and fun of the poor for pennies. This collection, issued about 1870, preserves ballads and gallows sheets that would else have rotted away. It is a rich store for anyone studying popular print.
4934-the-natural-history-of-wiltshire:
John Aubrey's natural history of Wiltshire gathers antiquarian notes, wonders, and weather from an English county and beyond. The sample chapter ranges past Wiltshire itself to hurricanes and hailstorms across England and Italy, including the great tempest linked in legend to Oliver Cromwell's death.

Aubrey, writing in the seventeenth century, records what he heard and saw with a collector's appetite for the remarkable. The volume mixes county lore with natural marvels, storms, and local custom. Readers get a cabinet of curiosities from an early naturalist, valuable as much for its period voice as for its facts.
49369-a-history-of-lancashire:
A History of Lancashire, by Colonel Henry Fishwick, was published by Elliot Stock at London in 1894 in the Popular County Histories series. Fishwick had already written the Lancashire Library and histories of Kirkham and Rochdale.

The preface confesses the difficulty: the material for a county history, printed and in manuscript, is enormous. Squeezing a faithful picture of the county into one octavo volume means leaving out much that readers would prefer included. Fishwick confines himself to the history of the county as a whole. He avoids personal and local details except where they illustrate his subject, and says nothing of Lancashire authors and celebrities, since personal notices belong to biography, not history. He also rejects everything that cannot be well authenticated and declines to encumber the text with references.
49516-bacon-and-shakespeare:
Albert Calvert wrote a small book gainst the claim that Bacon wrote Shakespeare. The book came out in London in 1902. A front plate shows Bacon from a small work by Oliver. That plate is the Duke of Buccleuch's own piece, the key says. Calvert grants no Bacon man may be won by his brief.

That faith is too stiff and wilful for cure, he holds in front. It rests on a false take of Bacon's own bent, he argues. It feeds on gross false tales of Shakespeare's life as well. While the claim held few minds, no fight was need, he says. Now it spreads, so he takes up arms in print. Stage past fans get a tart, brief plea.
49624-ballad-of-the-lost-hare:
Margaret Sidney wrote the Ballad of the Lost Hare, copyrighted at Boston in 1882, with designs furnished by Ida Roberts. The poem opens as an introduction in numbered verses. Near a hill and a winding glade lived the naughtiest hare ever made, the verses say. Father scolded and mother whipped, but every day away he slipped. Three brothers and two sisters cried as off he flew.

The father at last forbids him home until he can stay in his little bed. One more race, he warns, and the hare may beg and cry all day outside. The eleventh verse gives the end: alack, he never came back. Swallowed alive, hung on a rail, or dancing along the pale waters, none can say. The winds forgot his very name, and he became in truth the lost hare.
4994-five-thousand-miles-underground-or-:
Professor Amos Henderson calls for Washington across a big shed full of machinery, and this underground adventure answers with a joke. Washington hides beneath iron, steel, and aluminum. He replies in grand speech that he will attend to the professor's orders at the appointed time. Henderson wishes he had started when he began talking.

The professor's subterranean vessel carries the party five thousand miles underground toward the mystery of the earth's center. No byline appears in the catalog record. Readers get a boys' scientific romance of drills, caverns, and wonders below, in the tradition of voyages to places no one had ever seen.
50082-talks-on-teaching-literature:
Talks on Teaching Literature collects lectures by Arlo Bates on the schoolroom study of books. Houghton, Mifflin published them in Boston and New York in 1906. Bates first delivered them at a summer school in Illinois. That was in June 1905. Eighteen talks make up the volume. An index closes it.

The first talk states the problem baldly. Earnest teachers all meet black moments, Bates writes. In those moments literature plainly cannot be taught. A pupil who learns in literature learns it himself. Art conveys what no other language can express. Later talks weigh the conditions and difficulties. Prose, the novel, and Macbeth earn separate chapters. Criticism, workmanship, and biography follow. Voluntary reading closes the course.
50162-songs-of-love-and-empire:
Nesbit wrote Songs of Love and Empire, printed at Westminster in 1898. She had written Lays and Legends and A Pomander of Verse. A note at the front thanks the editors of the papers where many of these verses first appeared. After Sixty Years came out in the Daily News on June 22, 1897. To the Queen of England and other verses stood in the Pall Mall Gazette.

Nesbit gives the book to Hubert Bland, in a verse saying he taught her first what love and empire mean. The contents run in letter order. At the Sound of the Drum and the Ballad of the White Lady stand among them. A Song of Peace and Honour, a Song of Trafalgar, Trafalgar Day, and To the Queen of England suit the book's second theme. The first poem hails the Queen on the day of flags and flowers.
50209-the-mystery-of-the-sycamore:
The Mystery of the Sycamore is a detective novel by Carolyn Wells. It first appeared in 1920 under the title The Pardon Tree. The Lippincott Company reissued it under the new name in 1921. 

The opening chapter brings a letter that says come, and a man sorting his mail. Curtis Keefe divides his post into three neat piles by importance. Chapters that follow promise a big sycamore tree and a bugle sounding taps. Another heir, inquiries, and a chain of confessions drive the middle of the book. Fleming Stone, the author's series detective, enters in the eleventh chapter. Rachel's story and an awful truth wait near the close. A final confession ends the sequence of revelations the contents advertise.
50661-dave-dawson-at-singapore:
R Sidney Bowen wrote Dave Dawson at Singapore, held at New York in 1942 as part of the War Adventure Series. Bowen had writ Dave Dawson tales at Dunkirk, in Libya, and on convoy patrol. Seventeen chapters carry the tale. Dave Dawson and Freddy Farmer stand at its heart.

The tale opens on the British cruiser Harkness at sea. Freddy stares at the far line of land and breathes the name Singapore. Dave jokes of its ten thousand smells. Strange orders, a secret note, and flights north build the plot. Chapter heads name death, chaos, and brave wings. The book is a fast war tale for young readers of its day.
50945-point-of-departure:
Point of Departure, a science fiction story by Vaughan Shelton, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1956, with art by Weiss. The tale opens in the office of the president of a Research Foundation. A man named Halleck is on edge, near to attacking a man named Donner. The president has to order him to sit down.

Halleck feels answerable for the acts of Donner, and for the mess they have made. The hook of the story is a dark one. The troubles of Donner repeat something that made chaos thousands of years ago. That echo of an ancient disaster drives the plot. Shelton builds the tale on a clash between a rash researcher and the men who must judge his work. The story is a short piece of magazine science fiction.
51040-cuban-folk-lore:
Cuban Folk-Lore is a book by Terwilliger, printed at Havana in 1908. It opens with superstition and witchcraft in Cuba. Terwilliger says no place shows such a mass of superstitious customs. Even educated whites, he claims, fear the brujo, or witch doctor.

Most of the practices came from Africa with enslaved people. The Ñáñigos society, mixing Catholicism with witchcraft, reached Cuba in 1836. Its first chapter, Apapa Epi, rose at Regla under government license. Whites were first refused entry. In 1863 a traitor sold the order's secrets for twenty cents. The book records a folk religion at work in Cuban life.
51177-legends-of-lancashire:
Seven Lancashire legends gathered in one volume, published at London and Wigan in 1841. Whittaker and Company shared the issue with R Cocker of Wigan. Lady Stanley received the dedication, by her kind permission. The tales run from the Battle of Wigan Lane to Lancaster Castle. Witches of Furness, a devil's wall, and a spectre coach stand between.

The preface jokes at its own expense first. A preface before an introduction feels impudent, the chronicler admits. His prospectus calls Lancashire the antiquarian's richest county. Its rivers once flowed with blood, and its houses were towers and abbeys. Now fortresses are factories and heroes are clerks. The tales rescue the older, stranger county for fireside reading.
51194-made-to-measure:
William Campbell Gault sets a robot-age marriage tale in Galaxy Science Fiction, January 1951. L Woromay drew the pictures. Joe rides a pressure-tube train with his friend Sam.

The tube locks sigh a phrase at him: she's not right. Joe means his wife Vera. She is not what he wants. Sam directs the Domestic Center, which orders the mating market. With women far outnumbering men, the Center gives reason and order to the contest. It has nearly ended illicit relations, Sam boasts. It secures the children. But the big job, Joe says, was missed. The headnote shows that job plainly: somewhere an ideal mate waits for every man and woman. Joe, the great living authority on robots, was a man who rolled his own.
51271-the-history-of-the-highland-cleara:
History of the Highland Clearances is a history by Alexander Mackenzie, first issued in 1883. A second edition, altered and revised, followed in 1914 after his death. A new introduction by Ian Macpherson, a member of parliament, frames this printing. Contents begin with Sutherland, the county most famed for forced removals.

Witness voices fill the Sutherland part, from Donald Sage to Hugh Miller in print. Harriet Beecher Stowe praise of improvements draws a sharp reply from Donald Macleod. The trial of Patrick Sellar stands as its own grim section in the book. Ross shire cases such as Glencalvie carry the record north and west onward.
5161-the-treasure:
Selma Lagerlof's short novel, The Treasure, opens at Solberga parsonage in the days of King Frederik the Second of Denmark. Its ten chapters move from the quays and the town cellars to moonlight, haunting, unrest, and Sir Archie's flight over the ice, as a buried treasure draws thieves and lovers toward ruin.

Lagerlof tells a dark tale of greed and guilt in a coastal town, with the sea's roar closing the story. The book shows her gift for legend-like narrative, where landscape and conscience press together, and it offers a compact, haunting read for lovers of Scandinavian fiction.
51614-poems-of-pleasure:
Poems of Pleasure is a book of verse by Ella Wheeler Wilcox, who also wrote Poems of Passion. The Chicago edition is dated 1897, with roots in an 1888 printing. Her portrait and signature face the title page.

The poems fall into three parts, named Passional, Philosophical and Miscellaneous. The first poem, Surrender, tells of two souls meeting like planets in space. Old ties and aims fall away in that bright moment. Love's glory fills the whole of the scene. Later parts turn to thought and to mixed themes. The verse is bold, warm and full of feeling. Her lines move with a strong beat and plain, bold words.
5168-the-land-of-heart-s-desire:
W. B. Yeats's one-act play, first performed in 1894, is set in a cottage in County Sligo, where the Bruin family gathers around the hearth. A faery child enters their home and tempts the young bride, Mary Bruin, away from marriage, work, and mortal sorrow toward the land of heart's desire, where beauty never fades.

Yeats wrote the play from Irish folklore, and its short scenes carry his early themes: the pull of the otherworld against ordinary life, and the price of longing. The play is brief, lyrical, and strange, and it offers a fine first taste of Yeats as a dramatist before his later Abbey Theatre work.
5169-hardscrabble-or-the-fall-of-chicago:
John Richardson's Hardscrabble tells of the fall of Chicago in 1812. It opens on an April day in a farmhouse beside the Chicago River's southern branch, four miles from the fort. Four people rise from a midday meal by a blazing fire, unaware that war with the surrounding tribes is about to destroy their settlement.

Richardson, who knew the frontier wars first hand, writes a tale of Indian warfare, siege, and flight, grounded in the history of Fort Dearborn. The novel offers readers a dramatic, if dated, account of a famous frontier disaster, told from the settler side of a conflict that ended in massacre and captivity.
518-the-enchanted-island-of-yew-whereon-:
L. Frank Baum tells of Prince Marvel on the Enchanted Island of Yew in this fairy tale. A fairy gives Marvel a year in mortal form, and he roams with Nerle, meeting a king of thieves, gray men, a royal dragon, and the twin rulers of Twi. A tyrant, a magic book, and enchanted mirrors test his knightly heart.

Baum writes with gentle humor and bright invention, in the vein of his Oz books. Marvel wins fights by courtesy as much as sword. The book charms young readers as a quest where kindness, not force, proves the truest magic, and where a year of wonders ends in a hundred years of peace.
51997-a-book-of-poems-al-que-quiere:
Al Que Quiere is a book of poems by William Carlos Williams. The Four Seas Company of Boston published it in 1917. A Spanish epigraph by Arévalo Martínez stands at the front of the volume. Many of the poems had appeared in little magazines before this gathering.

Poetry, Others, The Egoist, and The Poetry Journal are named as those magazines. The contents open with Sub Terra and two pastorals of the countryside. Chickory and daisies, gulls, and a woman walking pass through the early pages. Love songs recur among the titles in several shapes and moods. Spanish-titled pieces, El Hombre and Mujer among them, thread the list. Liberty, equality, fraternity are cried in capitals in one title. The volume shows a young American poet finding a local, spoken music.
5202-the-golden-lion-of-granpere:
Anthony Trollope's novel is set in Granpere, a village among the Vosges mountains of Lorraine, near the baths of Plombieres. Its inn, the Golden Lion, is the centre of village life. The story follows its keeper's family, their hopes for marriage, and the arrival of outsiders who disturb a close community.

Trollope, writing of French provincial life, mixes romance with his usual close observation of money, pride, and family feeling. The novel is quieter than his English Barsetshire books, and it gives readers a charming picture of a mountain village where an inn's fortunes and a family's honour rise and fall together.
52367-the-story-of-the-east-riding-of-yo:
The Story of the East Riding of Yorkshire is a county history by Horace Browne, published in London in 1912 with one hundred and seventy illustrations. The frontispiece shows Beverley Minster, the pride of the East Riding. Browne dedicates the book to the boys and girls of the Riding, hoping their forefathers' story will inspire them to roll onwards the wheels of progress.

The acknowledgements map the making: council help, Trinity House records, and an architect's drawing. A companion volume on York in English history is advertised at the front. The Story is Edwardian county history in schoolroom form.
52441-baptism-according-to-scripture:
A theological treatise by E H Hoare, vicar of Barkby in Leicestershire. The Seeleys published the second edition at London in 1850. A clerical meeting prompted the work. Its question asked what Scripture alone deduces about baptism. Hoare, one of the members present, took the systematic path. He examined every passage bearing on the subject.

No text, he insists, may be read against another. The inquiry outgrew his expectations and cost him pains. The interest, he says, repaid the labour. His advertisement quotes the sixth Article of his church. What Scripture does not contain or prove is not required as faith. Hoare opens by tracing baptism talk to the deluge. Peter's words on the eight saved souls anchor the start.
52576-a-manual-of-american-literature:
A Manual of American Literature was edited by Theodore Stanton of Cornell University with members of the Cornell faculty. G P Putnam's Sons published it in 1909 as volume No 4000 of the Tauchnitz Edition. Stanton's preface explains that the Leipzig series, begun in 1841 as a Collection of British Authors, took in American books almost at once. Fenimore Cooper's The Spy was its fourth volume, in 1842.

Washington Irving followed, then Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter and Mrs Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin in 1852. The manual surveys that literature for European readers, and the volume is dedicated to President Theodore Roosevelt. Tauchnitz aimed, Stanton says, to spread love of English literature beyond the British Empire.
52724-glass-manufacture:
Glass Manufacture is a technical book by Walter Rosenhain, of the National Physical Laboratory, printed at New York in 1908. It belongs to the Westminster Series of trade handbooks. Rosenhain ran the laboratory's department for metallurgy and its chemistry. The book treats glass as a thing of science and of the works floor.

The first chapter takes up the physical and chemical properties of glass. It defines the term, calls glass a congealed fluid, and notes its amorphous build as the trait all vitreous bodies share. Glass, it stresses, is no fixed compound but a complex solution, open to a wide range of mixes. Later chapters turn to the raw stuffs: sources of silica in sand and sandstone, felspar, soda ash, salt-cake, and pearl ash. The book suits students and glassworks men alike.
52956-a-bitter-heritage-a-modern-story-o:
John Bloundelle-Burton wrote a modern story of love and adventure, issued in 1899. D Appleton and Company brought out A Bitter Heritage in New York that year. Press praise at the front calls Burton a master of dramatic scenes. His tales The Clash of Arms and Fortune's My Foe are listed with warmth.

Chapter heads name a crime's story, a land of golden sun, and a woman named Zara. A midnight visitor, a drop of blood, and a French man's memories stir the plot. The tale stands as Number 272 in Appletons' Town and Country Library. Readers get brisk romance in the school of Stevenson and Haggard.
53136-fig-culture-edible-figs-their-cult:
Fig Culture is Bulletin Number 5 of the United States Department of Agriculture, printed at Washington in 1897. Its Division of Pomology issued the pamphlet. Gustav Eisen of San Francisco wrote on edible figs, their culture and curing. Frank Earle of Auburn, Alabama, wrote on fig culture in the Gulf States.

The letter of transmittal says the two papers stand together for a reason. The fig-growing parts of the country differ so much in climate that one account cannot serve all. Together they give growers a full view of the trade. The bulletin opens the science of the fig, one species with some four hundred known kinds.
53193-intermere:
Intermere is a utopian novel by William Alexander Taylor of Columbus, Ohio. Its table of contents, added by the transcriber, lays out the whole design. A tourist lost in mid-ocean is mysteriously introduced into Intermere, where he meets the first citizen and other chief officials.

Xamas, the first citizen, explains the polity and principles of the Commonwealth, which govern for the interests of all its people. Maros, another guide, puts the visitor Anderton in touch with his mother and clears away his superstitious ideas with the possibilities of science. A trip by air, land and water shows provinces, cities, hamlets and gardens of matchless beauty. Only near the end is the secret of Intermere partly revealed, just as Anderton is restored, much to his regret, to his home and kindred. Taylor wrote in the great age of American utopias.
53198-penny-allen-and-the-mystery-of-the:
Penny Allen and the Mystery of the Hidden Treasure, by Jean McKechnie, came out in 1950. The World Publishing Company issued it in the Falcon Books line. A cover note sets the scene for girl readers. The Allens, Philip, Jimmy, Penny, and Marjorie, open their Michigan lodge as a summer hotel. Talk of buried treasure draws them to hunt for it. Others want the same prize, and danger follows.

Contents list fifteen chapters, from A New Adventure to Happy Ending. An anonymous letter, an abandoned well, and clues in a bottle drive the plot. Jimmy comes to the rescue in one chapter. Philip traps a thief in another. Chapter one opens in June wind off Lake Superior, with Penny hanging blankets at the lodge.
53206-selections-from-modern-poets-made-:
Selections from Modern Poets is an anthology made by J C Squire, printed at London in 1921. In his prefatory note Squire lays down his rule: no poet in the book was over fifty when he began to compile it in 1919. The eldest of them all was born in 1870.

Many good and some great living poets are therefore missing, he owns. Nothing is here by Hardy or Bridges, by Housman, Yeats, or Kipling. The date was arbitrarily chosen, but some date had to be fixed. His object was to show what many think an exceptional recent flowering of verse. He will not analyse the tendencies of the poems, saying such things are better seen at a distance. He notes one phenomenon: the rise of very many poets who write only or mainly in lyrical forms.
53216-an-essay-on-the-incubus-or-night-m:
An Essay on the Incubus, or Night-mare, a medical treatise by John Bond, was printed in London in 1753. Bond dedicated the work to Arthur Dobbs, governor of North Carolina. A passage from Virgil stands at the head of the title page. The subject, the crushing dream now called sleep paralysis, was then little understood.

Bond writes from his own suffering, since the night-mare afflicted him much. He found the ancient physicians gave little light on it beyond dreadful forecasts. Their accounts could not be sound, he argues, since they knew nothing of the circulation of the blood. Later writers who had never felt the thing did little better. The essay tries to give the first full account of its causes and cure.
53300-nature-s-teachings-human-invention:
Nature's Teachings, by the late Reverend Wood, argues that human tools were found in nature long before men made them. Wood was known for Homes Without Hands and other works on beasts and men. In his preface he says there is scarce a device of man that lacks a first form in the wild world.

The book sets nature and art side by side in plain, short terms, with more than seven hundred and fifty figures. Early parts treat rafts, oars, paddles, and screws, then war gear, nets, hooks, and armour. Wood holds that steam and current, once mere toys for boys, grew into engines and the wire that sends words far off. He urges new finders to look to nature first.
53477-the-relation-of-art-to-nature:
The Relation of Art to Nature is a short treatise by John W. Beatty, published in New York in 1922. Beatty sets out the base rules of art through one theme: how art stands toward nature. He lets artists and thinkers speak in their own words. His table of names runs from Socrates and Plato to Rodin and Whistler. Painters and sculptors get one long list. Writers and philosophers get a second.

Six short parts build the case. The artist and his purpose comes first, then old views of art. The proof of painters and sculptors fills the heart of the book. The views of philosophers and writers follow. A part on symmetry and a conclusion close the work. The whole runs to some seventy pages. Beatty holds that the great makers agree on the bond of art and nature more than men think.
53490-william-shakespeare:
William Shakespeare is a critical study by Victor Hugo, translated by A Baillot and published in Boston in eighteen sixty four. Hugo dedicates the book to England as the glorification of her poet. He wrote it in exile at Hauteville House, as his dedication is signed and dated. A portrait of Hugo fronts the volume.

Part one moves from Shakespeare's life to a roll of men of genius, from Homer and Job to Dante and Cervantes. Art and science, the ancient Shakespeare, and the souls follow as book heads. Hugo treats Shakespeare as a summit of human genius, in vast and sweeping prose. The book is as much a Hugo manifesto as a study.
53617-legendary-yorkshire:
Legendary Yorkshire is a set of lore tales of the great north shire by Ross, a fellow of a royal past lore guild. He had writ past books on the famed folk of its wolds and on its kin tales. Five hundred copies of this book were struck, each with its count mark.

It came out at Hull and London in the early eighteen nineties. Its parts roam the shire of tales: a charm cave, a town with a doom, and a great worm of a dale town. The devils shafts, a giants road, and a saints head fill the next run. The dead arm of a king saint, the move of a saints bones, and a deed of a famed saint join them.
53793-a-literary-history-of-ireland-from:
Douglas Hyde wrote a full past of Ireland's books from the first days. His book dates to 1899, and a case of old Gospels fronts it. Hyde gave the book to the Gaelic League with warm words. He calls it the one body in Ireland that grasps her past. That past holds a true hoard for the land, he holds.

Gaelic verse in his gift page thanks the League for great work. It was done with no gold and no aid, the verse says. Hyde traces song, tale, and lore age by age. Old faith books and bard songs stand in their due place. His aim is to make the present grow from that past. All who love Ireland's tongue gain a map here.
53849-the-symbolist-movement-in-literatu:
Arthur Symons wrote a study of the symbolist movement in literature, in a revised and enlarged edition printed in New York in 1919. Symons had written Cities of Italy and The Romantic Movement in English Literature. Without symbolism there can be no literature, he argues, indeed not even language. Words themselves are but symbols, he says, mere sounds agreed to carry certain meanings.

Symbolism began with the first words of the first man, as he named every living thing, or before them in heaven. A symbol, in Carlyle's phrase quoted here, is a conventional representation of idea by form, of the unseen by the visible. Symons traces that art through French poets and their English heirs in a landmark of modern criticism.
53860-country-life-in-the-poetry-of-john:
Country Life in the Poetry of John Clare, printed in 1922, is Mildred Coen's thesis for the bachelor of arts degree in English at the University of Illinois. Clarence Valentine Boyer supervised the work. Coen divides her study into three parts, with a bibliography at the end. The whole runs to about twenty-five pages.

The first part sets out the hard facts of enclosure in Clare's England. Open fields of small strips gave way to fenced farms, and many poor families lost their living. The second part gives Clare's own life. The third reads his poems as a record of the country world he knew: its work, its creatures and its passing ways.
53965-the-book-of-the-hamburgs-a-brief-t:
Frank Baum wrote The Book of the Hamburgs, a brief guide to the mating, rearing, and care of Hamburg fowls, printed at Hartford in eighteen eighty-six. Hamburgs, he says, were bred to feather by farm folk in Yorkshire and Lancashire long before fancy fowls had a name. The blacks were called Black Pheasant Fowls, and the spangled kinds were Lancashire Mooneys and Yorkshire Pheasants.

The penciled kinds came from Holland, where they were known as Dutch Everyday Layers. All Hamburgs share clear marks, Baum says, a lack of the sitting instinct, clean slender legs, and neat rose combs. Their small round white ear lobes and light, graceful lines set them apart from all other breeds. The guide serves keepers who breed for show and for eggs.
54016-in-search-of-treasure:
In Search of Treasure, by Horatio Alger, bears a copyright of 1894. Alger had written many tales of boys who rise by grit and good luck. The hero here is Guy Fenwick, a broad-shouldered boy of sixteen at Bayport, near New Bedford.

Guy's father is the pastor of a church in the town, and his purse is too thin for college fees. Guy is the best Latin and Greek scholar the academy has had in years, his father says. Harvard was the father's own path at the same age. Yet Guy owns to a stronger taste than study: a taste for adventure. He wants to see strange lands and meet strange folk. The tale sends him out to find his fortune.
5418-the-home-acre:
E. P. Roe wrote The Home Acre as a practical guide for people who dream of a country home. He opens with tree-planting, arguing that land hunger is a natural craving, and that city breadwinners often dream of a rural house as the crown of their working lives. The book then works through the whole smallholding in order.

Chapters cover fruit trees and grass, the garden, the vineyard and orchard, raspberries, currants, strawberries, and the kitchen garden. Roe writes plainly, for beginners who want food and beauty from their own acres. Readers get a friendly nineteenth-century handbook, useful as history and still clear about the work involved.
54259-chapters-on-spanish-literature:
Chapters on Spanish Literature is a set of lectures by James Fitzmaurice-Kelly. Constable published it in London in 1908. Fitzmaurice-Kelly was a fellow of the British Academy. He was also a corresponding member of the Spanish Academy. He dedicated the lectures to his fellow members of the Hispanic Society of America. The contents list ten chapters from the Cid to modern novelists. The Archpriest of Hita and the court of Juan the Second follow the Cid.

The Romancero, the old ballad stock, gets a chapter of its own. Two chapters treat the life and works of Cervantes. Lope de Vega and Calderon anchor the drama chapters. The first chapter argues that national heroes reveal a people's temper. A portrait discloses the artist's opinion of his sitter, it begins. So the choice of a hero is a kind of self revelation. The lectures survey a whole literature for English readers.
5429-preface-to-shakespeare:
Samuel Johnson wrote this preface for his annotated edition of Shakespeare's plays, published in 1765. He opens by complaining that praise is lavished on the dead and honors paid to mere antiquity, by critics who hope to seem clever through paradox. Johnson then turns to Shakespeare himself, judging the plays on their merits rather than their age.

The preface defends Shakespeare's mixture of comedy and tragedy, his characters, and his language, while admitting faults where Johnson finds them. Selected notes on plays such as Hamlet, King Lear, and Othello follow. Readers get a landmark of literary criticism, still readable as an argument about why Shakespeare endures.
54300-marks-first-lessons-in-geometry-in:
Bernhard Marks, head of Lincoln School in San Francisco, wrote these first lessons in geometry for young classes. Ivison, Phinney, Blakeman printed the book at New York in 1869. It comes in two parts, shown by things, not by rules alone.

Marks asks in his preface why sums fill the schools of the world while geometry is shut out. Sums count as a first branch, fit for the young, he says. Geometry is deemed a high branch, though its first steps are plain to the eye. His lessons start with shapes a child can see and handle. Grammar schools and academies form his stated ground, in an age when such a book was a bold new thing.
54351-in-beaver-cove-and-elsewhere:
Matt Crim wrote In Beaver Cove and Elsewhere, issued in New York by Charles L Webster and Company in eighteen ninety two. Crim gave the book to father and mother. Eleven stories fill the volume. In Beaver Cove stands first. S phiry Ann, An Onfortunit Creetur, and Bet follow in dialect titles. The title tale opens at a dance at the Woods cabin in Beaver Cove.

All the young people of the settlement were there, and many from adjoining settlements, the tale says. The main room had been cleared of its meagre furniture, it adds. The pine plank floor creaked under shuffling feet, while dust and lamp smoke made the air thick. Bill Eldridge sat by the hearth playing his fiddle with tireless energy, it notes. Armindy Hudgins and Elisha Cole were the leaders in the party, it says. Southern readers get Georgia mountain stories in local colour.
54392-a-complete-history-of-music-for-sc:
W J Baltzell wrote A Complete History of Music. The Theodore Presser Company issued it at Philadelphia in 1908. Schools, clubs, and private readers are its marks. Six scholars gave pieces to the work. Arthur Elson and Edward Burlingame Hill stand among them. Portraits and instrument pictures fill the pages.

Musical examples stand printed in the text. The plan joins class recitation with lectures, Baltzell says. Paragraph heads should be fixed in mind first. Heavy type and italics mark each lesson's spine. End questions test the pupils' mastery of it. Reference works should be sought for more, he urges. Each class member reads an abstract aloud. Review outlines serve for exam-style answers. A copyright of 1905 stands behind the 1908 issue. A classroom music history from the piano trade's great house armed teachers with lessons, tests, and pictures in one stout book.
54497-fort-concho-its-why-and-wherefore:
Gregory tells a frontier tale in Fort Concho, Its Why and Wherefore, a museum book from San Angelo, Texas. Printings run from 1957 to 1970. The Department of the Interior named the fort a National Historic Landmark on October 7, 1961. The fort stood from 1867 to 1889.

Gregory gives the book to the pioneer men and women of the Southwest. A Macaulay line on pride in the deeds of the past fronts the work. The tale starts before the purchase of 1803, with a trader who sold stolen stock to French traders near Natchitoches. Raids out of Mexico, red paint from cinnabar near Terlingua Creek, and the road by Persimmon Gap set the wild scene.
545-at-the-earth-s-core:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends two men into a hollow Earth in this adventure, told by a narrator who met the survivor in the Sahara. A drilling machine meant for coal bores past the crust into Pellucidar, a world lit by a central sun, ruled by winged Mahars, and full of ape men and dinosaurs. Dian the Beautiful, a captive, stirs love and revolt.

Burroughs writes at a gallop, with escapes, temples, and pursuits. His hero must learn Pellucidar's ways or die in them. The book charms as pure lost-world fun, where science serves as a door to a stranger, older Earth within our own.
54552-dutch-and-flemish-furniture:
Esther Singleton wrote this rich study of Dutch and Flemish furniture through the ages. McClure printed the book in New York in 1907, with many plates. A bed by Daniel Marot stands as the frontispiece view. Contents run from the Middle Ages to later court splendor.

Chapter one treats church art, wood carving, and castle furniture forms. Chests, sideboards, tables, chairs, and hangings get close, full notes. Tapestry, leather, glass, and gold work of Flanders fill the account. Chapter two turns to the lush Burgundian court and its great feasts. Singleton had written on French and English furniture before this.
54637-cornish-feasts-and-folk-lore:
Courtney gathered Cornish feasts and folk lore in a book dated 1890, first run in a folk lore sheet in 1886 and 1887. Her front words warn how wide charm craft and witch fear still run in the county. Some seek witches to lift the evil eye, while some shun them in dread of an ill wish.

Feasts for parish saints, kept on the near Sunday and Monday, lead the customs in the book. Each home, poor or rich, tries for a joint of meat and a figgy pudding on that day. Saffron cake, heavy cake with clotted cream, and plum cake baked on Saturday mark the rich fare.
54666-international-may-day-and-american:
Boris Reinstein contrasts International May Day and American Labor Day here. The Socialist Labor Party printed the pamphlet in New York. Its subtitle calls May Day a holiday of working class freedom. Labor Day is set against it as a holiday exalting chains.

The preface says the capital and labor struggle fronts the stage now. Material conditions for labor triumph ripen in America, he contends. The Weekly People ad in front hails class conscious workers power. A political victory alone is moonshine without union might, it teaches. The party paper sells at two dollars a year from Rose Street, New York City.
54701-gothic-architecture:
Édouard Corroyer wrote Gothic Architecture, edited by Walter Armstrong and issued at New York in eighteen ninety-three. Corroyer was an architect to the French government. Florence Simmonds translated the text under Armstrong's eye, and two hundred and thirty-six pictures fill the book.

Armstrong warns that Corroyer writes from a French standpoint. He credits France with the source of all that is fine in Gothic work. Armstrong grants that this bias does little harm to the book's broad picture. Corroyer traces how new means and finds changed the builder's forms step by step. The field stays mostly in France, with few trips beyond her frontier.
54766-the-traitor-a-story-of-the-fall-of:
The Traitor, a story of the fall of the Invisible Empire by Thomas Dixon, was published in New York in 1907 by Doubleday, Page. Pictures by Williams attend the tale. Dixon states in a preface that the volume closes his Trilogy of Reconstruction, after The Leopard's Spots and The Clansman. The book is dedicated to men of the South who, in its words, suffered exile, imprisonment, and death in the Klan's service.

The story opens with the order of dissolution by General Forest, in Dixon's spelling. The scene is the foothills of North Carolina; the time, 1870 to 1872. A cast list names John Graham, ex-chief of the Klan, a new Klan chief, a federal judge, and federal agents. Dixon's trilogy, written from a white Southern view of Reconstruction, was widely read and long contested.
54866-french-and-english-furniture:
French and English Furniture is a guide to distinctive styles and periods. Esther Singleton wrote it, building on her Furniture of Our Forefathers. Nichols drew the illustrations from original sources for the volume. McClure, Phillips issued it in New York in December 1903. Contents march by reign and by maker in strict time order.

Louis the Thirteenth and the Jacobean periods open the survey in turn. Louis the Fourteenth, Queen Anne, and early Georgian styles follow. Louis the Fifteenth, Chippendale, and Louis the Sixteenth fill the middle. Adam, Heppelwhite, Sheraton, and Empire close the long, plated march. Collectors and decorators got a room by room picture history here.
55115-the-city-of-pleasure:
The City of Pleasure, a fantasia on modern themes by Arnold Bennett, was published in New York in 1907. Bennett was known for The Old Wives' Tale and Clayhanger. Part one is named Carpentaria, for Charles Carpentaria, managing and musical director of a vast new pleasure city. Josephus Ilam is its president.

The tale opens over the city at the captive balloon, set to rise every half hour to a thousand feet for half a crown a seat, field glass included. A tall, red-haired, masterful figure crosses the crowd and taps a crooked sign straight. Staff snap to work as Carpentaria asks if all is ready. Bennett spins a light satire of show business, money, and the selling of fun.
55185-some-principles-of-frontier-mounta:
Major Bird's Some Principles of Frontier Mountain Warfare was published by Hugh Rees at London in 1909. Bird had been a professor at the Indian Staff College. The opening argues that the principles of strategy and tactics never change, while organization and procedure must shift with every campaign. There are no invariable rules in war, and formalism in military operations is disastrous. Each problem must be judged on its merits, with principles applied, not rules.

The problems in view are those of the Indian frontier and its transborder clans. Force size turns on the land: its features, its fertility, and the numbers and armament of its people. A great French king's saying on Spain is quoted: in mountain country, large armies risk starvation and small ones defeat. The Pathan tribesmen are brave, hardened to fatigue, and many were trained in the Indian army itself.
55771-a-history-of-spanish-literature:
A History of Spanish Literature surveys seven centuries of Spanish writing in one volume. Fitzmaurice-Kelly wrote the history. Appleton published it in New York and London. The copyright dates to 1898, this printing to 1921. The book belongs to a series of short histories of the world's literatures. Gosse edited that series.

Thirteen chapters divide the story by ages. The anonymous age opens in the twelfth century. The age of Alfonso the Learned follows. Didactic and courtly ages succeed in turn. The age of Lope de Vega takes the largest share. Bourbon centuries and the nineteenth century follow. Contemporary literature closes the survey. The first chapter praises Castilian force and humour. French writing is more exquisite, he grants, but none beats it for truth.
55857-cynthia-ann-parker-the-story-of-he:
James T DeShields wrote the story of Cynthia Ann Parker and her capture in Texas. The book was printed for the author at St Louis in 1886. DeShields gave the work, by leave, to General L S Ross of Waco. A portrait of Cynthia Ann Parker fronts the tale.

Parker was taken when Parker's Fort fell and lived a quarter century among the Comanches. She wed the war chief Peta Nocona in that long stay. Captain L S Ross and the Texas Rangers took her back at Pease River. DeShields sifted many tales and notes to set down plain facts of a famed frontier life.
55933-peggy-finds-the-theatre:
Virginia Hughes wrote this Peggy Lane theater story, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1962. Sergio Leone illustrated Peggy's discovery of the stage for the publisher that year. A plate shows Randy dancing, as Peggy had suspected he could, by its caption at the front.

Dramatic dialogue opens the contents, and a dramatic decision follows in chapter two. In the wings, two auditions, starting a new role and a cast of characters fill the list. Thomas Lane speaks to his daughter in the kitchen as the tale opens, telling her the news is no surprise to them, in a backstage story for girls.
56014-the-demagogue-and-lady-phayre:
The Demagogue and Lady Phayre is a novel by William Locke, printed by John Lane in London and New York, in a third edition of 1911. Chapter one is called The Eternal Feminine. It opens as a lecture at the Sunington Radical Club breaks up, and the local member of Parliament walks home with the speaker.

The member is Aloysius Gleam, member for Sunington: spare, bald, precisely dressed, with a gold rimmed eye glass and a shrewd face. The speaker is Goddard, twenty eight, a cabinetmaker by trade, self taught and flushed with the success of his lecture on the New Trades Unionism. Gleam, who has chaired the meeting, asks whether Goddard would care to take to politics seriously.
56165-neither-here-nor-there:
Neither Here Nor There is a book of humorous sketches by Oliver Herford, published in New York in 1922 and billed by its publisher as a mirror of frivolity. The pieces, most of them only a few pages long, take up revolving doors, billboards, the trouser crease, money and fireflies, Bolshevism for babies and the question whether cats are people.

The opening sketch retells Eden as a gossip column. Eve, bored, begs the Serpent to tell her something new, and he tells her everything he knew. A publisher's note singles out a more tender piece, The Bon Dieu's Birthday Party, as Herford's fantasy in full flower. The collection's method is the light paradox: a solemn subject tilted a few degrees until its absurdity shows, then set gently down again.
56476-the-life-of-voltaire:
S G Tallentyre wrote a life of Voltaire in a third edition from Putnam's, with a frontispiece of Voltaire from Houdon's statue at the Comédie Française. Voltaire's own line heads the title: I have no sceptre, but I have a pen. Contents open with the boyhood. Epigrams and the Bastille follow. Oedipe and the journey to Holland come next. The Henriade continues the young poet's rise.

Tallentyre had written The Women of the Salons. Her Voltaire is a full narrative life for general readers. The pen against the sceptre states her theme: the writer as a power in Europe. Putnam issued the book in New York and London.
56478-old-mines-of-southern-california-d:
Old Mines of Southern California is a mining survey reprinted in 1965 by the Frontier Book Company of Toyahvale, Texas. The text comes from the Report of the State Mineralogist of 1893, and the reprint was limited to a thousand copies. It covers the desert, mountain, and coastal areas, with the Calico, Salton Sea, and Colorado River districts.

The county sections describe mines one by one, with their rocks, veins, and faults. The Los Angeles County part, written by Storms, an assistant in the field, singles out the Kelsey Mine. It stands in the San Gabriel Canyon near Azusa and won fame for silver ore of great richness. The survey gives collectors and local historians a dated record of mines that were old even then.
56553-the-sugar-creek-gang-digs-for-trea:
Paul Hutchens wrote The Sugar Creek Gang Digs for Treasure, a boys’ camp tale. Van Kampen Press issued the book at Wheaton, Illinois, in nineteen hundred forty eight. The tale speaks in the voice of a freckled boy in the gang. Two brown tents stand at the lake camp in the first scene.

Camp rules force a dull nap after lunch each day. The teller has slept and slips out to a white rowboat. Sun beats up off the lake like a mirror. His skin burns and freckles while his mates tan brown. A tree-clad island a mile out sparks his dreams. Heat builds like a storm is on its way. The gang’s hunt for buried wealth grows from such slow camp hours.
56618-the-friends-of-voltaire:
The Friends of Voltaire is a set of ten biographical studies by Tallentyre. John Murray issued the book in London in 1906. Tallentyre also wrote a life of Voltaire itself. Portraits of each friend face their chapters. A line from Voltaire's letters serves as motto. Thinking souls, he wrote, must rub against each other to strike light.

The ten friends are picked as types of an age. D'Alembert is the thinker and Diderot the talker. Galiani is the wit and Vauvenargues the aphorist. D'Holbach is the host of the famous salon. Grimm is the journalist and Helvetius the contradiction. Turgot stands as statesman and Beaumarchais as playwright. Condorcet closes the list as the aristocrat. Together they form the circle of the Enlightenment. The book reads as a group portrait of that world.
5672-the-voice-on-the-wire:
Eustace Hale Ball wrote The Voice on the Wire as a mystery opening in a club grill-room. A large man awkwardly follows a servant downstairs, feeling every man at the Flemish tables must ask what he is doing there. He wishes Monty Shirley would meet him in the back room of a ginmill, where he would feel comfortable, rather than this classy joint, but that is Shirley's game to play.

Reaching Shirley, he exclaims eagerly that he is glad to find him, fearing he might arrive too late. Chapters titled When Three Is a Mystery and The Fleeting Prompter follow. Readers get a brisk early mystery of telephones, clubs, and tangled lives.
56759-a-chance-for-himself-or-jack-hazar:
Trowbridge wrote A Chance for Himself, or Jack Hazard and His Treasure, published in Boston by James Osgood in 1872. It continues Jack Hazard and His Fortunes, named under the author's name. The frontispiece is called The Adventure with the Basket of Coin, and treasure drives the tale from the first chapter.

A thunder-squall opens the book. Then comes what Jack found in the log: treasure-trove. Jack counts his chickens early, waits for the deacon, and argues about a half-dollar. He goes for his treasure and meets the squire. The Huswick tribe holds a mock court and delivers a verdict. Hod's trousers travel to the squire's house, and Jack rescues Lion but misses the treasure. Boys of 1872 got a buried-money tale with the whole village tugging at the hoard.
56893-nervous-ills-their-cause-and-cure:
Boris Sidis, head of a healing institute at Portsmouth in New Hampshire, wrote a book on nervous ills that Badger of Boston copyrighted in 1922. His theme is fear. At the root of all animal life, he argues, lies the urge to keep oneself alive.

The chapters give fear the first place among the forces of the mind. They trace its stages, its power, and its bond with superstition and disease. Sidis treats the half waking state he calls hypnoidal, the subconscious, and the laws of suggestion. Case histories and fear confessions fill the later part. Stammering, loss of voice, and trance states are all taken up. The cure he urges works through the quiet state, not through drugs.
57154-girls-of-the-morning-glory-camp-fi:
Girls of the Morning-Glory Camp Fire is a tale for girls by Isabel Hornibrook, put out in April of nineteen sixteen. Hornibrook was known for past tales of camp and trail. The tale is given to three girls by name. Its front list names past eighteen parts, full of lake scenes, a fire ring, and shore strife.

Props in the text thank two lore men for leave to use song words and tunes of two tribes, from their notes among those folk. Part names hint at a cast off, quick sands, a strange coin, and a torch post. The tale thus blends camp craft, tribe lore, and a thread of search and risk by the lake.
57210-the-substitute-millionaire:
The Substitute Millionaire is a novel by Hulbert Footner. Doran published the book at New York in 1919. Footner had written Thieves' Wit and Jack Chanty among earlier tales. The story opens on a crowded subway train in New York City.

Jack Norman rides to work reading his paper like any clerk. The news of the day is the killing of Silas Gyde, a millionaire miser blown up by a bomb in the street. The dead man earned perhaps six millions a year and spent almost nothing. He bought his clothes at a cheap outfitter and carried empty pockets. He walked a mile each day for a free lunch at a company office. It was at that office door that the bomb found him. Gyde died a bachelor with no known kin, and the mystery of his heir drives the plot.
573-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb retell Shakespeare's plays as short stories for young readers in this classic primer. The Tempest, A Midsummer Night's Dream, King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, and Othello lead the set, with comedies such as Twelfth Night and The Taming of the Shrew. The Lambs keep Shakespeare's words where they fit the tale.

A preface explains their method: tragedy lends itself to retelling, comedy less so, since dialogue resists turning into narrative. The tales aim only as a first taste, not a substitute for the plays. Generations of children have met Shakespeare here first, and then gone on to the plays themselves.
57548-the-principles-of-leather-manufact:
Procter, professor of leather industries at the Yorkshire College in Leeds, wrote this trade treatise in 1903. Spon published it in London and New York that year. A frontispiece plate shows a section of calf-skin, with a key to a figure later in the book.

Procter had led the International Association of Leather Trades Chemists as its past president. His subject runs from hides and tanning materials to the chemistry of making leather that lasts. Bark, liquors, dyeing and finishing belong to the craft he sets out, in a book meant for tanners, chemists and students of the trade.
57833-the-hill-of-adventure:
The Hill of Adventure is a novel by Adair Aldon, published by the Century Company in New York in 1922. Aldon also wrote At the Sign of the Two Heroes. Shepherd drew its pictures. The frontispiece caption reads: things have broken loose quicker than we thought. The first chapter is named for Gray Cloud Mountain.

It opens with Beatrice viewing what lies ahead with feelings near to dismay. The picture list promises grave words, a lifted voice breaking a long spell, and a confession from Beatrice herself. The tale belongs to the mountain adventure romances of its decade. It mixes wild scenery with a story of love and danger.
57885-the-tickencote-treasure:
The Tickencote Treasure is a mystery novel by William Le Queux, printed in London in 1913. Le Queux also wrote A Secret Service and In White Raiment. A frontispiece shows a skipper boasting he could take the old tub from Gibraltar to Naples without a compass. Job Seal stands at the story's start.

The chapters run on parchments and secrets. Job Seal borrows a fusee, the company sees and hears strange things, and a mysterious man appears. The narrator examines parchments and takes an expert opinion. What was written in the vellum book, the seven dead men, and the guardian of the secret follow. A seller of the secret and a silent man thicken the end. The narrator says plainly that rumours of his strange adventures moved him to write them down at last.
581-ginx-s-baby-his-birth-and-other-misf:
Edward Jenkins follows a foundling through Victorian charity, church, parish, and politics in this satire. Ginx's baby, born to a poor father named Ginx, is passed from hand to hand: first his father, then charities and churches, then parish guardians, then clubs and politicians. Each part asks what its keepers did with him.

Jenkins writes with sharp, comic anger, mocking laws, sects, and reformers who debate while a child waits. A preface stages a critic who calls the tale improbable, answered by an author who insists it may be true. The book endures as a witty indictment of how societies fail their poorest children.
58356-the-passing-of-empire:
The Passing of Empire, by Fielding-Hall, the author of The Soul of a People, is a book about British India in change. Hurst and Blackett published it in London in 1913. Its epigraph glosses the saying that man shall not live by bread alone: that is to say, Fielding-Hall adds, by ideas.

The book falls in three parts. The Old India treats Indian unrest, the people, the civilian and his training, criminal and civil law, the village, and opium and excise. Counsels of Despair takes up the provincial councils and the Indian as civilian. A New India then argues for a new civilian, law and courts reform, self-government and education. The first chapter notes that reports of sedition have quieted. The attempt on the Viceroy, officials say, was an isolated act. Fielding-Hall doubts the calm will last.
58577-the-fur-seal-s-tooth-a-story-of-al:
The Fur Seal’s Tooth, a story of Alaskan adventure by Kirk Munroe, was issued by Harper in 1894. A front plate shows a cry of the title words in mid scene. Munroe had written the whole Mates series of boys’ books before it. Wakulla and The Flamingo Feather stand in his list as well.

His tales sold at sixty cents in Harper’s Young People Series. Alaska, its seal islands, and its poachers give this book its ground. A fur seal’s tooth serves as the token and the title of the tale. Boys of the nineties read Munroe for wild coasts and true seamanship. His north is cold, rich, and fought over by hunters and guards. Adventure and natural history share his pages evenly.
58586-bird-houses-baths-and-feeding-shel:
Bird Houses, Baths and Feeding Shelters tells how to make and place them. Edmund Sawyer wrote the guide for the Cranbrook Institute of Science. It is Bulletin Number One, fifth edition, dated nineteen fifty five. The first edition, as Bird Houses, came out in March nineteen thirty one.

Later editions grew to add western species, baths, and feeding shelters too. Contents open with bird houses and common sense, correcting current notions. Material, entrance size, nails, slabs, and cleaning get plain rules first. Set dimensions follow for wren, chickadee, nuthatch, titmouse, and swallow houses. Bluebird, flicker, purple martin, and tree nesting duck boxes close the list.
58667-stage-coach-and-mail-in-days-of-yo:
Stage-Coach and Mail in Days of Yore is a fond history of the coaching age by Harper, and the hosted text is the first of two volumes. It was published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1903. Old prints and pictures fill its pages.

Harper had written a shelf of road books before this one. The Brighton, Portsmouth, Dover, and Bath roads each had a volume. Here he takes the whole world of the stage coach and the mail. The preface quotes a Southampton coachman in the year the railway opened. The man hung his old whip over the fireplace, sure he would need it no more. Harper calls the end of the coaching age a tragedy for such men, and a bitter uprooting for many more.
58668-stage-coach-and-mail-in-days-of-yo:
Charles Harper wrote Stage-Coach and Mail in Days of Yore, a picturesque history of the coaching age, and Chapman and Hall of London published it in 1903. This is the second of two volumes. Harper had written a shelf of road books, listed at the front.

The illustrations come from old-time prints and pictures, and one shows a mail coach passing Saint George's Circus in Southwark in 1797. The second volume opens with the later mails, the fast government coaches that crowned the age. Then it goes down the road in days of yore, starting with a journey from Newcastle-on-Tyne to London in 1772, told leg by leg. Harper writes for readers who loved the road as their grandfathers knew it. The history is told from the coach box as much as from the records.
58723-bernardin-de-st-pierre:
Arvede Barine wrote a life of Bernardin de Saint Pierre for the Great French Writers series, printed at Chicago in 1893 in Gordon's English dress. Augustin Birrell wrote the preface. The series set Boissier on Sevigne, Caro on George Sand, Sorel on Montesquieu and Madame de Stael, and Simon on Victor Cousin, at one dollar a volume. Youth and years of travel open the life.

A period of drift follows, with the voyage to the Isle of France, friendship with Rousseau, and a crisis. The later chapters treat the famed studies of nature and the tale that made him known round the world. English readers get a French critic's cool verdict on a writer England loved. Judgments of other nations on their own authors are weighed at the start.
58793-the-daughter-of-virginia-dare:
Mary Virginia Wall's The Daughter of Virginia Dare was published by the Neale Publishing Company of New York and Washington in 1908. Wall gives the book to her mother, Virginia, and her grandmother, England. The tale is of the Roanoke colony, told from the sailing of the ships that carried the first English settlers to Virginia.

The prelude opens at Portsmouth, sunbeams playing about three small vessels crowded with colonists. The good ship Admiral leads, Simon Ferdinando her master, with a pinnace and a flyboat behind, English flags at every masthead. They tarry eight days at the Isle of Wight and two at Plymouth. Eleanor Dare stands on deck as May hawthorn scent reaches the water, afraid of the unknown land, and hiding her fear from her husband's hope of home and fortune.
58840-colour-decoration-of-architecture:
Colour Decoration of Architecture is a treatise by James Ward, published by Dutton in New York in 1914. Ward wrote several earlier books on ornament and fresco painting. This one treats the colour and decoration of the interiors and exteriors of buildings. It adds historical notices of the art and practice of colour decoration in Italy, France, Germany, and England. The title page addresses it to decorators and students.

The book carries twelve illustrations in colour and twenty-two in half-tone. A sketch design for a wall decoration in fresco serves as frontispiece. Chapters open with an introduction and the value of colour in building. They proceed to the colouring of interiors and exteriors, and the use and modification of colour in decoration. Later chapters take up Italian decoration and ornament, then coloured building in France and beyond.
58879-hertfordshire:
Lydekker wrote Hertfordshire for the Cambridge County Geographies, a line under a general editor, printed at Cambridge in 1909. Maps, diagrams, and pictures go with the text. A physical map of the county stands at the front. Contents open with county and shire, and the name Hertfordshire, its origin and meaning. The general character of the county follows, then its size, shape, and bounds.

Surface and general features, watershed and rivers, and geology and soil come in turn. The wild life of the county, its weather and rainfall, and its people, race, speech, and numbers fill the next chapters. Farming, special crops, trades and making, and minerals follow. The history of Hertfordshire, its old remains from early, Roman, and Saxon times, and its building in church, castle, and house forms, close the run of heads. The volume thus treats the county whole, from its rocks to its great seats.
58895-bombers-training-and-application-o:
Lieut Ferris wrote Bombers' Training as a field guide for troops in trench warfare. Ferris served with a Canadian battalion of the war years. The book came out at Toronto in 1916.

A set of lectures builds the course step by step. The first treats explosives and the working knowledge a bomber needs. The next sorts explosives by kind, traits and strength. Later lectures study types of rifle grenade and hand grenade. The aim is plain and grim: to teach men to use bombs with skill and care. It is a stark relic of trench war craft. Short, clear heads make the drills easy to learn by rote.
58907-a-b-c-of-gothic-architecture:
John Henry Parker wrote an A B C of Gothic Architecture, issued by Parker and Company at Oxford and London in eighteen eighty one. Parker kept the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford. An advertisement to the first edition states the design. The little work is a stepping stone to larger and costlier works, he says. His own Introduction to the Study of Gothic Architecture stands among them.

The same examples are not used, save a few well known historical instances, Parker notes. His object was to make the book as simple as possible, so that a child may understand it, he says. A child who has seen many examples, with the features of each style explained, remembers them in a way that astonishes older folk, he holds. Accurate pictures of buildings teach the eye, he adds. Beginners get arches, windows, and mouldings in the plainest terms.
58981-history-of-sculpture-painting-and-:
Memes wrote a survey of the fine arts printed in Boston in 1834, in three parts on carving, painting, and building. The first part moves from Egypt and the East through the schools of Greece to Rome. Names such as Phidias, Lysippus, and Praxiteles mark the high points of the Greek art of the carved form.

Painting takes up Raphael, Titian, Rubens, and the schools of Italy, Germany, and England in turn. Building closes the book, with the Greek orders and the works of Egypt and India in view. Short lives, frank views on rise and fall, and praise for craft give the survey its shape.
59070-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Gustave Doré is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. It lists the books illustrated by Doré as issued by that library. The body of the file prints each volume's table of contents in full. A reader can thus see the shape of every Doré book at a glance.

Gargantua and Pantagruel leads the master list of the works. Don Quixote follows in its two illustrated volumes under his hand. The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations stands among the largest ventures. Dante's Divine Comedy appears as visions of hell, purgatory, and paradise. The Raven, the tales of Mother Goose, and the fables of La Fontaine follow. Sketches humorous and grotesque, Rhine myths, and Pyrenees travels widen the range. Arthurian pieces — Elaine, Enide, and their sisters — close the romantic side.
59388-memories-of-the-future:
Opal, Lady Porstock wrote Memories of the Future, being memoirs of the years nineteen fifteen to nineteen seventy two, written in the year of grace nineteen eighty eight. Ronald A Knox edited the satire. McClelland and Stewart in Toronto published the book, printed in Great Britain. A Herodotus line heads it, that all things may happen in the long lapse of time. Fifteen chapters and an index fill the volume.
