An editor preface plays a fugal variation on the author preface, it says. We do ill if we fail in veneration for the future, for we beget it and it is of our blood, the preface holds. Chapters run from Childhood through School Days, Oxford, and Travels on the Continent. My Marriage, London Society and Its Follies, and a parliamentary election follow. England on the Eve of the Great War closes the joke. Wit readers get a future history satire.
59455-a-history-of-roman-classical-liter:
Browne, a teacher of classics at King's College in London, wrote a history of Roman writing in its great age. The edition shown here was printed at Philadelphia in 1853. In his preface Browne notes that this whole span of fine writing fills less than four centuries. Rome had stood for five hundred years, he says, with no true author at all.

The book traces how Greek art and learning first reached Rome about two and a half centuries before Christ. It also looks back at the Latin tongue itself, how it formed from the speech of nearby tribes. Browne asks why men of letters had such a hard road under the Republic. The Roman love of action, he argues, made quiet study seem a small thing.
59463-his-great-adventure:
His Great Adventure is a novel by Robert Herrick, published by the Macmillan Company of New York in nineteen thirteen. The copyright runs nineteen twelve to the Frank A Munsey Company and nineteen thirteen to Macmillan. Herrick had written Together, One Woman's Life, and The Common Lot. Part one of the novel is called Fortune.

The opening stands on Fifth Avenue at dusk on an April day. A young man in a cheap rain-coat and steamer-cap gazes irresolutely up and down. His sallow face is unshaven, his eyes owlish behind round steel spectacles. The air about him is not youthful depression but the settled gloom of repeated failure. He checks a possession in his coat pocket with a bitter smile. Herrick launches his hero from the curb of the avenue, with one more throw-down behind him.
59499-the-gaspards-of-pine-croft-a-roman:
Ralph Connor wrote a romance of the Windermere valley, printed in New York in 1923. Connor was known for The Sky Pilot and The Man from Glengarry. Of all British Columbia valleys, the tale says, none has a finer sweep than the Windermere. It rolls on both sides of the Columbia River in wide grass lands.

Hugh Gaspard first saw the valley on a glorious autumn day and could never escape that first sight. Though trained as an engineer, he felt the land as a settler and a dreamer. Ranch life, family pride, and the pull of the wild valley shape the Gaspards of Pine Croft. Connor mixes faith, work, and love in his famed western manner.
59862-american-renaissance-a-review-of-d:
Joy Wheeler Dow, an architect, wrote on American home craft in a fresh age. His book came out in New York in 1904. Six and ninety half tone plates show the homes he praises. The Bennett House at New Bedford fronts it with its yard face. Rules of right lead his list, and art gainst trade comes next.

The old rule and Andrew Jackson fill the third long part. Small starts of a home school of craft stand in part four. The grand age and first work of the new age come in turn. A reign of fear and its odd use take the mid list's span. Style talk and a close end the book's scheme of homes. Plates prove each claim.
59988-poems-of-nature:
Henry David Thoreau wrote the poems in a small book first printed in 1895. Henry Salt and Frank Sanborn chose the poems and edited the book. It came out in Boston, New York, and London. Most poems turn on woods, water, seasons, and the quiet life of the mind.

Poems named Nature, Inspiration, Sic Vita, and The Fisher Boy open the book. Later poems sing of rain, mist, smoke, haze, the moon, and the fall of the leaf. Some were written at Walden. Others speak of friendship, poverty, conscience, and prayer. Short lines and plain speech carry Thoreau and his close watch of the world outdoors and his thoughts on how a man should live.
60392-a-treatise-on-electricity-wherein-:
Francis Penrose, surgeon at Bicester, wrote a treatise on electricity printed at Oxford in 1752. Its phenomena are accounted for, and the cause of the attraction and gravitation of solids assigned. A short account follows of how the electrical effluvia act upon the animal frame, and in what disorders they may be applied with success, and in what not.

They who are allowed the very greatest and wisest of men have been intent upon making observations and experiments, the motto from Woodward runs. Such work would be vain were no conclusions drawn and no theory raised from them. Mr Freke, surgeon to Bartholomew hospital, is praised for his penetration on the subject. Penrose writes when electric sparks were a wonder and a hoped for cure at once.
606-indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-e:
Frank Linderman retells Blackfeet why stories from War Eagle's lodge fire in this volume, dedicated to Charles Russell and George Bird Grinnell. Tales tell why the chipmunk's back is striped, why the curlew's bill is crooked, why the deer has no gall, and how Old-Man stole the sun's leggings. A preface praises Indian lore's closeness to nature.

Linderman writes in plain, warm prose, keeping the tales' childlike simplicity. Birds, beasts, winds, and moonlight explain the world in fanciful reasons. The book serves as a treasury of Montana Indian folk tales, saved before the blanket Indian and the buffalo vanished from the plains.
6066-king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance:
Talbot Mundy opens with the song of the Indian Secret Service. Its men are eyes of empire, skinned and puckered and quick to see. They shun display, yet stay hot on the trail of ties and pullers of roots of ruction. The men who govern India are few, while those who stand in their way with floods of words are a host.

Athelstan King might claim to know a little. Mundy answers cries that India is a home of thugs and hungry millions. He claims instead that she is the original home of chivalry. The romance follows King on the frontier, where loyalty, daring, and secret work decide the fate of border tribes and empire.
60668-essay-on-the-character-and-influen:
Guizot's essay on Washington began as the introduction to a French edition of Sparks's Life of Washington and the statesman's writings. This third American edition was published by James Miller at New York in 1868. Guizot, himself a historian and a practical statesman, was thought peculiarly qualified to judge Washington's character and his claims on the gratitude of his country.

The French publishers note that no foreign event ever stirred France like the American Revolution. No foreigner was so admired there as Washington, by the old court and the new nation alike. Louis the Sixteenth heaped testimonials on him; Napoleon ordered public mourning at his death. Hillard's translator's preface calls the essay the most accurate and profound European word on its subject. A Frenchman's tribute, meant to justify American veneration.
6074-lady-clare:
Alfred Tennyson's Lady Clare comes illustrated by Alfred Fredericks, Granville Perkins, Frederic Schell, Edmund Garrett, F. S. Church, and Harry Fenn. The plates mark the poem's turning points: lilies blowing, a lily-white doe, old Alice the nurse entering, and a cry of falsely, falsely have ye done.

Lady Clare speaks of birth and love, asking whether she is loved for herself and declaring, if I'm a beggar born, she will face it plainly. She clothes herself in a russet gown, while Lord Ronald steps down from his tower. Tennyson's ballad turns on rank, truth, and a nurse's secret, told in swift, musical verse.
60830-how-to-study-architecture:
How to Study Architecture is a survey of building history by Charles Caffin. Dodd, Mead and Company published it in New York in 1917, with illustrations. Caffin had already written a companion volume on how to study pictures. His subtitle states the plan of the whole book in one line.

Architecture, that plan runs, is the product of successive ages of civilization. Each period therefore pairs a chapter on a people's life with one on its buildings. The pre-classic books treat Egypt, Babylon, Persia, and the Aegean world. The classic books give the Hellenic and Roman ages their paired chapters. Early Christian, Byzantine, and Muhammedan building follow in the post-classic book. A Renaissance book closes the long march of styles and peoples.
60860-the-crystal-sceptre-a-story-of-adv:
The Crystal Sceptre is a story of adventure by Philip Verrill Mighels, the author of Nella, the Heart of the Army. It came out in New York in 1901 from R. F. Fenno and Company. The contents set out a tale of travel into wild lands. The first chapter is The End of the Voyage, and the second A Strange Alliance.

The Home of the Links, A Reconnoitre, and Hostile Neighbours stand next in the list. Language and Weapons, Important Discoveries, and Attacked and Besieged carry the tale on. The Cauldron of Gold, Daylight at Last, and A Camp on the Hill stand later. A Deadly Foe, The Night in the Jungle, and An Old Roué stand in the list as well. The book is a boys' adventure of a lost land, strange foes, and gold, in the manner of its day.
61061-og-son-of-fire:
Og, Son of Fire is a boys' tale of the stone age by Irving Crump, editor of the Boy Scouts' magazine, in print since 1921. Pictures by Charles Livingston Bull run through it; one shows two wolf cubs shivering beside the hero. The contents open with the call of cooked meat. The fire demon, a crack in the earth, and the first camp fire follow in quick heads.

In the fifth chapter the wolf becomes dog, the book's great taming. At bay with the wolf pack, a captive of the tree people, and a scar faced terror carry the middle. Sacrifice to a sabre tooth, stolen flames, and the wrath of the fire monster raise the stakes. A fire lighter, a traitor named Gog, and Gog's passing close the list. Fire, and its keeping, is the hero's whole world.
61069-german-spies-in-england-an-exposur:
William Le Queux, a famed writer of spy tales, turned reporter of real spies in this book. Langton printed German Spies in England at Toronto in 1915, from British plates. War fever runs through every page, by the author's own frank word.

Le Queux tells the reader he long held back, then felt duty drive him to write. The truth must be told and the peril faced, he says. How the truth was hidden and the Kaiser's secret head the list. How spies work, the spy and the law, and some fresh cases fill the middle. Twenty-seven thousand aliens at large in Britain is his stark count. How to end the spy peril closes his plea.
6112-nature-and-human-nature:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton's Nature and Human Nature dates from 1855. It promises surprises, clippers and steamers, and a woman's heart. A critter with a thousand virtues and but one vice appears, with a new way to learn Gaelic. Wounds of the heart, fiddling and dancing, stitching a button-hole, and the plural of moose follow.

Later chapters give a day on the lake, a betrothal, and a foggy night. Female colleges, gipsying, the world before the flood, lost at sea, and holding up the mirror follow. Town and country, honeymoon, clams, the devil's hole, and cucumber lake close the miscellany. Haliburton catches manners living as they rise, with humor.
61141-the-weird-picture:
John R Carling hangs a mystery on a portrait in a novel issued by Little, Brown, and Company at Boston in 1905. Cyrus Cuneo drew the pictures. Carling had written The Shadow of the Czar before it.

The contents move like a case file. The Red Stain opens the book, and The Veiled Lady follows. A wedding morning comes next, then a chapter named simply Waiting. The artist paints a notable picture. The Standard newspaper reports on it. High Mass brings a shock. One chapter asks whether the studio visitor is ghost or mortal. The artist's portfolio reveals its secret late. The mysteries of the studio lead to the dénouement. A letter in the close matter fixes a wedding with Daphne for Christmas Day.
61150-stair-building-and-the-steel-squar:
Fred T Hodgson and Morris Williams teach a trade in Stair-Building and the Steel Square, from the American Technical Society of Chicago in 1917. The subtitle calls it a manual of practical instruction in the art of stair-building and hand-railing, and the manifold uses of the steel square. Hodgson wrote part one, Williams part two and shares the first.

The contents open with stair construction: definitions, setting out stairs, the pitch-board, the well-hole, and close-string and open-newel stairs. Geometrical stairways follow, with wreaths and the tangent system. Part two turns the square to roof framing, hips, valleys, and polygons.
61178-history-of-indian-and-eastern-arch:
James Fergusson wrote a History of Indian and Eastern Architecture, issued at London in 1891 by John Murray. The book forms Volume Three of a new edition of his History of Architecture. A print of a temple at Kantonuggur heads the work. Fergusson held high posts in learned and building groups.

Front pages list his past books on rock cut temples and old building in Hindustan. Those books held tinted prints, plans, and wood cuts. A book on the true rules of beauty in art is named too. Palaces of Nineveh and Persepolis get a book of their own. Names in the text are spelt in more than one way, a note warns. The volume treats temples and old forms across India and the East.
61198-aide-memoire:
Aide Memoire, a science fiction tale by Keith Laumer, first ran in Worlds of If in July 1962. The hero is Retief, a cool and blunt young officer in a future Earth corps posted to odd worlds. Here he serves on Fust, home of the Fustians, a long-lived folk who look like turtles and move fast when they choose.

Ambassador Magnan wants each staff member to sponsor a Fustian youth group. One group, known by the short name SCARS, has waited weeks for a backer and the funds that come with one. Retief doubts the youths need his help at all. He fears the rival Groaci post will step in first, and the clash of manners drives the tale.
61211-boys-of-the-old-sea-bed-tales-of-n:
Boys of the Old Sea Bed, by Charles Allen McConnell, holds boyhood nature tales. The Nazarene church press at Kansas City issued it in nineteen thirteen. McConnell gives the book to his late brother Robert, one of the boys. Contents run from In the Bed of an Ancient Sea to College Days.

Tales treat catching a fawn, a great blue heron, and a forest fire. A first deer hunt, an Indian war dance, and a floating bog follow. Lake adventure, a paint mine, and bird trapping fill the middle chapters. Moundbuilders, camp cooking, and winter in the lumber woods add range. The Gift of the Flood and the Tragedy of the Mounds close in.
61330-elements-of-trench-warfare:
Elements of Trench Warfare, by Captain William Waldron of the 29th United States Infantry, is a pocket manual printed at Washington in 1917 and sold for sixty cents. Waldron, a graduate of the Army War College and author of Scouting and Patrolling, wrote it in plain words for the common soldier as America entered the Great War.

Chapters cover the layout of a position, wire and mines, listening posts, trench types and drainage, dugouts, mortar and machine gun posts, and revetments of sandbags and fascines. A note from the author offers the book to every army unit. It is field craft boiled down for men about to dig in.
61366-medical-thoughts-of-shakespeare:
Medical Thoughts of Shakespeare gathers what Shakespeare wrote about health and sickness, sorted by theme. B Rush Field, a member of the Shakespeare Society of New York, made the collection. The second edition, much enlarged, came out in 1885.

Field added whole chapters on the doctor, on surgery, and on the working of the body. More than four hundred new quotes swell the count in this edition. Sections cover fevers, wounds, childbirth, drugs and old age. The book shows how much sound lore on the body sits inside the plays. It is a handy tool for readers of both fields. Field even adds a few like passages from other authors under their proper heads.
6143-essays-on-work-and-culture:
Hamilton Wright Mabie dedicates Essays on Work and Culture to Henry Van Dyke. It opens with the line that along slender wires of speech some message from the heart is sent, though none can tell the whole that's meant. His contents ask tool or man, the man in the work, and work as self-expression.

Pain of youth, a year of wandering, the ultimate test, liberation, larger education, fellowship, and work and pessimism follow. Later essays treat training, concentration, relaxation, recreation, imagination in work, character, and freedom from self-consciousness. Mabie treats work as a path to culture and character.
61549-knock-at-a-venture:
Knock at a Venture is a set of tales by Phillpotts, author of past novels of prisons and hid wives. It came out at New York and London in the first years of the last age, with all rights kept. Its rights were set in law the year past.

Its gift word makes it out to a friend of the author. That friend is named the first live sage on the old and mid age moor of Dartmoor. The tales then take a mound by the way, a man whose name means a vow, and a grave dug with pick and spade. A pair of the old tale world, a gift of food, cross ways, and a true son fill the mid run. Two widows and a rovers tale close the set.
61810-revolt-in-the-ice-empire:
Ray Cummings wrote Revolt in the Ice Empire, a tale from Planet Stories in fall 1940. The front note calls Zura a frozen small world and a kind of utopia. Earth men come to topple the rule of its gentle queen. Their tools are the foul tools of revolt, the note says.

The teller says much writ on the first voyage to Zura is wrong. He and his wife Tara are, he thinks, the sole folk left to tell the tale. Zura came in from far space twice and has not come back. He sets out to fix the state record. Men bring love and hate, truth and lies, peace and war to any world, he holds. Zura was odd chiefly for its harsh clime.
61944-the-new-science-of-controlled-brea:
Edward Lankow, a singer of opera and a teacher of voice, set out a new science of breath control in lessons copyrighted in 1922. The Corrective Eating Society of New York issued the first volume. Breath, he says, is the secret of strength, energy, and beauty.

The first lesson gives the grounds of the art. Oxygen, Lankow holds, is the greatest cleansing force in all nature, and it can enter the body only by breathing. The priests of China and India, he tells, worked out the art two thousand years before Christ. Their calm, deep breathing cut the count from eighteen or twenty two breaths a minute to six or eight. Greeks and Romans took it up and used it to build the strong chests of their statues.
61945-the-new-science-of-controlled-brea:
Edward Lankow teaches breath mastery in The New Science of Controlled Breathing, volume two, printed in New York with copyright in 1922. The Corrective Eating Society issues the lessons. Lankow was a leading basso with the Boston, Metropolitan, and Chicago opera companies, a singer and teacher of the new science. The subtitle promises the secret of strength, energy, and beauty, through breath control. Lesson two treats controlled breathing as a means of exercise.

Many theories concerning the art of breathing have been exploited in recent years, he opens. The net results, however, have been poor. The truth as to the importance of right method in breathing may have been presented, he holds. But it has remained of no value, since it has not been accepted and acted upon. The fault lies in the teachers, he charges: they have been too vague, and have set out theory rather than practice.
62329-the-mate-of-the-good-ship-york-or-:
W Clark Russell wrote this sea novel, printed by L C Page of Boston with copyrights of 1900 and 1902, in its eighth impression by April 1907. Russell had written The Wreck of the Grosvenor and A Marriage at Sea. W H Dunton drew the front plate, showing Hardy turning to look at the York. Julia Armstrong opens the tale, and Bax's Farm follows.

The East India Dock Road, the Glamis Castle, and Captain Layard take the cast to sea. The ship's lookout, the French mate, and a lost boat fill the middle chapters. Russell writes the merchant sea as few could: docks, ships, and men, with the mate of the good ship York at the heart of her adventure.
62648-the-experiences-of-uncle-jack-bein:
The Experiences of Uncle Jack is a biography of the Reverend Andrew Jackson Newgent. It was written by the Reverend Snyder, a minister in the United Brethren Church. The book was printed in 1911 by the United Brethren Publishing House at Dayton, Ohio. A late photograph of Newgent forms the frontispiece.

The chapter headings sketch a frontier life. They open with ancestry, a picture of pioneer days, and tales of the boy Jack. Among them are a short-cut in the study of the stars and the fate of his first pair of breeches. His father's tragic death, a move to Parke County, schooldays, and conversion follow. Later chapters cover his call to the ministry, his first sermon, and his work as a boy preacher. The book is a warm church life of a preacher known as Uncle Jack.
62675-some-common-birds-in-their-relatio:
Some Common Birds in Their Relation to Agriculture is Farmers' Bulletin number 54 of the United States Department of Agriculture. F E L Beal, assistant ornithologist of the Biological Survey, wrote it. The bulletin is dated May 1897. The Government Printing Office issued this revised printing at Washington in 1898. Its question throughout is what each bird eats.

The introduction argues that a bird's benefit or harm depends almost entirely on its food. Farmers accuse crows in cornfields and woodpeckers in orchards too quickly. Careful study often shows the birds destroying noxious insects instead. The contents then run species by species. Cuckoos, woodpeckers, the kingbird, and the phoebe come first. Bluejay, crow, bobolink, and redwinged blackbird follow. Meadow lark, oriole, grackle, sparrows, and grosbeak continue the list. Swallows, cedarbird, catbird, thrasher, wren, robin, and bluebird close it. Each account weighs crop damage against insect service.
62899-the-lone-adventure:
Halliwell Sutcliffe opens a tale of loyalty and war at Windyhough, a grim old house in a moor gorge near Pendle Hill. The Royd family has held the house since Norman times, proud of an open record and a hardy name. Rupert, the heir, breaks the pattern, being weaker of body than his forebears and shy with his equals.

Chapter titles promise a fight on the moor, a night-rider, a horse-thief, and the coming of a prince to the south. Later chapters turn to rides, sieges, exile, and love. Readers get a northern English adventure of a slight, lonely heir caught up in great events, first issued in 1911 and full of moor, horse, and sword.
62908-submarine-warfare-past-present-and:
Herbert Fyfe, once librarian of the Royal Institution, told the whole tale of the submarine in this book. Grant Richards printed Submarine Warfare at London in 1902, with fifty plates. Admiral Fremantle wrote the opening, and Edward Reed the part on boats to come.

David and Goliath names its front plate: the Russian battleship Retvisan, 12,700 tons, set by the tiny Holland boat of 75 tons. Fyfe writes for the plain reader, he owns: no deep study is asked. Two years of gathering stand behind the sum. From old diving bells to the first true war boats, he runs the line. In 1902 the submarine was a toy of doubt; twelve years later it ruled the seas' fear.
62950-the-timber-treasure:
The Timber Treasure is a boys' novel by Frank Lillie Pollock, author of Wilderness Honey and The Woods Rider. The Century Company published it in 1923, after appearance in The Youth's Companion. Pollock thanks that magazine's publishers for leave to reprint.

Eleven chapters carry the plot from The End of a Trail through Indian Charlie, Burned Out, Across the Wilderness, and Defeat to The Treasure, Victory, and a Fight in the Dark. The opening brings Tom Jackson by stage, mud-splashed and chilled after a twenty-mile drive, into the sawmill town of Oakley with his canvas sack and cased rifle. Woodsmen, forest farmers, and settlers crowd the hotel, but nobody speaks to him. The uncle who was to meet him is not there. Tom is left to wonder whether his letter went astray.
63119-the-two-spies-nathan-hale-and-john:
The Two Spies: Nathan Hale and John Andre is a biographical work by Benson Lossing. Appleton published it in New York, with a copyright of 1886. Pen and ink sketches by Rosa illustrate the little volume. Anna Seward's monody on Major Andre is included in it. A foretalk introduces the two spies of the War for Independence. Both were young, well educated men of genius and ability, it says. They were brave soldiers, pure in private character, and beloved. Yet they were spies, the foretalk exclaims.

Vattel is quoted that spies are generally condemned to death. Not unjustly, since the mischief they do can scarcely else be prevented. A man of honour declines the spy's part, the quote continues. May not a spy act from disinterested patriotism, Lossing asks. Hale's birthplace illustrates the front of the book. Lossing pairs an American and a British martyr of espionage.
63134-minions-of-the-crystal-sphere:
Minions of the Crystal Sphere is a tale of worlds far from our own. Albert de Pina wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1944. Its scene is a vast clear globe that hangs in the black of space. The globe, named Plastica, hangs high over the far world Neptune.

In its heart burns the hate of a host of slaves in chains. They wait for a bell call to rise in war on their lords. The call will come from a man with no land of his own. The globe is clear as glass yet stronger than the best steel. In it sits the town of those who rule the whole realm. The tale is space war pulp of the raw, bright kind.
63148-men-who-have-made-the-empire:
George Griffith's Men Who Have Made the Empire, in its third edition from Pearson of London in 1899, tells the lives of twelve empire-makers for general readers. Griffith warns that school histories may make his first choice look strange.

He begins with William the Norman, a man taught as a foreign invader and ruthless oppressor, and argues his place as the first maker of the empire. The lives then run through Edward of the Long Legs, the queen's little pirate, Oliver Cromwell, William of Orange, James Cook, Lord Clive, and Warren Hastings. Nelson, Wellington, Chinese Gordon, and Cecil Rhodes close the list. Griffith writes stirring narrative rather than dry record, and dedicates the pages to the mighty dead and the living who carry on their work.
63242-hellenistic-sculpture:
Hellenistic Sculpture is a study of Greek sculpture after Alexander, by Guy Dickins, a fellow and lecturer of Saint John's College, Oxford. The Clarendon Press published it at Oxford in 1920, with a preface by Percy Gardner. An introductory note explains the book's state. Dickins wrote these chapters as a brief sketch of the period, to which he hoped to devote years of study.

They foreshadow theories he meant to work out in full, and for that reason the editors believed them useful to students. Plain gaps remain: paragraphs on the Barberini Faun and the Attic Gaul were left blank in 1914, and no attempt was made to fill them. The pictures favour less accessible pieces, with references to standard works for the rest. Many come from casts in the Ashmolean Museum and from famed photo archives.
63293-the-fasting-cure:
Upton Sinclair wrote The Fasting Cure, issued by Mitchell Kennerley in New York and London in MCMXI, with a copyright of nineteen eleven. Sinclair had written The Jungle, The Metropolis, and The Moneychangers, among many books. He gave the book to Bernarr Macfadden in cordial praise of his person and teachings. Photos show Sinclair before and after systematic fasting. Chapters and an appendix fill the volume.

Sinclair argues for perfect health by fasting in the opening chapter. A letter to the New York Times, notes on fasting, and fasting and the doctors follow. Humours of fasting and a symposium on fasting add voices. Later heads treat death during the fast, fasting and the mind, and diet after the fast. An appendix holds letters from fasters, a fruit and nut diet, and Horace Fletcher fast. Health seekers get a bold, first hand plea.
63421-glass-and-glass-manufacture:
Glass and Glass Manufacture, by Percival Marson, is a Pitman trade handbook. Pitman issued it at London, reprinted in June 1918 and June 1919. Marson was a consultant on refractory materials and a medallist in glass manufacture. An old glass house of 1790 fronts the book as its frontispiece.

Pliny tale of Phoenician sailors and soda lumps opens the history chapter inside. Chemistry of glass, its properties, and the kinds of glass follow in order. Coloured glass, artificial gems, decolorizers, and furnace refractories fill the middle chapters. Pots, lehrs, tools, and machines show the craft at work in plates. Crown, sheet, plate, tube, and optical glass close the survey.
63443-twenty-unsettled-miles-in-the-nort:
T C Mendenhall wrote Twenty Unsettled Miles in the Northeast Boundary for the American Antiquarian Society. Charles Hamilton printed the talk at Worcester in eighteen hundred ninety seven. Mendenhall gave it at the group’s fall meet in October eighteen hundred ninety six. His theme is a gap in the line with Great Britain.

Most folk thought the Webster-Ashburton pact of eighteen hundred forty two had fixed all bounds. One stretch, he shows, was never drawn in words. From the mouth of the Saint Croix River to the open sea runs about twenty one miles. Tides there rise eighteen to twenty feet in Passamaquoddy Bay. No clear main channel marks a line. Maine and New Brunswick both claim by vague right.
63448-madame-claire:
Madame Claire is a novel by Susan Ertz, published by Appleton at New York in 1923. Contents list the chapters in bare numbers, opening at page one in the file. An old French lady in London, wise and serene, gives the novel its title. Her grandchildren loves and troubles come to her for judgment and healing.

Ertz writes the postwar young with sympathy and the old with reverence in the tale. Madame Claire past in France shadows the family present in England in the plot. The novel was a quiet bestseller and a stage success in its day. Readers gain a gentle comedy of generations from a once loved novelist.
63599-when-thoughts-will-soar-a-romance-:
When Thoughts Will Soar is a romance of the immediate future. Baroness Bertha von Suttner, author of Lay Down Your Arms, wrote it. Nathan Haskell Dole translated her German text into English prose. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in June 1914. Contents open with a prelude and with Franka Garlett as heroine.

Chlodwig Helmer, Franka's new home, and life in Sielenburg Castle follow. A count's will, an anonymous message, and Franka's salon build the plot. The outlines of a great plan and a debut shape her career path. Evenings at Lucerne and in a rose palace vary the social scene. Suttner, a famed peace worker, dreams of thought set free in time.
63671-conservation-archaeology-of-the-ri:
Raab and Moir wrote this report for the Archaeology Research Program of Southern Methodist University in 1981, with funds from the Tarrant County water district building the dam. It explains the Richland Creek Archaeological Project, near Corsicana, Texas, as conservation archaeology in action.

The introduction argues against the popular picture of archaeologists digging remote tombs. Modern fieldwork, it says, may study anything from American Indian sites ten thousand years old to farms of the early twentieth century, and much of it is laboratory work and report writing. Laws passed since 1906 require such study before public works destroy sites. The report sets out what the project had done in its first phase, in 1980 and 1981, and why the heritage matters.
6368-here-there-and-everywhere:
Lord Frederic Hamilton, encouraged by the kind reception of The Days Before Yesterday, ventures into print again with personal experiences in many lands, seen from unaccustomed angles. This is less a book of reminiscences than a recapitulation, he says, and its chapters range from big game shooting at Cooch Behar to Himalayan sunrises. A confidential elephant named Chota Begum, a first tiger, a leopard and an orchestra, and a charging rhinoceros fill the Indian chapters.

Jamaica and Barbados planters, East India soldiers and civil servants shaking the pagoda tree, and merchants retiring to England with yellow faces and torpid livers give the book its wider sweep. Hamilton writes as a traveller who has lived in the places he describes, with humour and a sharp eye for ceremony, sport, and empire's odd corners. The volume is anecdote as history, told by a man who was there.
63852-the-marquis-of-le-torie-re:
The Marquis of Letoriere is a French novel put into English, and issued in Boston by Nichols and Hall in 1873. The title page says only that it comes from the French. Twenty chapters carry the tale from a tailor's shop to a duel and an abbey.

The scene opens in 1769 in the Rue St Honoré in Paris. Master Landry keeps the Golden Scissors, a small tailor's shop near the Palais Royal. He is a lean, pale, quiet man, no match for his wife. Madelaine is robust and quick, with a man's gait and a voice that rules the house. Their apprentice is a stout young German named Martin Kraft. On a dark, rainy December day the wife's bad humour rules the shop, and her hand falls on husband and lad alike. The debtor, the lawsuit, and the cavalier of the chapter heads grow out of this shop.
63997-martian-nightmare:
Martian Nightmare is a novelet by Bryce Walton from Planet Stories magazine. The tale ran in the January 1951 issue of that pulp sheet. Three tough fighting-men of Earth stand named in its opening blurb. Danton, Keith, and Van Ness rise from a tomb of forgetfulness. They find themselves space-wrecked on Mars in that strange awakening.

Earth's last hope against the evil, immortal Oligarchs rests on them. The blurb calls it weird, incredible, a horrible dream that is real. John Burton opens the tale in a contented New World of ease. Burton works ten hours a week overseeing machines in a coal mine. No hate, no violence, no fear of the future mark that world. Yet bad dreams come, in which he seems somebody else entirely. What he was in those dreams strikes him as too horrible to recall.
6423-history-of-american-literature:
Reuben Post Halleck, author of a History of English Literature, writes its American companion after earnest requests from readers across the United States. He followed his rule of careful first hand study, which delayed the book, and plans it on the same model. Colonial literature opens the story, for American letters did not begin independent: colonists brought English language, books, and modes of thought.

Shakespeare had died four years before Pilgrims landed at Plymouth, Halleck notes, and an American in Paris without French can neither read books nor talk with citizens. Later chapters cover New York and New England groups, southern and western literature, and eastern realists, with Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales as a peak. Leatherstocking, Hawkeye, Natty Bumppo, embodies pioneer fearlessness and rugged honesty. Halleck writes a school history, clear and patriotic.
64267-girl-of-the-silver-sphere:
Harvey Haggard wrote Girl of the Silver Sphere, a tale in a planet magazine of 1947. Beautiful and impossibly savage, the girl is loved madly by Prince Ilon. For her he would almost dare the blackest secret of the cosmos. Almost, but not quite, the blurb teases. The tale opens on a silver sphere swimming in vague depths.

A frame of intricate mechanism glows softly round the sphere. A young man in rich gossamer robes leans over its controls. The sphere leaps upward in his vision plate, swelling like a balloon. Continents, seas, a city, a street, and a room come into view. She walks her room in the scant dress of her age and world. She never leaves the floor, having no control over gravity. Oh beautiful, primitive girl, the watcher whispers, savage girl of lost ages. Haggard gives a pulp romance across the stars.
64307-the-emerald-story-book-stories-and:
Ada Skinner and Eleanor Skinner gathered a book of tales and poems of spring, nature, and Easter, printed in New York in 1915. Maxfield Parrish drew the front picture of spring. The editors thank many writers for leave to use their work. Helen Keller, James Whitcomb Riley, and Oscar Wilde all have pieces in the book.

A small acorn, a little brown wren, and Mister Hop Toad appear in its pages. Poems on sheep and lambs, jonquils, and joy sit beside tales of bees and Easter for children. The Selfish Giant and pieces from fairy books round out the set. The whole book greets the return of warm days, new growth, and young life outdoors.
6436-castle-nowhere:
Constance Fenimore Woolson sets Castle Nowhere on the northern curve of Lake Michigan, a shore that was wilderness not many years ago and still shows on school maps as empty waste. Pale, cold yellow paper runs from Point St. Ignace to the iron ports on Little Bay de Noquet, a hundred miles of nothing, according to map makers who know nothing of the region. Long legged tribal names stretch across townless territory farther west, but not here.

This northern curve is and always has been a place apart, the book's opening insists, withholding even the names other regions get. A mid scene finds Waring holding a girl wrapped in furs, while an old man chafes her icy hands and feet. He cries that if she but comes back to life he will say not one word more. Woolson writes lake country romance with wilderness, rescue, and a father's remorse.
6439-nan-sherwood-at-rose-ranch-or-the-o:
Annie Roe Carr sends Nan Sherwood to Rose Ranch for an old Mexican's treasure, after school reopens and introductions at Lakeview Hall. Laura Polk, of irrepressible spirits and flamboyant hair, drawls that a Rhoda from the rolling prairie will ride up on a pinto pony, gun at belt and lariat swinging, to rope Dr. Beulah and bear her captive to a lair. Amelia Boggs corrects her metaphors: only four legged beasts bear victims to lairs.

Rhoda, red haired, answers that movies show more wonders in the wild west than philosophy dreams. Later, a tennis ball from a court whizzes over the back stop and bangs a grey pony on the nose. The beast leaps all four feet in air at once, crazy in an instant. Carr writes a girls' school and ranch tale, where jokes, ponies, and a Mexican girl's treasure braid into a summer's adventure.
64397-tad-coon-s-great-adventure:
John Breck wrote Tad Coon's Great Adventure, book six of the Told at Twilight Stories, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1923. William Andrews drew the pictures. The series tells animal tales at twilight, mostly about Nibble the bunny and his woodland friends.

In this volume the woodsfolk watch a boy named Louie Thomson, who keeps animals in a kind of prison and later takes lessons from them. Chapters follow Nibble Rabbit's family, dark hours in Louie's prison, and Tad Coon going back to prison himself. The animals wonder whether a little boy could go wild. By the end, Louie's tent delights the woodsfolk. Breck writes nature stories that give wild animals speech, families, and feelings a child can follow.
6440-elsie-dinsmore:
Martha Finley opens Elsie Dinsmore with Mrs. Welby's verse on an eye bright and soft, swimming in liquid light and tears. The school room at Roselands is pleasant, though its ceiling runs lower than the modern portion, since its wing dates before the Revolution. Windows reach floor to ceiling and open on a veranda over a flower garden, with fields, woods, and hills beyond, and rosewood desks inside.

Within this pleasant apartment the story's young heroine takes shape, a girl of feeling and conscience in a grand southern house. A mid scene shows Adelaide urging Elsie to hurry for a party, sure her papa never said she should not go, until Mr. Dinsmore steps from the library and answers dryly that Elsie is not to go. Finley writes a girls' story of duty, family rule, and a child's tender heart.
64529-a-history-of-italian-literature:
A History of Italian Literature is a survey by Richard Garnett. It belongs to Heinemann's Short Histories of the Literatures of the World. Edmund Gosse edited that series of national surveys. Murray's Ancient Greek Literature stands in the series list. Dowden's French Literature and Gosse's Modern English Literature are there too. Each volume was a large crown octavo in cloth at six shillings. Garnett was a keeper of printed books and a man of letters. His volume carries Italian writing from its Latin roots.

Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio anchor such a history at its start. The Renaissance and the centuries after fill its later span. A short history must choose and compress with judgment. Garnett's name promised learning in brief compass for general readers. The series aimed to map world literature volume by volume.
64587-augustus-carp-esq-by-himself-being:
Augustus Carp, Esquire, by Himself, calls itself the autobiography of a really good man. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1924, printed in Great Britain, with illustrations by Robin. A photograph shows the author at 21, and the book is dedicated to the memory of his father, Augustus Carp of Camberwell.

The contents promise comedy from the first line. Carp opens by refusing to apologize for writing the book, calling it an imperative duty. He describes his parents, their home, Mon Repos in Angela Gardens, and the long anxiety before his birth. Chapter two covers the trials of his infancy, his varieties of indigestion, and the hunt for a second godfather. His father's church, Saint James-the-Lesser-Still at Peckham Rye, enters in chapter two as well. Readers get a smug narrator who never sees how funny he is.
64642-frontier-humor-in-verse-prose-and-:
Frontier Humor in Verse, Prose and Picture, by Palmer Cox, author of Queer People and The Brownies, was entered at Washington in 1889. A publishers' preface argues that truth is not only stranger than fiction but funnier also. Some men, it says, have no eye for fun and are fun blind; Cox is presented as one who sees the fun, tells it, and pictures it for other eyes.

The contents list runs to dozens of pieces. Comic yarns include a deadly pie, a balloon ascent, a greased pig, and a startling catastrophe. Verse pieces give odes on a bumble bee and on a flea, and a sermon on a pin. Sketches treat trials of the farmer, an impatient undertaker, a countryman's tooth, quaint epitaphs, and the champion mean man. Jim Dudley recurs through the book, in a flight, a fight with a Texan, and a sermon of his own.
64673-pillar-of-fire:
Pillar of Fire is a story by Ray Bradbury, taken from Planet Stories for the summer of 1948. The magazine's own note refuses to classify it: we cannot tell you what kind of a story this is, the editors write, it is too tremendous for that. Its hero comes out of the earth, hating. Hate was his father; hate was his mother.

It was good to walk again, to leap up out of the earth and stretch cramped arms. But he could not breathe. He flung his arms over his face and tried, forcing a little air halfway down his throat with withered moves of long-dormant muscles. He was dead, and he knew he was dead, and yet he stood upright. A passage preserved in the copy holds him in the graveyard, hating. The wind roared on his newly opened ears.
64679-who-goes-there:
Charles Davis wrote a tale of space war called Who Goes There, first run in Planet Stories in the spring of 1950. Two great ships flash through the outer dark of our sun's realm, one hurt and one in chase. The lead ship is an Alarian cruiser, torn by a force beam, with water spouting from her side to freeze in the cold.

Her guns lash back with a heat ray, and atom torpedoes zigzag toward the foe ship of Ru'ukon. Most are caught and blown up mid flight by force beams. The head note frames two worn foes, Ekrado and Ronaro, who gaze with joy at a fair water world below, sure they will find friends and the help they need.
64771-sword-of-fire:
Emmett McDowell wrote a tale of Jupiter Jones and a sword of fire. The tale ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1949. Bare and weak in slime, Jones curses the warp that threw him. That warp flung him down on a vile world of base bred folk. Their low cries hail him a knight in bright gear in the blurb.

The bright blade in his hands is their lone hope, it claims. Eight leg beasts of dread are the foes in that dire claim. The Mizar, a bright spike with swept wings, starts the tale. It arcs to a high road round the world at great height. Fuel runs low as Jones reads the gauge with red eyes. Pulp fire rules it.
65084-the-boy-scout-pathfinders-or-jack-:
The Boy Scout Pathfinders is a boys' adventure novel by Major Robert Maitland. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it in 1912. It is volume six of the Boy Scout Series. Its subtitle calls it Jack Danby's best adventure. The contents list eighteen chapters in the Adirondacks. Ho for the Adirondacks opens with a train's arrival. The logging camp and the old snake hunter follow. The Fight and The Bear's Surprise Party come next in order.

Trapped in the Cave and the scouts to the fore raise the pace. Busy as Beavers and a bog fill the middle chapters. The Broken Trestle and The Saving of the Train give a railroad climax. Jack's Run for Life stands late in the contents. The first chapter crashes with locomotive bells and steam. A score of khaki clad boys tumble onto the platform. Maitland writes camp adventure for the new scout movement.
65149-the-house-of-adventure:
House of Adventure is a novel by Warwick Deeping, copyrighted by Macmillan in 1921. Burt of New York reissued the book by arrangement with Macmillan in 1922. Deeping, author of Sorrell and Son, dedicates it to Bedford Fenwick for great kindness. Chapter one finds two stragglers sleeping in an orchard near the village of Beaucourt.

Morning sun hangs as a great yellow disc in the purple beech boughs beyond the stream. Hoar frost silvers the grass under a thin, cloudless March sky in the opening. War stragglers in France and a ruined house give the romance its ground. Deeping postwar fiction of healing and home found a vast quiet readership.
65276-a-history-of-sculpture:
A History of Sculpture is a survey by Ernest Short, printed at London in 1907 with many pictures. Short presents the art across the ages, as a manual for students and general readers. The front matter also carries word of a kindred manual, Reinach's history of art, praised as a store drawn from all the great galleries.

Short owns that his scheme forced him to deal curtly with the art before the Greeks, above all the Mycenaean age. His reason is plain: ivory work and goldsmith work, where that age shines, fall outside the scope of sculpture proper. The book thus keeps its eye on carved and modelled work in stone, bronze, and clay.
65291-the-pinafore-picture-book-the-stor: The Pinafore Picture Book retells a famous comic opera for children. The opera is Pinafore, the Gilbert and Sullivan hit. George Bell and Sons of London published the book. It stands in the same line as The Peter Pan Picture Book. That volume won praise for its rich color plates. This book follows the same dress. It has large pages and full-page pictures in color. The tale is told in plain prose. Young readers meet the captain and the lovers. They get the whole plot without the songs.
65552-on-time-or-bound-to-get-there:
On Time, or Bound to Get There is a boys' adventure novel by Oliver Optic, reprinted by Street and Smith in New York in their Alger Series at fifteen cents. Oliver Optic was a prolific writer of boys' books. The series bound his work with Alger's.

The edition's front matter is the series catalogue itself. It runs from Driven From Home to Joe's Luck. The publishers boast that Alger is to boys what Dickens is to grown-ups, and that boys of foreign parents absorb fair play and clean living from these peculiarly American books. On Time, as number 149 of the series, is that formula in uniform dress: a boy hero, a journey, and punctual pluck rewarded.
65557-highways-of-canadian-literature:
Logan and French wrote this synoptic introduction to the literary history of Canada, published at Toronto in 1924. Logan lectured on Canadian literature at Acadia University in Nova Scotia. French, his partner, edited the Standard Canadian Reciter and wrote on the appeal of poetry.

Their history runs in English from 1760 to 1924, as the subtitle promises. The book goes to Colonel Thompson, a Dalhousie governor, for the gift of loyal friendship, in the dedication. A line from Belloc stands there, that nothing is worth the wear of winning save laughter and the love of friends, a fit motto for a national literature's highway.
65560-the-land-of-afternoon-a-satire:
The Land of Afternoon, a satire by Gilbert Knox, was printed in Ottawa in 1924. Knox states plainly in a foreword that the novel is meant as satire on parts of social and civic life in Canada. The book falls in three parts named They Came, They Saw, and They Conquered. A verse from The Lotus Eaters sets the drowsy mood.

Knox warns that satire attacks folly in a class or a crowd, not real persons, and that all his figures are made up. He takes pride in his hero, Raymond Dilling, as a man of sound, active morals. Knox holds that many plain men, if pressed by a hard test, would act with the same firm right spirit.
65653-memorials-of-old-lincolnshire:
Sympson edited this volume of essays on old Lincolnshire and its churches. Allen printed it in London in 1911 in a counties memorials set. A plate shows Lincoln Cathedral at evening as frontispiece art. The book is given to Earl Brownlow, lord lieutenant of the county.

Contents start with prehistoric Lincolnshire and the Romans in the county. Saxon churches, Kirkstead Chapel, and south county churches follow in turn. Heckington church, Boston, Grantham, and Stamford get full chapters here. Tattershall Castle, brasses, rood screens, and the Civil War close it. Lincolnshire families and Doddington Hall add house lore to the church record.
65732-the-hybrids-an-epi-comic-satire:
The Hybrids is an epi-comic verse satire entered at Washington in 1871. F H Harwood published it at Milwaukee. The title page credits only an M D as author. Its subtitle names the species mocked: mollusks, saurians, pachyderms. A mock advertisement frames the poem as a cordial. The cordial, it claims, heals whatever the purchaser pleases. It is specially suited, the joke runs, to female diseases.

A section called the As-cription opens the verse. It hails blest stupidity as an impervious shield. Long ears wave triumphant at each bray, in the donkey joke. The prelude then invokes the gods in the minor key. Its theme is woman hatching into masculine. The bard sings the birth of the Amazonian age. No feeble waif was born that day, the prelude boasts. A fierce volcanic creature came instead. The satire belongs to the era's backlash against women's rights.
65782-her-christmas-at-the-hermitage-a-t:
Helen Topping Miller sets a Christmas tale at the Hermitage, the Tennessee home of Andrew Jackson. Longmans, Green and Company issued it at New York, London, and Toronto in 1955. It is a first edition, printed in the United States.

The tale opens in the kitchen, with old Hannah on her stool before the fire. Her knees are stiff, and rising is a groaning misery. She snaps orders at the women: a heap of company is coming. Betty must put more sage in the dressing. Mrs Jackson likes her turkey seasoned high, and Hannah raised those turkeys herself. Old Moll, who came down the river from Virginia, watches privileged and workless. Miller builds the holiday around Rachel Jackson's household. Her servants' talk carries the history of the place.
65848-theodore-savage-a-story-of-the-pas:
Cicely Hamilton, who wrote Diana of Dobson's and William, an Englishman, built this tale of a world undone. Theodore Savage came out at London in 1922. Its subhead is a riddle: a story of the past or the future.

Savage himself, the first page says, would grant that the tale's hold lies in its circumstance, not in him. He was what his world made him: public school, Wadham, and the Civil Service in youth. His clerk's rounds in the Distribution Office bored him, and at times all that was best in him cried out at the cage. But no revolt came. Then circumstance itself broke, and the clerk became a toiler with his hands among men who lived brutishly. Hamilton's cold tale of civilization's fall.
65919-history-of-the-fylde-of-lancashire:
John Porter wrote a history of the Fylde district of Lancashire, printed in 1876 at Fleetwood and Blackpool. The first chapter runs from the ancient Britons through Romans, Anglo-Saxons, and Danes. Porter says he drew on Baines, Fishwick, Thornber, and the books of learned groups for much of his tale.

Thanks in the front pages name churchmen, landowners, and town bailiffs who gave help with facts. Porter aimed at a full and clear book, free of dull or showy style, in set bounds. The work is given to Benjamin Whitworth, praised for his drive, open hand, and good works in the Fylde.
65921-highways-and-byways-in-lincolnshir:
Willingham Franklin Rawnsley walks a whole county in Highways and Byways in Lincolnshire, published by Macmillan in 1914 with drawings by Frederick L Griggs. The road runs from Stamford and Bourne through Grantham and Sleaford to Lincoln, its cathedral, and the saints Paulinus and Hugh. Gainsborough, the Isle of Axholme, Grimsby, Caistor, and Louth follow in turn.

The last half roams the marsh and fen churches, Spilsby and the Tennysons' Somersby, Bardney Abbey, Boston, the Black Death, and Croyland. A chapter on Lincolnshire folksong adds local voice. Ramblers and church hunters get a full, fond county survey.
65929-the-illustrators-of-montmartre:
The Illustrators of Montmartre is an art book by Frank Emanuel, issued as the third volume of a series of art monographs. The series, edited by Selwyn Brinton, covers print makers in England, colour prints of Japan, and the sculptor Rodin. A front picture shows a work by Steinlen, a dressmaker's apprentice, before the title page.

The series notice promises books richly pictured, with colour plates and fine prints, bound in art canvas. Emanuel's volume turns that format on the artists of one Paris quarter. Montmartre's illustrators made their art for books, papers, and the street life around them. The monograph places their drawings in the wider line of the series, which treats each art and city in a short, pictured study.
6614-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Captain Kidd leads the ninth volume, which asks where buried treasure might lie between Key West and Halifax. Skinner notes that if Kidd saved his pirate gains with care, pots of gold could hide at Gardiner's Island, Dunderberg, Coney Island, Cape Cod, and a dozen more spots. Hope of such finds has cost real wealth in the search.

Storied waters, cliffs, and mountains follow, with sea serpents, stone-throwing devils, lovers' leaps, and gods on high peaks. The volume mixes greed, wonder, and caution in equal parts. As to Buried Treasure is a fun, skeptical tour of America's gold fever and its watery myths.
66320-the-young-diana-an-experiment-of-t:
The Young Diana: An Experiment of the Future, by Marie Corelli, was printed at Toronto by William Briggs, with a Canadian copyright of 1918. Corelli, who wrote Barabbas and Romance of Two Worlds, opens in the old grand style: Gentle Reader. She begs a fair, calm read for a tale most will deem past belief. It is not, she swears, a tale of the Sex Problem sort. Her lead, Diana May, comes to no bad end.

No end can be brought for her at all: she is still alive and thrives. Life, says Corelli, is a mask of two faces, mirth and grief, and men spend their years in sense thrills they then tell. Diana's strange feats fill that frame. Tale fans get Corelli's high, warm plea for a woman out of time's grip.
66383-the-kings-of-the-east-a-romance-of:
Kings of the East is a novel by Sydney Grier, billed as a romance of the near future. It stands third in her Balkan series and came out with Blackwood in 1900. Chapter heads promise a movement and its man, a first shot, and a crown matrimonial. Silver slippers, a disturbing element, and breaking with the past fill the early acts.

Later heads turn to the church militant, a fool errand, and the house of Lady Zenobia. Face to face meetings, the penalty of greatness, and the breaking point raise the stakes. Man and wife and the bitter close of all end the listed tale. Politics and love drive this Balkan tale of crowns and plots.
66496-the-omnipotent-self-a-study-in-sel:
The Omnipotent Self is a mind lore book by Paul Bousfield, out in nineteen twenty three. Its next name calls it a study in self cheat and self cure. A Kegan Paul house of London brought the book out that year. Bousfield healed at a London nerve clinic for war fund men. Part one treats the hid mind, push back, and the forces that shape cast.

Will law, self love, fact and dream, and twin self heads fill that part. Cross mood and self plea parts close the first part scheme. Part two turns to use with self probe and aim reset heads. Thought reset and self hint parts fill its cure scheme in rank. Most of our thoughts lie out of plain sight, part one opens.
66518-labour-and-the-popular-welfare:
Labour and the Popular Welfare, by Mallock, is a study of work and well being in the Britain of its day. The title joins two great terms of the age, labour and welfare. Mallock wrote much on society, wealth, and the claims of socialism. His books took the side of property and gradual change.

A work of this title treats wages, unions, and the lot of the worker. It asks what truly raises the welfare of the people at large. Mallock distrusted easy schemes of leveling and state control. He argued that capital and direction earn their keep in the world. Readers meet a conservative answer to the labour question of the nineties. The book is a document of the great debate on wealth and poverty.
66533-benton-s-venture:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this boys' novel, published by Appleton in New York and London in 1914. The contents open with Tom having an idea, and Willard having one too. Their father, Benton, says yes, a bargain is sealed, and the venture at the heart of the book gets under way.

Willard goes on strike, Jerry comes to the rescue, and Tom learns to run a craft called the Ark. A first passenger, help from the News-Patriot paper and a brush with the police follow in quick order. Work, pride and pay drive a lively tale of boys trying to run a small business well.
66775-bottoms-up-an-application-of-the-s:
George Jean Nathan wrote Bottoms Up, an application of the slapstick to satire, published by Philip Goodman in New York in 1917. Nathan was America's sharpest theatre critic. His first sketch shows his method. A magazine love scene runs in lush style until the page turns, and an advertisement for tomato soup interrupts the lovers at their crisis. The story then resumes mid-sentence. Nathan calls the piece Magazine Fiction à la Mode.

The contents promise more of the same: glossaries, stories of the operas, a French vest pocket dictionary, and a study of what you get for your money. Three modern dramatists get a chapter. Nathan's satire is urban and unsparing, aimed at the magazines, the stage, and the reading public's habits. Bottoms Up gathers the jeux d'esprit of a critic who believed laughter was a weapon, and used it weekly.
66796-historical-record-of-the-thirty-fi:
Historical Record of the Thirty-First, or the Huntingdonshire Regiment, belongs to a famed army series. Richard Cannon compiled the records of the British Army from the adjutant general office. The series set out to give the history of every regiment in her majesty service. Command of the late King William the Fourth stands at its head.

Printed by authority and under royal patronage, the records march regiment by regiment. Raising, campaigns, honours, and changes of name and uniform fill each such volume. The Thirty-First Foot served in many wars of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Cannon dry official style preserves dates, places, and officer names for each campaign. Regimental pride and army history meet in these crown printed records.
66837-portrait-of-a-man-with-red-hair-a-:
Portrait of a Man with Red Hair is a romantic macabre tale by Hugh Walpole. Doran published it in New York with rights held in 1925. Walpole dedicates it to his friends Ethel and Arthur Fowler in a letter. That letter is dated at Brackenburn in April of the year 1925. Much of the book was written under their roof, he tells them.

Walpole calls the work a romance in an unfavourable time for romances. He wrote it as a rest and refreshment after a long lecture tour. That tour through America taught him to love their country more. He enjoyed writing it very much, he confesses in frank terms. Whether tales are meant to be enjoyed, he muses, stern days deny.
66863-the-plot-that-failed-or-when-men-c:
Nick Carter tales fill the New Magnet Library set praised in these front pages. The blurb says one specialist wrote no other kind of fiction. His mind stayed fixed on new plots for his detective hero. Carter lands the crook behind bars at the end of each tale.

A long list names the best tales, from Wanted A Clew onward. Titles promise tangled skeins, bullion theft, and men of riddles as cases. The house urges new readers to try any one volume first. This volume holds The Plot That Failed, or When Men Conspire.
66908-letters-of-the-late-ignatius-sanch:
Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African, with memoirs of his life prefixed, reached a third edition in London in 1784. The editor states in an advertisement that the letters were never written for print and were gathered from the friends who received them. Her aims were to show that an untutored African may have gifts equal to a European, and to serve Sancho's worthy family.

The life tells that Sancho was born in 1729 on board a slave ship days out from Guinea, and baptized at Carthagena by the bishop. His mother died of the new climate, and his father took his own life to escape slavery. At two years old his master brought him to England and gave him away. Wit, music, and sharp moral talk fill the famed letters.
66911-eline-vere:
Louis Couperus's Dutch novel Eline Vere appears here in English in a translation by J T Grein, issued in New York in 1892. Edmund Gosse adds a long introduction on a new school of Dutch writers. Gosse calls them Sensitivists and places Couperus among young authors in revolt against older Dutch taste.

Inside, Gosse traces how the young group read Rossetti, Keats, Flaubert, and Poe, then sought a finer, more exact art of their own. The novel itself follows Eline Vere, whose story gives the book its title. Readers new to Dutch fiction get both the novel and a guide to the movement that produced it, written close to the time.
6700-sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-:
Volume one of William Meinhold's Sidonia the Sorceress opens with a portrait of Sidonia von Bork in her prime. Golden hair lies under a gold net. Jewels cover her neck and arms, and she wears a purple bodice with an azure velvet robe. Behind her beauty, the painter adds a second, spectral Sidonia in death garments, a sorceress in white with black stripes. The contrast sets the tale.

Young Sidonia, richest and fairest maid of Pomerania, loves a duke who leaves her for a princess, then hides in a convent and turns to magic for revenge. Meinhold, in Lady Wilde's translation, leaves it open whether this is history or fancy. Volume one is a dark, romantic tale of pride, love, and witchcraft.
6701-sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-:
Volume two of Meinhold's Sidonia carries book three from her reception into the convent at Marienfliess to her execution on August 19, 1620. Chapters tell how Sidonia talks Dorothea Stettin out of office, wounds a rival with an axe, and prays a porter to death, until the chaplain refuses her shriving. Witch burnings, a sun-angel, and a burning at her window follow.

Diliana Bork and George Putkammer at last marry, while Sidonia, stripped of rank, is chained to the witches' tower at Saatzig. The volume closes with the sad fate of Pomerania's last princes. Volume two is the grim, gripping end of Sidonia's dark tale.
67078-the-lady-from-long-acre:
Victor Bridges wrote this adventure novel, published by Putnam in 1919 with illustrations by Ray Rohn. It opens over tea, where Lady Jocelyn, at seventy-two, confesses to her nephew Tony that age has decayed her conscience: she likes immoral and useless people more.

Tony, a baronet with misdeeds to report, is exactly her favorite. The contents promise a prize fighter, two yellow-faced foreigners, affairs in Livadia, and a run-away queen. Later chapters bring an artistic forgery, kidnapping the bride, and getting access to Isabel. The frontispiece shows a man grappling with a cart driver in the nick of time. Bridges, author of A Rogue by Compulsion, mixes society talk with Ruritanian plot.
67334-course-of-empire:
Richard Wilson's story, printed in Infinity Science Fiction in February 1956, is a satire told on a hillside. Roger Boynton, once a fellow commissioner in World Government, sits above an orchard with a young man named Allister. He recalls his years as commissioner of colonies, when he had to choose who should run each new planet. The data were skimpy, he admits, and the choices were mostly guesses.

Mars was sandy, so they put a Bedouin in charge, and Jordan donated a thousand camels. Venus was rainy, so an Englishman got it, and England sent a crate of Alligator raincoats. Boynton calls the aid scheme Point Four point four, Mars being the fourth planet. Jupiter comes next in his telling. The story smiles at empire-building done by rule of thumb.
67496-over-the-wire:
Over the Wire is a railroad telegraph tale by Eugene Jones in first person. Snow and ice bury the mountain tower where the narrator works his key. Semaphore lights blur through the storm as night shuts down hard. Donaldson, the agent at Hastings, reports by wire that his coal is gone.

Big Ben, the senior operator, prophesies that Donaldson can fend for himself. Ben Morse snaps like a track torpedo, fast yet true, on the key. He can near read the colour of your eyes over a wire, Jones says. Tower BB seventeen on the Mountain Division is their post of three years. Ben never showed flurry, even when a freight ran wild once.
67582-jerry-todd-and-the-oak-island-trea:
Jerry Todd and the Oak Island Treasure is a boys' novel by Leo Edwards. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York, with drawings by Bert Salg. The book opens with a letter headed Jerry Todd Says. Jerry pitches the story. The gang fixed up his dad's clay scow as a canal-boat show. It has a stage, audience seats, and a merry-go-round hand organ for an orchestra.

Scoop plays the magician, billed as the Great Kermann. Red sells the tickets. Peg hopes for the price of a bicycle. A ghost helps the boys against the Stricker gang. Was it a real ghost, Jerry asks, or a man playing ghost? Buried treasure on a lonely island drives the mystery. A piano leg and a piano tuner add puzzles. The volume follows Jerry Todd and the Whispering Mummy and The Rose-Colored Cat in the series.
6766-the-press-gang-afloat-and-ashore:
J. R. Hutchinson tells how the press-gang came in, why it was deemed needful, what it was, and whom it might take. Chapters follow the gang afloat and ashore, at grips with victims, at play, and in its dealings with women, ending with how the gang went out. Pictures show an unwelcome visit, a seizing on Tower Hill on a wedding morning, and Jack in the bilboes.

The press-gang, which seized men for the navy, was feared and hated across Britain. Hutchinson writes with a historian's care and a storyteller's pace. The Press-Gang Afloat and Ashore is a vivid, grim account of a harsh old naval custom.
67942-the-honey-bee-a-manual-of-instruct:
Frank Benton wrote a manual of instruction in bee culture for the public. The Government Printing Office issued The Honey Bee at Washington in 1899. It stands as Bulletin Number 1, new series, of the Division of Entomology. A front plate shows an apiary in Maryland. Benton held the post of assistant entomologist, and this issue is the third edition of the bulletin.

A letter dated May 27, 1899, tells the manual's path to print. The first run of 1,000 copies sold out fast on strong demand. Congress then ordered a reprint of 20,000 copies in April 1896. Bee keepers gain clear, official teaching from the man in charge of the work. His manuscript went in on September 20, 1895.
68066-on-poetic-interpretation-of-nature:
On Poetic Interpretation of Nature is a set of lectures by Shairp. Shairp was principal of the United College at St Andrews in Scotland. Houghton, Mifflin issued the Boston and New York edition in 1900. The small book grew from lectures to a large popular audience. Shairp has since rewritten and recast them into their present shape.

The lectures formed a literary supplement to courses on physical subjects. Colleagues lectured on chemistry, geology, and physiology at the same time. Shairp aimed to show that each science explains part of nature's mysteries. Poetry reads the same world with feeling and with awe beside them. Wordsworth and the poets stand as witnesses in his argument here.
68268-the-loves-of-pelleas-and-etarre:
Zona Gale's book of linked stories, first published in nineteen seven, circles the long marriage of Pelleas and Etarre. The elderly couple's names borrow from Arthurian romance. The pieces first appeared in magazines such as Appleton's, the Cosmopolitan, and the Saturday Evening Post. Gale gathers them into one arc of a shared life.

The chapters run from The Odour of the Ointment and The Elopement through The Honeymoon and The Baby. They end with The Golden Wedding and Christmas Roses. The opening scene sets the tone. It is Easter morning, and the drawing room is crowded with Ascension lilies sent by friends. The two old people are in fine health, yet for the first time in fifty years together they are forbidden to leave the house. Gale writes tenderly about love grown old without going stale.
68277-the-blood-of-the-vampire:
The Blood of the Vampire is a novel by Florence Marryat. The Tauchnitz edition for readers on the Continent carries the text in one volume. Marryat was a busy and well known writer of tales in her day.

The front pages list her many earlier novels, from Love's Conflict to Phyllida. That long list gives a sense of her range and her fame. The title points to a dark tale with a vampire at its heart. Readers who like strong sensation and gothic dread in a late Victorian novel will find the promise plain on the cover. The Tauchnitz list at the front also shows the wide reach of her tales abroad.
68337-a-caution-to-great-britain-and-her:
A Caution to Great Britain and Her Colonies is an anti-slavery tract by Ant Benezet, reprinted in London by James Phillips in 1784. Its full title promises a short representation of the calamitous state of the enslaved Negroes in the British dominions.

The tract says thousands are yearly brought by the slave trade into bondage, and many to miserable, untimely ends. It marvels that the trade has not only gone unchecked by those in power but has had their countenance. Benezet charitably supposes that rulers and clergy do not know the corrupt motives that keep the trade alive. He quotes James Foster calling the practice a defiance of the God of the Gentiles. Temporal evils are promised next: the trade breaks natural affection and saps the peace of every country where it prevails.
68409-the-martian-shore:
The Martian Shore, by Charles Fontenay, is a science fiction story taken from Infinity Science Fiction of April 1957. A headnote sums its hero: Shaan made the longest crawl in history, to avoid crawling before tyrants.

Robbo Shaan trudges across the Hellas Desert toward Alpheus Canal, in the low gravity of Mars. Soldiers of the Imperial Government dropped him from a jetcopter hours before, to die. The Imperial Constitution forbids killing a man outright, so the government brands its traitors instead. The brand on Shaan's forehead means any loyal citizen must shoot him on sight. His crime was simple: he talked democracy. Mars had won free of the Earth corporations in the Charax Uprising, then lost its freedom to the new empire. Shaan has no map, no radio, and an hour of oxygen. They took his vial of suspensene, the drug that could have kept him alive in suspension.
68440-the-long-trail-a-story-of-african-:
The Long Trail, a story of African adventure by Herbert Strang, was published in London in 1919 for boy readers. Pictures by H Evison and a colour frontispiece fill the book.

The chapters open with a ruined village and a fight at dawn, then tell the story of Goruba. The party is rushed by enemies, put under the lash, and driven on a northward trail past pythons and a broken bridge. Later chapters bring a stampede, an attack by lions, a fight with crocodiles, and a charge by rhinoceroses. The hunters discover the hoard of Rabeh and train an army of their own. A blow for liberty and the end of Goruba close the tale. Strang's long list of war and adventure stories fills the front pages.
68554-rustlers-beware:
Arthur Chapman wrote Rustlers Beware, a Western tale by the author of Held for Ransom. Chapter One is named Sealed Orders. Two men talk in a railroad station in the heat. Asa Swingley, called Two Bar Ace, urges Milt Bertram to throw in with his crew. Cow work for a crusty uncle is the lot Milt would leave.

Swingley is tall, lean, and long jawed with keen grey eyes. He has awed foes by looks and beaten or shot the rest, the tale says. Milt is near his size and just as firm. Milt agrees to come but holds the right to quit if things are not on the level. A trip from Texas to Wyoming and a bit of shooting are held out as bait. Guns, belts, and spurred boots mark both men as the plot starts.
68555-the-night-wire:
H F Arnold wrote The Night Wire, a short weird tale told by a night telegraph man. A flash opens it: New York, September thirty, Ambassador Holliwell died here today. There is something ungodly about these night wire jobs, the narrator says. You sit on the top floor of a skyscraper and listen in to the whispers of a civilization, he writes.

Along in the quiet hours between two and four, the operators doze over their sounders and the news comes in, he says. Fires and disasters and suicides fill the wire. Murders, crowds, and catastrophes follow. The night wire man takes it down almost in his sleep, he notes. Sometimes, though, queer things happen, he warns. One did the other night, and he has not got over it yet. Weird tale readers get a classic of the wire room.
68597-landmarks-in-russian-literature:
Landmarks in Russian Literature is a critical survey by Maurice Baring, first published by Methuen in London in March 1910. The hosted edition is the second of the same year. Baring dedicated the book to Arthur Christopher Benson, and he had earlier written With the Russians in Manchuria and A Year in Russia.

A bibliography opens the volume. It lists translations of Tolstoy, studies of Dostoievski, lives of Tolstoy, and histories of Russian literature in French, German, and English. Baring praises one newspaper estimate of Tolstoy as the best he had seen in England. His own task, the text soon admits, is hard. Explaining Russia to an English public invites confusion at every step. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
68604-europe-and-elsewhere:
Europe and Elsewhere is a posthumous gathering of Mark Twain's essays and papers, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1923. Brander Matthews supplied an appreciation and Albert Bigelow Paine, Twain's biographer, an introduction. The Mark Twain Company held the copyright, and this is the first edition.

The contents show the older Twain at war. Letters to Satan stand in the list beside The United States of Lyncherdom. To the Person Sitting in Darkness, his attack on the imperial missions, and To My Missionary Critics follow, with A Word of Encouragement for Our Blushing Exiles for relief. A sketch of Thomas Brackett Reed and a piece called The Finished Book close the run. Paine gathered pieces Twain had published in magazines or left in manuscript, and the volume keeps his late, bitter voice before the public.
68799-a-successful-venture:
A Successful Venture, by Ellen Douglas Deland, is a girls novel of family pluck. Wilde of Boston issued it with rights in 1897, plates by Alice Barber Stephens. A Shakespeare tag on merry hearts fronts the story of the Starr sisters. Chapter one brings a Wentworth Ward visit to Glen Arden on a rainy day.

Four girls sit by the dining room fire while wind drives the rain outside. Honor Starr, the eldest, rests on the sofa with camphor at hand. Chapters promise a family council and a declaration of independence in the family. Katherine as financier and Victoria in search of funds drive the venture. Midnight marauders, a river scene, and changed opinions close eighteen chapters.
68811-black-no-more:
Black No More, a novel by George Schuyler, was first published in 1931. A 1969 reprint by McGrath at College Park, Maryland, is the copy described here. Its subtitle calls it an account of the strange workings of science in the land of the free. The years 1933 to 1940 are given as the frame of the tale.

A dedication addresses all Caucasians who can trace their ancestry back ten generations. It dares them to assert no black leaves or branches on their family trees. Max Disher stands outside the Honky Tonk Club in chapter one, puffing a cigar. Crowds of white and black folk enter the cabaret in that opening scene. A process that turns black skin white drives this biting satire of America.
68875-the-lion-s-share:
Octave Thanet wrote The Lion's Share, a novel published in Indianapolis in 1907 with pictures by Ashe. Thanet was known for The Man of the Hour and Stories of a Western Town. The title promises a fight over who takes the largest part of something, and the contents promise a puzzle that only falls into place near the end.

The first chapter opens in 1903, when Colonel Rupert Winter, home from the Philippines, visits Harvard and hears a pistol shot in a dormitory room. Inside, young Cary Mercer lies slumped over his study table, a revolver on the floor and blood in his dark curls. Chapters ahead bring train robbers, a vanished boy named Archie, a voice in the telephone, and a haunted house. Readers get a mystery of money and family secrets, built scene by scene until the pattern clears.
68886-king-edward-s-realm-story-of-the-m:
Dawe, a clergyman, told the story of how the British Empire was made in a book of 1902. The Educational Supply Association of London published it under the name of the reigning king, Edward. A glance at the map, Dawe begins, shows the red of empire spread over one sixth of the lands where men can live. That spread is more than one hundred times the size of England itself.

The chapters march by dates. First comes the age of printing, firearms, and the sea road to India, with Elizabeth and the defeat of the Armada.
