Then come the first colonies, the wars with France, and the gain of India and Canada. Nelson and Wellington fill the years of trial. The last parts treat self rule in the colonies, gold, and men who died exploring. A final chapter binds the whole in one theme, the unity of the empire.
68988-on-reading-in-relation-to-literatu:
On Reading in Relation to Literature is a lecture by Lafcadio Hearn, issued in Boston by the Atlantic Monthly Press in 1921 as number seventeen of the Atlantic Readings. Hearn promises his students a series on literary life and work. The lectures rest on his practical years among the makers of literature in different countries.

His subject, he warns, looks simple and is not. Very few persons, he begins, know how to read. Taste and discrimination come only from long experience with literature. Without them, learning to read is almost impossible, though rare men gain the gift by nature. Hearn speaks as a teacher near the close of term, keeping a promise to lecture without texts or authorities. The essay survives as the credo of a great stylist on the discipline that formed him.
69017-memorials-of-old-derbyshire:
Memorials of Old Derbyshire is a county history volume edited by Charles Cox. Bemrose published it in London and Derby in 1907. It belongs to the Memorials of the Counties of England series. A water-colour of Haddon Hall and Dorothy Vernon's bridge fronts the book. Cox also wrote the Churches of Derbyshire in four volumes.

The book is inscribed to the eighth duke of Devonshire, the county's lord-lieutenant. Cox opens with an essay on historic Derbyshire. Other pieces treat the county's churches, halls, families, and customs, with many illustrations. Such memorial volumes gathered a county's past between two covers for its own people.
69035-the-public-square:
Will Levington Comfort wrote a novel of rooms, work, and love in a city. The book came out in New York in 1923. Comfort also wrote Routledge Rides Alone. He gave the book to Dorothy Mosher. Harrow Street, number 54, starts the tale's world.

A fish meal, a knock at the door, and lunch at Sharpe's build the start. Fanny Gallup steps in, and April breathes once more. A baby coach, a shared lamp, and a red room mark the turns. New lodgers come to Harrow Street as hearts shift. Town life in small rooms is the true theme here.
69037-don-hale-over-there:
W Crispin Sheppard wrote Don Hale Over There, published at Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company in nineteen eighteen. H A Bodine drew the pictures. Sheppard had earlier written Don Hale in the War Zone and books in the Rambler Club series. Twenty three chapters carry Don Hale through the war in France. The contents open with the new arrival and a mystery.

On Duty, Underground, and Under Fire follow. Chapters treat the chateau, a man hunt, and the light in the window. The Big Gun, the observation post, and the attack stand in the middle. Later chapters bring the Chemin de Mort, barrage fire, and a charge of deserter. The Red Cross, a discovery, the treasure, and the Count close the tale. Boys get a war story of shells, duty, and mystery behind the lines.
6908-the-air-ship-boys-or-the-quest-of-t:
Ned and his friends build an air ship and fly south in search of Aztec treasure, in a tale by H L Sayler. The early chapters set the scheme in motion, with Major Baldwin Honeywell, Miguel Vasquez, a contract, and liquid hydrogen for lift. A dinner party on the Placida and a newspaper man from the Kansas City Comet add color before the ship takes shape in New Mexico.

Once afloat, the boys fight Indians with a searchlight, drop a cordite bomb, and make a thrilling rescue in mid air. Camp Eagle in the mountains leads to a secret tunnel in the mesa, a turquoise temple, and the golden eagle of the Aztecs. The quest ends with a quarter of a ton of treasure, won by nerve and by flight.
69177-mirth-and-metre:
Frank E Smedley and Edmund H Yates, billed as Two Merry Men, wrote Mirth and Metre. George Routledge and Company issued the book in London and New York in eighteen hundred fifty five. M’Connell drew its plates. A Shakespeare tag on fools and mirth fronts the set.

Lays and legends in comic verse fill the book throughout. The pair own up front that Barham set their pattern. His Ingoldsby Legends had made a school of gay rhyming tales. No shred of his mantle fits them, they grant with a laugh. Yet a young hand may use a proved form, they argue. New thoughts in an old tune beat strained hunts for the new. Waterloo lost no shine for Caesar’s Gaul, their preface quips. Judge the sport on its own feet is their plea.
69479-the-garden-as-a-picture:
Garden as a Picture is a garden essay by Beatrix Jones, with pictures by Henry McCarter. A garden of the Villa of Castello fronts the piece as its first image. Jones opens by mocking garden books that claim authority on all of life. Astronomy, cookery, philosophy, and even matrimony fall under garden writers, she jokes.

Old quotations return in garden books like the burden of a song, she notes. Bacon stately essay opening is the one readers feel cheated without in such books. Against bedding plant beds of atrocious colour she sets gardens composed like pictures. Landscape taste in America owes much to this plea for the planted scene.
695-glaucus-or-the-wonders-of-the-shore:
Charles Kingsley wrote this guide to the seashore for readers who walk the rocks at low tide and wonder what they see. First issued in 1855, it leads the reader from pool to pool, naming sea anemones, crabs, shells, and weeds, and noting how each lives, feeds, and breeds. Colour plates in later printings help the eye match the page to the shore.

Kingsley urges the reader to keep live specimens, watch them at home, and learn by close looking rather than by books alone. His tone is warm and eager, full of praise for small wonders most walkers pass by. The book helped make seaside natural history a popular pastime, and it still serves as a friendly first guide to tide-pool life.
6950-the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-seashore:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to the seashore, opening with a busy departure and a chase after a duck. Dinah climbs into the big depot wagon, Freddie brings his pet cat Snoop in a box, and Flossie guards ferns wrapped in wet paper from the sun. Mrs Bobbsey trusts Bert with a satchel holding glasses of jelly, while Nan fears someone will sit on her hat box.

Uncle Daniel readies old Bill the horse, Aunt Sarah counts boxes, and Freddie's little duck Downy in a blue shoe box nearly gets left behind. The chapter promises a holiday of small mishaps and family fun at the shore. The twins, their pets, and their elders set out in a bustle that young readers will know well.
69558-congo-life-and-folklore:
John Weeks wrote Congo Life and Folklore, at London in 1911. The Religious Tract Society put out the missionary's book. Life on the Congo makes the first part of the volume. A brass rod describes that life, its title jokes. Thirty-three native stories make the second part of it.

They were told round evening fires, the title adds. A native village stands photographed at the book's front. The main path on Wathen station shows a welcome banner there. I am packed in a box, the brass rod begins its tale. Sent to Congoland, it rides an ocean steamer in chapter one. Curious names of the Kroo boys fill its early pages. Weeks gave his colleagues, living and dead, the dedication of it. Their labours established a kingdom in Congoland, he writes. Weeks gives the Congo a missionary's double record.
69595-the-life-of-john-metcalf-commonly-:
The Life of John Metcalf tells the story of the man called Blind Jack of Knaresborough. Printed at York in 1795, it came out while its subject still lived. Metcalf lost his sight young, yet built a name across the north of England. The title page lists his exploits in hunting and card playing. It also notes his part in the expedition against the rebels of 1745.

The greater fame rests on his works as a road maker. He took contracts for roads and bridges across four counties. Yorkshire, Lancashire, Derbyshire, and Cheshire all saw his hand. A portrait of him at age 78 fronts the book. The preface calls him a surprising exception to the common lot of the blind. Most blind men of his day could only amuse society to earn a living. Metcalf, blind and poor, instead built the roads society travelled on.
69619-character-of-renaissance-architect:
Charles Herbert Moore wrote Character of Renaissance Architecture, issued in New York by the Macmillan Company in nineteen oh five. Moore had earlier written Development and Character of Gothic Architecture. Twelve plates in photogravure and many illustrations aid the text. He gave the book to his daughter. Chapter one argues that Renaissance fine arts character has not been correctly set forth.

The fine arts always express the conditions and beliefs of a people, he holds. Medieval Christianity as a source of artistic inspiration opens the argument. Renaissance works were qualified by the immoral tendencies of the time, Moore argues. Luxury and extravagance marked Florence at the close of the fifteenth century, he says. The fine arts were made to minister to sensuous pleasure, he adds. Architecture students get a stern, learned critique of Renaissance building.
6965-alice-sit-by-the-fire:
J M Barrie's play Alice Sit by the Fire opens with a wish to peep into Amy's diary, an octavo book with Amy in gold letters wandering across soft brown leather. The narrator notes that novels often invite readers to look over shoulders, while plays are more coquettish things. Yet the book is padlocked, though its hiding place in a lower drawer is known, and Amy's own feelings, not the author's, are the true subject.

The play that follows turns on Amy, her family, and the gap between what she thinks happened and what others think. Barrie writes with his usual blend of wit and tenderness, letting a girl's diary stand for a young mind finding its voice. The comedy grows from secrets kept, read, and half understood at home.
69678-memoirs-of-a-millionaire:
Lucia True Ames presents Memoirs of a Millionaire, printed at Boston and New York in 1889. She gives the book to her sole brother, Charles Ames. The front pages frame it for all who hold both the rights of the land and the charge of wealth.

An editor's first word tells how the book was made. A noble woman has died young, yet her name is a household word. Fans pressed for a life, so the editor drew on news reports, letters, and diaries. The pages show her many projects and her gifts to the cause of mankind. Her work, though cut short, was done, the preface says.
69856-orpheus-or-the-music-of-the-future:
Orpheus, or the music of the future, is a book of essays on music by Turner, issued at New York in 1926. Its chapters begin with a definition of music. Is music knowledge or life, the second asks. The general idea of progress and the idea of progress in music follow, then chapters on absolute value and on feeling in music.

Turner opens with a jest and a claim. The dullest books on literature, he says, are those that begin with a history of the alphabet. His own book is not a history but a phantasy, or, if you like, a philosophy. If it is a good phantasy it will be a good philosophy, he argues, since all philosophy is phantasy, the imagining of love. A line of Dante in Italian seals the claim.
69978-types-of-prehistoric-southwestern-:
Fewkes wrote this paper on types of prehistoric Southwestern architecture, reprinted from the Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society for April 1917. The Society printed it at Worcester, Massachusetts, that year. Fewkes opens by tying the calendar, sun worship, and farming close together among early peoples. Land left to rest, he notes, forced early farmers to shift their planting places.

In the Southwest, he argues, that shifting life gave way to a settled farming stage. Irrigation brought water and food for the soil year after year. With farms fixed in one place, strong and lasting homes rose beside them. A sound calendar, read from the sun and moon on the horizon, told farmers when to plant and when rains would come.
70079-architecture:
Henry-Russell Hitchcock wrote Architecture, Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries for the Pelican History of Art, edited by Nikolaus Pevsner. Penguin Books first published it in 1958 and issued a second edition in 1963; plates, a bibliography, and a long index fill out the volume.

The history runs in three parts. The first covers 1800 to 1850: romantic classicism, the doctrine of Durand, the picturesque and the Gothic Revival, and building with iron and glass. The second covers 1850 to 1900, from Second Empire Paris and High Victorian Gothic to Norman Shaw, Richardson, and the rise of commercial building. The third runs to 1955: the Art Nouveau of Horta, Mackintosh, and Gaudí, then Perret, Wright, Behrens, and the generation of Gropius, Le Corbusier, and Mies van der Rohe.
7008-the-city-of-fire:
Grace Livingston Hill sets The City of Fire in Sabbath Valley, a green jewel cupped in mountain hands under a serene morning sun. Clean smooth streets, white houses with green blinds, clear cut maples, a wide winged brick schoolhouse, a vine clad stone church, and a low roofed stone parsonage fill the opening view. The word manse had not yet reached the valley, and no affectations troubled its air.

Billy Gaston waits two miles away and a few degrees up the mountainside, on the little station platform at Pleasant View. A note on the text records chapters renumbered from chapter twenty four and the name Fenning changed to Fenner throughout. Hill's tale follows valley folk through fire, faith, and the testing of a quiet town.
70083-the-tower-treasure:
Franklin Dixon wrote this Hardy Boys tale of a tower treasure hunt. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York, copyright 1927. Rogers drew the plates, boys at the old tower among them. Contents open the speed demon, then the stolen roadster case.

Traces of the thief, the hold up, and tire tracks follow. A mansion robbery, an arrest, and red hair fill the middle. The search of the tower and a flash in the tower come. Two boys ride motorcycles on a shore road that spring morning. The chief gets a bomb and a confession come before the tower search begins there.
7017-a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore:
Fay Cooper Cole offers this study in Tinguian folk lore as a doctoral thesis for Columbia University, published in Chicago in 1915. It rests on a collection of Philippine folk tales from the Field Museum. It was gathered during sixteen months among the Tinguian, a powerful pagan tribe of the mountain districts of Abra, Ilocos Sur, and Norte in northern Luzon. In social order, government, house building, and material culture the tribe differs sharply from the neighboring Igorot.

Cole finds their religious order and ceremonies more highly developed than those of nearby tribes, a claim his tales and notes support. The study gives English readers direct access to a mountain people's stories, rites, and world view. It stands as early American field work in the Philippines, careful, plain, and rich in tale matter.
70281-st-domingo-its-revolution-and-its-:
St Domingo, Its Revolution and Its Hero, was written by Elliott. Dix published the discourse at New York in 1855. It was condensed for the New York Library Association, February 26, 1855. Elliott states two aims at the start. First, to weaken the bitter prejudice of colour. That prejudice, he says, bars black men from citizen rights, the communion table, and even the omnibus. Second, to spur black readers to earn respect as Toussaint did: by industry, wealth, learning, and bravery.

Twenty sections carry the tale. Columbus called the island the Paradise of God, Elliott writes. Spaniards who followed cared only for gold. A million natives were sacrificed to the mines, he charges. The mulattoes, the feast of St Louis, and the man himself follow. Enfranchisement, prosperity, Napoleon, treachery, and death close the life of Toussaint Louverture.
70412-scripture-texts-illustrated-by-gen:
Francis Jacox wrote notes that pair Bible texts with lines from wide reading. Jacox was a clergyman with a degree from Oxford or Cambridge rank. The book came out in New York in 1871. Its short title is Scripture Texts Illustrated by General Literature. Each part takes one verse and builds a short essay round it.

Heads run from Achan's fall to the lilies of the field. Jacox draws on poets, tales, and works of fact for each text. The aim is to make old verses feel close and clear. Church readers get fresh light on known lines, text by text. The verse and prose sit side by side on each page for ease of use.
7056-along-the-shore:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop sings along the shore in poems dedicated to G P L, opening with a verse on sky, spring wind, and souls tender as May tints. For such large ecstasies, she asks, what can we bring, save wild flowers of love laid on affection's altar to win unexcelled protection. The contents list Inlet and Shore, Impersonality, A Protean Glimpse, Power Against Power, and Life's Priestess.

Love Now, One and One, The Violin, Gertrude, and Unity in Space follow, with The Shell and the Word, The Clock Tower Bell, and Ours to Endure. Broken Waves, The Ghosts of Revellers, Life's Burying Ground, and Beyond Utterance lead to The Suicide, For Others, and Zest. Lathrop writes shore, sea, and spirit in brief, musical lyrics.
70589-tarzan-and-the-lost-empire:
Tarzan and the Lost Empire is an adventure novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs. The first book edition appeared in 1929. This Ace edition follows that text. Frank Frazetta drew the cover art. A foreword by an editor of a Burroughs magazine defends the real Tarzan. It corrects errors spread by the films.

The plot begins with a missing archaeologist. He was hunting the secret of a lost tribe in the Wiramwazi Mountains. Tarzan speeds into deep Africa to rescue him. He finds twin cities of Roman soldiery. They are outposts of an empire fallen fifteen hundred years before. The tale mixes ancient intrigue with modern schemers. Gladiators and enraged lions await the hero.
70731-a-history-of-english-literature:
A History of English Literature, a practical text book by Edward Albert, was published by Crowell at New York in 1923. Albert taught at George Watson's College in Edinburgh. Its motto bids us praise famous men whose names live for evermore. The contents walk the whole road of English letters in twelve chapters.

The Old English period opens the book, then the Middle English period and the age of Chaucer. From Chaucer to Spenser leads into the age of Elizabeth, the book's longest span. The ages of Milton, Dryden, and Pope follow, then transition and the return to nature. The Victorian age and the post Victorian age close the survey. Albert begins in the fifth century, with the Romans leaving Britain in the year 410. The book served schools as a single, orderly map of a thousand years of writing.
71126-animal-portraiture:
Animal Portraiture pairs fifty studies by Wilhelm Kuhnert with prose by R Lydekker, issued by Frederick Warne in London in 1912. The plates run from the lion and the Manchurian tiger through seal, elk, capercaillie, and roe-deer. Polar bear, mandrill, wolf, red kangaroo, and the Nile crocodile fill the middle of the book.

Later plates take in the bison, the platypus, the spiny ant-eater, the black swan, the Somali ostrich, and the razorbill, each with its Latin name. The lion's essay opens on his mane and his crown as king of beasts. Animal lovers get fine art with sound facts.
71158-three-textile-raw-materials-and-th:
Three Textile Raw Materials and Their Manufacture was put out by the International Acceptance Bank of New York under a 1924 copyright. The book treats cotton, wool, and silk, from the raw stuff to the cloth. James Paul Warburg, a vice president of the bank, wrote the cotton part.

Part one treats the cotton plant, the making of cotton, and the road from mill to buyer. It closes on the place of the United States in the trade. Part two treats wool, worsted making, woolen making, and the money side. Part three treats silk, reeling, the marketing of raw silk, and the making of thrown and spun silk. Weaving and finishing, and artificial silk, close the set. Photos come by courtesy of the Pacific Mills and the Keystone View Company. Trade fans get a bank clear survey of cloth stuffs.
71335-kaffir-folk-lore:
Kaffir Folk-Lore is George McCall Theal's selection of the traditional tales current among the people living on the eastern border of the Cape Colony. Swan Sonnenschein and Company of London issued this second edition in 1886, with the copious explanatory notes the title promises. Theal also wrote a history of the colonies and states of South Africa.

His preface argues the new science of folklore. The traditionary tales of a people, he holds, are a key to their ideas and a standard of their powers of thought. They guide the student through the religious belief, the form of government, and the marriage customs of those who tell them. The best narrators, he notes, are almost invariably ancient dames, and the time chosen for storytelling is always the evening. Theal's collection stands early in the record of South African oral literature.
71377-maurice-and-the-bay-mare:
Maurice and the Bay Mare is a horse story by Henry Herbert Knibbs. Knibbs also wrote The Stray and The Fighting Gringo. An opening note sets out the creed of the true horseman. Such a man, born to horses, admires a spirited animal. Old Maurice, the groom, once rode steeplechases in Ireland. 

Maurice sidles up to the narrator with a hand half raised. He begs the narrator not to take the bay mare out himself. The mare has stood in her stall for three days, he warns. Better to let one of the boys give her a half hour in the ring first. Both men have been hurt by horses before, he reminds him. They are not as young as they were, he adds. The tale opens as a stable yard warning.
71448-fire:
Fire is the first issue of a quarterly devoted to the younger Negro artists. Its foreword rings like a bell: fire that burns, sears and melts steel and iron bars. A printed spiritual cries that fire will burn the soul. The issue thanks nine patrons by name, among them Carl Van Vechten of New York City.

The magazine calls itself a non-commercial product interested only in the arts. To fund a second issue it asks fifty people to subscribe ten dollars each. Fifty more are asked for five dollars each. No eloquent plea follows: the editors say Fire speaks for itself. The number stands as a bold bid by young Black artists to print their own work.
7148-lectures-on-dramatic-art-and-litera:
August Wilhelm Schlegel's lectures on dramatic art and literature open with a Herschel epigraph praising a taste for reading above all gifts. Give a man that taste and the means to gratify it, Herschel says, and he can hardly fail of happiness, unless handed a most perverse selection of books. Reading places him among the best society of every age, with the wisest, wittiest, tenderest, bravest, and purest characters who adorned humanity.

He becomes a denizen of all nations and a contemporary of all ages, with the world created for him. Schlegel's lectures, with a translator's preface and the author's own preface, then survey drama from ancients to moderns, in the romantic criticism that shaped a century. The volume remains a classic guide to the stage as literature.
71538-robespierre:
Ange Galdemar made Robespierre, the story of Victorien Sardou's play, adapted and turned into a novel under Sardou's own leave, printed in New York in 1899. A front picture shows Ellen Terry as Clarisse de Mauluçon in the play. Sardou's letter stands at the front, praising how happily the novel catches the play's stage events.

Contents run to fifteen chapters: the discovery, the voice of the past, the Englishman, and the arrest. The scaffold amid flowers, the prison of La Bourse, and the feast of the Supreme Being follow. Hours of anguish, the tumbrils, a broken idol, and the knell of the tocsin lead to the end. The first chapter opens in June 1775, at the Hôtel de Pontivy in the Marais quarter of Paris. Behind its ivy-clad walls, where life seems asleep, the master of the house keeps watch.
71765-on-the-sweeny-wire:
On the Sweeny Wire is a comic novel by Charles R. Barnes, part of his Sweeny series about the widow Belle Sweeny. The title points to the party telephone line, shared by several households, where everyone can listen to everyone else's calls. Belle finds her neighbours' talk irresistible, with near-disastrous results.

The story opens with a telephone inspector working in the flat while the widow watches him. Over a chat with her boarder she explains the party-line habit of listening in. She settles in to tell how eavesdropping once nearly ruined her and her husband Danny.
7201-a-history-of-english-literature:
Robert Huntington Fletcher wrote this history as a general manual for college students and readers beyond high-school age. He aimed to outline the growth of English literature with due regard for national life. He also gave an appreciative reading of the most important authors, choosing a limited set rather than crowding the page with names.

Fletcher notes that he found no other book combining those two ends to his mind, so he wrote his own. The volume moves from early writing toward modern work, linking books to the times that made them. Its steady, classroom prose helps a student see both the line of development and the value of single writers along the way.
72134-the-bible-of-nature:
The Bible of Nature, or the Principles of Secularism, by Felix L Oswald, came out in New York from the Truth Seeker Company. Oswald gives the work to the memory of Benedict Spinoza. He calls it a gift toward the faith of the future. Its motto, from Lessing, says light is help from heaven.

Twenty chapters of maxims sort life by kind. First come rules of the body, on health, strength, and plain living. Next come rules of mind, on facts, free thought, and grit. Moral rules treat justice, truth, and care for man. Last rules treat woods, rest, home reform, and law reform. Free thinkers get a full creed of life with no church at its head.
72176-captains-of-adventure:
Roger Pocock profiles bold men in Captains of Adventure, from the Bobbs-Merrill Company, copyrighted in 1913, with portraits. A front plate shows Napoleon Bonaparte. The opening chapter, Adventurers, asks what an adventurer is and rejects the dictionary answer about seeking a fortune.

The true adventurer, Pocock argues, seeks not money but the perilous enterprise itself, and the type is the lone-hand pioneer. Saint Paul, Francis Drake, Livingstone, and Gordon stand as his examples, saints and scoundrels alike among the breed. Men in regular standing forces, like Tromp and De Ruyter, are ruled out of the class. Boys get heroes with salt air.
72181-sunfire:
Edmond Hamilton wrote this space tale for Amazing Stories, where it ran in September 1962, with plates by Finlay. Hugh Kellard comes home from space to an old house on Earth. Walking in a pine grove wakes a smell he once met far from Earth.

All in the house seems the same as before he left, and that sameness stuns him. The life is gone from it now: no voices, no comings and goings, as when his grandfather lived. Kellard stands in the front hall, tired in body, mind, and nerve. Coming back feels like travelling into the past, he thinks. A voice in his mind bids him forget the far smell of pines; he knows he never will.
72316-angel-esquire:
Edgar Wallace wrote this mystery about Angel Esquire of Scotland Yard, as its cover copy announces. Angel helps Jimmy Stannard, as the criminal element of London knows him, in the tale. Their puzzle is the great safe that held the fortune of old Reale, the copy explains at the front.

Reale hid the combination in a bit of doggerel verse serving as a cryptogram, it says. When his will was read, four people might benefit by it, the copy goes on. Two of them belonged to the Borough Lots gang and would stop at nothing, so Jimmy and Angel race crooks to a fortune locked in rhyme.
72412-mahan-on-naval-warfare:
Allan Westcott, an instructor at the United States Naval Academy, chose pieces from the writings of Rear Admiral Alfred Mahan. The book came out in Boston in 1918 with maps and diagrams. A list at the front names Mahan's famed works, from The Influence of Sea Power upon History onward. A portrait shows Mahan in uniform.

Westcott draws the extracts from books and papers written across thirty years. Sea power, strategy, and the great operations of navies in the war of American independence all appear. A sketch tells of Mahan's father Dennis, a West Point graduate and professor of engineering. Students of war at sea get Mahan's core thought in one handy volume.
72502-the-spirit-of-american-sculpture:
The Spirit of American Sculpture is a survey by Adeline Adams, written for the National Sculpture Society. The society held the rights and issued the book at New York in 1923. A study for a head by Augustus Saint-Gaudens faces the title page. An editors' note praises the author's husband, the sculptor Herbert Adams, with care.

The contents begin with Patience Wright speaking a prologue on the art's first days. A chapter of three leaders treats Ward, Saint-Gaudens, and French with moral earnestness in art. Later chapters cover expositions, statues and busts, and horse monuments. Garden sculpture, relief work, and small bronzes each receive a chapter. The society itself is treated near the close. Adams writes as an insider, judging American carving by truth and fitness.
72624-family-fare:
Family Fare is a guide to food management and recipes issued by the United States Department of Agriculture. It is Home and Garden Bulletin number one. The book opens with nutrition: food at work for the body, a guide to eat by, and notes on keeping a desirable weight.

The contents move from planning to the table. Chapters cover smart buying of meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and fresh, canned, and frozen produce. Wise storing gets its own pages, as do ingredients and how to measure them. The recipe sections give main dishes of meat, poultry, and fish, dishes of eggs, cheese, and dry beans, and ways with fresh, frozen, and canned vegetables. Salads, soups, sauces, breads, sandwiches, and desserts follow. A last section covers ways to use leftovers, a fitting close for a book on managing food well.
72648-better-babies-and-their-care:
Anna Steese Richardson, national chairman of hygiene for the Congress of Mothers and Parent-Teacher Associations, wrote this guide to infant care. Stokes published it at New York in 1914, and this copy is its second printing. It grew out of the Better Babies contests, and a dedication addresses the hundred thousand babies, mothers, and helpers who had taken part in them.

Richardson's contents treat motherhood as a profession requiring training. They begin with preparation for motherhood and the baby's birthday: choosing nurse and doctor, the sanitary bedroom, the layette, and preventing blindness in the newborn. Chapters on the nursing baby claim three hundred thousand babies are sacrificed yearly to ignorance, and set out the mother's diet and regular nursing. Artificial feeding, milk formulas, guarding digestion, teething and weaning, cleanliness, and fresh air and sleep follow in order.
72969-the-girl-from-nowhere:
Baillie Reynolds wrote this novel, copyrighted by Doran in New York in 1910. Despair opens the contents, and flight follows it in the second chapter. A refuge of straw and a journey up river carry the girl of the title onward in the list.

Separation, the outcast's brother and the first letter fill the middle chapters in turn. The squire defies conventions, the hunt is up and Rona finds a knight in the tale. A strange land, a Kirgiz yourt and the despair of Vronsky widen the map, in a romance of a girl with no past who must make a future.
73028-the-soul-of-the-moving-picture:
The Soul of the Moving Picture is a study of film art by Walter Bloem. Allen Porterfield turned the German text into English for this print. Stills from famed screen works crowd the plates of the book. The book bears a rights line of the year nineteen twenty four.

Nine parts treat tools, texts, tricks, scenes, and sets in close order. The poet of film and the range of screen verse earn twin parts next. How tales shift from page to screen gets its own late part in turn. A last part asks how film can climb to true art rank. Plates from Caligari and the Nibelung tale show the new screen craft.
73099-the-hidden-treasure:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey sets a tale of faith in the Somerset of 1527 in a new edition issued by John F Shaw and Company at London. The frontispiece shows Anne with a lamp in her hand.

Chapter one, The Gold Medal, opens on a mild spring evening at Bridgewater. Sun breaks through gray cloud and gilds the tower of St Mary's church. Boats shine on the river below. Beams slip into the shop of John Lucas, the master baker in Bridge Street. Master Lucas knits his brows over crabbed accounts, peering through huge horn spectacles. Chapters bring a shepherd's tale, seed by the wayside, and a Christian brother. A trial and a sorrowful parting lead toward the close. Guernsey wrote church tales for the young.
73156-out-of-nowhere:
Out of Nowhere is a science fiction tale by Grosser, first printed in Future combined with Science Fiction in October 1941. Its frame names Valnar, a time traveller from nowhere in particular. On his last stop in this line of time he raised havoc. His acts brought about the rise of Dodson, a mental dictator who now threatens the whole planet. Barlow and Laurine mean to make the traveller undo his work this trip.

The tale opens in a park at dusk. Barlow and Laurine walk as lovers, for the eyes of the civic guard. Once past him, she gives the word: the group is to scatter and sleep. Dodson has got agents inside it. The New Orleans headquarters was raided in mid meeting. Then her eyes widen at something over Barlow's shoulder. She flees, and a violet haze stands in the air before him.
73208-an-address-to-british-females-on-t:
An Address to British Females speaks on the moral care of pregnancy and labour, by William Cooke. Cooke was a surgeon accoucheur, and Cox printed the pamphlet in London in eighteen seventeen. Its spur was the death of Princess Charlotte Augusta of Wales that year. A defence of her doctors, Croft, Baillie, and Sims, forms its second half.

The preface says the nation's grief fixed all minds on the one sad event. Cooke wrote in haste, and owns his style and order may be faulted. He meant only to quiet groundless fears and make childbirth safer at home. His rebukes aim at faults of practice, never at men's characters, he protests. The doctors he defends were strangers to him, so his plea is free of interest. The address itself calls Charlotte's death a sorrow without match in memory.
73335-aberdeenshire:
Aberdeenshire is a county guide in a set of shire books from Cambridge. Alexander Mackie wrote the guide from his post at the town school. Maps, charts, and prints dress the text of the school survey. The book came out in the year nineteen eleven.

First parts ask what shire and county mean, then take the lands broad marks. Size, shape, and bounds of the north east shire fill the next heads in line. Hills, streams, shore, farms, and towns earn parts in a set school plan. The set aims sound home lore at youth in each shire of the realm. Fine maps from a great map house give the book its clear frame.
73658-when-mother-lets-us-make-paper-box:
When Mother Lets Us Make Paper Box Furniture is a craft book for children. Its author taught art and hand work at a Brooklyn school for teachers. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen fourteen. Drawings by the author show each step of the work.

Lessons show how to make toy house gear from stuff that costs near nothing. Full plans cover a divan, a bed, a dresser, a desk, and chairs. Sets are grouped for parlour, bedroom, dining room, kitchen, and hall. Each piece has a build page and a page of fine points to check. The book tells young makers their cheap toys can please as much as shop toys.
73708-margie-s-venture:
Margie's Venture, or When the Ship Comes Home, by Mary Ropes, was published in London by the Sunday School Union. Ropes had written The Mystery of Hoyle's Mouth and Vassia before it. The tale opens with Harry Mayne, first officer of a big steamship, taking leave of Fay Grayling, the girl he is pledged to marry, before a cruise of more than a year.

Seven chapters carry the story from Harry's farewells to a close of penitence and peace. At Garden Lodge the talk turns to half-sisters, and a plot is laid against an innocent girl. A frontispiece cries out against the evil thought aimed at her. The charge is made, the plot fails, and the book ends in sorrow owned and forgiven. It is a Sunday school tale of the old kind.
73723-studies-in-jocular-literature:
Hazlitt wrote these studies of jocular literature for Elliot Stock in 1890, in the Book-Lover's Library edited by Wheatley. A popular subject more closely considered is the subtitle. The first chapter argues the real use and importance of jests and anecdotes: an Anglo-Saxon king, he notes, gave the manor of Walworth to his jester. Jest-books, on this showing, are documents of social history.

The chapters trace the jest from Greece and Rome: the Deipnosophistae of Athenaeus, the Noctes Atticae, Diogenes Laertius, and the Greek Anthology. The formulation of the jest and the marred anecdote get chapters. Reynolds, Johnson, and Garrick appear at the literary club. The Hundred Merry Tales and Merry Tales and Quick Answers carry the line, and Joe Miller's Jests closes the history, with Mottley its editor. Hazlitt, the bibliographer, treats fooling as a library science, and the footnotes are half the entertainment.
73763-dave-fearless-after-a-sunken-treas:
Dave Fearless After a Sunken Treasure, or the Rival Ocean Divers, is a boys adventure book by Roy Rockwood. George Sully and Company published the book at New York, copyrighted in 1918. Rockwood is named as author of Dave Fearless on a Floating Island in the same series. A frontispiece shows the terrific mouth of a monster wide open at page twenty eight.

Contents promise a run of dangers for Dave and his friends in the tale. Punishing a Sneak and The Hankers Move open the action of the book. A strange hotel adventure and an ocean monster follow in the list of chapters. Rockwood was a house name of the Stratemeyer syndicate, whose series books taught two generations of American boys to read for plot. Sunken treasure and rival divers give this volume its salt water share of that schooling.
73798-mystery-of-the-inn-by-the-shore:
The Mystery of the Inn by the Shore is a novel by Florence Warden, author of The House on the Marsh. Bonner's Sons published the book at New York in 1895. A frontispiece shows a painter praised at his easel. The scene is Stroan, a decayed port on the Scottish coast.

Sea and prosperity left Stroan together, Warden writes. The town dwindled as its harbour emptied, its streets twisting and moss grown. Then golf came down from the north and made the bare sands fashionable. A new hotel rose for visitors, and life stirred again. Three London friends arrive one warm September to play the links. A journalist, an artist, and a barrister make the party. Their holiday turns toward the mystery of the book's title.
73819-an-awfully-big-adventure:
Bartimeus, writing under that pen name, published this book of naval sketches and stories with Cassell and Company in 1919, one piece reprinted from Blackwood's Magazine by leave. The contents mix humour and war. A group called Behind the Veil tells the story of the Q boats in 1918. Another gives the action between a British ship named Prize and the German submarine U93.

The title piece opens in play: children run toy boats, the Mantis and the Moth, down a moorland stream, waging war on an invisible Turkish enemy in the bracken. The captain of the Moth is one small person whose petticoat has caught in a bramble, and the senior officer orders the beastly thing off. Casualties mount in make-believe as trout flee upstream like bronze flashes. Later sections, dated 1913 to 1919, include The Forfeit, Supper Beer, The English Way, and Unto the Hills.
73903-wanderings-in-new-south-wales-bata:
Volume two of George Bennett's Wanderings in New South Wales, Batavia, Pedir Coast, Singapore, and China was published by Bentley in London in 1834. Bennett, a fellow of the Linnean Society and of the Royal College of Surgeons, kept the journal of a naturalist through 1832, 1833, and 1834. A Canton factory view, from a sketch by Chinnery, fronts the volume.

This volume's contents start on the Pedir coast: a treaty with the Acheenese, trade in areka-nut, and talks to restore a Penang brig. Then Singapore, and the sail for China past the Lemma Islands to Macao. The museum there, and Beale's splendid aviary and gardens, fill two chapters with pheasants, pigeons, and a paradise bird. Whampoa and Canton close the contents, with the tea shrub and dwarf orange trees noted.
73950-schwartz-of-tanjore:
Jesse Page wrote Schwartz of Tanjore, a life of the famed India mission man. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued it in London in nineteen hundred twenty one. Eight plates show Christian Frederick Schwartz and his wide field. The book stands in the Ecclesiastical Biographies of that house.

Henry Martyn caught his fire for heathen lands from Schwartz’s pen. As a Cambridge lad he read the old man’s journal and letters through. Ten years after Schwartz died, Martyn reached India in his wake. He sought out men who had known the grey saint at first hand. Clive, Hastings, and Cornwallis fill the age’s fame in most books. Page claims a niche for Schwartz among those founders of rule. Mild heart and iron aim met in him, a Bayard of the faith. He served the civil power well since foes could find no flaw.
7397-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Before the Curfew gathers Holmes's late poems, written when evening was coming on. At the Saturday Club recalls his circle of friends meeting by King's Chapel in Boston. Poems to Harriet Beecher Stowe on her seventieth birthday, to Lowell, and to Whittier on his eightieth, honor the writers of his generation one by one as they aged.

The volume also marks public milestones. There is a poem for Harvard's two hundred and fiftieth anniversary, a welcome to a scientist, and verses for a festival and for a volume printed in raised letters for the blind. The tone is warm and valedictory without self-pity. Holmes writes as a man still at his fireside, taking stock of friends, books, and a city he had sung for fifty years.
74357-the-whore:
An anonymous satirical poem in heroic couplets, sold at one shilling from Fleet Street pamphlet shops, claims to be written by a woman of quality in the trade it names. Its motto says that of all crimes condemned in womankind, the title word stands first in the catalogue. A mock dedication recommends the poem to ladies whose names are dashed out. The piece calls itself a truly Sapphic production.

Thanks to the age, the poem opens, the satirizing muse has themes enough to choose. Vulgar scenes of strife supply them. Such Grub Street satires sold scandal under cover of moral condemnation. The pamphlet belongs to the early eighteenth century trade in bawdy verse.
74438-albyn-or-scotland-and-the-future:
Grieve wrote Albyn, or Scotland and the Future, printed at London in nineteen twenty-seven in the Today and Tomorrow set. Grieve had written studies of Scottish music and letters before this tract. He opens on the forces moving toward a Scottish renaissance. The movement began, he says, as a purely literary one some seven or eight years before, then took on political and religious bearings.

It is at once radical and conservative, he grants, and it has not set the heather on fire. Yet it has made more headway than the English press allows. Grieve links it to the Clyde rebels, the home rule movement, and the drive to revive Braid Scots and Gaelic. He reads it, in Spengler's terms, as a bid to reverse the ruling order of Scottish life.
74467-jerry-or-the-sailor-boy-ashore:
Jerry, or the Sailor Boy Ashore, is the seventh Aimwell story, left unfinished. Walter Aimwell died before he could finish the tale for his young readers. Gould and Lincoln of Boston brought the fragment out in 1864. A memoir of the author, with his likeness, stands added at the front. The preface owns the tale lacks the full completeness of its fellows.

Its design shows the folly of chafing under parental restraint at home. Low and vicious company blights character, the tale warns its readers. Jerry's own account holds much useful lore of sailor life at sea. Ports and lands he visited fill his story of adventures abroad. Filial duty and high aims stand as the basis of manly character. Oscar Preston's sway over Jerry and an escape darken the fragment. The Aimwell Stories had won great popularity with the young by then.
74477-essays-in-miniature:
Essays in Miniature is a book of short literary essays by Agnes Repplier, published by Charles Webster at New York in 1892. It belongs to the Fiction, Fact, and Fancy Series, edited by Arthur Stedman, which also held tales by Mark Twain and poems by Walt Whitman. Each volume sold bound in bright cloth for seventy-five cents.

Repplier's pieces open with Our Friends, the Books, and pass to the trials of a publisher and the weight of notes. Talk in novels, a short defence of villains, and a by-way in fiction follow. Pieces on the custom house, on Wilde's Intentions, on the humors of fine eating, and on children in fiction show her wit at its lightest. Three famous old maids and the charm of the familiar close the set.
7479-dorothy-dainty-at-glenmore:
Amy Brooks wrote and illustrated the Dorothy Dainty books, and this volume, published in August 1917, takes Dorothy to Glenmore. A letter from Vera, answered by Dorothy on the third page, sets the story moving. The familiar pleasures of the series follow: friends, holidays, and small adventures told in a gentle, old-fashioned voice. The author's own illustrations picture the scenes.

Dorothy Dainty was a popular girls' heroine of the era, and Glenmore gives her a new setting for kindness, mischief, and growing up. Brooks writes for young readers without talking down to them, and the book's charm lies in its warmth. It belongs on the shelf with the other Dorothy Dainty volumes, a quiet story of a good girl's summer.
75030-mr-petre:
Hilaire Belloc wrote Mr Petre, a novel from McBride at New York in 1925. Chesterton drew the pictures for the book, issued in August of that year. Belloc gives it to all poor gentlemen. The front plate shows Mr Petre wondering who or what he may have been. That loss of self stands at the heart of the tale. A later scene is dated April 3, 1953, years ahead of the book.

There a rotor craft comes up through the Sound at the end of ten days from New York. A passenger aboard holds a key place in the strange plot. Plates show two ex-lord-chancellors in agreement and a club admonishment in St James's. One plate notes that a man used to think in three figures, and now thinks in five. Belloc mixes amnesia, money, and high place in a comic fable of England.
75105-the-garden-of-desire:
Edna Underwood wrote these love sonnets to a Spanish monk in verse. Mitchell Kennerley printed the book in New York and London in 1913. A Kalidasa line on the God of Love stands as motto. The first sonnet rushes home through twilight with kisses like flame.

Spain rises in vision as wet gray streets fade from sight. The speaker waits by a window for one she owes but loves not. Sonnet two takes up wooing in soft speech and tongues of love. Spanish, Italian, and English are weighed as speech for passion here.
75110-a-history-of-land-mammals-in-the-w:
William Scott, who taught geology and fossil lore at Princeton, wrote a history of the land mammals of the Americas, issued by Macmillan in 1913. Thirty two plates and more than a hundred drawings by Bruce Horsfall fill the book. A front plate shows a tar pool in California, with dire wolves and a sabre tooth tiger on a dead elephant.

Early parts teach how rocks and fossils are read, how mammals are classed, and how skeletons and teeth tell a tale. Later parts trace the shape of the Americas in late earth time and the spread of beasts north and south. Horse kin, cattle kin, elephants, and lost orders each get a history part. Scott gave the book to two classmates of 1876.
75148-boy-bird-house-architecture:
Boy Bird House Architecture, by Leon Baxter, director of manual training in the public schools of Johnsbury, Vermont, was copyrighted by the Bruce Publishing Company of Milwaukee in 1920. Baxter dedicates it to the lover of the open, the woods, the fields, and the waterways, and offers the results of six years of study and observation of birds and their ways.

An introductory note from the Fairbanks Museum vouches for the method in practice. About two hundred suitable nesting boxes had been placed in proper localities in three years. The museum offers prizes each year, and an April exhibit of bird houses draws crowds of proud parents. Every drawing in the book, Baxter states, is of a proven house, one that has served as a home for songsters. He quotes a Farmers' Bulletin of the Department of Agriculture and a contribution by Forbush for the Audubon societies.
75202-balbus-or-the-future-of-architectu: Balbus, or The Future of Architecture is an essay by Christian Barman in the To-Day and To-Morrow series, printed at London by Kegan Paul, Trench and Trubner, with Dutton in New York. Barman also wrote The Danger to Saint Paul's and The Bridge. His opening argument weighs a common comparison. Architecture and dress are both coverings, he notes, the one for the body and the other for the body politic. Their likeness holds only so far, and the essay builds its forecast of building on that distinction.
75227-hungarian-literature:
Hungarian Literature, by Emil Reich, is a survey of Magyar writing for English readers. Page of Boston issued the book, with a map of Hungary bound in. Reich calls it the first bid in English at a joined tale of that literature. He himself was Hungarian and held a doctor title in law.

Reich aim is a vivid view of chief currents and leading persons. Magyar letters are too vast for full treatment in a small essay, he grants. His method sets Hungarian works beside English, French, German, and classic works. That matching, he hopes, gives a life like sense of an unknown field. Fame of a few Magyar novelists in English lands helped prompt the book.
75230-the-doctor-looks-at-literature:
Joseph Collins wrote The Doctor Looks at Literature, mind studies of life and letters. George H Doran issued the book in New York with a nineteen hundred twenty three copyright. Collins had written books on nerves and on Italy. Portraits of the writers face their chapters.

The first chapter asks what mind study can give tales and poems. James Joyce gets a bold chapter as Ireland’s new rebel. Feodor Dostoevsky stands as seer and soul searcher. Marcel Proust wins praise as a master of the mind. Katherine Mansfield, Rebecca West, and Virginia Woolf each get a study. D H Lawrence closes the roll of the great. Diary men get two chapters of their own in the midst.
75304-the-house-without-windows-eepersip:
The House Without Windows, published by Knopf in 1927, is Barbara Newhall Follett's tale of Eepersip. Eepersip lives with her father and mother in a brown shingled cottage on the foothills of Mount Varcrobis. She persuades her parents to make a garden. In a few years it is the most beautiful garden ever seen, ringed with fruit trees and crowded with roses.

Still the child grows lonely among her flowers. One July day she packs sandwiches and crackers in a small lunch-basket. Before dawn she slips out without telling a soul and walks east through the woodlands. The book falls into three parts: the meadow, the sea and the mountains. A historical note closes the strange, wistful tale.
75377-the-life-of-henry-labouchere:
Algar Labouchere Thorold wrote The Life of Henry Labouchere, printed in nineteen thirteen and given to his cousin Mary Dorothea. The first part traces the family from the Huguenots of Orthez, through exile and a Dutch counting house, to a home in England. Henry was born in eighteen thirty-one. His youth takes in Eton, boy fights, and views on fagging that were his own.

At Trinity College, Cambridge, he was suspended for defiance and lived for a time at a London tavern. Travels with a tutor, a voyage to Mexico, and gambling fill his early manhood. Later parts follow him as an attache at Washington, Munich, Stockholm, and Frankfort, where he met Bismarck. His bids for Parliament, his unseating on petition, and his turn to journalism close the parts shown in the contents.
75425-portuguese-literature:
Aubrey F G Bell wrote Portuguese Literature, a survey. Oxford's Clarendon Press issued it in 1922. Humphrey Milford published for the university. The book goes to the true Portugal of the future. A Leopardi line heads that dedication page. Literature alone can ground a nation's rebirth, it says.

The book stood ready in October 1916, Bell notes. War delayed its printing for years in full. A few changes brought it up to date since. Bell writes from Sao Joao do Estoril in Portugal. July 1921 dates that short preface. An intro treats the last two centuries first. Carolina Michaelis de Vasconcellos stands praised there. Theophilo Braga shares that praise of scholars. Part One runs from 1185 to 1325. The Cossantes open that first age's verse. An English scholar's one-volume map of Portugal's letters served students who had no other road into that literature.
75561-some-old-masters-of-greek-architec:
Some Old Masters of Greek Architecture, by Harry Douglas, profiles Greek builders. Quarter Oak at Great Barrington issued the book in eighteen ninety nine. Douglas was curator of Kellogg Terrace when the study appeared. He gives the book to Edward Francis Searles for his high ideals.

Chapter one treats how the public values architects, or fails to value them. Mythical and archaic builders follow, then the makers of the three orders. Early Grecian architects and the age of Pericles fill the middle chapters. Later Greek and Alexandrian builders close the survey of the masters. An index of architects and sculptors ends the small volume.
75637-winged-warfare:
Winged Warfare: Hunting the Huns in the Air is Major Bishop's memoir of the flying war. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London, New York, and Toronto in 1918. Bishop held the Victoria Cross, the Distinguished Service Order, and the Military Cross. The first chapter explains how he took to flying. It was the mud, he writes, that decided him.

Bishop had crossed to England with the Mississauga Horse of Toronto. He expected battle to mean a galloping charger's saddle. Instead July 1915 brought rain, horse-lines, and cavalry mud of a special meanness. Mired to the knees one day, he watched a trim aeroplane land and rise again. It climbed into clean grey mists and summer sunshine. His mind was made up on the spot. He had entered the Royal Military College at Kingston at seventeen. But the training stood him in good stead when Canada rushed to enlist.
75991-the-bonfire:
Francis Paget wrote a village tale for children round a bonfire night. Paget was rector of Elford and held a master's degree. The book came out in 1844 in the Tales of the Village Children set. Jasper Crabbe, a sour old man, stands at its start. He dwells alone and likes no one's children, the boys say.

His coat is old in cut, and his garb is patched and darned. Loose clothes hang on his thin frame like a scarecrow's dress. He came from far off to a broke farm by the common. None knows why he chose that sad, lone place to dwell. Yateshull boys watch him with fear and awe. A bonfire night will test what they think of him.
76025-joe-strong-on-the-high-wire:
Joe Strong on the High Wire is a boys' circus novel by Vance Barnum, printed at New York in 1916. Its subtitle promises motor-cycle perils of the air. Barnum had already written Joe Strong the Boy Wizard and Joe Strong on the Trapeze. The plates show Joe falling toward the net.

The chapters open with a good-bye, a shaky bridge, and a car turned turtle. Joe makes his apparatus, fails, and finds a new idea. His first exhibition leads to days of daring, a bad fall, and a new machine. A big climb and a crossing of a chasm build to Madison Square Garden. Marksman work, a wild ride, a cablegram, and an inheritance close the book. Joe is the classic series hero: brave, handy, and always one wire above disaster.
762-british-airships-past-present-and-fu:
George Whale, late Major in the Royal Air Force, wrote this history of British airships from their early days to the post-war years. Chapters trace private firms, army airships, and the naval airship section, from Parseval and Astra-Torres types to the non-rigids of coastal patrol and the great rigids, No. 1 and No. 9.

Whale writes as an insider, with technical detail on design, lift, and service, but in prose a general reader can follow. He covers triumphs and wrecks with equal candour. The book is a key source on the age when Britain bet on the airship, before the aeroplane won the skies, and it still serves historians of early flight.
76555-the-attic-theatre:
Haigh's The Attic Theatre, a description of the stage and theatre of the Athenians and of the dramatic performances at Athens. It is kept here in its third edition, revised and in part re-written by Pickard-Cambridge. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued it in 1907. A frontispiece shows the theatre at Athens from the east.

Four long chapters divide the subject. The first covers the dramatic contests: the City Dionysia, tragedy and comedy there, the Lenaea, the judges, and the prizes. The second treats preparation, the poets, the choregi who paid, the choosing of actors, and the training of the chorus. The third is the building itself: the old wooden theatres, the stone theatre, the auditorium, the orchestra, and the stage-buildings. The rival theories of Puchstein, Wieseler, and Dorpfeld are argued here. Scenery, its machines and entrances, fills the fourth.
76559-terpander-or-music-and-the-future:
Terpander, or Music and the Future, is Edward J Dent's essay on where music is going, published by E P Dutton and Company of New York in 1927. The title names the Greek musician who added three strings to the four-stringed lyre. Sparta's Ephori fined Terpander for his innovations, yet his strains also appeased a sedition.

Dent opens with an old musician leaving a Debussy concert in the century's early years. If this is the music of the future, the man says, he is glad he shall not live to hear it. Debussy has since passed over to the classics, but the apprehension remains. Music-lovers who survived Brahms, Wagner, Strauss, and Franck as scandals now face Schönberg and Stravinsky like a language with no kin to any they know. Dent asks whether the jargon has significance, and what the future of such an art can be.
76696-little-eyebright-and-her-pund-o-ca:
Agnes Giberne wrote a tale for young readers about a girl named Euphrasia, called Eyebright. John F Shaw and Company issued this new form in London without a date on the title page. Sixteen chapters run from her home and plans to a late choice about care. Friends, kin, and hard tests shape the girl's path.

Early scenes show Mrs Mackenzie worn down by worry and fear of flu. Talk with Mrs Landor frames the book's plea for trust over dread. Heads such as A Prisoner, Never Sent, and Not Cast Down hint at trials to come. The tale teaches calm faith through a child's own load of care.
76789-oration-on-voltaire:
Oration on Voltaire is a speech by Victor Hugo, delivered at Paris on 30 May 1878, the hundredth anniversary of Voltaire's death. James Parton translated it. The Haldeman-Julius Company printed it at Girard, Kansas, in 1923 in its Ten Cent Pocket Series. The booklet also holds a sketch of Voltaire and an essay on him by Georg Brandes.

Hugo opens with the death of the man a century before. Voltaire died laden with years, with works, and with the most fearful of responsibilities, the human conscience informed and set right. He went cursed by the past and blessed by the future. Hugo calls him more than a man: he was an age. The eighty-four years of his life span the space between the monarchy at its height and the revolution at its dawn. The speech is a set piece of nineteenth-century praise for the champion of reason.
77101-the-gaelic-state-in-the-past-futur:
Darrell Figgis wrote on the Gaelic state in the past and future, sold at one shilling net by a Dublin house. The book gives a careful historical analysis, in clear and simple terms, of the Gaelic state, the cover says. It shows exactly what that state was and how it worked. It further shows in what way it could be adapted for the modern requirements of a nation.

On the basis of that analysis it outlines a state for the future that claims to be a continuity of Ireland's historic past. A nation is crowned when it exists in the world not only by a continuing national life, Figgis writes, but by a state in which its intuitions and desires are expressed. The same list sells Connolly's Labour in Ireland and Milroy's Memories of Mountjoy. Ireland in revolution gets a blueprint drawn from its own old law and kingship.
77119-sally-cocksure:
Sally Cocksure is a school story by Ierne Plunket for girls. Gordon Browne drew the illustrations for the Oxford University Press edition. That edition was reprinted in Great Britain in the year 1929. A front plate shows Sally clasping the door of the next carriage. Chapters open with Sally at home and on the way to school.

Unpopularity and a cold shoulder greet the new girl at first frost. An escapade, penalties, and a rift in the lute complicate her first term. A night adventure, a fair, and sheer silliness vary the school year. A blotted essay, games and toffee, and lost property fill later heads. Reconciliation and rescue close the list on a warm, forgiving note.
77129-dot-dot-dash-dot-fire:
Dot Dot Dash Dot Fire is a girls' story by Clarice Detzer, illustrated by Robb Beebe. The title spells a signal in flag code, and its heroine is at home with signals. Edna James has grown up around life saving stations on Lake Michigan. Her uncle, Captain Eli James, commands the Whitefish Bay coast guard station.

Miss Mills, captain of the Whitefish City Girl Scout troop, proposes a change for Edna. Camp with other girls, she argues, will make the lonely girl happier. Edna joins Troop Number One at Cummings Point, knowing none of the fifteen girls. She feels useless among the patrols pitching tents and swinging kettles. But a coast guard captain's niece owns skills no ordinary scout can match. The fire of the title will call them out.
77441-the-homosexual-in-literature:
Noel I Garde compiled The Homosexual in Literature, a dated bibliography. The Village Press issued the first edition at New York in 1959. Its span runs from about 700 BC to 1958. All known English fiction books in the field are its aim. Novels, tales, poems, and plays all count. Fictionalized lives join the list as well.

Works in other tongues stay out of the list. Books on female homosexuality stay out too — except where men also figure. Medical and study works are barred from it. Plato and Gide's Corydon fall under that bar. Magazine tales count only if bound as books later. Two lines run side by side, primary and lesser. Primary means the theme stands at the tale's core. A brave early shelf list, the book mapped a hidden literature for readers who had no other map.
77447-scottish-chapbook-literature:
Scottish Chapbook Literature is a study by William Harvey, printed at Paisley in 1903. Harvey also wrote Scottish Life and Character and a life of Burns in Stirlingshire. His preface says that the spread of knowledge by chapbook began with the coming of printing to Scotland.

From the days of the Wedderburns' Gude and Godlie Ballates to the middle of the last century, the chapman was a travelling publisher of real weight. In crowded market and on lone moor he sold his broadsides and small books. He spread knowledge and lined his own pockets at once. Harvey's aim is a brief account of that man and his wares. The book gives much fact about the authors, printers, and publishers of the trade. It recovers a cheap literature that reached folk no bookshop served.
77455-god-s-drum-and-other-cycles-from-i:
God's Drum and Other Cycles from Indian Lore is a book of poems by Hartley Alexander. Dutton published it in New York in 1927. Anders John Haugseth drew the illustrations. The edition was limited to 750 numbered and signed copies. The contents group the poems into cycles. The Chanting Earth opens the book with sun and morning songs. God's Drum itself stands inside that first cycle. The Cities of White Men appears there too, in pointed contrast.

On the Prairie gives winds, dust eddies, and tumbleweeds their poems. The Thunder, Mirage, and The Blizzard follow in that cycle. Spirit Songs form the third group of the contents. The Red Apocalypse closes the named cycles in the list. Alexander also wrote Manito Masks on kindred themes. The poems take up Native song forms in English verse.
77587-the-chief-elizabethan-dramatists-e:
The Chief Elizabethan Dramatists, Excluding Shakespeare, is an anthology of selected plays edited by William Allan Neilson. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1911. Neilson, a professor of English at Harvard, took the texts from the original quartos and folios. Notes, biographies, and bibliographies go with each play.

Sixteen dramatists stand in the contents. Lyly's Endymion and Peele's Old Wives Tale open the book. Greene's Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay follows. Marlowe gets four plays: Tamburlaine, Doctor Faustus, The Jew of Malta, and Edward the Second. Kyd's Spanish Tragedy, Chapman's Bussy D'Ambois, and three plays of Jonson, among them Volpone and The Alchemist, fill the middle. Dekker, Marston, Heywood, Beaumont and Fletcher, Webster, Middleton, Massinger, Ford, and Shirley complete the set.
77717-passage-to-anywhere:
Passage to Anywhere is a science fiction story by Sam Merwin the younger. An editor's note frames its fancy: suppose men could step into a matter transmitting machine. They could be teleported instantly to Venus or Mars, it says. A battle of political titans would have to be waged first, it warns. The note predicts the reader will not lay the story down.

Park Hamilton sits down behind his desk as the tale opens. A shocking pink envelope lies atop the neat tower of his morning's mail. A distinct sense of foreboding fills him at the sight, the text says. In six years of a difficult office he has grown sensitive to small events as signs of larger patterns. He reaches slowly for the envelope. His office directs science projects research, the tale explains.
77735-crab-shrimp-and-lobster-lore:
Crab, Shrimp, and Lobster Lore is a book of seaside natural history by Lord. Routledge published it in London in 1867. Its subtitle promises lore gathered among rocks, riversides, and forests. Lord had written Sea-Fish, and How to Catch Them, before it.

The preface invites the reader on a ramble among rock pools. Weed-covered ledges and bright sea gardens border those pools, it says. The expedition reaches as far as tropic islands raised by coral insects. Palm groves, surf, and still lagoons set the scene for the hunt. The quarry are the mailed hosts of the submarine world, in his phrase. Crabs, shrimps, and lobsters are the armour-clads under study here. Their keeps, caverns, and points of vantage are to be explored in turn. Their armoury and equipment are inspected like a soldier's kit.
77771-ukrainian-literature:
Clarence A Manning of Columbia University wrote studies of leading Ukrainian authors, copyrighted in April 1944, with a foreword by Watson Kirkconnell. The Ukrainian National Association at Jersey City published the book. Manning opens with the background of Ukrainian culture. He argues that Ukrainians are not new: they have played a part for over a thousand years.

Chapters treat Hrihori Skovoroda, Ivan Kotlyarevsky, and Hrihori Kvitka Osnovyanenko in turn. Taras Shevchenko gets the longest early place. Pantaleimon Kulish, Marko Vovchok, and Ivan Franko follow. Lesya Ukrainka and Vasil Stefanyk close the author studies. A chapter on writing after 1918 and a bibliography end the book.
77866-memorials-of-old-nottinghamshire:
Everard L Guilford edited Memorials of Old Nottinghamshire, in the Memorials of the Counties of England series under general editor P H Ditchfield. George Allen and Company in London issued the book in nineteen twelve. Guilford gave the book to the inhabitants of Nottinghamshire. Many illustrations aid the text, including the old Trent Bridge at Nottingham. A dozen essays by county scholars fill the volume.

Guilford opens with Historical Nottinghamshire. A Hamilton Thompson treats the medieval church architecture of the county. J Charles Cox treats Newstead Priory and the religious houses, and the Forest of Sherwood. J A Gotch treats Wollaton Hall. Bernard Smith treats the ancient and modern Trent. Essays on roods and screens, the Civil War in the county, and Nottinghamshire poets follow. W P W Phillimore treats Nottingham town, and W E Hodgson treats Southwell. County lovers get a rich, pictured survey.
77901-puck-in-pasture:
Puck in Pasture is a book of verse and pictures by Elizabeth Mackinstry, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1925. It was a first edition from Doubleday, Page and Company, given to Emily Howland Lyman. The poems draw on the fairy world of Ireland and the open fields, with Puck himself as the lead figure.

The title poem finds Puck waking after a hedgerow night and hearing a parson at prayer under a white thorn. Ashamed of his ill spent life, he goes to Farmer Brown to ask for work as a man among men. Around it stand poems on leprecauns, the wild geese, Merlin, and a captive field mouse.
78156-trial-by-fire:
Ernest Haycox sets a tale at the birth of a war in Trial by Fire. Doctor Brent is up before dawn on a call to the widow Potter, a mile down the road. Her scared grandson had tapped at his door in the dark. The old lady burns with fever.

Brent does his work, waits for a good sign, and rides home slow near breakfast. The June day will be hot, and Boston town glows in the sun. He pities Gage and his soldiers, shut in the town with scant fresh food. Brent is a staunch Tory and frowns at the siege. He had thought the clash would end in a stale mate of rage and sense.
78213-shrapnel-shell-manufacture:
Shrapnel Shell Manufacture, by Douglas T Hamilton, was published in New York in nineteen fifteen by the Industrial Press. Hamilton was an associate editor of Machinery and an author of machine shop treatises. The title page calls the book a comprehensive treatise. It covers forging, machining, and heat treatment of shells.

Further chapters cover cartridge cases and fuses for field and mountain artillery. Full directions for tool equipment and machine setup are given throughout. The back half prints government specifications for this class of munitions. They include the Russian three-inch shell, the British eighteen-pounder, and American shrapnel. American shops took war orders from every side in nineteen fifteen, and Hamilton's manual told them how to fill those orders.
7855-the-vision-of-desire:
Margaret Pedler's The Vision of Desire quotes the Rubaiyat on heaven as fulfilled desire and hell as a soul on fire. It follows Ann's legacy through the Brabazons of Lorne, a man with a scar, and a lady from the priory. Chapters promise rats in a trap, oldstone cottage, dream flowers, and a sprig of heliotrope.

Later headings run from an eternal triangle and a battle of wills through refusal, return, and wild oats. The teeth of the wolf, a patch of sunlight, and a vision fulfilled close the book. Through romance and mystery, Pedler asks whether desire, once seen plainly, can be kept or must be paid for.
78556-cup-bearers-of-wine-and-hellebore:
Cup-Bearers of Wine and Hellebore is a book of literary essays by Llewelyn Powys, issued as Little Blue Book number 702 by the Haldeman-Julius Company at Girard, Kansas, in 1924. The Little Blue Books sold serious writing for pennies by mail. The essays had appeared in the New York Times, The Dial, and The Freeman.

Six writers fill the contents. Francois Rabelais opens the book: few books, Powys writes, have drawn more of the unregenerate body of the earth into their pages than Rabelais's works. Jonathan Swift follows, then Matthew Prior, William Cowper, and James Thomson. Padraic Colum, a living Irish poet, closes the set. The title names the two gifts these writers bore: wine for joy, and hellebore, the old cure for madness, for sorrow. Powys dedicates the book to Orage, the great editor who first encouraged him.
79071-samphire:
Samphire is a book of poems by John Cowper Powys, issued at New York by Thomas Seltzer in 1922. A line from King Lear on the samphire gatherer heads the title page. Half way down hangs one that gathers samphire, dreadful trade, says the motto. Powys dedicates the book to his brother Llewelyn Powys.

The Ultimate and Demogorgon open the table of the poems. The Old Pier Post and The Castle of Gathore follow in the list. The Twilight of the Gods and The Face stand among the titles. A heron’s nest, an old satyr, and a malice dance fill out the run. Powys writes wild, earthy lyrics of coast and myth. His verse here is early, strange, and full of sea wind.
79116-atmosphere:
Atmosphere is a tale by Murray Leinster. It was put out in Argosy on 26 January 1918. The tale opens with a claim about its place: it was all in the atmosphere. Men do not take wild revenge in civil places, the first lines hold. In any other part of the world the thing would have been out of the question.

The heat and the sun, with the neat and well-kept horror across the water, set the scene. A riot of green growth and waves that plash soft on the shore stand round it. That horror is the leper village of Molokai, in sight each time the men of the small post look across the strait. It got on their nerves, the tale says, and left them unfit for calm thought. The narrator then turns to the affair he means to tell.
79159-jane-eyre:
Jane Eyre, in this cheap edition, is not the novel but a stage version of it, adapted by John Brougham. It stands as number 400 in Dicks' Standard Plays, complete, priced at one penny, and printed at London by John Dicks of the Strand. A note promises the play can be performed without risk of infringing any rights.

The little book belongs to the great age of penny drama, when famous tales were cut down for the stage and sold to players and readers alike. Its pages also carry lists of Dicks' British Drama, twelve volumes of celebrated plays at a shilling each. Brougham's version squeezes the governess's story into a play fit for quick performance.
79183-the-japanese-empire:
The Japanese Empire, by Harry Franck, is a geographical reader for schools. The Owen Company issued it at Dansville, New York, in 1927 with photos. It belongs to the Travels in Many Lands set for young readers. Franck sails from Seattle, crossing the north Pacific the short way round.

Twenty chapters move from Tokyo life to the far north of Japan. Living with the Japanese, work and play, and evenings fill the middle. The Ainu of the north get a chapter as Japan wild men of old. Formosa, Japan tropical island, and Korea under Japanese rule extend the tour. Maps, photos by the author, and a pronunciation list aid the student.
79192-the-fire:
Helen Hull wrote a tale of a girl in a small land office who longs for more. The tale ran in The Century Magazine in November 1917. Crompton drew its pictures. Cynthia works at a desk with a green felt top and an old ledger. Her chief sells lots and acts as a town scribe out front.

Moriety pays fifty cents a week on her lot and leaves the door ajar. Old Fleming, a law man down the hall, comes for chess with her father. Cynthia waits two full ticks, then darts to speak her mind. Her young face twists with a brave, shy resolve. Hull sets a small town's hopes in one keen scene.
79206-the-death-of-a-millionaire:
Cole and Margaret Cole plot a crime tale in The Death of a Millionaire, printed in New York in 1925. The tale moves in short, brisk parts with long, sly heads. A very great man is kept waiting in part one, and a prim hotel is badly shamed.

Inspector Blaikie draws his first sums, and Lord Ealing starts a probe of his own. Superintendent Wilson hears of a great concession and grows alarmed. A lawyer then lays out the dead man's will and hints at a motive. Hugh Radlett tells his own story late in the book. Crime fans get a cool, witty puzzle of wealth and death.
79400-the-greatest-adventure:
The Greatest Adventure is a science fiction novel by John Taine, copyrighted in 1929 and here reprinted by Ace Books of New York. A biographical note explains the pen name. Taine is the mathematician Eric Temple Bell, a professor at the California Institute of Technology since 1926. He wrote fifteen science fiction novels under the alias.

The publisher's blurb shouts the premise: they ripped the veil off the past. Doctor Eric Lane's party of five creeps across the frozen Antarctic seeking the discovery of the ages. Lane is following the account of a sea captain who fished a lifeless organism from nearby waters. The thing was a devilish monstrosity that fit no pattern of nature's. Lane knew what it meant when he saw it. Taine, a research mathematician born in Scotland, brought a scientist's relish to lost worlds and deep time.
79464-monster-no-more:
Basil Wells wrote Monster No More, a space tale of a lost handful of humans. A front note calls their fate a nightmare of breeding gone wild. The Starship was the first ship to span the void between solar systems. Her voyage had lasted for hundreds of years. No crew member had ever set foot on a planet.

Hull shielding was flawed and jets had cracked past repair. Air leaked to space and air plants broke down again and again. For each normal birth there were five or six mutant young. Cosmic rays through thin shielding wrought the harm. Crops changed and food grew scarce, with sickness close behind. The ship dives to Ghakk, a desert world of Rhebus Nine, and breaks up. Escape craft drop to the sands as the tale begins.
79612-in-case-of-fire:
In Case of Fire, a comic story by Walter Kellogg Towers, opens with a request at a fire chief's desk. The narrator and his friend Jim ask to borrow two fire helmets. The chief's suspicion dissolves when they lead him outside, where his men are admiring their vehicle: a fire rig on a truck chassis.

Jim explains the errand. The rig has been demonstrated at county fairs with no result but crowds, and the Springfield branch thinks it might sell to a small town nearby. The two mean to drive it down over the holidays. To impress Springfield they need helmets to complete the outfit: siren, gong, hooks, ladders, axes, and hose are aboard.
