The chief laughs that he will never see the hats again, and lends them from the rack. Rolling into the town of Kane, they give the crowd the gong and the siren wide open.
823-the-life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore:
Rev. P. Power translated and introduced this life of St. Declan of Ardmore, edited from a manuscript in the Royal Library at Brussels. Declan, an early Irish saint, is praised in the Martyrology of Oengus as the head of a hundred thousand, a champion of battle for Erin. His life blends history with legend.

The tale follows Declan's birth, his mission, and his works in Munster, with miracles and journeys that mark the early Irish church. Power's introduction sets the text in its place and weighs its sources. The book serves readers of Irish saints' lives, and of the faith that shaped Ireland before the Normans came.
8323-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-23-eccl:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, and the book that follows tests every human project and finds it wind. Ecclesiastes, in Challoner's Douay-Rheims text, is the voice of an old king who tried wisdom, wealth, building, and pleasure, and watched each fade. Work, riches, and fame all end the same way, in death, and the writer says so with bleak honesty.

Yet the book is not despair: it urges readers to eat, drink, and enjoy honest work as gifts, and closes by advising fear of God and keeping his commands. Its refrains, a time for every purpose and the wisdom of the quiet word, have passed into common speech. Ecclesiastes suits readers who want Scripture to argue with easy optimism.
8470-the-life-of-john-clare:
Frederick Martin wrote The Life of John Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet hailed as the English Burns. Martin's preface recalls how, some forty years before, the literary world rapturously hailed Clare's appearance. Rossini set his verses to music, and Madame Vestris recited them before crowded audiences, before neglect and madness closed his story.

Clare, a farm laborer who wrote of fields, birds, and village life, became a Romantic celebrity and then a patient in asylums. Martin's biography, an early life of the poet, tells that rise and fall with sympathy. Readers get the classic story of a working-class poet, loved, lionized, and left, in Victorian England.
8487-dame-care:
Hermann Sudermann's novel Dame Care, translated by Bertha Overbeck, opens at a hard time: just when Meyerhofer's estate is to be sold by auction, his third son Paul is born. Frau Elsbeth, haggard and melancholy, lies in her big four-post bed, the newborn's cradle near her, listening to events that will shape the family's fate.

Sudermann, a leading German dramatist and novelist, writes of care itself as a dame, a presence haunting a family through debt, birth, and loss. Readers get a naturalist novel of rural Germany, where money troubles and human feeling intertwine. The book's opening, a birth beside a ruin, sets its tone: life beginning as fortune ends.
8555-initiation-into-literature:
Émile Faguet wrote Initiation into Literature as a guide to the world's literatures, translated from French by Sir Home Gordon, with additions the author made specially for the English version. Contents open with ancient India, the Vedas and Buddhist literature, and move through the great literatures in order, giving beginners a map of what to read and why.

Faguet, a leading French critic, writes for readers who want to enter literature without a university course. The translator acknowledges Faguet's courtesy in adding material for English readers. The book suits students and self-taught readers, as a companion to a lifetime of reading, clear, opinionated, and wide-ranging.
8737-robert-elsmere:
Mrs Humphrey Ward's Robert Elsmere, published in Boston by DeWolfe, Fiske and Company. Follows a young clergyman whose faith is shaken by historical criticism and by the suffering he sees. Dedicated to two friends separated by diversity of circumstance and opinion, Thomas Hill Green, Oxford moral philosopher. Laura Octavia Mary Lyttelton, the novel links them by the love of God and the service of man. That dedication states the book's theme.

Elsmere leaves orthodox belief but not religious duty, founding a new brotherhood of service among London's poor. Ward's long, earnest novel became a sensation, debated in pulpits and drawing rooms on both sides of the Atlantic. It remains the classic Victorian novel of doubt, valuable for its portrait of a mind moving from creed to conscience. For its picture of late Victorian religion in crisis.
8894-latin-literature:
J. W. Mackail, sometime fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, writes this history of Latin literature as a tribute to his friend and master, Professor William Sellar. Sellar was to have written the volume for a series of manuals. After his death Mackail, one of his old pupils, was asked to carry out the work Sellar had undertaken. The book is offered as a last tribute to Sellar's memory, and its preface states that debt plainly.

Contents move from the republic's origins, early epic and tragedy with Andronicus, Naevius, Ennius, Pacuvius. Accius, through comedy with Plautus and Terence, to early prose, the satura, jurists, annalists, and orators, with Cato, the Scipionic circle, and Lucilius. Lucretius, Catullus and lyric poetry, and Cicero follow. Mackail's compact survey remains a clear guide for students, and a readable introduction for anyone wanting the shape of Latin letters whole.
9073-the-roof-of-france-or-the-causses-o:
Matilda Betham-Edwards wrote this travel book, the third of her published travels in France, and dedicated it to President Sadi Carnot. Its subject is the Causses of the Lozère, high limestone plateaus she calls the roof of France. She made two journeys in search of them, from Le Puy to Mende and onward.

Chapters cross the Morvan, the Rhône valley, and the Tarn canyon, with rapids shot and strange rock towns viewed. Betham-Edwards writes with a keen eye for land and folk. The book still charms as a record of rural France before the age of cars.
9154-salted-with-fire:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel in broad Scots speech, opening with a shoemaker, or soutar, and his daughter Maggie. Maggie runs to Stanecross for chaff to fill her father's hungry bed, while the minister is due that morning. Father and daughter spar in dialect about the minister, a man Maggie cannot abide.

The title, salted with fire, points to trial that purifies. MacDonald's Scots folk argue faith, pride, and love in their own tongue. The novel gives readers a vivid taste of Scottish village life, its humor, its kirk, and its stubborn hearts.
9813-santo-domingo-a-country-with-a-futu:
Otto Schoenrich published this survey of Santo Domingo in 1918, when the Dominican Republic was little known to most American readers. He traces the island's past from Columbus's landing in 1492 through conquest, colony, revolution, and the American influence of his own day.

After the history, Schoenrich turns to the land itself: its coasts and climate, minerals, plants, people, faith, schools, and roads. The book argues that the country had room to grow, and it still serves as a clear, fact-packed portrait of the Dominican Republic at the start of the twentieth century.
9973-yorkshire:
Gordon Home both painted and described Yorkshire in this travel book, with illustrations of the county he loved. His chapters cross the moors from Pickering to Whitby, follow the Esk valley, and trace the coast from Whitby to Redcar and to Scarborough.

Home writes as a walking companion, noting villages, abbeys, cliffs, and the light on the moors. The book belongs to the painted travel books of its age, where pictures and prose share the work. Readers planning a visit, or dreaming of one, get Yorkshire town by town, valley by valley, at a walker's pace.
a-drama-on-the-seashore:
Honoré de Balzac places his short tale on the rocky coast of Brittany, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. The narrator, walking by the sea with a companion, falls into thought about youth and ambition. They meet a poor fisherman whose worn face and silence hide a dreadful story.

The fisherman's tale, told in brief, concerns a father, a son given to crime, and a punishment the father felt God required of him. The sea and the barren shore frame the confession, and the narrator leaves shaken. Balzac packs guilt, faith, and fate into a few pages, and the stark ending has kept the story in print.
a-girl-of-high-adventure:
A Girl of High Adventure is a 1914 girls' novel by L T Meade, one of the most prolific writers of fiction for young people in her day. Its heroine, Margot St Juste, lives under the care of her Uncle John and his wife. The opening pages show the aunt lecturing the girl on gratitude, warning her that without their kindness she would be a miserable little beggar.

Margot answers her uncle's kindness easily, but life in that strict household is harder than the lectures suggest. From this constrained start, Meade builds the adventure promised by the title, in her usual manner for girl readers of the period. The book preserves a lively example of Edwardian girls' fiction and its mix of duty, spirit, and escape.
a-history-of-english-literature:
Robert Huntington Fletcher wrote A History of English Literature as a college manual, and his preface is dated August 1916. He aimed to outline how the literature grew with the nation's life, judge the chief authors fairly, and still leave students time to read the works themselves rather than books about them.

The survey runs by periods, from the Britons and Anglo-Saxons through the Norman-French age and on toward the nineteenth century, which Fletcher treats at greatest length. Chapters mix biography, criticism, and lists of cheap editions a class could actually buy. Questions and assignments at the end turn the volume into a working textbook, not just a shelf reference.
a-journey-in-other-worlds-a-romance-of-t:
John Jacob Astor imagines a voyage to Jupiter and Saturn, in a romance whose contents include a historical sketch of the world in the year 2000, given by Professor Cortlandt. President Bearwarden speaks, plans are laid, and the ship Callisto is built. Book one handles the future earth before the travelers say goodbye.

Book two explores Jupiter: mastodons, strange hunters, a Jovian Niagara, and polar discoveries. Book three reaches Saturn, where the travelers meet spirits and hear sermons on the soul's fate. Astor, one of America's richest men, mixes science guesses, hunting scenes, and theology. The novel is a curious window into what the future looked like from his decade.
a-man-four-square: William MacLeod Raine tells of a man four square in a western novel. Its prologue calls the hero Jimmie Go Get Em, and chapters follow Shoot a Buck Canyon, Ranse Roush pays, and Pauline Roubideau says thank you. On the trail, a fight, and Billie stands pat drive the action. Raine writes a western of rustlers, fugitives, and square dealing.
a-short-biographical-dictionary-of-engli: John William Cousin compiles this short biographical dictionary of English literature, published by Dent in London and Dutton in New York. Its entries give lives in brief, with contractions for born, circa, flourished, married, and collected. Its sources run from Allibone and Hazlitt to Chambers and the Dictionary of National Biography. The volume serves readers who need a life, a date, and a book list without turning to a shelf of authorities.
a-short-history-of-english-agriculture: William Henry Ricketts Curtler writes this short history of English agriculture, published at Oxford in 1909. The chapters move from communistic farming and the growth of the manor through its thirteenth-century zenith and fourteenth-century decline, marked by the Black Death and the Statute of Labourers. Enclosure, the break-up of the manor, leases, the peasants' revolt, and the corn laws carry the story toward a farming shaped by markets and law.
a-soldier-s-sketches-under-fire: Harold Harvey, a private soldier, offers annotated drawings made under fire in this unpretentious volume. The forenote contrasts faked pictures of the war with sketches taken on the spot. Often the artist's rifle lay briefly aside while he drew, always in open or hidden peril of life. All that Harvey drew he saw, though he saw much he could not draw, and the sketches gain in realism what they lose in elaboration.
a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore:
Fay-Cooper Cole submitted this study for his doctorate at Columbia University, publishing it at Chicago in 1915, as the title page states. It rests on a collection of Philippine folk tales he gathered during sixteen months with the Tinguian, a pagan people of the mountain districts of Abra and northern Luzon. He notes their social organization and ceremonies differ sharply from the neighboring Igorot.

Cole analyzes the tales by motif and type, comparing Tinguian stories with those of other peoples to trace how folklore travels and changes. The study is technical, written for fellow anthropologists, but its subject is living story: creation, spirits, and heroes. It stands as an early, serious piece of Philippine folklore scholarship.
a-study-of-shakespeare: Algernon Charles Swinburne studies Shakespeare in three periods: lyric and fantastic, comic and historic, and tragic and romantic. Appendices add a note on the historical play of King Edward the Third, proceedings of the Newest Shakespeare Society, and additions and corrections. The opening compares Shakespeare to the sea, crossed by students in every sort of boat, from the paltry fishing craft to majestic galleys steered by Coleridge and Goethe.
a-very-pleasaunt-fruitful-diologe-called: Desiderius Erasmus speaks in this pleasant and fruitful dialogue called the Epicure, newly translated in 1545. The dialogue opens under Saint Paul's charge to the Ephesians not to be deceived by false doctrine or vain talk. It bids readers hearken to godly things and the doctrine of the Gospel. Its greeting invokes the mercy and grace of the heavenly father upon the noble and virtuous Prince Edward, in the spelling of its own day.
act-declaration-testimony-for-the-whole-: The Reformed Presbytery of North America puts out this act, declaration, and testimony for the whole of the sworn reform in Great Britain and Ireland. It covers the years 1638 to 1649, against falls from faith of former and later times to the present day, with an add-on dated 1850. Motto lines from the Psalms, Isaiah, Jude, and Revelation frame the paper. The opening says that soon after its start the group saw good reason to put out a court witness to set forth its rules.
adventure:
Jack London's novel was taken from the 1911 Thomas Nelson edition named on its opening page. It begins with a very sick white man carried on the back of a servant in the Solomon Islands. The sick man runs a plantation, and fever has nearly finished him. A ship's arrival brings Joan Lackland, a young woman who wants to become a planter herself.

Twenty-eight chapters follow storms, labour troubles, rival traders, and the hard bargain of island planting. Joan shoots, rides, and argues as an equal, and feeling grows between her and the recovering planter. London fills the tale with trade goods, copra, disease, and the rough rules of the South Seas.
alice-sit-by-the-fire:
J. M. Barrie begins, in his stage directions, by wishing he could peep into Amy's diary. It is octavo, with Amy in gold letters across its soft brown leather covers. It lies padlocked in the lower drawer of a hand-painted escritoire. Amy is sixteen, and today she is washing her hair. Her parents are coming home from India after years away, and she has built a romance around the mother she barely knows.

Alice, the mother, finds grown children who treat her as a stranger and a daughter bent on a tragic love affair copied from novels. Barrie turns the tangle with tenderness: scenes of misunderstanding mend into recognition. The play shows the Peter Pan author writing family feeling without magic, and finding it harder.
along-the-shore:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop gathers her poems under a shore title, dedicating the volume to G. P. L. The contents open with Inlet and Shore and run through Impersonality, A Protean Glimpse, Life's Priestess, The Shell and the Word, The Clock-Tower Bell, Broken Waves, and The Ghosts of Revellers. Sea pieces stand beside studies of grief, faith, and endurance.

Later titles — The Suicide, For Others, A Song Before Grief, The Baby, Twenty Bold Mariners, In the Artillery, The Lost Battle — show the range from lyric to narrative. Lathrop, Nathaniel Hawthorne's daughter, wrote verse of real feeling before she gave her later life to nursing the poor with cancer. The poems keep her early, literary self in view.
anglo-saxon-literature: John Earle writes on Anglo-Saxon literature, as Rawlinson Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford and rector of Swanswick, under the committee of general literature and education. The study surveys Old English poetry and prose, from Beowulf to the chronicles. Earle's book guided Victorian students into England's earliest literature. Notes guide the new reader through hard names.
aspects-of-literature:
John Middleton Murry collected these critical essays in a volume printed in 1920. Most first ran in the Times Literary Supplement, the Nation, or the Athenaeum, papers where Murry was then making his name. He places his piece on the function of criticism first, although written last, because it states the standard of value the other essays quietly use.

Studies follow on Rousseau's religion, the poetry of Edward Thomas, and the fiction of Chekhov, whose essay appears in two linked parts. A chapter on Ronsard praises the French poet's open delight in Petrarch-style love verse. Throughout, Murry treats criticism as serious reading: patient, personal, and ready to say plainly why one writer endures and another fades.
at-a-winter-s-fire:
Bernard Capes published this set of tales in 1899, gathering pieces that had mostly run in English and American magazines such as the Cornhill and Macmillan's. Capes, a clerk turned writer, favoured eerie stories told beside a fire, and the title suits the mood. Twelve tales mix ghost lore, crime, and strange romance.

Openings include The Moon Stricken, set on a desolate road in the Bernese Oberland, plus The Vanishing House, Dark Dignum, and Black Venn. Later pieces offer The Black Reaper, A Voice from the Pit, and Dinah's Mammoth. Quiet narrators, old houses, and sudden reversals carry the dread; Capes rarely shouts, letting one wrong detail chill the whole scene for fireside readers.
at-aboukir-and-acre:
G. A. Henty published this boys' historical novel in 1899, sending a young English hero through Napoleon's invasion of Egypt. Edgar, the lad of the story, makes a Bedouin friend, gets left behind, and reaches the fighting around Cairo. Henty built his career on such tales, pairing exact campaign history with a brave boy at its centre.

Chapters cover the Battle of the Pyramids, a rising in Cairo, and rescue from an Egyptian tomb. Sir Sidney Smith enters, then a sea-fight, and the desperate siege of Acre, where Napoleon failed. Plans of the Nile battle, the siege, and Alexandria support the narrative. Abercrombie's expedition and the Battle of Alexandria close the campaign in rousing style.
at-the-earth-s-core:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens At the Earth's Core with a narrator who warns that nobody will believe his story. He tells how David Innes and inventor Abner Perry bored into the earth in a great iron mole. They emerge in Pellucidar, a hollow world lit by a central sun, where time barely moves. Dinosaurs, beast-men, and the reptilian Mahars rule there.

Enslaved, Innes meets Dian the Beautiful, escapes, and fights the Mahars, who paralyze victims in their temple before eating them. The contents promise slavery, freedom, pursuit, and a return to earth. Published in 1914, the novel launched Burroughs's Pellucidar series and mixes lost-world adventure with his usual swift, cliff-hanging pace.
babylonian-and-assyrian-literature:
Epiphanius Wilson edited this anthology of Mesopotamian writing, issued in a revised edition in 1901. The title page promises the Epic of Izdubar, hymns, tablets, and cuneiform inscriptions, with Wilson's special introduction. Izdubar is the hero readers now know as Gilgamesh, in the early translation that first carried the flood story to a wide public.

Wilson explains how Assyrian scribes wrote fast on clay with a bevelled stylus, each stroke a narrow wedge. Skilled hands turned off vast amounts of copy for kings and temples. Hymns follow in stately rendering: a noble ruler, king of the gods, opens canals and treads the wide earth, nourishing heaven and earth. The volume captures the first excitement of decipherment, when Babylonian texts were new wonders in English dress.
beatrix-of-clare:
John Reed Scott published this romance of Richard the Third's England in 1907, here in the Grosset and Dunlap reprint with illustrations by Clarence F. Underwood. Scott had won his public with The Colonel of the Red Huzzars. Ruddy tresses and great eyes introduce Beatrix, Countess of Clare, while Richard of Gloucester takes the second chapter and the story's dark centre.

Sir Aymer de Lacy serves as the knightly hero, summoned with Sir Ralph de Wilton while Richard paces alone after supper, watching a crowded courtyard from an open window. Arrests, a wayside skirmish, the queen of archery, and Buckingham's revenge drive the plot through Windsor and Northampton. Scott writes the Wars of the Roses as cloak-and-sword romance, with Richard fascinating and dangerous at its heart, two years before Bosworth settles every fate.
beautiful-stories-from-shakespeare:
E Nesbit retold twenty of Shakespeare's plays as Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare, opening with Dr Johnson's praise that Shakespeare alone gave his country more practical wisdom than all his successors. Her preface calls his works the richest and fairest uninspired genius ever penned, instruction delivered through delight. A brief life of Shakespeare precedes the tales.

A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Tempest, As You Like It, King Lear, and Romeo and Juliet lead the contents, each play compressed into clear prose for young readers. Macbeth demanding which of them has placed Banquo's ghost in his chair shows her fidelity to the drama. Nesbit's versions, like Lamb's Tales before them, started generations toward the plays themselves.
bismarck-and-the-foundation-of-the-germa:
James Wycliffe Headlam wrote this life of Bismarck for a heroes-of-the-nations series, copyrighted in 1899. Most pages were finished before the Prince's death; Headlam apologises for the year's delay and warns that Busch's memoirs, lately published, have been much exaggerated as a source. A Lenbach portrait fronts the volume, under Ovid's line that the hero's deeds and hard-won fame shall live.

Schleswig-Holstein gives the sampled crisis. Austria, lenient in Holstein, allowed full press freedom and a mass meeting of four thousand men at Altona. The King took offence, and any Austrian act that offended the King was most useful to Bismarck. Headlam writes the cool English account: the three wars, the empire proclaimed at Versailles, and the chancellor's system weighed by a historian who admired the statecraft and distrusted the man.
black-bartlemy-s-treasure:
Jeffery Farnol published this pirate romance in 1920, dedicating it to his two nephews. Martin Conisby, the narrator, begins on Pembury Hill and hears a song in the wood at midnight. Contents in the old style tell how he stole his breakfast, met Adam Penfeather, came to Conisby Shene, and heard tell of Black Bartlemy's treasure. A blood-brotherhood oath and a fight in the dark launch the voyage.

Aboard ship, Martin crouches chin on fist, scowling across tempestuous waters, cursing Penfeather and all his works. His companion, the Lady Joan Brandon in disguise, reads him like weather: you frown, Martin, though the storm is done and we alive. Have patience. Farnol writes the treasure hunt as his readers loved it — archaic talk, a nameless black ship dogging the Faithful Friend, and honour among thieves tested chapter by chapter.
books-and-culture:
Hamilton Wright Mabie published Books and Culture with Dodd, Mead and Company of New York, under an 1896 copyright. Mabie writes for the common reader who wants more from books than passing amusement. Twenty-four short chapters build one plea for reading as a way of life.

Early chapters treat method, time, and place, then the first delight of a real book. Mabie argues that great books free the mind from its own time and place. Tragedy, fiction, and action each teach in their own way, he holds. A chapter on village narrowness shows what reading cures. The close looks back over the whole path to a wider life. Mabie's calm, warm counsel suited the self-taught readers of his day.
brandes-main-currents-in-19th-century-li:
Georg Brandes opens his landmark survey of European writing with The Emigrant Literature, here in English. Exiles driven out by revolt carried new ideas from land to land after the French Revolution. The Danish critic treats their books as sparks in a broad fire.

Brandes links life, politics, and art in one flowing account. He asks how writers in exile shaped the taste of a whole continent. Later volumes would take up France, Germany, and England in turn. This first book launched a six-volume work that changed how Europe read its own nineteenth century.
bright-wits-prince-of-mogadore:
Burren Loughlin and L L Flood made Bright-Wits, Prince of Mogadore, a puzzle tale copyrighted by H M Caldwell in 1909. Loughlin sends Prince Bright-Wits to Parrabang, where the beautiful Azalia waits. Marriage hangs on tasks set by the plotters Garrofat and Doola.

Each chapter poses a working puzzle: a rug to read, eight provinces to bound, three fountains and three gates to plumb. Onalba's game, nine disks, and an endless chain test the prince in turn. Ablano the Brahman counsels patience when jealousy bites. The last decree of Onalba fells the plotters, and Bright-Wits wins his bride. A closing part prints full solutions. Children could race the prince, pencil in hand, through every task.
britannica-1911-aberdare:
Aberdare receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Glamorgan market town stands where the Dâr meets the Cynon above the Taff. Its urban district held 43,365 folk in 1901, fed by rail from Cardiff and London.

A mere village in 1800, the town grew tenfold in fifty years on coal and iron. Ironworks at Llwydcoed and Abernant rose in 1799 and 1800, then died by 1875. Steam coal for export, begun in 1836, became the town's chief support. Fifty acres of park, a dozen Anglican churches, and over fifty Welsh chapels mark its civic life. Cairns and a British camp crown the mountain toward Merthyr.
britannica-1911-aberdeenshire:
Aberdeenshire receives a county entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The north-eastern Scottish county fronts the North Sea for sixty-five miles and ranks sixth in area. Five districts divide it: Mar, Formartine, Buchan, Garioch the granary, and Strathbogie.

Ben Macdhui at 4,296 feet, second height in Britain, crowns the Grampian mass in Mar. Lochnagar, Bennachie, and the Buck of Cabrach mark the skyline. Dee, Don, Ythan, Ugie, and Deveron carry salmon and trout, and pearl mussels in the Ythan gave a pearl to the Scottish crown, the entry says. Bullers of Buchan boil through a sea arch on the coast. Schists, limestone, and quartzite form the rock frame, cut by later igneous masses. Chalybeate springs at Peterhead and Pannanich close the survey.
britannica-1911-acre-land-measure:
Acre is a land measure used by English-speaking peoples. The word comes from Old English acer. It is kin to Latin ager and Greek agros. All carry the sense of open country. Phrases like God's acre keep that sense alive. As a measure, an acre first meant a day's ploughing. It was the land a yoke of oxen could plough in a day.

Statutes fixed the value over centuries. Edward I, Edward III, and Henry VIII all legislated. The Act of 1878 now defines the acre. It contains four thousand eight hundred and forty square yards. Local acres survive in a few places, though. The Scottish acre is larger than the statute acre. The Irish acre is larger still. Welsh and county measures vary widely.
britannica-1911-acupressure: Acupressure is a method of restraining haemorrhage, or bleeding, introduced by Sir James Young Simpson. Its name joins the Latin acus, a needle, and premere, to press. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single sentence: the direct pressure of a metallic needle, used alone or assisted by a loop of wire, closes the vessel near the bleeding point. The whole technique is in that sentence — pressure from a needle, precisely placed, doing the work of stopping the flow.
britannica-1911-acupuncture:
Acupuncture is a surgical operation performed with a needle. The name joins Latin words for needle and pricking. The needle pricks the part affected. Chinese practitioners have used the method for ages. Their cases include headaches and lethargies. Convulsions and colics were treated the same way. The 1911 Britannica entry is very brief. It records the technique and its Chinese history. No theory of why it works is offered.

Readers are sent to the article on surgery. Fuller treatment of the operation belongs there. The entry's value lies in its plain record. Western medicine in 1911 knew the practice existed. It knew the complaints acupuncture claimed to treat.
britannica-1911-agriculture:
Agriculture is the science, art, and industry of the soil. Its name joins Latin words for field and cultivation. It produces the means of human subsistence. Livestock rearing stands inside its widest sense. Crop raising stands there as its core. The entry calls its history man's most permanent story. Antiquity ascribed agriculture a divine origin. Brahma, Isis, Demeter, and Ceres founded it in men's tales.

Stages of progress structure the survey. Exhausting one patch then abandoning it came first. Fallow and manure made permanent fields possible. Antiquity practised intensive culture in developed form. New plants later dispensed with bare fallow. Science then revolutionized husbandry through soil knowledge. The huge article's sections cover crops, livestock, machinery, and wages. America receives a closing section of its own.
britannica-1911-ajmere:
Ajmere, or Ajmer, is a city of British India in Rajputana. It gives its name to a district and to a small province, Ajmere-Merwara. The city lies on the low slopes of Taragarh hill in the Aravalli range. To the north lies a large lake made by man, the Anasagar. The city draws its water supply from that lake.

The chief sight is the tomb of a famed Muslim saint, Mayud-uddin. The tomb stands at the foot of Taragarh hill in a block of white marble halls. The emperor Akbar walked from Agra to this shrine with his empress, in keeping with a vow made as he prayed for a son. Tall pillars set two miles apart still mark his daily halts on the way. An old Jain temple, now a mosque, stands on the same hill slope.
britannica-1911-allix-pierre:
Pierre Allix, who lived from 1641 to 1717, was a French Protestant divine born at Alencon. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from a Champagne pastorate to Charenton near Paris. When the edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685 he fled to London for safety. There, with the leave of James the Second, he opened a church for French exiles.

His learning won him divinity degrees from both universities soon after arrival in England. In 1690 Bishop Burnet gave him a treasurer post and a canonry at Salisbury. He died in London in March 1717 after a life of exile and study. His many works plead the Protestant cause and must be used with care.
britannica-1911-anglo-norman-literature:
Anglo-Norman literature is the French-language literature of England after the Norman Conquest. French came over with William the Conqueror and shared with Latin the standing of England's literary language through the whole twelfth century, remaining in use at court until the fourteenth. Not until Henry IV's reign did English become the native tongue of England's kings.

After England lost its French provinces, schools taught French at places like Marlborough, yet the language slowly changed under individual authors until an Anglo-Norman language, properly so called, ceased to exist. One fourteenth-century writer still praised French as the most beautiful and gracious language in the world after school Latin. The long survey that follows works through genres and authors across three centuries, with manuscripts, romances, chronicles, and religious writing, and closes with a substantial bibliography of French, English, and Swedish scholarship.
britannica-1911-anna-baldasarre:
Baldasarre Anna was a painter of Venice. He flourished across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His birth came probably about 1560. Flemish descent is said of him. The date of his death is uncertain. He seems alive still in 1639. Leonardo Corona was his teacher for years. Corona's death left works unfinished. Anna completed several of those paintings.

His own activity stayed within Venice. Churches there received most of his pieces. A few private houses held others. Old guide-books notice many paintings by him. Descriptions of the city list them in numbers. Scarcely any have survived, though. The entry is short and frankly sparse. It records a once-visible local painter. Time has erased nearly all his work.
britannica-1911-apollonius-of-tyre:
Apollonius of Tyre, a tale from the middle ages thought to come from a lost Greek source, is summed up in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first known note of the story is in the sixth century. The romance may date from three centuries before that. It shows a marked likeness to a Greek tale by Xenophon of Ephesus.

King Antiochus guards a dark secret about his daughter by a riddle that costs failed suitors their heads. Apollonius solves it and flees the king wrath by sea. He weds a king daughter in Cyrene, then loses her at sea in childbirth. His daughter Tarsia is left with false guardians at Tarsus. Father, mother, and child meet again only after fourteen years apart.
britannica-1911-arboriculture:
Arboriculture is the science and art of tree cultivation. Food crops occupied human attention for ages. Domestic animals' fodder did the same. Timber came from native woods meanwhile. Houses, ships, and machines used that timber. Fuel also came from wild forest. Egyptians practised fruit-tree culture early. Greeks and Romans did likewise occasionally. Ornamental trees and shrubs received some care.

Large-scale timber cultivation is modern, though. Charlemagne's France was mostly immense forest. He rooted up portions of it beneficially. Orchards and vineyards replaced cleared woodland. Germany formed artificial plantations early, apparently. The fifteenth century saw them begin there. Britain began planting a century later. Henry VIII's church land seizures changed matters. New owners sold much timber quickly. Prices fell from the glut, Hollingshed reports. The entry points to the forestry articles for details.
britannica-1911-argyllshire:
Argyllshire is a large county on the west coast of Scotland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ranks it second in size among Scottish counties. Sea lochs cut deep into its coast at many points. Mainland districts and Hebridean islands both fall within its bounds in full.

Named districts run from Ardnamurchan in the west to Cowall in the east. Kintyre forms a long thin peninsula toward Ireland in the south. No rivers in the county can bear boats, the entry notes. Mountain streams such as the Orchy and Awe drain its lochs instead. Mull, Islay, Jura, Staffa, and Iona count among its chief islands.
britannica-1911-armoire:
Armoire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a tall movable cupboard, taking its French name. It has one or more doors, and its shape and size have varied greatly over time. The carving of its doors and sides has faithfully followed shifts in fashion and in use, the entry says.

At first these cupboards were very heavy, with chief ornament in hinges and locks of beaten iron. Finer church pieces, used to keep vestments, vessels, and relics safe, were often painted with sacred scenes. Some were painted inside as well. The cathedrals of Bayeux and Noyon hold famed examples, and York holds the most typical English one. By the end of the fourteenth century, carving was taking the place of paint.
britannica-1911-atmosphere:
Atmosphere, from Greek words for vapour and sphere, is the airy envelope around the earth, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article surveys what was known of it. The word also names the envelope of gas about any solid or liquid. Weather events seated in the air drew notice early. Hesiod guessed at the origin of winds from the sun's heating of the air. Greek thinkers founded pneumatics on observed properties of air.

Anaximenes made air the first substance of all things. Galileo gave direct proof of its material nature by weighing a ball of compressed air. Before the rise of pneumatic chemistry, air was held a single element. Studies of burning later showed it is chiefly a mix of two gases, oxygen and nitrogen. Cavendish measured their shares from more than 500 tests.
britannica-1911-auxerre:
Auxerre is a town of central France. It is capital of the Yonne department. Sens lies thirty-eight miles north-north-west. The Paris-Lyon railway serves it between Laroche and Nevers. Population in 1906 was 16,971. The town climbs an eminence's slopes and summit. The Yonne's left bank holds it. Two bridges lead to right-bank suburbs. Streets are steep, narrow, and irregular.

Wide tree-lined boulevards surround the town pleasantly. They replaced the ancient fortifications completely. St Étienne, the former cathedral, is a fine church. It is a majestic Gothic building. Its fabric spans the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries. Three richly sculptured portals admit visitors. A rose window crowns the middle portal. One massive tower rises over the north portal. Its southern counterpart is unfinished. An eleventh-century crypt extends beneath the choir. Twelfth-century mural paintings decorate that crypt.
britannica-1911-ayrshire:
Ayrshire is a south-western county of Scotland fronting the Firth of Clyde, with seventy miles of coast and an area of 1,142 square miles. Old districts still name its parts: Cunninghame in the north, Kyle in the middle, and Carrick in the south, where Robert Bruce held an earldom.

Hills rise modestly, Black Craig topping them at 2,298 feet, while no river is navigable. Six streams win fame for quiet beauty, the Ayr longest at some thirty-eight miles, and Burns's verse lifted lesser burns like the Afton and Lugar above them. Loch Doon is the largest lake. Ailsa Craig and smaller islands stand off the coast, and the county splits for politics into North and South Ayrshire.
britannica-1911-azure: Azure comes, through the Romance languages, from the Arabic al-lazward, the name of the precious stone lapis lazuli, its first letter l having dropped away in the passage between tongues. The word thus names first the stone itself, lapis lazuli, and then, from the stone, its colour: blue. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry rests on that double sense, a gem and the deep blue taken from it.
britannica-1911-bagneres-de-bigorre:
Bagnères-de-Bigorre is a town of south-western France. It is capital of an arrondissement in the Hautes-Pyrénées. The town stands on the Adour's left bank, at the Campan valley's end. Fine mountain scenery surrounds it. Its 1906 population was 6,661, more than doubled in the season from May to October.

Some fifty mineral springs make it one of France's chief watering places. They are rich in sulphate of lime or iron. They run from 59 to 122 degrees. Rheumatism, nervous troubles, and indigestion bring visitors to them. Marble ornaments many houses, and marble working, woollen weaving, and barège cloth making employ the town. Romans frequented it as Vicus Aquensis; a 12th-century count gave it a liberal charter, and its baths rose for good in the 1500s.
britannica-1911-balasore:
Balasore was a town and district of British India, in the Orissa division of Bengal. The town stands on the right bank of the Burabalang river, a short way inland from the sea. English traders settled there in 1642, close to an even earlier post at Pippli.

The 1911 Britannica entry tells how those traders built a strong post and dealt in cotton goods and muslins, and how the town later fell back as sand blocked the river mouth. It then moves to the district itself, a strip of low land between hills and sea, and gives its size, crops, and people.
britannica-1911-baltard-louis-pierre:
Louis Pierre Baltard (1764–1846) was a French architect and engraver, born in Paris on 9 July 1764. He began as a landscape painter. Travel in Italy, and the beauty of its buildings, turned him toward architecture, where he won great success and planned some of the largest public buildings in Paris.

Yet his fame rests chiefly on engraving. The 1911 Britannica entry names his plates of Paris and its monuments. It also names his work for Denon's book on Egypt. His series on Napoleon's wars and on the Grand Prix de l'Architecture, carried on alone for a time, get mention too. He also cut portraits. Two of his children became architects, Victor Baltard the better known.
britannica-1911-baltimore:
Baltimore is a city and seaport in Maryland, in the United States, ranked seventh in the country by population. It stands at the head of tide-water on the Patapsco river, where its branches form an estuary reaching twelve miles to Chesapeake Bay. The city lies 40 miles by rail from Washington and 97 miles from Philadelphia.

Its people numbered 508,957 in 1900 and 558,485 in 1910, among them many German, Russian, and Irish born residents, the entry records. Railways such as the Baltimore and Ohio and steamship lines to Atlantic and foreign ports made it a great trade hub. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, goes on to the city's streets, history, trade, and public life in full detail.
britannica-1911-bancroft-sir-squire:
Sir Squire Bancroft (born 1841) was an English actor and manager, born near London on 14 May 1841. He first trod the stage at Birmingham in 1861 and played the provinces with success for years. London saw him first in 1865, at the Prince of Wales's theatre under Effie Marie Wilton, whom he married in 1868.

Together the Bancrofts staged all the Robertson comedies, from Society in 1865 to M.P. in 1870, and later revivals of older plays with a fine company. The 1911 Britannica entry calls their management of the little Prince of Wales's a new era for the English stage, reviving London interest in modern drama. In 1879 they moved to the Haymarket theatre.
britannica-1911-banffshire:
Banffshire is a north-eastern county of Scotland, bounded by the Moray Firth to the north, Aberdeenshire to the east and south, and Elgin and Inverness to the west. It covers 403,364 acres. The northern half is mostly fine, open, rolling country with rich, well-farmed soil. The south is mountainous, though its glens hold wide farms.

Cairngorm, on the county's edge, rises 4,084 feet and is famous for the amber quartz crystals sold as cairngorms in Scots jewellery. Ben Rinnes and Corryhabbie are among the other heights named. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, treats the county's rivers too. The Spey and Deveron form its borders. Shorter streams such as the Avon, Fiddich, and Isla are stocked with trout.
britannica-1911-bangalore:
Bangalore is a city of India, capital of the native state of Mysore and the largest British cantonment in the south of India. It stands 3,113 feet above the sea and 219 miles west of Madras by rail. Its population in 1901 was 69,447.

The founding of the present fort is laid to a descendant of Kempe Goude, a farmer of the neighbourhood. In the 1500s Goude left his village to escape a local ruler's tyranny. He settled a few miles north of the present city. His family built forts at Bangalore and Savendrug, then lost the place to Bijapur. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, traces the city's passage through the hands of Shahji's family and later powers.
britannica-1911-bangor-carnarvonshire:
Bangor is a city and seaport of Carnarvonshire in north Wales, 240 miles north-west of London by rail, with 11,269 people in 1901. Once called Bangor Fawr to set it apart from other Bangors, it lies near the northern entrance of the Menai Straits and draws many visitors. Upper and Lower Bangor make up the town, the Lower being practically one street.

Its small cathedral stands where a church attributed to St Deiniol, from about 525, once stood. Burned and wrecked across the centuries, it was restored by Sir Gilbert Scott in 1866–1875. The 1911 Britannica entry also names the University College of North Wales, founded in 1883, and points to Lord Penrhyn's great slate quarries at Bethesda, six miles off.
britannica-1911-barbed-wire:
Barbed wire is a fence wire with sharp points fixed into twisted strands. Its farm entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The form was first urged for the western states of America by need. Large cattle herds ranged where timber for wood fences was scarce there.

Plain iron wire stretched in heat and snapped in cold on the frontier. Cattle rubbed smooth fences, loosened posts, and broke the wire in time. Farm hands sought a wire that stock would learn to avoid at once. Their work led to barbed wire, then to machines that set barbs fast. Cheap machine made wire soon won favour with farmers round the world.
britannica-1911-barre:
Barre, a city in Washington county, Vermont, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a granite town about six miles south-east of Montpelier. Its population reached 10,734 in the 1910 census, and railways plus electric street lines linked it with the state capital. The township around it was settled after the War of Independence, organized in 1793, and named for Isaac Barré, who had defended American rights in the British parliament.

Granite work dominates the entry. Barre made monuments and tombstones, stone-cutting tools, and other machinery, and those memorial stones made up most of the value of its factory output in 1905. The city also had the Aldrich public library, Goddard Seminary, a granite statue of Burns raised by local Scots in 1899, and waterworks owned by the city itself. The city charter dates from 1894.
britannica-1911-barriere-theodore:
Théodore Barrière (1823–1877), a French dramatist born in Paris, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from a family of map engravers tied to the war department, and he spent nine years in that same service himself. A vaudeville staged at the Beaumarchais theatre, then taken up at once by the Palais Royal, showed him that playwriting was his real calling.

His output over the next thirty years was large. Alone or with partners, Barrière signed more than a hundred plays. Named successes include La Vie de bohème in 1849, worked on with Henri Murger from Murger's own book, Manon Lescaut, Les Filles de marbre, Les Faux Bonshommes, and Le Gascon. One play, Malheureux vaincus, was banned by the censor. Barrière died in Paris in October 1877.
britannica-1911-baudelaire-charles-pierr:
Charles Pierre Baudelaire (1821–1867), a French poet born in Paris, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. His father died in 1827; his mother soon wed Aupick, later an ambassador. Baudelaire was schooled at Lyons and at the Collège Louis-le-Grand. On leaving in 1839 he chose a life of letters. His wild living led his guardians to ship him to India in 1841 to mend his habits.

Art and scandal mark his work. His Salons of 1845 and 1846 drew notice for bold new views on art. Slow and fussy in writing, he brought out his great book of poems, Les Fleurs du mal, only in 1857. Its craft won a small public, but its dark choice of subjects, drawn from sickness, vice, and death, made the book a by-word for unwholesomeness with staid critics. He also gave France its Poe, in renderings praised as masterpieces of translation.
britannica-1911-beaucaire:
Beaucaire, a town of south-eastern France, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the department of Gard, on the right bank of the Rhone. Tarascon faces it across the river, joined by two handsome bridges. The census of 1906 counted 7,284 people there.

Above the town, a rocky pine-clad hill holds the remains of a counts' château. Its chapel, dedicated to St Louis, shows fine sculpture of the Romanesque end. Beaucaire's fame rests on its great July fair, held since the twelve hundreds. That fair has now lost its former weight in trade. The town is still a working port on the Rhone. Wine and freestone from nearby quarries fill its water-borne commerce. Its industries include distilling, furniture making, and food trades. The site is that of the Roman town of Ugernum.
britannica-1911-bed-furniture:
Bed is a general term for a resting or sleeping place, and a long entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the bedstead through history. The word is a common Teutonic one, perhaps linked to a root meaning to dig, a dug-out place for safe rest. Bedding and coverings have varied greatly across the ages.

The entry begins with the Egyptians, who used high bedsteads climbed by steps, with bolsters, curtains, and head-rests of stone, wood, or metal. Assyrians, Medes, and Persians had like beds, often inlaid with metal, mother-of-pearl, and ivory. The Greek bed had a wooden frame with hide bands laced across it, and later beds were veneered with costly woods or made of solid ivory.
britannica-1911-bedfordshire:
Bedfordshire, a small shire in the south midlands of England, fills a land entry in the 1911 Britannica. It ranks as the fourth least shire in the land by size. The River Ouse winds through its rich vale past the town of Bedford. Low waves of land rise north of that vale. A spur of the Chiltern Hills parts the vale from a flat side vale to the south.

Rock lore takes up most of the shown text in fine points. Clay beds of the mid oolite group rule the low north ground. Sand beds form a high tract from Woburn through Ampthill to Potton. Sand is dug at large scale at Leighton Buzzard for trade. Beds of fuller earth sit in that sand tract at Woburn.
britannica-1911-bedsore:
A bedsore is a sore caused by long lying in bed. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties it to pressure and to sweat and dirt on the skin. It strikes folk kept in bed by sickness or old age. Weak feeding of the tissues sets the stage for it. The more helpless the patient, the greater the risk. Those who cannot feel or move are in most danger.

Good nursing is the entry's whole answer. In large hospitals the sore had become a rarity by 1911. The bed must be firm and smooth, with sheets changed when soiled. The patient's pose must shift often from the first day. Parts under pressure are washed, dried, and dusted with zinc powder four times a day. A water pillow or a ring of felt eases the load on bone.
britannica-1911-beljame-alexandre:
Alexandre Beljame (1842–1906) was a French writer born at Villiers-le-Bel, near Paris. Part of his childhood was spent in England, and he kept visiting London all his life. At the Sorbonne a chair was made for him, and his lectures there did much to spread the study of English writing in France.

Beljame gave the Clark lectures at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1905–1906, the year before his death at Domont. His best known book studies literary life in England in the 1700s through Dryden, Addison and Pope, and the French Academy crowned it in 1897. His editions of Macbeth, Othello and Julius Caesar also won a prize.
britannica-1911-bellaire:
Bellaire is a city of Belmont county, Ohio, on the Ohio river, five miles south of Wheeling, West Virginia. Its people numbered 9,934 in 1890 and 12,946 by 1910. Three railways serve it: the Baltimore & Ohio, the Pennsylvania, and the Ohio River & Western.

Bellaire ships out the coal of the Belmont field, which in 1907 yielded nearly a fifth of all Ohio’s coal. Iron, limestone and fireclay lie near, and its works make iron and steel, glass, enamelled ware, farm tools and stoves. Settled about 1795 and laid out in 1836, the place became a village in 1858 and a city in 1874.
britannica-1911-belon-pierre:
Pierre Belon (1517–1564) was a French naturalist born near Le Mans. He took a doctor’s degree in medicine at Paris, then studied under the botanist Valerius Cordus at Wittenberg and travelled Germany with him. Cardinal de Tournon then funded a great scientific journey for him.

From 1546 to 1549 Belon crossed Greece, Asia Minor, Egypt, Arabia and Palestine, and printed a full illustrated account in 1553. His books on strange fishes, on water animals and on birds give him a place among the first workers in comparative anatomy. Favoured by two French kings, he was murdered one April evening in 1564 in the Bois de Boulogne.
britannica-1911-benoit-de-sainte-more:
Benoît de Sainte-More was a French trouvère, or verse-maker, of the twelfth century, probably from Sainte-Maure in Touraine. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his title of maître, which hints at university training. He was a loyal man of Henry II of England and wrote at that king’s court.

Two great works carry Benoît’s name. His Roman de Troie retells the fall of Troy, and scholars credit him with the Chronique des ducs de Normandie, a poem of over forty thousand lines. That chronicle carries the Norman dukes from Rollo to Henry I, a task Henry II seems to have taken from Wace and given to him. The likeness of handling between the two poems is the main proof they share one author.
britannica-1911-bent-james-theodore:
James Theodore Bent (1852–1897) was an English traveller born at Baildon House near Leeds, son of James Bent. Repton and Wadham College, Oxford, schooled him, and he graduated in 1875. His wife Mabel, married in 1877, went with him on every journey that followed.

Bent wrote on San Marino, Genoa and Garibaldi, then on the Greek islands in The Cyclades. From 1885 he turned to digging and field research, working in Asia Minor and the Bahrein Islands, where he found signs of an early Phoenician home. A year in South Africa followed, and his claims for a Semitic origin of the Mashonaland ruins won pioneer credit, though scholars rejected the theory itself.
britannica-1911-berlin-new-hampshire:
Berlin, New Hampshire, is a city on the Androscoggin River in the northern part of the state, about 98 miles northwest of Portland, Maine. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its growth in figures: 3,729 people in 1890, 8,886 in 1900, and 11,780 in the 1910 census, served by the Grand Trunk and Boston and Maine railways.

Set in the White Mountains, 16 miles from the base of Mount Washington, the city grew on water power from Berlin Falls. Its sawmills, pulp and paper mills, and sulphite fibre mills drew timber from New England and Quebec; factory output in 1905 was valued at $5,989,119.
britannica-1911-berryer-antoine-pierre:
Antoine Pierre Berryer (1790–1868) was a French advocate and parliamentary orator. His father was an eminent advocate to the parlement. Berryer studied at the Collège de Juilly and entered the law. He was admitted advocate in 1811. Like his father he was an ardent Legitimist. In 1815 he followed Louis XVIII to Ghent as a volunteer.

The 1911 Britannica entry charts his fame in hard political trials. He helped defend Marshal Ney, and won acquittal for General Cambronne. He defended journalists in many press cases. He spoke boldly for press freedom against harsh police measures. His long career closed with protest at the coup of 1851. He entered the French Academy in 1854 and died in 1868.
britannica-1911-berthier-louis-alexandre:
Louis Alexandre Berthier (1753–1815), Prince of Neuchâtel, was a French marshal and Napoleon's chief of staff. He was born at Versailles, son of an officer of engineers. He entered the army at seventeen. He served in the staff, the engineers, and dragoons in turn. In 1780 he sailed to North America with Rochambeau. By 1796 he was chief of staff to the army of Italy under Bonaparte.

The 1911 Britannica entry gives him a clear, limited verdict. His power of work, accuracy, and mastery of detail made him the ideal chief of staff. He was not a great commander on his own, as Bavaria showed in 1809. His fame rests on carrying out Napoleon's orders to the smallest point. He died in 1815, in uncertain circumstances.
britannica-1911-berwickshire:
Berwickshire is a Scottish county at the country's south-eastern corner. The North Sea bounds it north and east, the Tweed and Roxburghshire south. Its area is 457 square miles, with 21 miles of coast. The 1911 Britannica article divides it into three districts. Lauderdale is the valley of the Leader in the west. Lammermuir is the northern upland, and the Merse is the large southern lowland.

The Lammermuir hills are round-backed, averaging about 1,000 feet. Says Law, the highest summit, reaches 1,749 feet. The coast is lofty and rocky, broken by ravines. Only Eyemouth harbour takes small vessels along it. St Abb's Head, with its lighthouse, rises to 310 feet. The article then covers rivers, towns, history, and border affairs at length.
britannica-1911-beza-theodore:
Theodore Beza (1519-1605) was a French theologian and the heir of Calvin at Geneva, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his path. He was born at Vezelai in Burgundy, the son of a local bailli, and was raised by an uncle in Paris. The uncle placed him under Melchior Wolmar, who had taught Greek to Calvin and grounded Beza in Scripture from a Protestant view. Beza then studied law at Orleans and began practice in Paris.

Though not in orders, he held two church livings, and he printed a book of loose Latin verses that he later regretted. A grave illness changed his course: he married and in October 1548 joined Calvin's church at Geneva. In 1549 he became professor of Greek at Lausanne. There he served as Calvin's right hand in print, including a defence of the burning of Servetus in 1554.
britannica-1911-bonfire:
Bonfire began as bone-fire, a fire of bones. The entry digs into the word before the custom. Early English used bone-fire, and Scots used bane-fire. The bone spelling held on until about 1760. The earliest proof of the sense is ban fyre, in the Catholicon Anglicum of 1483. Its Latin gloss means fire of bones.

Other guesses at the word's birth are set out and rejected. One derives it from Baal-fire. Another makes it boon-fire, a fire built from neighbours' gifts. The meanings are then sorted into four. A fire of bones comes first. A corpse fire, or funeral pile, comes next. Third is a fire for burning heretics or banned books. Fourth is a great open-air fire for national joy. Such fires also served as alarm signals. The beacons lit against the Armada are the case in point.
britannica-1911-bore:
Bore, as a tidal wave, is a high wall of water that rushes up a narrowing river mouth, and the entry opens with the Severn's famous example. There the tide rises 18 feet in an hour and a half. Squeezed in the funnel-shaped estuary, the water heaps into a wave running from bank to bank, also seen at its best in the Bay of Fundy.

The word's root is guessed to be a Scandinavian term for a wave, and its other name, eagre, is of unknown birth. The entry then parts company with sound-alike words: the bore that drills holes, the bore of a gun that gives its calibre, and the tiresome person called a bore. Each is treated as its own word with its own history.
britannica-1911-borgia-cesare:
Cesare Borgia (1476–1507), duke of Valentinois and Romagna, was the favourite son of Pope Alexander VI by Vanozza dei Cattanei. Born at Rome while his father was still a cardinal, he was made archbishop of Valencia on Alexander's election in 1492 and a cardinal a year later. The pope's family favouritism was practised most of all for him.

In his father's first years Cesare lived wildly at the Vatican. Sent as hostage with Charles VIII toward Naples in 1495, he escaped at Velletri. In 1497 his brother Giovanni, duke of Gandia, was murdered, and the deed was laid, in all likelihood rightly, to Cesare. The long entry follows his giving up the cardinal's hat, his French marriage and dukedom, his conquest of the Romagna, and his fall and death in Spain after his father's death.
britannica-1911-bouguer-pierre:
Pierre Bouguer (1698–1758) was a French mathematician who made some of the first measures of light. His father John Bouguer, a noted hydrographer, held the royal chair of hydrography at Croisic in Brittany and wrote on navigation. In 1713 the son, at fifteen, followed him in the chair.

Three academy prizes came his way in 1727 and after, for papers on the masting of ships and on observing star heights and compass variation at sea. In 1729 his Essai d'optique set out to measure how much light is lost passing through air. He found sunlight 300 times stronger than moonlight, an early step in photometry. He became professor at Havre in 1730 and associate geometer of the Academy, and invented a heliometer, the account goes on to tell.
britannica-1911-breconshire:
Breconshire, also called Brecknockshire, is an inland county in South Wales and the fourth largest county in Wales. Hills and high peaks ring it on the east and south, with the Vale of Usk cutting through at Crickhowell. Its best known summit, Pen y Fan, rises to 2910 feet, while Pen y Gader and Fan Brycheiniog both pass 2600 feet.

North of the Usk the land turns rougher, crossed by the Mynydd Eppynt range and stretches of barren hill country. The entry sets out the county bounds against Cardigan, Radnor, Monmouth, Glamorgan and Carmarthen, then works through its rivers, valleys and uplands in detail. Moist but mild weather and rich soil in the valleys make parts of it notably fertile.
britannica-1911-briare:
Briare is a town of north-central France in the department of Loiret. It stands on the right bank of the Loire. The rail line to Nevers puts it 45 and a half miles south-east of Orleans. In 1906 it held 4613 people. The Romans knew the place as Brivodorum.

Its place on the map turns on a canal. Briare stands at the end of the Canal of Briare, built from 1605 to 1642 and about 36 miles long, which links the Loire by the Loing to the Seine. Local work covers fine pottery and odd porcelain buttons made from felspar and milk by a method devised by Bapterosses, whose bust stands in town. Canal loads run to wood, iron, coal and building goods, and a canal bridge 720 yards long carries the side canal across the Loire.
britannica-1911-brissot-jacques-pierre:
Jacques Pierre Brissot (1754–1793), who took the added name de Warville, was a leading French Girondist born at Chartres in January 1754, where his father kept an inn. Well schooled, he entered a Paris law office. His first books, a theory of criminal laws (1781) and a philosophical library for the lawmaker (1782), dealt with legal thought and showed how deeply Rousseau's moral teaching had marked him.

Voltaire praised the first book, dedicated to him, and Brissot's quick pen won work on the Mercure, the Courrier de l'Europe and other papers. He dreamed of uniting all Europe's learned men and started a London paper as their voice, but the plan failed. Back in Paris he was lodged in the Bastille for a work against the government. Freed after four months, he wrote on, fled to London again, met leading abolitionists there, and later founded a society in Paris.
britannica-1911-brongniart-adolphe-theod:
Adolphe Theodore Brongniart (1801–1876) was a French botanist, son of the geologist Alexandre Brongniart, born in Paris on 14 January 1801. He showed an early bent for natural science, working first at geology and later at botany, training himself for what became his life's main task: the study of fossil plants. In 1826 he took a medical doctorate with a thesis on the Rhamnaceae, yet chose botany over medicine.

In 1831 he became assistant to Desfontaines at the Museum of Natural History. Two years later he succeeded him as professor. He held the chair until his death in Paris on 18 February 1876. A tireless worker and prolific writer, he left many books and memoirs. A paper of 1822 on the classification and distribution of fossil plants opened his line of research. It compared extinct with living forms. That line led toward his great history of fossil vegetables.
britannica-1911-brongniart-alexandre:
Alexandre Brongniart (1770–1847) was a French mineralogist and geologist born in Paris on 5 February 1770, son of the noted architect who designed the Bourse. He studied chemistry young under Lavoisier, passed through the Ecole des Mines and took honours at the Ecole de Medecine, then joined the army of the Pyrenees as a pharmacist. A slight political offence landed him in prison for a time.

Freed, he became professor of natural history at the College des Quatre Nations. In 1800 he was made director of the Sevres porcelain factory, a post he kept until death and where he did his greatest work. Under him Sevres became the leading porcelain factory in Europe. His team's research laid the foundations of ceramic chemistry. He also succeeded Hauy as professor of mineralogy in the Museum of Natural History, and his science ranged well past minerals alone.
britannica-1911-brumaire:
Brumaire was the second month of the republican calendar set up in France by a decree of the National Convention on 5 October of the year II, 1793. Its naming completed by Fabre d'Eglantine. The month began on 22 or 23 October of the old calendar and ended on 20 or 21 November. Like the other months it was divided into decades of ten days.

Its name alludes to the fogs and mists common at that time of year. One date made the word famous: the coup d'etat of the 18th Brumaire in the year VIII, 9 November 1799. By which General Bonaparte overthrew the Directory government and replaced it with the Consulate. The short entry closes by pointing readers to a study of the republican calendar in a journal of the French Revolution for 1884-1885.
britannica-1911-buchon-jean-alexandre:
Jean Alexandre Buchon (1791–1849) was a French scholar and editor. This 1911 Britannica entry sums up his work. He was born at Menetou-Salon on 21 May 1791. He died on 29 August 1849. He was an ardent Liberal under the Restoration. At the same time he joined the revival of historical study. He travelled Europe hunting old French chronicles.

His Collection of national chronicles ran to 47 volumes. It appeared between 1824 and 1829. After 1830 he founded the Panthéon littéraire series. It reprinted mystics, Greek historians and French memoirs. His travels in Italy and the East led him further. He studied the medieval French settlements in Greece. His books on the Morea broke new ground there. The entry grants that his work was not fully scholarly. Still, it served history well, and the eastern studies had real original value.
britannica-1911-buckinghamshire:
Buckinghamshire is a south midland county of England. Its short name is Bucks. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the whole county. Its area is 743.2 square miles. Northamptonshire bounds it to the north. Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Middlesex lie east. Berkshire and Surrey lie south, and Oxfordshire west.

Two river basins drain the county. The Ouse crosses the northern part. The Thames forms the whole southern boundary. The article describes the chalk hills of the south. It covers the chief towns and their trades. It gives the county's soil, farming and roads. It also treats railways, local government and history. Population figures and parish details close the survey. The result is a full county portrait of its period.
britannica-1911-caere:
Caere is an ancient city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Caere, the modern Cerveteri, was a city of Etruria in Italy. It stood about five miles from the sea and twenty miles from Rome. Its first name was Agylla, until the Etruscans took it and renamed it.

The entry follows the city's long dealings with Rome. Caere was one of the twelve cities of Etruria, with busy trade through its port. After the Gauls struck Rome in the year 390 before Christ, Rome's sacred objects were kept safe at Caere. War in the year 353 ended with Caere half absorbed into the Roman state. Its people held a limited citizenship without a vote, a status named from the town itself. The article is a compact guide to a city that stood between Etruscan and Roman worlds.
britannica-1911-cambridgeshire:
Cambridgeshire is a county article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an eastern county of England of 858.9 square miles. Lincolnshire bounds it on the north, Norfolk and Suffolk on the east, Essex and Hertfordshire on the south, and three more counties on the west. The greater part of the county falls within the Fens, flat land only a few feet above the sea and cut by endless drainage channels.

Away from the fens, the south and south east rise in gentle swells. The Gog Magog Hills near Cambridge and the low hill that carries Ely stand out from afar across the level. By its rocks the county splits into three regions: chalk uplands in the south, a clay and greensand belt in the south west, and the alluvial fenland over the rest.
britannica-1911-capital-architecture:
A capital is the crowning part of a column in architecture. The word comes from the Latin caput, meaning head. This 1911 Britannica article explains the member and its types. The capital flares out as the column rises. It carries the abacus above it. It joins the square abacus to the round shaft below. Its bulk can be convex, concave or bracketed out.

Those three forms define the great classical types. The Doric capital is convex in its bulk. The Corinthian bell is concave instead. The Ionic capital brackets outward to its volutes. All later capitals rest on these three types. The entry notes the capital's key place in building. It crowns every monumental column in view. For that reason it drew the richest ornament. It has become the clearest sign of any style. The earliest capitals copied the lotus and papyrus.
britannica-1911-capture:
Capture, in international law, is the seizure of a ship at sea. A belligerent vessel takes an enemy or neutral merchant ship. This short 1911 Britannica entry explains the rules. The French term is prise maritime. An enemy ship, once captured, becomes lawful prize at once. A neutral ship stands in a different position. Her papers may not settle her status.

If her papers are not conclusive, the captor may search her. Contraband on board gives grounds for seizure. So do papers or cargo that raise serious suspicion. The master must be given a chance to clear the doubt. If he fails, a prize crew boards the ship. They take her to the nearest port with a prize court. There her case is tried in proper form. The word capture also names the vessel so taken. The entry is signed by Thomas Barclay.
britannica-1911-cardiganshire:
Cardiganshire is a county of South Wales. Its Welsh names are Ceredigion and Sir Aberteifi. Its area is 688 square miles. It ranks fifth in size among the Welsh counties. Cardigan Bay, on the Irish Sea, bounds it west. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the county. Merioneth bounds it north, and Montgomery east. Carmarthen and Pembroke lie to the south.

The county is hilly or undulating almost throughout. Great bogs at Borth and Tregaron are the exception. Its mountains have little grandeur, the entry admits. Plinlimmon rises 2463 feet on the eastern boundary. Even it lacks boldness of outline, the article says. The river Teifi is by far its most important stream. It rises above Tregaron and crosses the county. The article covers towns, farming, roads and antiquities. It gives the county's history and its local government in turn.
britannica-1911-caricature:
Caricature is the art of ridicule in pictures. It applies the grotesque to the purposes of satire. This long 1911 Britannica article traces the art and its name. The Italian word caricatura means a ridiculous portrait. It comes from caricare, to load or charge. The French form of the term is charge. Sir Thomas Browne first used the word in English.

Browne used it in his Christian Morals, a posthumous work. It next appeared in the Spectator, still in Italian form. Johnson adopted it in his dictionary of 1757. It took its modern shape late in the 18th century. The article then turns to caricature among the ancients. Little there is certain, it warns the reader. Few traces of the comic survive in Egyptian art. Some satirical papyri are known, and are weighed. The article follows the art through Greece, Rome and the middle ages.
britannica-1911-carlyle-joseph-dacre:
Joseph Dacre Carlyle (1759–1804) was a British orientalist. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in Arabic studies. He was born at Carlisle, where his father was a physician. He went to Cambridge in 1775. In 1779 he was elected a fellow of Queens' College. A native of Bagdad, David Zamio, helped him learn Arabic. With that help he gained great proficiency in its literature.

In 1795 Carlyle became professor of Arabic at Cambridge. His translation of Yusuf ibn Taghri Birdi appeared in 1792. His Specimens of Arabic Poetry followed in 1796. It ran from the earliest times to the fall of the Caliphate. In 1799 he sailed as chaplain to Lord Elgin's embassy at Constantinople. He toured Asia Minor, Palestine, Greece and Italy on research. He gathered Greek and Syriac manuscripts on those travels. They were meant for a critical edition of the New Testament. He died in 1804 before that work could be finished.
britannica-1911-carmarthenshire:
Carmarthenshire is a county of South Wales. Its Welsh name is Sir Gaerfyrddin, or Sir Gar. Its area is 918 square miles. It is the largest of the South Welsh counties. Cardigan bounds it north, and Brecon and Glamorgan east. Pembroke lies west, and Carmarthen Bay south. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the county.

Almost the whole surface is hilly and irregular. Marsh and sandy burrows fringe the coast-line. The upper Towy valley scenery is praised as beautiful. The Black Mountains rise on the eastern border. Carmarthen Van, their peak, reaches 2632 feet. Few other hills in the county pass 1000 feet. The river Towy drains the central part of the county. Its tributaries include the Gwili, Cothi and Sawdde. The article covers towns, farming, coal and county history.
britannica-1911-carnarvonshire:
Carnarvonshire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a county of north Wales, bounded by the Irish Sea, Denbigh, Merioneth, and the Menai Straits. The county covers 565 square miles, and about half its length is the Lleyn peninsula, which runs south-west into the Irish Sea. Its mountains include Snowdon, at 3560 feet the highest summit in England and Wales, along with Carnedd Llewelyn and the Glydyr peaks.

The entry describes the Conwy, the county's largest river, and names Carnarvon, Pwllheli, and Llandudno among its principal towns. It notes rich minerals, including lead, copper, and some gold, and many good slate quarries. A closing history runs from the Segontiaci and Roman occupation through the kingdom of Gwynedd to Edward I, whose castles at Conwy, Carnarvon, and Criccieth still mark the county.
britannica-1911-castiglione-baldassare:
Baldassare Castiglione (1478-1529) was an Italian courtier and man of letters. He was born at Casanatico near Mantua and schooled at Milan under famed teachers. In 1496 he joined the service of Lodovico Sforza, duke of Milan. When Lodovico was taken to France as a prisoner in 1500, Castiglione went back to Mantua. In 1504 he joined the court of the duke of Urbino.

In 1506 the duke sent him on a task to Henry VII of England. After the duke died without a child in 1508, Castiglione served the next ruler of Urbino. He acted as envoy at the court of Pope Leo X. In 1524 he crossed to Spain to help settle a dispute between the pope and the emperor. There he was made bishop of Avila.
britannica-1911-caussin-de-perceval-arma:
Armand Pierre Caussin de Perceval (1795–1871) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French orientalist born in Paris. His father held the Arabic chair in the Collège de France. In 1814 the son went to Constantinople as a student interpreter. He then travelled in Asiatic Turkey, spent a year with the Maronites in the Lebanon, and became dragoman at Aleppo.

Back in Paris, he became professor of vulgar Arabic at the school of living Oriental languages in 1821 and at the Collège de France in 1833. The Academy of Inscriptions elected him in 1849, and he died in Paris during the siege in January 1871. His grammar of vulgar Arabic went through several editions. His great name, though, rests on one book: the Essai on the history of the Arabs before Islam and in the age of Mahomet, three volumes published from 1847 to 1849.
britannica-1911-cawnpore:
Cawnpore, also called Kanpur, is a city and district of British India in the United Provinces. A 1911 Britannica entry places it on the south bank of the Ganges river. From old times it stood as a frontier post for Oudh and Bengal folk. Clive chose it as the camp for troops lent by the nawab of Oudh.

In 1801 it became the chief British frontier station under the East India Company. By Mutiny time the frontier had moved on and troops had thinned there. Four railways meet at the city in the years the entry covers. Its trade in harness, shoes, and leather work leads the survey of its business.
britannica-1911-chandernagore:
Chandernagore, also spelled Chandarnagar, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places the French settlement in India on the right bank of the river Hugli, twenty miles above Calcutta. It gives the area as three square miles and the population in 1901 as twenty five thousand.

Inside, the article traces how the town became a lasting French settlement in 1688 and grew under Dupleix. It tells of an English fleet taking the town in 1757, of its return to France in 1763, and of a second English hold that ended in 1816. By 1911 its old trade had faded, and it read as a quiet suburb of Calcutta under the governor at Pondicherry.
britannica-1911-charente-inferieure:
Charente-Inferieure is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a department of France. It is a maritime department of the south west. It takes in the old provinces of Saintonge and Aunis. It also holds a small portion of Poitou. The islands of Re, Oleron, Aix, and Madame belong to it. Its area is given as 2791 square miles. A count from 1906 puts its people at 453,793.

Vendee and Deux-Sevres bound it on the north and north east. Charente, Dordogne, and Gironde bound its other sides. The Bay of Biscay washes its western coast. Plains and low hills occupy the interior land. The coast is flat and marshy in character. The department takes its name from the river Charente. That river crosses it for the last part of its course. The climate is temperate and, off the coast, healthy.
britannica-1911-charles-ii-king-of-navar:
