Charles II (1332-1387), called the Bad, was king of Navarre and count of Evreux. He was a son of Jeanne II, queen of Navarre, by her marriage to Philip, count of Evreux. He became king on his mother's death in 1349. He put down a rising at Pampeluna with great cruelty. Acts of that kind earned him his surname of the Bad in full.

In 1352 Charles wed Jeanne, a daughter of John II of France. The match tied him still closer to the French crown. Through his mother he was a grandson of Louis X. Through his father he was a great-grandson of Philip III. He thus had a claim to the throne of France. He also held lands under the French king's rule, whose son-in-law he now was. The article calls him able and well spoken, yet without scruple.
britannica-1911-chassesriau-theodore:
Théodore Chassériau (1819–1856) is the subject of a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French painter. He was born in the Antilles. He studied under Ingres at Paris and at Rome. Later he fell under the influence of Paul Delaroche. That double schooling shaped a painter who stood between two schools.

The entry calls him a well known painter of portraits and historical pieces. It names one work in particular. His “Tepidarium at Pompeii,” painted in 1853, is in the Louvre. The whole entry runs to a few lines. It gives the painter's birth and death years, his two masters, his field, and his best known canvas. Readers who want more must go beyond it, but the outline it leaves is exact as far as it goes.
britannica-1911-cheadle-cheshire:
Cheadle is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Cheshire, England, in the Altrincham parliamentary division. It stands six miles south of Manchester. It is included in the urban district of Cheadle and Gatley, which counted 7916 people in 1901. The entry calls it one of the many townships of modern growth that fringe the southern edge of Manchester. In effect they form suburbs of that city. Stockport lies just to the east.

The name survives in the formerly separate villages of Cheadle Hulme, Cheadle Bulkeley, and Cheadle Moseley. Cotton printing and bleaching works operate in the locality. The parish church of St Giles is built in the Perpendicular style. It contains an altar tomb of the fifteenth century for two knights. The short entry gives a mill and suburb township in Manchester's orbit, with one old church as its chief monument.
britannica-1911-cheadle-staffordshire:
Cheadle is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town in Staffordshire, England, in the Leek parliamentary division. It stands 13 miles north east of Stafford. It is the terminus of a branch line from Cresswell on the North Staffordshire railway. Its population in 1901 was 5186. The Roman Catholic church of St Giles, with a lofty spire, was designed by Pugin and built in 1846. Its interior is lavishly decorated.

Considerable collieries work in the neighbourhood. Silk and tape works operate in the town. In the nearby Froghall district limestone is quarried. Copper is manufactured there as well. Two fairs of ancient origin are held at Cheadle each year. The short entry gives a small industrial market town: coal, silk, tape, limestone, and copper around it, and one admired Pugin church at its centre.
britannica-1911-cherubini-maria-luigi-ca:
Cherubini, Maria Luigi Carlo Zenobio Salvatore (1760–1842) was an Italian composer, born at Florence on 14 September 1760 and dead at Paris on 15 March 1842. His father played harpsichord at the Pergola theatre, and the boy learned music at six and composition at nine. From 1777 he studied four years under Sarti at Bologna, in both church music and drama. His first complete opera, Quinto Fabio, was produced in 1780.

Paris became his home from 1786, and his first French opera, Démophon, came in 1788. Lodoiska in 1791 began the series of his masterpieces, and Médée in 1797 fixed his fame. Napoleon disliked his severe manner and favoured lighter Italian music, so high office came slowly. Les Deux Journées, first heard in Paris in 1801, thrilled its hearers with a tale of restored humanity. The entry stresses his superb craft, checked by a lack of warmth.
britannica-1911-cheshire:
Cheshire is a north-western county of England, bounded by Lancashire, Yorkshire, Derbyshire, Staffordshire, Shropshire and Welsh counties, with the Irish Sea to the north-west. Its area is 1,027.8 square miles, and the estuaries of the Dee and Mersey form its coast. Between those estuaries lies the low peninsula of Wirral. The Weaver is the chief river inside the county, joined by the Dane at Northwich.

Most of the surface is low and flat, though the Peckforton hills flank the Weaver valley and high ground rises in the east. Small lakes called meres, such as Combermere and Rostherne, dot the county and draw fine houses to their banks. Geology rests mostly on Triassic strata, whose Keuper marls hold thick beds of rock salt. More than four fifths of the land is cultivated, much of it in lasting pasture.
britannica-1911-chimere:
Chimere, in modern English use, is a garment worn as part of the ceremonial dress of Anglican bishops, a long sleeveless gown of silk or satin. It opens down the front, gathers in at the back between the shoulders and has slits for the arms. Bishops wear it over the rochet, in black or in scarlet for convocation robes. Its name reaches back through French and Italian forms, perhaps to a Greek word for wintry dress.

Origin was long debated, but the entry holds it proved that the chimere derives from the medieval tabard. That tabard was a civil upper garment worn by men of rank. The gown thus passed from lay dress into the bishop's ceremonial wardrobe over the centuries. Form, dress order and descent from the tabard are the points the notice establishes.
britannica-1911-chromosphere: In astronomy, the chromosphere is the red layer of gas that wraps the sun outside its bright photosphere. Its name joins Greek words for colour and for a sphere. The layer can be seen with the naked eye at the start or end of a total eclipse of the sun. With a spectroscope it can also be seen at other times when the light is right. The short entry sends readers on to the articles on the Sun and on eclipses for more detail.
britannica-1911-clackmannanshire:
Clackmannanshire is the smallest county in Scotland, bounded by the Forth, Stirlingshire, Perthshire and Fifeshire, with an area of about 55 square miles. An elevated ridge runs through its middle, widening eastward above the carse lands of the Forth and Devon valleys. North of that ridge the Ochil hills form a picturesque feature, with Ben Cleuch at 2,363 feet the principal summit. King's Seat, Whitewisp and the Law are other named heights over 2,000 feet.

The river Devon, noted for romantic scenery and excellent trout fishing in its upper parts, winds 33 miles to the Forth at Cambus. The Black Devon flows west over coal strata and drives many mills and collieries with its water. Ships of 500 tons run up the Forth as far as Alloa on the county boundary. Gartmorn, the only lake, was dammed to furnish water to Alloa and power to mills.
britannica-1911-clermont-tonnerre:
Clermont-Tonnerre is the name of a French family whose members played some part in the history of France, especially in Dauphiné, from about 1100 to the Revolution. Sibaud, lord of Clermont in Viennois, who first appears in 1080, founded the family line. A descendant aided Pope Calixtus II against an anti-pope and was allowed, it is said, to add two keys and a tiara to the family arms. In 1547 Clermont was made a county for Antoine, governor of Dauphiné.

Later members include Gaspard (1688–1781), a soldier at Fontenoy and Lawfeldt who became duke and peer and, as senior marshal, assisted at the coronation of Louis XVI. His grandson was guillotined at Lyons in 1793, and his son in July 1794. Catherine de Clermont-Tonnerre won fame as the tenth muse for her learning. Aimé Marie Gaspard served as minister of marine and of war under Charles X before retiring after 1830.
britannica-1911-closure: Closure, from the French clôture, is the parliamentary term for the closing of debate according to a certain rule. Debate closes under that rule even when certain members are anxious to continue it. The entry gives no history of the device, no house, date or case in its brief text. It sends readers to the article on Parliament and its procedure for the working detail. Closure thus stands as a rule-bound ending imposed on discussion.
britannica-1911-clotaire:
Clotaire, or Chlothachar, is the name of four Frankish kings, and the entry treats their reigns in sequence from the sons of Clovis. Clotaire I, who died in 561, received Soissons, Laon, Noyon, Cambrai and Maastricht as his share in 511. Ambitious, he instigated the murder of his brother Clodomer's children in 524 and gained Tours and Poitiers. Burgundy, Provence, Thuringia and Spain campaigns enlarged him, until by 558 he was king of all Gaul.

Clotaire II, son of Chilperic I, was recognised as king in his cradle in 584 through his mother Fredegond's devotion and his uncle Gontran's protection. After defeat at Dormelles in 600 he recovered, and by 613, having put Brunhilda to death, he was master of the whole Frankish kingdom. Great concessions to the aristocracy followed in the constitution of 18 October 614. Comparative tranquillity rewarded those concessions for the rest of his reign, the entry argues.
britannica-1911-coimbatore:
Coimbatore is a city and district of British India in the Madras presidency. The city stands on the left bank of the Noyil river, 305 miles from Madras by rail. Its people numbered 53,080 in 1901, up fourteen per cent in ten years. It sits 1,437 feet above the sea. Slopes of the Nilgiri hills give it a fine setting.

Trade and schools fill out the account. Cotton weaving and spinning lead its work, with tanning and distilling beside them. Makers turn out coffee, sugar, manure and saltpetre. Two colleges, a farm college and a forestry school serve the town. The district covers 7,860 square miles of flat, open land. Mountains hem it on three sides. Grain, cotton, cattle and hides lead its exports. Two rail lines cross the district.
britannica-1911-coire:
Coire, called Chur in German and Coira in Italian, is the capital of the Swiss canton of the Grisons. It stands 1,949 feet above the sea on the right bank of the Plessur torrent. The town sits where that stream leaves the Schanfigg valley. It lies about a mile above the stream's meeting with the Rhine. Two hills guard the valley mouth.

In 1900 the town held 11,532 people. Most spoke German, with Romonsch and Italian speakers beside them. Protestants outnumbered Roman Catholics. The old town in the east holds the chief sights. Saint Lucius cathedral there was built between 1178 and 1282. Coire forms a hub of Alpine routes. Passes to Italy and the Engadine all meet there. Rail links it to Zürich, 74 miles away.
britannica-1911-colin-alexandre:
Alexandre Colin, a Flemish sculptor of the sixteenth century, is set down in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Colin was born at Malines and lived to a great age. In 1563 the emperor Ferdinand called him to Innsbruck. There a grand tomb for Maximilian the First was rising in a church. Colin cut twenty of its twenty-four marble relief panels.

The panels show the chief acts and wins of Maximilian's reign. Colin is said to have cut all twenty in three years. The work mixes life and force with care like a fine cameo. One great judge called it the finest work of its kind. Colin served the emperor and his son as court sculptor. More of his tombs stand in the same church.
britannica-1911-commodore:
Commodore is a naval rank explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is a form of commander, written commandore in the sixteen hundreds. In the British navy it is a temporary rank. It goes to an officer placed in command of a squadron.

Two kinds of commodore serve in that navy. One keeps a captain under him in his own ship. He holds the temporary rank and pay of a rear-admiral. The other kind ranks and is paid only as a captain. The title is also a courtesy for the senior officer of a squadron of more than three ships. In the United States navy it began as just such a courtesy title. It was made a true commissioned rank in 1862, then abolished in 1899. Ashore, the name belongs to the president of a yacht club. It also marks the senior captain of a merchant fleet.
britannica-1911-condottiere:
A condottiere was the leader of a hired military company in old Italy. Such companies could run to several thousand men. States hired them to fight their wars. The word comes in the end from a Latin verb meaning to lead or to hire. In common use it covers the soldiers as well as their chief. These captains shaped Italian history for two centuries.

Their great age ran from the mid 1200s to the mid 1400s. The wars of Guelphs and Ghibellines gave them room to rise. Italy lacked a strong feudal horse force. Rich city life softened its people, and city militias could not wage wars of attack. War thus became the condottiere's trade and his monopoly. That grip let him claim a price and a place past his worth. The entry closes with the fall of the pure hired company.
britannica-1911-conge-d-elire:
Conge d elire is a French phrase for leave to elect. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the English church custom behind it. The crown grants the permit under the great seal. It lets a cathedral dean and chapter choose a new bishop.

Old custom once let kings hand out bishop posts by ring and staff. King John granted free choice in 1214, with royal leave asked first. A law of 1534 fixed the form still used in 1911. The chapter must pick the person named in a royal letter. They have twelve days, or the crown may name its own choice. Church heads then check and confirm the pick. The rite kept royal power inside a church vote.
britannica-1911-coote-sir-eyre:
Sir Eyre Coote (1726–1783) was a British soldier, son of a clergyman, born near Limerick. He entered the 27th regiment as a young man. He saw active service in the Jacobite rising of 1745. Some years later he gained a captaincy in the 39th regiment. That unit was the first British regiment sent to India, and India made his name.

In 1756 part of the regiment went from Madras to join Clive against Calcutta. The city fell back into British hands with ease. Coote won local rank of major for his good work in a surprise of the Nawab's camp. At the council before Plassey his soldierly advice helped bring the battle on. After the win he chased the French for 400 miles in hard country. That work won him a regiment of his own, the 84th. It also broke his health for good. Fresh wars in India fill the rest.
britannica-1911-corneille-pierre:
Pierre Corneille, a French dramatist and poet who lived from 1606 to 1684, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Rouen in June 1606, he was the son of a king's advocate at the Table de Marbre. His father also held office over waters and forests in Rouen. In that post he was a vigorous magistrate who suppressed brigandage without fear. The family was ennobled in 1637.

Corneille was taught by the Jesuits of Rouen. At eighteen he was entered as an advocate and took the oaths early, by special leave. He later held posts tied to the admiralty and to waters and forests. Those posts proved worth little, and he sold them in 1650 for 6,000 livres. Readers get the family and legal ground of his early life, before the plays that made his name.
britannica-1911-correnti-cesare:
Cesare Correnti (1815-1888) was an Italian rebel and statesman born at Milan on 3 January 1815. He came of a poor but noble family. While he worked in the office of the public debt, he spread rebel pamphlets through Lombardy. They were meant to stir hate of the Austrians. In 1848 he urged the Milanese to give up smoking as a protest. That act helped spark the revolt known as the Five Days.

Correnti was a lead spirit of the revolt and ran the work of its ruling body. When Austrian troops took Milan back, he fled to Piedmont. There he lived by journalism and kept sending his pamphlets into Lombardy. He was chosen as a deputy in 1849 and worked hard for the national cause. He backed Cavour on the Crimean war, though he sat with the Left.
britannica-1911-coverture:
Coverture is a term in English law for the state of a woman during marriage. The word is an old French form of the modern word for a covering. A wife is held to be under the cover, sway and guard of her husband. That state shields her in set cases from punishment for crime. The crime must be done in his presence and on his presumed force.

The hosted entry is short and holds no more than that core rule. It sends readers to the entry on husband and wife for the full account. No case, act or date is named in the piece itself. Place in law, root of the word and one shield form its whole matter. The description stays within those bounds and adds no rule the stub does not print.
britannica-1911-crozat-pierre: Pierre Crozat, a French art collector who lived from 1661 to 1740, is covered in a brief life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Toulouse to a famed banking family, he became treasurer to the king in Paris. He built a grand store of pictures and fine objects. A rich pictured work called the Cabinet Crozat showed the best French collections. His treasures passed to his nephews and were later split up.
britannica-1911-cuddalore:
Cuddalore is a town of British India in the South Arcot district of Madras, on the coast 125 miles south of Madras by rail. Its population in 1901 was 52,216, up a tenth in the decade. Low-lying, it is still held unusually healthy and serves as a sanatorium for the district round it. Its chief exports are sugar, oil-seeds, and indigo. Two colleges and two high schools serve the town.

Near Cuddalore stand the ruins of Fort St David, on the river Gadilam, bought by the English in 1690. The sale covered the fort and all land within a cannon shot, and those villages are still called cannon ball villages. From 1746 the fort was the British headquarters for the south, and it beat off Dupleix's attack. Clive governed it in 1756, the French took it twice, and in 1785 it passed finally to Britain. That fort's stirring history fills most of the entry.
britannica-1911-curie-pierre:
Pierre Curie (1859-1906) was a French physicist, and his work is set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris and educated at the Sorbonne, he became professor of physics there. He had already done valued work on piezoelectricity and on how bodies' magnetic traits shift with heat.

The entry centers on his joint work with his wife Marie on radium. Noting that some uranium minerals were more active than uranium itself, they reasoned that a new, strongly active substance must hide inside. In 1898, after hard labor on pitchblende, they announced two new substances, polonium and radium. In 1903 they shared a Nobel prize for physics with Henri Becquerel.
britannica-1911-dasyure:
Dasyure is a book name for beasts of the family Dasyuridae. The 1911 Britannica entry says the name fits best the genus Dasyurus. Those beasts are the true dasyures of science in that strict sense. Most live on the continent of Australia and in Tasmania. In nature they fill the place of small flesh eaters of other lands.

Cats, civets, and weasels hold that place in the Old World instead. Dasyures hide by day in rock holes or in hollow trees. By night they prowl for small mammals and birds as prey. Some climb trees in part, as their foot pads seem to show. The spot tailed kind is the size of a house cat in bulk.
britannica-1911-daumier-honore:
Honore Daumier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French caricaturist and painter. The hosted text opens with the tail of another entry, then gives this life in full. He lived from 1808 to 1879. He was born at Marseilles in France. From his earliest youth he showed a strong bent toward art. His father tried in vain to check that bent. 

Daumier mastered the technique of lithography early. He began by producing plates for music publishers. When Philipon launched the comic journal La Caricature, Daumier joined its staff. There he began his campaign of scathing satire. His targets were the foibles of the bourgeoisie and corrupt law. A caricature of the king as Gargantua brought him prison. He served six months at Sainte Pelagie in 1832. For the Charivari he later made his famous social caricatures.
britannica-1911-del-credere: Del credere is an Italian phrase meaning of belief or of trust. In English law a del credere agent sells goods for his principal on credit. For an extra fee he vows to sell only to buyers who are fully able to pay. His place is thus that of a surety for the buyer. If the buyer fails to pay, the agent owes his principal. The pact need not be put in writing to hold. The entry sends readers to the articles on brokers and on guarantees.
britannica-1911-delfico-melchiorre:
Melchiorre Delfico, who lived from 1744 to 1835, was an Italian writer on trade and law. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits his books with real reforms. He was born at Teramo in the Abruzzi in August 1744. He was schooled at Naples in law and state economy.

One paper by Delfico killed harsh curbs on farm sales at Naples. Those rules had blocked the sale and export of crops. A later work helped end feudal rights over land. He served as a state councillor under Joseph Bonaparte. After the old king came back, he led the state archives board. He quit that post in 1825 and died at Teramo in 1835. Late works weighed the worth and doubt of history itself.
britannica-1911-denbighshire:
Denbighshire is a county of North Wales bounded by the Irish Sea and by Flint, Cheshire, Shropshire, Montgomery, Merioneth and Carnarvon. Its area is 662 square miles, and its surface is broken and varied. The bleak Hiraethog hills slope to the Conwy and the Clwyd, while the Clwyd and Elwy valleys soften the uplands. Rivers drain to the Clwyd, Conwy and Dee, and the Pistyll Rhaiadr fall and Moel Sych, the county's highest point, mark the Berwyn side.

The geology runs through every main stratum from the Ordovician to the Triassic, and the Ruabon side is rich in minerals. The article closes with the county's churches, rood lofts, brasses and stained glass. Near Abergele a cave is named as the refuge of Richard II before his capture in 1399.
britannica-1911-derbyshire:
Derbyshire, a north midland county of England, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bounded by Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Staffordshire and Cheshire, and it covers a little over a thousand square miles. The face of the county varies a great deal, from the flat, plain south to the hills of the north.

The Peak District in the north, though less grand than the Lake District, holds some of the finest hill scenery in England. Richly wooded glens and dales, such as those of Castleton, Glossop, Dovedale and Millersdale, give it its special beauty. The landscape runs from wild moorland and grey rocks to the park lands of Chatsworth. Some woods are noted for fine oaks, those at Kedleston among the largest and oldest in the kingdom. The county's streams flow out from the northern hills, most of them to the Trent.
britannica-1911-devonshire:
Devonshire, a county in the south west of England, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. Its area is near 2,605 square miles, topped by just two English counties. It is bound by the Bristol Channel, the English Channel, and Cornwall. Near all of its land is uneven and hilly.

Devon holds the highest land in England south of Derbyshire, the piece says. Dartmoor, its chief feature, is a broad high waste of moor in the south. Its top point rises to 2,039 feet. Heather uplands of Exmoor reach in from Somerset, home to red deer and hardy ponies. Rich farm tracts, such as the South Hams with its apple groves, set off the wild moors.
britannica-1911-dorsetshire:
Dorsetshire, or Dorset, is a south-western county of England bounded by Wiltshire, Hampshire, the Channel, Devonshire and Somersetshire. Its area is just under 988 square miles, and a line of downs strikes across it from Shaftesbury toward Devon, sometimes topping 900 feet. The Stour breaches the central hills between Sturminster Newton and Blandford, while the Frome and the Piddle cross the plain to Poole Harbour. The Vale of Blackmore is the county's well-watered farming heart.

The coast is the county's glory: Poole Harbour's lake-like inlet, the bold headlands of Ballard Down and Durlston Head, and the Isle of Purbeck between them. The long article then works through Dorset's geology, towns, history and antiquities in gazetteer detail. A full bibliography of county histories, from Hutchins onward, closes the piece.
britannica-1911-edinburghshire:
Edinburghshire, also called Midlothian, is a county of Scotland on the Firth of Forth. The 1911 Britannica article gives its area as 366 square miles. Haddington and Berwick bound it east, and Linlithgow west. The island of Cramond in the Firth belongs to the county. It has no true mountains, but the Pentland Hills push boldly in from the south-west. Scald Law, at 1,898 feet, is their high point.

The Moorfoot Hills in the south-east top out at 2,136 feet on Blackhope Scar. Lone hills near the city include Arthur's Seat, at 822 feet, and Blackford Hill. The Esk is the longest river of the county. It drains the land between the Pentlands and the Moorfoots and meets the sea at Musselburgh. Its two branches join in the grounds of Dalkeith Palace.
britannica-1911-elginshire:
Elginshire, also called Moray, a northern county of Scotland, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The Moray Firth bounds it to the north, and Banffshire, Inverness, and Nairnshire lie around it. The county covers only the eastern part of the old province of Moray. That province once ran from the Spey to the Beauly. The county itself covers 477 square miles.

The land falls into two sections. Along the coast lies the Laigh o' Moray, a level and fertile tract some 30 miles long. South of it the country turns hilly, though no high mountains rise there. The Cromdale Hills, on the Banffshire border, reach 2,329 feet. Two great rivers, the Spey and the Findhorn, both rise in Inverness-shire. About 50 miles of the Spey run in or beside the county. Readers get a full account of the county's shape, hills, and waters.
britannica-1911-ellesmere:
Ellesmere is a market town in the Oswestry parliamentary division of Shropshire, England, on the Cambrian railway, 182 miles north-west from London. The urban district had 1945 people in 1901. The town stands on the west shore of the mere, or small lake, from which it takes its name. Other sheets of water nearby include Blake Mere, Cole Mere, White Mere, Newton Mere, and Crose Mere.

The church of St Mary shows styles from Norman onward and was partly rebuilt in 1848. The castle site is now pleasure gardens on high ground with a wide view. The town hall holds a library and a natural history collection, and the college is a large boys' school. Ellesmere is a key farming centre for its district. Its canal, a famous work of Thomas Telford, joins the Severn with the Mersey, crossing the Vale of Llangollen on an aqueduct 336 yards long and 127 feet high.
britannica-1911-ellore:
Ellore is a town of British India in the Kistna district of Madras, on the East Coast railway, 303 miles from Madras. Its population in 1901 was 33,521. The two canal systems of the Godavari and Kistna deltas meet at the town. Ellore was formerly a military station and the capital of the Northern Circars.

The town has manufactures of cotton and saltpetre, and an important Church of England high school. At Pedda Vegi, north of the town, stand extensive ruins. Those ruins are believed to be remains of the Buddhist kingdom of Vengi. From them the Mahommedans, after conquering the district in 1470, took material for building a fort at Ellore. The short entry thus ties the modern town to a much older Buddhist past lying in ruins just beyond it, and to the later fort raised from those same stones.
britannica-1911-elsinore:
Elsinore, in Danish Helsingör, is a seaport of Denmark in the county of Frederiksborg, on the east coast of Zealand, 28 miles north of Copenhagen by rail. Its population in 1901 was 13,902. The town stands at the narrowest part of the Sound, facing the Swedish town of Helsingborg three miles away. Its harbour takes vessels of 20 feet draught.

Shipbuilding yards, a foundry, and engineering shops line the port, and the chief export is farm produce. Helsingör gained town privileges in 1425, was taken and burnt by Lübeck in 1522, and was retaken by Christian II in 1535. The town is famed as the Elsinore of Shakespeare's Hamlet. East of the town stands Kronberg castle, a great Gothic pile built by Frederick II late in the 16th century. Its Flag Battery is the platform where the ghost appears in the play.
britannica-1911-equation-of-the-centre: Equation of the centre is an astronomy term defined in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the angular gap between a planet's true place and its mean place. A planet in an ellipse does not travel at a steady pace. The term measures how far it strays from where steady motion would put it. Applied as a correction to the mean anomaly, it yields the true anomaly. The effect is zero at the nearest and farthest points of the orbit, and greatest midway between them.
britannica-1911-esquire:
Esquire is the subject of a rank article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a French word for a shield bearer. At first an esquire was the attendant on a knight. He carried the knight's helm, shield, and lance at the tournament or in battle. He ranked just below a knight, and his post was the training stage of knighthood. The title was one of function, not of birth, and was not passed down.

The article tells how that first sense was lost in time. Esquire became a title of honour between knight and gentleman, as it still stands in strict use. Holders of knight's fees who had not taken knighthood were called esquires. The chief landowner of a parish is still called the squire by custom. Camden in the fifteen hundreds set out four classes with a right to the style.
britannica-1911-etagere: An etagere is a light piece of French made goods much like the English what-not. It was made in large count in the late part of the past age but two. As its name shows, it is a set of shelves in tiers. They hold small trim goods and keep sakes. It was most oft built to fit a corner. The best forms from the reign of Louis the Sixteenth use rare woods. They are known for their grace and fine lines.
britannica-1911-euchre:
Euchre is a card game played with a deck of 32 cards, the ordinary pack cut down below the seven. The joker, when used, is the highest trump. Next comes the right bower, the knave of trumps, then the left bower, the knave of the other suit of the same colour. Aces and court cards follow in whist order. With the joker in play the game is called railroad euchre. Two, three or four people can play.

Each player receives five cards, dealt two then three or three then two. The next card turns up for trumps. In the two-handed game the non-dealer may order it up or pass. The dealer may adopt the suit or pass in turn. If both pass, either may name another suit, making it next or crossing the suit. The entry then works through the play of tricks, marches and lone hands.
britannica-1911-exeter-new-hampshire:
Exeter is a New Hampshire town and a county-seat of Rockingham county, on the Squamscott river. It lies about 12 miles south-west of Portsmouth and 51 miles north by east of Boston. Its population was 4,284 in 1890, 4,922 in 1900 and 4,897 in 1910. The Boston & Maine railway serves it. The town keeps a public library and colonial-era houses. Its fame rests on Phillips Exeter Academy, incorporated in 1781 and opened in 1783.

Dr John Phillips, a Harvard graduate who made a fortune, founded the academy. Its charter pledges it to promote piety and virtue. It teaches English, Latin and Greek, writing, arithmetic and music. Oratory, practical geometry, logic and geography also appear in the founding list. The charter leaves room for other liberal arts as opportunity permits. The entry sets the school in a small mill and market town of some 17 square miles.
britannica-1911-fabre-d-eglantine-philip:
Philippe François Nazaire Fabre d'Églantine, a French dramatist and revolutionist who lived from 1750 to 1794, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Carcassonne in July 1750, his real name was plain Fabre. The added name marked a golden eglantine he won at the floral games of Toulouse. After touring the provinces as an actor, he came to Paris.

His first comedy in Paris failed in 1787, and a tragedy at the Théâtre Français failed as well. One play alone kept its fame, Philinte, a sequel to Molière's Misanthrope, staged in 1790. Its hero is not Molière's man but a study of pure egotism. The play carried a political charge as well. Alceste stands for the citizen patriot, while Philinte is a dangerous aristocrat in disguise. Fabre became president and secretary of the club of the Cordeliers.
britannica-1911-falloux-frederic-alfred-:
Frédéric Alfred Pierre Falloux (1811–1886) was a French politician and author, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his party roots. He was born at Angers on the eleventh of May 1811. His father had been ennobled by Charles the Tenth. Falloux began his career as a Legitimist and clerical journalist.

In 1846 Falloux entered the legislature as deputy for Maine et Loire. With many other strong Catholics, he gave real or feigned support to the revolution of 1848. Louis Napoleon made him minister of education in 1849. Quarrels with the president led him to resign within a year. In that short term he still secured a lasting law. The Loi Falloux of March 1850 set the order of primary and secondary schooling in France.
britannica-1911-fantin-latour-ignace-hen:
Ignace Henri Jean Theodore Fantin Latour, a French artist who lived from 1836 to 1904, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Grenoble, he studied first with his father, a pastel painter. He then trained at the drawing school of Lecoq de Boisbaudran and later under Couture. He was the friend of Ingres, Delacroix, Corot, and Courbet, among others.

Fantin Latour first showed at the Salon of 1861, and many of his chief works hung there in later years. In 1863 he showed with the rejected artists, with Monet, Legros, and Whistler among them. Whistler brought him into English art circles, and he lived for a time in England. His group portraits, set out in the manner of the Dutch masters, are stressed in the text. One such work shows Whistler, Legros, Baudelaire, and the artist himself in honour of Delacroix.
britannica-1911-felibien-andre:
Andre Felibien, sieur des Avaux et de Javercy, was a French architect and royal historiographer. The heading gives his dates as 1610 to 1695. Its text, though, says he was born at Chartres in May 1619. He went to Paris at fourteen, then to Rome in 1647 as secretary of embassy. There he studied ancient monuments and libraries. He also made friends, among them the painter Nicolas Poussin.

Back in France, Felibien won the favour of Fouquet and then of Colbert. He was among the first members of the Academy of Inscriptions in 1663. He became historiographer to the king in 1666 and secretary of the Academy of Architecture in 1671. He also kept the cabinet of antiques. Amid office he wrote much. His best-known work is the Entretiens, talks on the lives and works of the greatest painters.
britannica-1911-feltre: Feltre, called Feltria in ancient times, is a town in Venetia, Italy, noted in a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on a lone hill in the province of Belluno, west of that city by rail. In nineteen oh one the town had over five thousand folk. Its cathedral has a fine apse from the fifteen hundreds. A council palace, now a theatre, is credited to Palladio. Parts of the old castle remain.
britannica-1911-flour-and-flour-manufact:
Flour and its manufacture form the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word flour comes from a French word for flower, the best part. In plain use it names the fine ground meal of the wheat berry. It is used as well for other grains and beans ground fine, as in rye flour or bean flour.

In Britain wheat flour was most often called meal in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The article goes back to the first tools of the trade. The root of the millstone was a round stone the size of a man's fist. With it grain or nuts were pounded on a flat stone that wore hollow with use. Such stones, called bullan stones, still lie in Ireland, and like marks show in the Orkneys and Shetlands. In early times the grind was the work of women.
britannica-1911-flumini-maggiore:
Flumini Maggiore is a town in the province of Cagliari, Sardinia, ten miles by road north of Iglesias and five miles from the west coast. Its population in 1901 was 3,908 in the town and 9,647 in the commune. It is the centre of a considerable lead and zinc mining district, and mining gives the short entry its whole theme. The ground around it was worked for metals long before the modern town took shape.

Three miles south stand the ruins of a temple probably built in the time of Commodus. They seem to mark the site of Metalla, meaning mines, a station on the coast road from Sulci to Tharros and the centre of the district in Roman times. At Flumini Maggiore itself two lead ingots were found. One bears a stamp with the name of the emperor Hadrian, tying the town's trade to the Roman age.
britannica-1911-forfarshire:
Forfarshire, or Angus, is an eastern county of Scotland. It is bounded north by Kincardine and Aberdeen, west by Perthshire, south by the Firth of Tay and east by the North Sea. Its area is 559,171 acres, or about 874 square miles. The island of Rossie and the Bell Rock belong to the shire. Few Scottish counties show so great a variety of surface within so small a frame, and the entry divides it into four clear sections for the reader.

In the north stand rugged masses of the Grampians. Below them runs Strathmore, the Howe of Angus, a fertile valley six to eight miles broad. Then come the Sidlaw Hills and scattered heights, and last the coastal plain and the Firth. The long county article treats its rivers, towns, farming, manufactures and history section by section. It is a full Edwardian county survey.
britannica-1911-forfeiture:
Forfeiture comes from forfeit, first an offence, then a fine exacted for it, through Old French from late Latin foris factum, a thing done outside the law. In English law the term has two uses. It means the loss, or liability to loss, of property for an offence or a breach of contract. It also means the property of which a party is deprived by that loss. The article that follows works through the rules under the common law of England.

Under the old law, attainder for treason or felony cost the offender his lands and goods as well as his life. In treason all his lands went to the king. In felony the felon's lands escheated to his immediate lord, subject to the king's right to waste them for a year and a day. Special rules for gavelkind land are noted.
britannica-1911-franceschini-baldassare:
Baldassare Franceschini (1611-1689), Italian painter of the Tuscan school, was named Il Volterrano from Volterra, his birthplace. He was the son of a sculptor in alabaster. At a very early age he learned the elements of art from Cosimo Daddi and began as his father's assistant. That work was plainly below his talents. The marquises Inghirami therefore placed him, at sixteen, under the Florentine painter Matteo Rosselli, and his rise in the art was rapid from that schooling onward.

Within a year Franceschini had advanced enough to paint frescoes in Volterra, skilful in foreshortening. Other frescoes for the Medici family followed. In 1652 the marchese Filippo Niccolini, meaning to employ him on the cupola and back wall of his chapel in Santa Croce, Florence, sent him travelling through Italy to perfect his style.
britannica-1911-franklin-new-hampshire:
Franklin is a city of Merrimack county, New Hampshire, set where the Pemigewasset and Winnepesaukee rivers join to form the Merrimac. Its population rose from 4085 in 1890 to 6132 in 1910, over an area of about 14 square miles. Rail lines link it with Concord, Bristol, and the White Mountains division.

River power drives works making foundry goods, paper and pulp, woollen goods, hosiery, saws, needles, and knitting machines, and the waterworks are run by the city. Daniel Webster was born within the present bounds, and the New Hampshire orphans home stands on the Webster farm. Franklin was formed in 1828 from parts of four towns and became a city in 1895.
britannica-1911-frechette-louis-honore:
Louis Honoré Fréchette (1839-1908), French-Canadian poet, was born at Levis, Quebec, on 16 November 1839, the son of a contractor. Called to the Canadian bar in 1864, he started the Journal de Lévis, and his revolutionary views drove him into exile in the United States, where he worked in Chicago journalism. In 1874 voters sent him to the Canadian parliament as the Liberal member for Levis.

Beaten in 1878 and 1882, he turned wholly to letters, edited French papers, and in 1889 became clerk of the Quebec legislative council. He long urged political union with the United States, though he accepted the C.M.G. from Queen Victoria in 1897. His verse includes Les Fleurs boréales and Les Oiseaux de neige, crowned by the French Academy in 1880, and La Légende d un peuple. Called the Canadian Laureate, he died on 1 June 1908.
britannica-1911-galilee-architecture: Galilee, in architecture, is a porch or chapel forming the entrance to a church, as at Durham and Ely cathedrals. At Lincoln the name is sometimes given to the south-west porch. The word is said to come from the phrase Galilee of the Gentiles in Matthew. Such porches probably served chiefly for penitents not yet admitted to the church, and in abbey churches as the vestibule where women might see their monk relatives or hear the service. Corpses were sometimes laid there before burial.
britannica-1911-galuppi-baldassare:
Baldassare Galuppi is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Italian writer of operas born near Venice in seventeen hundred and six. His father, a barber who played fiddle in a local theatre, first taught him music. A first opera at age sixteen failed and drove him to hard study.

The entry follows his busy years writing operas for Venetian stages. He worked in London and then led music at a great church in Venice. His comic operas, made with a famed play writer, won huge crowds. A Russian empress called him to her court for a time. The entry praises his craft in harmony and his fresh way with group song ends.
britannica-1911-gassendi-pierre:
Pierre Gassendi was a philosopher and man of science whose bronze statue was raised at Digne in 1852. The hosted 1911 Britannica text opens in mid-course, at his works rather than his life. His collected works, headed by the Syntagma philosophicum, came out in six volumes in 1658, with another six-volume edition in 1727.

The volumes hold his attacks and comments on Epicurus, Aristotle, Descartes and others. They also hold his astronomy, his commentary on Diogenes Laertius, and lives of Epicurus, Peiresc, Tycho Brahe and Copernicus. The entry praises the Lives highly, quoting Gibbon's praise of Gassendi as writer and thinker. It credits him less with new knowledge than with clear writing and a strong push for experiment. His system, built on Epicurean lines, is judged inconsistent.
britannica-1911-gerard-jean-ignace-isido:
Jean Ignace Isidore Gerard (1803-1847) was a French caricaturist, known by the name Grandville, his actor grandparents' stage name. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born at Nancy on 13 September 1803, taught drawing by his father, a miniature painter, and in Paris at twenty-one. Fame came with Metamorphoses du jour in 1828.

Those seventy scenes gave men animal faces and let them act out a human comedy, with great skill in matching traits to features. Periodicals such as Le Charivari took his work, and his political caricatures won wide popularity. He illustrated Beranger, La Fontaine, Don Quixote, Gulliver's Travels and Robinson Crusoe, and issued sets such as Les Fleurs animees. The entry praises his keen character-reading and inventive humour. He died of mental disease on 17 March 1847.
britannica-1911-german-literature:
German Literature is the subject of a letters entry in the 1911 Britannica. Set next to other letters, it shows a broken course. It falls in lone groups split off from each other. Dark spans of weak work part those groups starkly. No peer case is found in other lands of Europe. The cause lies less in the chequered past of the folk. It lies more in the bent of the national mind.

That mind met waves of force from Italy and France. It could not bend to those waves like neighbours did. Its past is a fight for its own free voice. That fight went on even when outside force seemed kind. In poor ages it sank to slavish copying of forms. The first sign of health was a cast off of such force. Hence its best ages rarely match those of other lands.
britannica-1911-gioja-melchiorre:
Gioja, Melchiorre is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Italian writer on thought and public wealth. Melchiorre Gioja was born at Piacenza on the twentieth of September 1767 and died in 1829. He was meant for the church and took orders. In 1796 he gave them up and went to Milan to study how states grow rich.

He won a prize for an essay on the kind of free rule best fit for Italy, and chose the life of a public writer. When Napoleon came, Gioja backed a republic under French sway in print. Under the Cisalpine Republic he was made record keeper and head of statistics. He was jailed more than once, in 1820 for eight months on a charge tied to the Carbonari plot.
britannica-1911-glamorganshire:
Glamorganshire, in Welsh Morganwg, is a maritime county in the south-east corner of Wales. The 1911 Britannica entry bounds it by Carmarthenshire, Breconshire and Monmouthshire, with the Bristol Channel to the south. It runs 53 miles from east to west and up to 29 miles inland, and its shape follows the fall from the Breconshire mountains to the sea.

Four rivers, the Rhymney, Taff, Neath and Tawe, drain it from the northern hills. The highest point, Craig y Llyn, reaches 1,970 feet. South of that peak lie the great coal-fields of mid-Glamorgan, the county's wealth and the entry's great theme. The long county article works through the land in order: surface, rivers, geology, climate, farming, coal and industry, towns, people and history. It is a full county survey of Wales's most industrial shire as it stood in 1911.
britannica-1911-gloucestershire:
Gloucestershire is a county in the west midlands of England. Six shires touch it on the north, east, and south, and two more lie to the west. Its shape is rough and long. The entry splits it in three clear parts, the hills, the vale, and the woods.

The east holds the Cotswold hills, whose west face stands high in a long line. That line splits the Thames flow from the Severn flow. Below it lies the rich vale of the lower Severn. Three famed streams join that river on its course. Past the Severn lies a fair tract of woods with a long past.
britannica-1911-goitre:
Goitre, in the 1911 Britannica medical entry, is a swelling at the front of the neck caused by enlargement of the thyroid gland. Its other names are given as Bronchocele and Derbyshire Neck. The gland sits against the windpipe, and in health makes no outward show.

In goitre the swelling is conspicuous and unsightly, and it can press hard on the windpipe and other parts of the neck. The entry cites cases recorded by Alibert where the tumour hung over the breast, or even to mid-thigh. It usually appears early in life, often between the eighth and twelfth years, growing slowly at first. Later changes can make the gland cystic or hard. The article then treats causes, the districts where goitre is endemic, and the treatment of the condition as practised at the time.
britannica-1911-goujet-claude-pierre:
Claude Pierre Goujet, a French abbé and man of letters who lived from 1697 to 1767, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Paris in October 1697, he studied at the Jesuit college and at the Collège Mazarin, yet became a strong Jansenist. He entered the Oratorians in 1719 and was soon made a canon.

For his extreme Jansenist views, Goujet suffered much persecution from the Jesuits, and several of his works were suppressed. In his last years his health failed and he lost his sight. Poverty forced him to sell his library, a sacrifice that hastened his death in 1767. He wrote a supplement to Moréri's dictionary and helped compile a literary history of France in eighteen volumes. He also wrote lives of the saints and a history of the Inquisitions.
britannica-1911-goujon-jean-marie-claude:
Jean Marie Claude Alexandre Goujon, a French publicist and statesman who lived from 1766 to 1795, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bourg, the son of a postmaster, he went to sea young and saw fighting at the age of twelve. In 1790 he settled at Meudon and set out to make up for his lack of schooling.

As the officer charged with feeding the folk of Seine et Oise in 1792, Goujon did hard work with skill and tact. He entered the Convention on the death of Hérault de Séchelles and sat with the Mountain. Sent on a mission to the armies of the Rhine and the Moselle, he acted with rare restraint. He spoke for peace inside the republic, yet fought the counter revolution in the Jacobin Club and from the Mountain benches. He spoke against letting Girondin survivors back in 1795.
britannica-1911-gouthiere-pierre:
Pierre Gouthiere, a French metal worker, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Troyes in seventeen forty, he went to Paris at an early age as a pupil of Martin Cour. In his career he made a vast amount of metal work of the utmost variety. The best of it was unsurpassed by any rival.

It was long believed that he took many orders for furniture from the court of Louis the Sixteenth. The queen Marie Antoinette was named as a chief patron. Later searches suggest his work for the queen was confined to bronzes. The entry weighs that revision and holds that his fame can bear the loss.
britannica-1911-grasmere:
Grasmere, a village and lake in Westmorland, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places it in the heart of the English Lake District, on the small river Rothay. The village lies near the head of the lake, on the road from Keswick to Ambleside.

The scene is the heart of the piece. Woods cloak much of the vale by Grasmere and Rydal Water. High hills rise on the east, with Loughrigg Fell and Silver How on the west. The village draws many guests yet keeps a calm, tucked away look. The text notes the house where William Wordsworth lived from seventeen ninety nine to eighteen hundred and eight. His grave is here too. The entry will help walkers and readers of the Lakes alike.
britannica-1911-greenore: Greenore is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a seaport and watering place in county Louth, Ireland. It stands on the western shore at the north of Carlingford Lough. The town owed its importance to the London and North-Western railway company. A steamer service run by the company crossed to Holyhead in Wales, eighty miles away. A steam ferry crossed the lough to Greencastle, serving Kilkeel and the resorts of county Down. The company also owned the hotel and laid out the golf links.
britannica-1911-gringoire-pierre:
Pierre Gringoire (c. 1480–1539) was a French poet and dramatist. He was probably born at Caen. His first work was Le Chasteau de labour (1499). That didactic poem praises diligence. It then turns into an allegory of married troubles. Care, Need and Discomfort visit a young couple.

In Paris he directed mystery plays for noble visitors. He rose through the Enfans sans Souci to Prince des Sots. He led that confraternity for some twenty years. His plays staged the popular mind of the moment. His Jeu du Prince des Sots et Mère Sotte dates from 1512. It defended Louis XII against Pope Julius II. Mère Sotte appeared disguised as the Church. Later he served as herald at the court of Lorraine. He turned orthodox in his final years.
britannica-1911-haddingtonshire:
Haddingtonshire, or East Lothian, is a south-eastern Scottish county. The Firth of Forth bounds it on the north. The North Sea and Berwickshire close the east and south. Edinburghshire lies to the west. The county covers 267 square miles. Its coastline measures 41 miles. The Bass Rock and Fidra Isle belong to it. The northern half slopes gently to the coast.

The southern half is hilly Lammermuir country. Several peaks there exceed 1,500 feet. Traprain Law and North Berwick Law break the level tract. The Tyne is the only important river. It runs 28 miles to the sea. Its trout are a very fine variety. A long geology section follows the county's strata. Farming, towns and antiquities fill later sections. Dunbar in 1650 and Prestonpans in 1745 were its last battles.
britannica-1911-hampshire:
Hampshire, or the county of Southampton, is a southern English county. Berkshire bounds it on the north and Surrey on the east. The English Channel washes its southern coast. Dorsetshire and Wiltshire close the west. Its area is 1,623.5 square miles. The Isle of Wight belongs to the county. The Solent and Spithead separate island from mainland. Southampton Water drives twelve miles inland from that strait.

The county shows gently rising hills and fruitful valleys. Mansions and pleasant villages stud the landscape. Extensive woodlands survive, above all the New Forest. That western district is a rare ancient afforested tract. The Western Downs reach 850 feet near Highclere. Rivers Avon, Test and Itchen get full treatment. Long sections follow for geology, farming and towns. Antiquities, administration and Civil War history close the survey.
britannica-1911-hanover-new-hampshire:
Hanover is a township of Grafton county, New Hampshire. It stands on the Connecticut river, 75 miles by rail north-west of Concord. Its population in 1910 was 2,075. No railway actually enters the township. The Ledyard Free Bridge links it to Norwich, Vermont, and its station. Rugged hills and deep gorges rise near the river. Moose Mountain tops them at 2,326 feet. Laura Bridgman was born near that mountain's foot.

Farming, dairying and lumbering are the chief pursuits. The village of Hanover occupies Hanover Plain in the south-west. Dartmouth College makes the village famous. Its campus is strikingly beautiful, with fine colonial buildings. Dartmouth Hall is the showpiece among them. The Mary Hitchcock memorial hospital opened in 1893. Governor Wentworth chartered the township in 1761. First settlement came in May 1765.
britannica-1911-hardy-alexandre:
Alexandre Hardy (born about 1569, died 1631), a French playwright, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, he was one of the most fertile writers for the stage of any age. He claimed to have written some six hundred plays, of which just thirty-four survive. All his life he was tied to a troupe of actors, whom he kept supplied with new work.

The article follows the troupe through the provinces and its spells in Paris. It played at the Hotel de Bourgogne in 1599 and held the house again in later years. Quarrels with the guild that owned the rights to the theatre drove it elsewhere for a time. In 1628 the company, long called royal, settled at that house for good. For all his output, Hardy never won riches or strong patrons from his many dedications.
britannica-1911-hay-breconshire:
Hay is a market town of Breconshire, south Wales. It stands on the south bank of the Wye. Hereford lies 20 miles east and Brecon 17 miles south-west. Its population in 1901 was 1,680. Two railway lines start from the town. Leland and Camden ascribed a Roman origin to it. Roman coins, called Jews' money locally, were reportedly found nearby. No other record confirms that report.

The earliest settlement probably dates from about 1088. Bernard Newmarch's Norman conquest of the district began then. The manor of Hay went briefly to Sir Philip Walwyn. It soon reverted to Newmarch and followed Brecknock lordship. Its forfeiture to the crown came in 1521. The castle was probably built in Newmarch's time. William de Breos, his great-grandson, rebuilt it. Henry VIII's act of 1535 named Hay's manor in the new county. Welsh tenures long prevailed in its Welsh part.
britannica-1911-hellebore:
Hellebore is a genus of plants, Helleborus, of the buttercup order Ranunculaceae. Its species are natives of Europe and western Asia. They are coarse perennial herbs with lobed leaves. Five persistent petaloid sepals form the showy flower. Minute tubular petals inside hold the honey. Stamens are very numerous and spirally arranged. Carpels vary in number and split along the ventral suture.

Black hellebore, Helleborus niger, is the famous Christmas rose. It blooms in mid-winter in southern and central Europe. Gerard already grew it in English gardens. Market gardens now force it for Christmas decorations. The Lenten rose, H. orientalis, has bred fine hybrids. Green hellebore yields alkaloids including jervine and veratrine. Pharmacology closes the long account. Black hellebore acts as purgative and uterine stimulant. Green hellebore is a cardiac and nervous sedative.
britannica-1911-herculano-de-carvalho-e-:
Alexandre Herculano de Carvalho e Araujo (1810–1877) was a Portuguese historian, born in Lisbon of humble stock. He learned Latin, logic and rhetoric at the Necessidades Monastery, then mathematics at the Royal Marine Academy. Under D. Miguel's absolute rule, he joined a failed rising in August 1831 and fled to England and France.

In 1832 he landed at the Mindello among D. Pedro's 7,500 men who took Oporto, and fought through its siege. His poems A Voz de Propheta (1832) and A Harpa do Crente (1834) sing of exile and that defence. In 1837 he founded the Panorama, modelled on the English Penny Magazine, and became royal librarian at the Ajuda Palace. Entering parliament in 1840, he turned from editing to history. A tomb raised by public subscription at Belem honours the greatest modern historian of Portugal.
britannica-1911-hertfordshire:
Hertfordshire, a county of England also called Herts, is mapped in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cambridgeshire and Bedfordshire bound it on the north and north west. Essex lies east, Middlesex south, and Buckinghamshire south west. Its area of about 635 square miles makes it the sixth smallest county in England.

The face of the county stays pleasant the whole way across. The ground rolls in gentle waves for the most part. Where hills and valleys follow in quick train, the woodland views turn truly fine. The upper Lea valley near Tewin by Hertford shows that charm at its best. To the north west a line of hills, part of the Chiltern chain, tops 800 feet near Dunstable. Those bare uplands hold far fewer people than the home counties at large.
britannica-1911-hindostani-literature:
Hindostani literature covers the writings in the home tongue of a wide tract of north India. The 1911 Britannica entry first fixes the ground: the vales of two great rivers and the lands south of them, but not the Punjab proper or lower Bengal. It then sets out the speech map of the region in care.

Town folk, the entry says, mostly use a form stocked with Persian words and writ in a Persian script. Country folk, the vast bulk, speak kinds of Hindi drawn from older tongues and writ in local scripts. The entry names the chief speech zones from west to east, and notes how a high form of Hindi grew for books from the speech round Delhi.
britannica-1911-hoche-lazare:
Lazare Hoche is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hoche was a French general who lived from 1768 to 1797. He was born of poor parents near Versailles. At sixteen he enlisted as a private soldier in a royal guard unit. He spent all his spare time earning extra pay by civil work. His aim was to buy books for study.

The article tells how he rose through line regiments to a commission in 1792. He earned further rank in the defence of a frontier town that year. When a French general deserted to the Austrians, Hoche fell under suspicion of treason. In 1793 he took command of the Army of the Moselle. Within weeks he stormed enemy lines and swept the foe to the middle Rhine in four days.
britannica-1911-horticulture:
Horticulture, in the long 1911 treatment, is the practical art of the garden, and the hosted text is a large portion of that article rather than its opening. The surviving pages work through operations in detail. Drainage comes first: the drain must sit lower than the general level of the subsoil, or soakage gathers in every hollow. Fruit-tree borders should not be cropped with vegetables, since digging tears the roots.

Shallow planting is preferred for wall trees and standards alike, with a mulch of dung or litter to hold moisture. Young standards are tied to stakes against the wind. The best planting time runs from late September to late November. Later pages turn to glasshouse work: air and vigilance against red spider, syringing, disbudding and thinning fruit. A calendar then walks through the months, listing the work of plant houses, flower garden and shrubbery season by season.
britannica-1911-huntingdon-huntingdonshi:
Huntingdon is a market town and county town of Huntingdonshire in England. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the Ouse, north of London. One main street, about a mile long, forms most of the town.

The parish church of Saint Mary stands on an old priory site. That priory of Augustinian Canons stood there in the tenth century past. Church records from fifteen fifty eight are kept, with older parish books too. They hold the baptism entry of Oliver Cromwell from fifteen ninety nine. The house where Cromwell was born still stands in the town today. Hinchingbrooke House, a Tudor mansion, lies at the town edge near by.
britannica-1911-huntingdonshire:
Huntingdonshire, a county of England, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It sits in the east midlands. Northamptonshire bounds it on the north and west. Bedfordshire lies to the south-west and Cambridgeshire to the east. Among English counties it is one of the smallest. Only Middlesex and Rutland are smaller, the text says.

Its area is 366 square miles. The surface is low and mostly bare of trees. A low ridge of hills enters from Cambridgeshire in the south-east. It runs across the western half of the county. A strip of it also lies north of the Ouse river. These hills never top 300 feet. Still, they form a pleasant, rolling surface. The north-east of the county covers some fifty thousand acres of flat fen-like land. County readers get shape, bounds, and ground in a tight survey.
britannica-1911-hyde-cheshire:
Hyde is a market town and borough in Cheshire, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its mills, mines, and rule. It lies on the river Tame east of Manchester. The river there marks the border with Lancashire. Its count in 1901 was near thirty-three thousand.

Cotton spinning and weaving mills anchor the town trade. Print works, iron foundries, and machine shops stand beside them. Hat making and margarine works add more jobs. Large coal mines work in the ground nearby. Hyde is a town of modern growth, the entry says. A few old houses still stand, among them Newton Hall. The old Hyde family held the manor as far back as King John.
britannica-1911-inverness-shire:
Inverness-shire, a Highland county of Scotland, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the largest shire in Scotland, at more than 4,200 square miles. More than a third of that area belongs to islands, since it takes in part of the Outer Hebrides and several of the Inner Hebrides. Ross and Cromarty bound it on the north, and the Atlantic washes its west shore.

The article stresses how wild and hilly most of the county is. More than fifty peaks pass 3,000 feet, among them Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the British Isles. Small rich tracts lie in the north by the river Ness, in some glens, and on the shores of sea lochs. The rest is rough high ground, noted for fine and at times grand scenery.
britannica-1911-jeannin-pierre:
Pierre Jeannin is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Jeannin was a French statesman who lived from 1540 to 1622. He was born at Autun and learned law at Bourges. He became a lawyer at Dijon in 1569 and rose to lead the parlement of Burgundy. He tried in vain to stop the Saint Bartholomew killings in his province.

The article tells how he served a rebel duke, yet sought peace with King Henry the Fourth. After a royal victory in 1595 the king took him into his council. In 1602 he was named to oversee royal funds. He helped make a treaty with Savoy and a pact with the Dutch in 1608. Under Louis the Thirteenth he kept charge of funds and worked for peace at court.
britannica-1911-joffrin-jules-francois-a:
Jules Francois Alexandre Joffrin lived from 1846 to 1890 and was a French politician. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Troyes, where he was born in March 1846. He served in the war with Germany as a young man. Caught up in the Commune, he fled to England in exile. Eleven years abroad kept him from French public life for a time.

Back home he joined the gradual wing of the socialist party. That wing stood against the sweeping plans of Jules Guesde and his men. In 1882 he won a seat on the Paris town council. Foes in the press hit him hard, and he sued for libel. In 1889 he stood against General Boulanger for the Chamber itself.
britannica-1911-jointure:
Jointure, in law, is a provision for a wife after the death of her husband, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. As defined by Coke, it is a fit freehold living from lands. It takes effect in possession or profit right after the husband's death. It lasts for the wife's life at least, unless she herself causes its loss.

A jointure is of two kinds, legal and equitable. The legal kind was first allowed by the Statute of Uses. Before that act, settlements on marriage were the usual path. The most general form settled an estate to the use of husband and wife for their lives. The whole then went to the survivor. The entry lists the marks a legal jointure must meet, on timing, length, and when it is made.
britannica-1911-jubbulpore:
Jubbulpore, or Jabalpur, was a city, district, and division of British India in the Central Provinces. The city stood 616 miles northeast of Bombay by rail and 220 miles southwest of Allahabad, with 90,316 people in 1901. Gorges in the rocks around it had been used to form a ring of lakes.

The city was modern, laid out in wide, straight streets, with the civil station and cantonment split from the native quarter by a stream. It had been the capital of the Saugor and Nerbudda territories and was now a brigade headquarters. As the junction of two great railways, it ranked among the chief rail centres of India. It held a steam cotton mill, a government college, high schools, and training schools for teachers. Waterworks were built in 1882. The district lay mostly in the Nerbudda valley, with its Marble Rocks gorge.
britannica-1911-junot-laure:
Laure Junot, duchess of Abrantes (1783–1834), was the wife of General Junot and was born at Montpellier. She was the daughter of Mme Permon, to whom, by the daughter's own account in her famed Memoirs, the young Bonaparte once offered marriage. The family settled at Paris, and Bonaparte was often at their house after Thermidor in 1794.

She married Junot early in the consulate and plunged into the gay life of Paris, noted for her beauty, her sharp wit, and her wild spending. Napoleon called her petite peste, yet treated the pair with great generosity, a fact that did not soften her barbs against him in the Memoirs. Her spending at Lisbon left Junot deep in debt. She later fell from favour for her free talk and her guests, and after 1815 she lived mostly at Rome among artists.
britannica-1911-jurieu-pierre:
Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713) was a French Protestant divine, born at Mer in Orléanais, where his father was a Protestant pastor. He studied at Saumur and Sedan under his grandfather Pierre Dumoulin. After further study in Holland and England he took Anglican orders, then, back in France, was ordained again and followed his father as pastor at Mer.

His first work appeared in 1671, and a treatise on devotion in 1674 won him the chair of theology and Hebrew at Sedan. Foes called him the Goliath of the Protestants. When the academy of Sedan was closed in 1681, he left for Holland ahead of a new book that put him at risk. He was pastor of the Walloon church at Rotterdam until his death in January 1713, and he did much to help those who suffered after the Edict of Nantes was revoked.
britannica-1911-kenmore:
Kenmore is a village and parish of Perthshire, Scotland, 6 miles west of Aberfeldy. The parish held 1271 people in 1901. The village stands at the foot of Loch Tay, near the point where the river Tay leaves the lake. Taymouth Castle, the seat of the Marquess of Breadalbane, stands near the base of Drummond Hill in a great park through which the Tay flows.

The castle is a stately four storeyed building with corner towers and a central pavilion. It was built in 1801, with the west wing added in 1842, on the site of a mansion of 1580 built for Sir Colin Campbell of Glenorchy. The old house was called Balloch, from a Gaelic word for the outlet of a lake. Two miles southwest are the Falls of Acharn, 80 feet high. Wordsworth and his sister visited them in 1803, when the grotto at the falls was fitted as a hermit's mossy cell.
britannica-1911-kincardineshire:
Kincardineshire, or the Mearns, is an eastern county of Scotland, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It is bounded east by the North Sea, south by Forfarshire, and north by Aberdeenshire, and covers 381 square miles. In the west and north-west the Grampians rule the scene, with Mount Battock at 2,555 feet the highest peak.

To the north the county slopes down to the wooded valley of the Dee, and to the south it falls to the Howe of the Mearns. Its chief rivers include the Bervie Water, the Feugh, the Dye, and the Luther Water, and the Dee and North Esk serve as border streams for part of their course. The article notes only two small lakes, and praises glens such as Glen Dye for their beauty.
britannica-1911-kinross-shire:
Kinross-shire, a county of Scotland, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Perthshire bounds it on the north and west, and Fifeshire on the south and east. Its area is 52,410 acres, or about eighty two square miles. Save for Clackmannan, it is the smallest county in Scotland in both area and population.

Hills ring its borders, with peaks of the Ochils to the north and the Lomond hills east. Loch Leven is its only lake, famed more for its history than its looks. Most streams in the shire are short, the Leven among them. The entry praises the scenery on the Devon river near the Crook. There the stream rushes through a rocky gorge at the Devil's Mill and passes under the Rumbling Bridge. The falls of Caldron Linn lie a little farther west.
britannica-1911-kintore:
Kintore is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Kintore is a royal and police burgh in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It stands on the River Don, north-west of Aberdeen. The entry gives its small population, just 789 in 1901.

The article stresses the town's age and its old stones. Kintore was made a royal burgh in the reign of William the Lion. It formed one of the Elgin group of parliamentary burghs. A mile away stand the ruins of Hallforest Castle, once a hunting seat of Robert Bruce. Sculptured stones and stone circles dot the parish. Nearby lay the site of Bruce's camp and Thainston House, home of a British envoy to Frederick the Great. The entry packs a small town's long past into a short space.
britannica-1911-kirkcudbrightshire:
Kirkcudbrightshire, also known as the Stewartry of Kirkcudbright and East Galloway, is a southwestern county of Scotland. Ayrshire bounds it north and northwest, Wigtownshire west and southwest, the Irish Sea and Solway Firth south and southeast, and Dumfriesshire east and northeast. It takes in the small islands of Hestan and Little Ross, used as lighthouse stations. Its area is 899 square miles.

The northwestern part of the shire is rugged, wild, and lonely. There stands Merrick at 2764 feet, the highest ground in the south of Scotland, with the group of the Rinns of Kells near by. Toward the southwest rise Lamachan and Larg, and the bold mass of Cairnsmore of Fleet. In the southeast the one striking height is Criffel at 1866 feet. The county survey that follows treats hills, rivers, farms, and towns in the full gazetteer order of its age.
britannica-1911-laconia-new-hampshire:
Laconia is a city and the county-seat of Belknap county, New Hampshire, on both sides of the Winnepesaukee river, 28 m. N.N.E. of Concord. Its population was 8042 in 1900 and 10,183 in 1910. The Boston & Maine railway has a granite passenger station, built in 1892, and repair shops in the city. Laconia sits in the lake district, with Lake Winnisquam to the south and west and Lake Winnepesaukee to the north-east, and draws many summer visitors.

At The Weirs, within the city, are the camp-meeting grounds and the reunion camping place of the New Hampshire Civil War veterans; Lakeport is another summer-resort ward. The city holds the State School for Feeble-minded Children, a cottage hospital, the public library in the Gale Memorial building of 1903, and the state fish hatchery. In 1905 Laconia ranked first in the state for hosiery and knit goods, which made 48.4% of its factory product value.
britannica-1911-laffitte-pierre:
Pierre Laffitte (1823–1903), French Positivist, was born at Béguey in the Gironde on the 21st of February 1823. Living in Paris as a teacher of mathematics, he became a disciple of Comte, who made him his literary executor. When the Positivist body split after Comte's death, Laffitte was recognized as head of the section that accepted the full Comtian doctrine. The other section followed Littré, who rejected the religion of humanity. From 1853 he gave Positivist lectures in the room Comte had used in the rue Monsieur le Prince.

His books include Les Grands Types de l'humanité (1875) and the Cours de philosophie première (1889). In 1893 he was appointed to the new chair at the Collège de France for the general history of science. A statue of Comte was erected in the Place de la Sorbonne in 1902, largely through his efforts. He died on the 4th of January 1903.
britannica-1911-lahore:
Lahore is a city of British India and capital of the Punjab, at 31° 35′ N. and 74° 20′ E., near the left bank of the Ravi. It stands 1706 ft. up and 1252 m. by rail from Calcutta, in about the latitude of Cairo but far hotter inland. It is among India's hottest places in summer. The native city is walled, about 1¼ m. long by ¾ m. broad, and much of it stands high on earlier remains, so old buildings now lie below ground level.

Hindu tradition traces Lahore's origin to Loh, or Lava, son of Rama. Alexander's historians do not mention it, and no Graeco-Bactrian coins are found in its ruins, It was probably of no importance in the earliest period. The Chinese Buddhist Hsüan Tsang, though, noticed the city. The modern city held 202,964 people in 1901, its parts include the native city, the civil station called Donald Town, and the Anarkali bazaar.
britannica-1911-lanarkshire:
Lanarkshire is a county in the south-west of Scotland, built around the valley of the Clyde. The 1911 Britannica article gives its area as 879 square miles. The shire falls in three wards: Upper, Middle, and Lower. The Upper ward takes the whole south half and more. Hamilton is the chief town of the Middle ward. The land slopes down from high southern hills to the Firth of Clyde in the north.

Culter Fell, at 2,454 feet, is among the high border hills named. The Clyde is the great river, fed by streams such as the Douglas, the Avon, and the Kelvin. The county has no large lochs, only small sheets of water in the north. Its best known sights are the Falls of Clyde at Bonnington, Corra, and Stonebyres. The entry then turns to the rocks and soils of the shire.
britannica-1911-lancashire:
Lancashire is a county article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a county in the north-west of England. It is bounded by Westmorland, Yorkshire, and Cheshire, and by the Irish Sea to the west. At about 1,880 square miles, it is the sixth county of England in size.

The coast is for the most part flat, cut by great inlets with wide sands at low tide. The chief inlets are the estuary of the Duddon, Morecambe Bay, and the mouths of the Ribble and the Mersey. Morecambe Bay takes in the Crake, the Leven, and the Kent. The bay also cuts off the district of Furness from the rest of the county. Off the Furness coast lies Walney Island, eight miles long, with smaller isles in the strait behind it.
britannica-1911-largentiere: Largentière is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a town of south-eastern France. It is the capital of an arrondissement in the Ardèche department. It sits in the valley of the Ligne river, south-west of Privas. Its people numbered 1,690 in 1906. Chief buildings are a church from three centuries and the castle of the bishops of Viviers, then a hospital. The town has silk mills and wine-growing, with trade in fruit and silk. Its name comes from silver mines worked nearby in the middle ages.
britannica-1911-larivey-pierre:
Pierre Larivey, a French dramatist who lived from about 1550 to 1612, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was of Italian origin, the son of one of the Giunta, the famed printers of Florence and Venice. The family was set at Troyes and had taken its French name as a rendering of the word giunto, arrived.

Larivey seems to have cast horoscopes and to have served as clerk to the chapter of a church, of which he became a canon. He has no claim to be the first maker of French comedy. His gift was to plant the Italian comedy of intrigue on French soil. He shaped, more than he turned word for word, twelve Italian comedies into French prose. The first book of his merry comedies came out in 1579 and the second in 1611.
britannica-1911-laromiguiere-pierre:
Pierre Laromiguière was a French thinker who lived from the mid seventeen hundreds into the next age.
