Born at Livignac, he taught at Toulouse, where a thesis on tax and the rights of goods brought him blame from the local court. He then moved to Paris, taught logic, and later sat in the Tribunate and in a learned body for moral and civic thought.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his books and then sums up his views. He pushed back against the view that the mind is just a part of the body at work. In his scheme, the soul acts on its own, notes facts, groups them, and then reasons over them, and so it is free and does not die.
britannica-1911-latreille-pierre-andre:
Latreille, Pierre Andre is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French naturalist who rose from poverty to lead the study of insects. Born in humble state at Brives-la-Gaillarde on the twentieth of November 1762, he entered the priesthood in 1786 and used his spare hours at Brives for entomology. The Revolution drove him from Paris, and he was held for a time in prison at Bordeaux.

His Precis of the generic marks of insects appeared in 1796, and in 1798 he was set to order the insect collection of the new Museum of Natural History. When the chair of invertebrate zoology was split after the death of Lamarck in 1830, Latreille took the chair for crustaceans, spiders, and insects. He joked that they gave him bread when he had no teeth left. He died in 1833.
britannica-1911-leicestershire:
Leicestershire is a midland county of England, ringed by six sister counties and just touching a seventh. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its area and paints its face as a rolling table land. Its high points are the rough hills of an old forest in the north west, one of which tops nine hundred feet.

Most of the county drains to a great river that forms a short part of its north bound. The chief stream of the county feeds that river, and the county takes its name from the old name of that stream, it is said. That stream rises in the south east and hugs the border for a long reach. A second stream joins it from the east border, and more small feeds swell the main flow.
britannica-1911-lewes-delaware:
Lewes is a town in Sussex county, Delaware, in the south-east of the state on Delaware Bay, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. Its people numbered 2,158 in 1910. Its harbour is formed by the Delaware Breakwater, built by the national state and finished in 1869, with a second breakwater above it finished in 1901.

The cove between the two works makes a harbour of refuge of about 550 acres, and the pilots of Delaware Bay make their base at Lewes. The town trades in fruit and vegetables with northern cities. Its past reaches back to the first European settlement on Delaware soil, made near here in 1631 by Dutch colonists. They called the place Zwaanendael, the valley of swans, but the settlement was soon wiped out by the native peoples.
britannica-1911-lincolnshire:
Lincolnshire is a large eastern county of England. Only Yorkshire tops its 2,646 square miles. The Humber bounds it north and the sea east. Some 110 miles of coast run low and marshy. Banks of earth guard field and town from sea floods.

Sea eats some shores and leaves others. Holbeach now stands six miles from the water. Wide Wash ground has been won back by drain and bank. A third of the county is fen and marsh, cut by drains with local names. Two limestone ranges run north and south through the plain: the Cliff and the Wolds. Sand beaches at Cleethorpes, Skegness, and Mablethorpe draw crowds in season. The Wash, full of banks and silt, makes the east coast's hardest sailing. Mist hides its low shores from ships close in.
britannica-1911-linlithgowshire:
Linlithgowshire, also called West Lothian, is a county in the south east of Scotland, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica maps its bounds. The Firth of Forth bounds it to the north, and Edinburghshire to the east and south east. Lanarkshire lies to the south west and Stirlingshire to the north west. The county covers 76,861 acres, or 120 square miles.

Its coast line runs for seventeen miles along the Firth. The land rises very slowly from the shore to a hilly district in the south. A valley a few miles inland stretches from east to west. Hills between the county town and Bathgate include Knock, at 1,017 feet. Cairnpapple stands at about 1,000 feet, and Cocklerue at 912 feet. Binny Craig, a sharp crag like those at Stirling and Edinburgh, ends the Riccarton Hills to the east.
britannica-1911-loti-pierre:
Pierre Loti was the pen name of Louis Marie Julien Viaud (1850–1910 era author), a French writer whose life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Rochefort on the fourteenth of January 1850. The Viauds were an old Protestant family, and Loti kept at least a formal hold on that faith. His childhood scenes fill his book Le Roman d’un enfant, printed in 1890.

His schooling began at Rochefort, but the navy was his set path. At seventeen he entered the naval school, Le Borda. He rose by slow steps to the rank of captain in 1906. In January 1910 he was placed on the reserve list. His pen name is said to come from his deep shyness as a young man. Shipmates gave him the name, and it stayed with his books.
britannica-1911-louys-pierre:
French novelist and poet Pierre Louys, born in Paris in eighteen seventy, is given a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At nineteen he founded a review that brought him into touch with the leaders of a school of French verse. Swinburne, Maeterlinck, and Mallarme were among those who wrote for it.

He won wide notice with a novel in eighteen ninety six that gave a vivid picture of morals at Alexandria. That was at the start of the Christian era. An earlier book claimed to be a version from the Greek. Its fine prose is held as typical of a modern French school, and some of its songs were set to music by Debussy and others. Later novels and story sets followed over the next decade. He wed a poet's daughter in eighteen ninety nine.
britannica-1911-macdonald-jacques-etienn:
Jacques Macdonald is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a marshal of France who lived from 1765 to 1840. He was born at Sedan in November 1765. His father came of an old Jacobite family. That family had followed James the Second to France. Flora Macdonald was a near kin of his house. In 1785 he joined a legion raised for Holland.

He then took a post in a loyal regiment. Love for a girl of reform views kept him from flight. He wed her and served as aide to a general. Brave acts at Jemmapes won him rank as colonel in 1793. He refused to desert with his chief to Austria. That loyalty won him a brigade in the Holland drive. His grasp of the land helped seize a Dutch fleet. Later service took him to the Rhine and to Italy.
britannica-1911-macedonian-empire:
The Macedonian empire is the name given to the empire founded by Alexander the Great of Macedon. It covered lands now held by Greece, Turkey, Egypt, Syria, and Persia. It ran east as far as northern India at its widest reach. The entry gives a general account of the empire in all its aspects. It falls into two main parts by its own plan.

The first part covers the reign of Alexander himself in full. The second covers his successors, the Diadochi, and their royal houses. At the start of the fourth century two kinds of state faced each other. Persia held strength in its size, its men, and its treasure under one hand. Greece held strength in spirit and in the skill of its soldiers. No Greek city state could match Persia alone in bulk.
britannica-1911-manley-mary-de-la-rivier:
Mary de la Riviere Manley, an English writer who lived from about 1663 to 1724, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. She was born on April 7, 1663, in Jersey. Her father governed the Channel Islands. Left an orphan at sixteen, she was tricked into a false marriage by a kinsman.

Manley wrote plays first, then turned to sharp tales of scandal. Her Secret History of Queen Zarah came out in 1705. Her big hit, a scandal tale from the New Atalantis, came in 1709. She was held for libel that fall but freed by the court in 1710. In 1711 she wrote tracts and many parts of the Examiner.
britannica-1911-mare:
Mare is a short word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English term for the female of the horse family. A mare is the female of any animal of the family Equidae, of the ass, or of the zebra, but the word points most of all to the horse. It is used of the camel as well.

The second half of the entry splits the word nightmare away from the horse. In that compound the ending is a Teutonic word, seen as mar, maer, and mara, for a goblin thought to sit on a sleeper's chest and cause such dreams. The same goblin word lives in the French cauchemar, whose first part comes from caucher, to tread or trample, from the Latin calcare. So one spelling in English hides two wholly separate words with separate roots.
britannica-1911-martin-sir-theodore:
Sir Theodore Martin is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Martin was a British author and translator, born at Edinburgh in 1816. He was the son of a solicitor and trained in that trade himself. He practised in Edinburgh before moving to London in 1846.

In London he became senior partner in a firm of parliamentary agents. Writing ran beside his legal work from the start. He gave pieces to Fraser's Magazine and Tait's Magazine under the name Bon Gaultier. With Professor Aytoun he published the Book of Ballads in 1856, under the same pen name. The book won popular favour at once. Translations followed: poems and ballads of Goethe in 1858, then a Danish lyric drama by Henrik Hertz. The entry follows a lawyer whose second career, in verse and translation, outshone the first.
britannica-1911-massena-andre:
Andre Massena, called the greatest of Napoleon's marshals, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He lived from 1756 to 1817 and was born at Nice on May 6, 1756. He was the son of a small wine merchant and was very poor. He began life as a cabin boy, then joined a regiment in 1775.

Massena rose fast as an officer, but his low birth barred a full commission, so he quit in 1789. War and the republic drew him back in 1791. By late 1793 he was a general of division. He won at Saorgio in 1794 and shared the win at Loano in 1795. In the great Italian drive of 1796 to 1797, he was Bonaparte's most trusted division chief.
britannica-1911-mercier-honore:
Honore Mercier was a Canadian lawyer and statesman who lived from eighteen forty to eighteen ninety-four. He was born at Saint Athanase in Quebec and trained for the law after school in Montreal. He worked as a paper editor and then in law for some years. He sat in the House of Commons and later led the Liberal Party in Quebec.

The entry traces his rise step by step. It tells how anger over the death of Louis Riel helped his party win in eighteen eighty-six. He then served as premier and passed the Jesuit Estates Act. Readers get a clear view of French Canadian politics in that age.
britannica-1911-mere:
Mere is a word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica covering three separate English words spelled the same. The first, from the Latin merus, means pure and unmixed: mere wine is wine with nothing added, and mere folly is folly pure and simple. Modern use gives the word a slighting tone, though law keeps the older sense in phrases like mere motion and mere right.

The other two words are native. The second mere, kin to the German Meer, is an arm of the sea or a lake. The third, from an Old English word for a wall, means a landmark or boundary, and also a road that divides two places. In Derbyshire lead country a mere was a measure of ore-bearing land.
britannica-1911-metochita-theodore:
Theodore Metochita was a Byzantine author, scholar, and statesman of high learning. He thrived under Andronicus the Second, who ruled to thirteen twenty eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. After his patron fell, Metochita lost his chancellor post and faced exile.

He was soon called back, but left public life for a convent home. There he died in the year thirteen thirty two, at rest. His pupil Nicephorus Gregoras called him a living library in praise. Only a few of his many works have survived to this day. His best known work holds some one hundred twenty essays on mixed themes.
britannica-1911-metre: Metre is a short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains the measure that sets verse apart from plain prose. Verse lines match in count of beats and in sound at the line end. Old Greek and Latin verse rests on long and short sounds in a set flow. The entry sends readers to a full entry on verse for the rules of each system. A split use of the same word for a unit of length is also noted.
britannica-1911-mignard-pierre:
Pierre Mignard (1610–1695) was a French painter, called Le Romain, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica centres on his feud with the Academy. He was born at Troyes in 1610, of a family of artists. His brother Nicholas was also a painter of note. In 1630 he left the studio of Simon Vouet for Italy.

Mignard spent twenty two years in Italy and built a strong reputation there. That fame brought him a summons home to Paris. His portrait of the king pleased the court, and he rose in royal favour. He then set himself against Le Brun, the head of the Academy. He declined to enter that body and made himself the centre of opposition to its power. The entry calls that struggle a key one. It matched the old guilds of France against the new Academy that Colbert upheld.
britannica-1911-moliere:
Moliere, born Jean Baptiste Poquelin in Paris in 1622, was the great French playwright of his age. The 1911 Britannica entry opens with care over the exact facts of his birth. His christening record dates to the fifteenth of January that year. His birth house stood most likely on the Rue Saint Honore in the city.

His father was an upholsterer who held a valued post in the royal household. The Poquelin family came from Beauvais, where they had thrived as tradesmen for ages. A tale of Scots descent is set aside as disproved by research. The entry then turns to his mother and his early schooling in Paris.
britannica-1911-monmouthshire:
Monmouthshire is a western border county of England, set against Wales. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 534 square miles. It is bounded by Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, and Glamorgan. The Severn estuary washes its south shore. The land varies much, with fine scenery along the Wye valley. Hills in the west and north rise to good height. Sugar Loaf, at 1,955 feet, is the top named.

Marsh levels flank the Usk mouth on the coast. Strong banks guard those levels from the tide. Five rivers are traced in the entry. The Wye forms most of the east border. The Usk flows south through the centre of the county. The Monnow, Ebbw, and Rhymney complete the list. Salmon crowd the Wye and the Usk. Trout fill many of the smaller streams. A section on the rocks of the county follows the rivers.
britannica-1911-montausier-charles-de-sa:
Montausier, Charles de Sainte-Maure is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French soldier and courtier. Born on the sixth of October 1610, he was raised a Huguenot and educated at Sedan. He served with distinction at the siege of Casale in 1630. In 1635 his brother's death made him marquis and the known suitor of Julie d'Angennes.

The article lingers on the famous courtship. For Julie he and a circle of poets made the Guirlande de Julie, a garland of verses painted with flowers. He had become a Roman Catholic before the marriage, stayed loyal to the crown through the Fronde, and rose high under Louis the Fourteenth. He took a dukedom, and from 1668 governed the dauphin's education.
britannica-1911-monte-vulture:
Monte Vulture is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a mountain in the Basilicata region of Italy, in the province of Potenza. The peak is an old volcano that no longer erupts. In Roman times the land around it lay on the border of two regions.

The entry gives the height of the peak and notes the thick woods on its crater. Oaks and beeches grow there, and wild boars and wolves live in the woods. Two small lakes lie on the mountain. A ruined church and a monks house stand by the upper lake. The town at the foot of the hill is also described.
britannica-1911-morellet-andre:
André Morellet, a French economist and miscellaneous writer who lived from 1727 to 1819, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Lyons in March 1727, he was one of the last survivors of the philosophes. He appears in many memoirs of the age. He was taught by the Jesuits at Lyons and at the Sorbonne. He took holy orders, but the title of abbé was the chief clerical thing about him.

Morellet had a ready and biting wit, and Voltaire gave him a punning nickname for it. A sharp pamphlet against a play landed him briefly in the Bastille. He also answered Galiani on the grain trade in 1770. Later he served in discreet dealings with English statesmen and received a pension. In 1785 he was elected to the Academy. A year before his death he issued four volumes of selections.
britannica-1911-nairnshire:
Nairnshire, a county in the north east of Scotland, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Inverness shire bounds it west and south, Elginshire east, and the Moray Firth north. It holds just past a hundred thousand acres. That makes it the fourth smallest county in Scotland, with nine miles of coast.

Sand banks fringe the shore and put ships at risk. Low dunes line it and run on into the next county. A strip of sand and gravel reaches four or five miles inland. Behind it lies a plain of low swells, the west end of the rich low land of Moray. South the land climbs fast to border hills. More than one top passes two thousand feet. Two rivers of note cross the county.
britannica-1911-normanton-yorkshire:
Normanton is an urban district in the West Riding of Yorkshire in England. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the river Calder near Wakefield. Three rail lines serve the town from sundry points of the compass. Its count in 1901 was 12,352 souls in the district. The church of All Saints mixes Norman and late Gothic work.

A square tower, rebuilt in 1717, crowns that parish church. Fine old stained glass and prized monuments fill its walls and aisles. A grammar school there was founded late in the 1500s in town. Traces of a moat that once ringed the town still show in places. A mound called Haw Hill near by may be an old barrow.
britannica-1911-northamptonshire:
Northamptonshire is an east midland county of England, and a long entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica surveys its land, rivers, and rocks. The county covers about 1,003 square miles and is ringed by seven other counties. Its surface rolls gently, richly farmed and in places well wooded, with few hills above 700 feet.

The entry stresses that the county is the main watershed of central England, where many great rivers start. It follows the Avon, Nene, Welland, and Cherwell on their paths out of the county. It also praises the county ash trees and old oaks, and notes that the north-east tip belongs to the Fen district.
britannica-1911-nottinghamshire:
Nottinghamshire is the subject of a county entry in the 1911 Britannica. The county is an inland shire of England. Four shires bound it on its land sides round. Its area is given as over eight hundred square miles. The north lies in the great plain of York. Marsh land lies in the far north of the county. Flat vales mark the lower Trent and the Idle.

In the south west the ground swells into hills. Near Mansfield those hills rise over six hundred feet. That district holds the old Sherwood Forest of fame. Some parts keep their old state to this day. Very old oaks stand in the part called the Dukeries. The chief rivers are the Trent, Erewash, Soar, and Idle. The Trent flows north east past Nottingham and Newark. Notes on the rocks below ground follow the rivers.
britannica-1911-ogre: Ogre is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a monster of fairy tale and folk lore. An ogre is a cruel giant who lives on human flesh. The word is French and first shows in the tales of Perrault, printed in 1697. The first English use was in 1713, spelled as hogre. Some have linked it to the Magyar folk name Ugri. The held view ties it to a Spanish word for Orcus, Latin god of the dead.
britannica-1911-overture:
Overture is the subject of a music article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An overture is the opening music played before a stage work or choral work. The idea of such a piece has no place before the sixteen hundreds. A flourish at the start of an early opera may count as the first of its kind. As an art form the overture began with the works of Lully.

The article describes the French overture that Lully devised. It joins a slow opening in marked dotted rhythm with a lively movement in fugue style. The slow opening was always repeated. The form thus came to serve as the opening of a suite of dances. Bach used the French overture form even for choruses and hymn tunes. With the rise of drama music and the sonata style, the French form lost favour for opera.
britannica-1911-oxfordshire:
Oxfordshire is an inland county of England, and a survey entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its land and rivers. It covers about 756 square miles and is ringed by six other counties. The county lies almost wholly in the basin of the upper Thames.

The entry follows the Thames along the southern border for seventy-one miles, from Kelmscot to below Henley. It then traces the side rivers that join it on the county side, none of which rise inside the county. The Windrush runs through Witney, the Evenlode past Blenheim Park, and the Cherwell forms part of the eastern border before joining the Thames at Oxford.
britannica-1911-paoli-cesare:
Cesare Paoli, an Italian scholar of old hand script and state papers, gets a life note in the 1911 Britannica. Born and schooled in Florence in eighteen forty, he was the son of a senator. At age twenty one he took a post in the town record office. He spent six years at the Siena files, then came back to Florence. In eighteen seventy four he took the first chair in his field there.

He spent his work years reading and printing old state papers by hand. From eighteen eighty seven he ran a famed past journal for Italy. His own works span past essays, script studies, prints of papers, and reviews. A full list of his works sits in a note in that same journal.
britannica-1911-parker-theodore:
The life of Theodore Parker fills a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Parker was an American preacher and social reformer born at Lexington, Massachusetts, in 1810. He was the youngest of eleven children of a small farmer. His grand-father led the minute-men in the fight at Lexington.

Parker taught school in winter, then worked his way through Harvard. He farmed while he studied and went to Cambridge for exams. He learned many tongues, from Hebrew and Arabic to the main modern tongues of Europe. In 1843 he brought out his English version of a German work on the Old Testament. The entry tracks a self-made scholar who reached wide fame.
britannica-1911-peeblesshire:
Peeblesshire, also called Tweeddale, is a southern inland county of Scotland, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lays out its hills. Edinburghshire bounds it to the north and north east. Selkirkshire lies to the east and south east, Dumfriesshire to the south, and Lanarkshire to the west. The county covers 222,599 acres, or near 548 square miles.

The surface is a run of hills, highest in the south of the county. The vale of the Tweed breaks that run, with glens cut by its many branches. South of the Tweed, Broad Law and Cramalt Craig each rise to 2,723 feet. North of the river, Broughton Heights stand at 1,872 feet. Trahenna Hill and Penvalla follow close behind in height. The Pentland hills reach into the north west corner of the shire.
britannica-1911-peine-forte-et-dure:
Peine forte et dure, French for hard and severe punishment, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The term names a torture used on prisoners who refused to plead when arraigned for felony. Under early English law a prisoner had to plead guilty or not guilty before trial. Those who stood silent were first imprisoned and starved. In the reign of Henry the Fourth the peine took their place.

The prisoner was stretched on his back, and stone or iron weights were laid on him. The pressing went on until he submitted or died. Pressing to death was abolished in 1772. Standing mute was then made equal to conviction. By an act of 1828, a plea of not guilty is entered for any prisoner who refuses to plead. The article records cases from 1442 on, including Margaret Clitherow in 1586.
britannica-1911-pembrokeshire:
Pembrokeshire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a county of South Wales. It is the most westerly county of that region. Cardigan bounds it on the north east. Carmarthen bounds it on the east. The Bristol Channel lies along its southern side. Saint Bride's Bay and Cardigan Bay wash its west. Its area is given as 615 square miles. The whole coast is extremely indented in character.

That coast extends over 140 miles in length. Milford Haven is the principal inlet of the county. Headlands run from Cemmaes to Saint Gowan's along the shore. Five islands of moderate size lie off the coast. Ramsey, Grassholm, Skomer, and Skokholm lie in Saint Bride's Bay. Rare birds are not uncommon along that coast. Peregrine falcons, ravens, and choughs are all named. Sea fowl breed in immense numbers on the Stack Rocks.
britannica-1911-perthshire:
Perthshire is an inland county of Scotland, the fourth largest county in that land. It is bounded by Inverness, Aberdeen, Forfar, Fife, Stirling, and Argyll. Its area runs to near two thousand five hundred square miles in all. By far the greater part of the county is mountainous in character. At least fifty peaks rise above three thousand feet in height.

Ben Lawers, near Loch Tay, is the best known of those peaks. Ben More, Ben Lui, and Schiehallion are also named in the entry. Four lesser hills were made famed by a poem, The Lady of the Lake. The Ochil hills split Perthshire from the shires to its south. The chief stream is the Tay, which rises on the Argyll border. It flows to the North Sea after a long course through the county.
britannica-1911-peruzzi-baldassare:
Baldassare Peruzzi, an Italian designer and painter who lived from 1481 to 1536, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born near Volterra and passed his youth at Siena. While still young he went to Rome to study building and paint. There he first walked in the path of Perugino.

His villa on the Tiber for a rich banker of Siena made his name. That house, now called the Farnesina, is praised for its grace and fine detail. In 1520 the pope made him a designer of Saint Peter's, though his plan was never built. In the sack of Rome in 1527 he barely kept his life. He then worked at Siena on its walls, and late works in Rome round out his tale. He lies by Raphael in the Pantheon.
britannica-1911-pisciculture:
Pisciculture, the art of breeding and rearing fish, opens a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin for fish. Few kinds of fish can be kept in bonds from egg to full growth all their lives. Goldfish are the stock case, and the carp is near the one food fish that bears such a life.

The entry splits the art into two main kinds. One rears young fish in ponds till they reach a size fit for the table. The other stocks wild waters with eggs or fry from caught parents. Carp ponds are a great trade in China and Germany, but dead in England. On the Adriatic coast, young sea fish are let into walled lagoons by sluice. There they are kept and fed till grown.
britannica-1911-pithou-pierre:
Pierre Pithou, a French lawyer and scholar who lived from 1539 to 1596, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Troyes, he was called to the Paris bar in 1560. A Calvinist, he fled to Sedan and Basel when the second war of religion broke out in 1567. He came home under an edict of peace and just missed death in the St Bartholomew massacre.

He then gave up the Protestant faith, and Henry as king gave him legal posts. His chief work was his share in the Satire Ménippée of 1593, which did deep harm to the League. His rich library passed in large part to the national library at Paris. He first made the Fables of Phaedrus known to the world in 1596, the year of his death.
britannica-1911-pleasure:
Pleasure in plain speech means much the same as enjoyment of any kind. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws the word through French from the Latin placere, to please. It covers both high mental joys and plain bodily ones. When and why people feel pleased is a question for two fields at once.

Mind study and moral study both take up the topic, the entry notes. Pleasure tends to follow success in some effort, it says. It can also come from mere sensation or from linked memories. Some moral thinkers held that all acts seek pleasure in the end. Aristotle took a middle path, tying pleasure to good action as its crown.
britannica-1911-porto-alegre:
Porto Alegre is a city and port of Brazil and capital of Rio Grande do Sul state. Its own article follows a word study entry in the hosted text. The 1911 Britannica entry places it at the north end of Lagoa dos Patos. It held about seventy three thousand people in 1900, many of German and Italian stock.

Rail lines and river steamers tie the port to colonies and to the west of the state. Five rivers flow into the Guahyba inlet and bring trade to its wharves. Shallow draft limits sea trade, since ships must cross a bar at the lake mouth. The entry gives a full port survey of routes, counts, and growth.
britannica-1911-portraiture:
Portraiture is the art of picturing a single person, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its first steps in Egypt and Greece. The earliest tries at likeness are found in Egypt. They appear in spirit figures and in the painted cases of mummies. Egyptian painting never went past fixed forms, mere outlines filled with flat colour.

In Greece the art likely began with shadow painting, called skiagraphy. A tale tells of a Greek girl tracing the shadow of her parting lover on a wall. The art grew fast from that start. In 463 before Christ, Polygnotus brought single likeness into the painting of public buildings. Near a century later, Apelles showed a genius for character and expression. Alexander the Great made Apelles his own painter for that gift.
britannica-1911-pugin-augustus-welby-nor:
Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin, an English architect who lived from 1812 to 1852, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Augustus Charles Pugin, a Frenchman who settled in London as a draughtsman of buildings. The younger Pugin was born in Bedford Square and schooled at Christ's Hospital, then entered his father's office.

His father spent years on a large series of books on the Gothic buildings of England, with accurate drawings of medieval work. The son's youth was spent making fine measured drawings for those books, and in that way his love of Gothic art was first lit. All his life he kept drawing, in England and on many trips to Germany and France. His sketches are praised for delicacy and touch. In 1827 he was hired to design furniture in a medieval style for Windsor Castle.
britannica-1911-quagmire: Quagmire is a word for a bog or marsh, ground so soaked with water that it cannot bear any weight, and this short 1911 Britannica entry explains how the word is built. Its first part is quag or quake, from an old English verb kin to quaver and quiver. Its second part is mire, meaning mud, from an Icelandic root. The entry adds a guess linking quag to the root seen in quick, meaning alive.
britannica-1911-radnorshire:
Radnorshire is a county article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an inland county of Wales, the smallest of the six South Welsh counties at 471 square miles. The county is lozenge shaped and almost wholly hilly, with the mountain tract of Radnor Forest at its centre rising to 2,163 feet. Toward the south the hills sink and the valleys widen into plains full of rivulets.

The Wye, the chief river, crosses the north west corner and then forms the border to England. Its waters hold salmon, trout, and grayling in plenty, drawing anglers to it and to its branches. One branch, the Elan, feeds the great reservoirs of Birmingham. The most famed waterfall is Water-break-its-Neck, west of New Radnor. By its rocks the county runs from Ordovician beds in the west through the Silurian to Old Red Sandstone in the south east, with an old ridge at Old Radnor.
britannica-1911-renfrewshire:
Renfrewshire is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a county in the south west of Scotland, on the river and firth of Clyde. Low hills and moor edge most of the shire, and one green vale cuts through it. Lakes and stored water serve the towns of Greenock and Glasgow.

The entry gives the size of the county and names its main heights and lochs. A long part on rocks explains the coal and lime beds under the ground. Old coal, iron stone, and oil shale beds are all mapped in turn. Building stone from one quarry is also noted. The account suits readers who want both the land and its wealth set out plainly.
britannica-1911-ricotti-magnani-cesare:
Ricotti-Magnani, Cesare is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Italian general who rebuilt his country's army. Born at Borgo Lavezzaro in 1822, he served as an artillery officer and was wounded at the siege of Peschiera in 1848. In 1852 he won praise for stopping the blast of a burning powder store. He ran the Artillery School from 1856 to 1859 and led the fifth division at San Martino.

On the death of General Govone in 1872 he became minister of war and reformed the army on the lessons of the Franco-German War. He cut the term of service, extended the draft to all able bodied men, and built a standing army with a mobile militia and a reserve. Italy could then place 1,800,000 men on a war footing. He fell with the Right in 1876, served again under Depretis, and entered the senate in 1890.
britannica-1911-robert-of-auxerre:
Robert of Auxerre, a French chronicler who lived from about 1156 to 1212, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was an inmate of the monastery of St Marien at Auxerre. At the request of its abbot, Milo de Trainel, he wrote a Chronicon, or universal history. The work runs from the creation of the world to the year 1211.

For the years before 1181 the chronicle is a compilation from older writers such as Prosper and Sigebert. From 1181 to 1211 it is an original authority. It is a key source for France under Philip Augustus. It also covers other lands, the Crusades, and affairs in the East. Molinier calls the author one of the best historians of the middle ages. The article praises his diligence and sound judgment. Two continuators carried the work to 1228.
britannica-1911-robinson-theodore:
Theodore Robinson is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Robinson was an American artist, born at Irasburg, Vermont, in 1852. He went to Paris to study painting as a young man. His teachers there were Gerome and Carolus-Duran, two masters of the French schools.

He also worked alongside Claude Monet, the great painter of light. That company shaped his own mature manner. Prizes marked his rising name on both sides of the ocean. The Webb Prize came in 1890 for his Winter Landscape. The Shaw Fund prize followed in 1892 for In the Sun, a study of a peasant girl. He had joined the Society of American Artists back in 1881. He died in New York City in April 1896, only forty-four years old. The brief entry fixes the outline of a short career spent between Vermont, Paris, and the circle of Monet.
britannica-1911-rochester-new-hampshire:
Rochester, a city in Strafford county, New Hampshire, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on two rivers, about thirty miles east of Concord. Its population rose from 7,396 in 1890 to 8,868 in the census of 1910. The city covers about thirty four square miles and is served by four rail lines.

The rivers give strong water power for varied making trades, the entry says. Rochester was named for Lawrence Hyde, earl of Rochester, and chartered as a town in 1722. No one settled there until 1728, though. Parts of the first town later split off to form two other towns. The place was the birthplace of John Parker Hale, and it gained a city charter in 1891.
britannica-1911-roxburghshire:
Roxburghshire is a border county of Scotland, set against England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 665 square miles of land. Only the north and the river valleys lie low. The whole south is marked by hills. The Cheviot range forms much of the line with England. Peaks named include Peel Fell and Greatmoor. Near Melrose stand the three Eildon hills.

Rivers take up much of the entry. The Tweed crosses the north of the shire. Its feeders include the Bowden, the Teviot, and the Eden. The Teviot is the chief stream wholly in the county. It runs 37 miles north east to join the Tweed at Kelso. A long list of its side streams is given. The Liddel leads the waters of the south. The entry reads as a careful map in words of a hill county.
britannica-1911-sacchini-antonio-maria-g:
Antonio Maria Gaspare Sacchini, an Italian composer who lived from 1734 to 1786, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Pozzuoli, he was the son of a poor fisherman. Durante heard him singing on the sands and took charge of his schooling at a music school in Naples. Durante and Piccinni taught him composition there.

The entry says his first work for the school theatre came in 1756, and his first serious opera was staged at Rome in 1762. Many more followed, nearly all with success. In 1769 he went to Venice, where one opera won such praise that he was made head of a music school. There he trained fine women singers and wrote church music. In London in 1772, despite a cruel plot against him, he won bright success.
britannica-1911-saltpetre:
Saltpetre is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on naturally occurring nitrates. The name joins Latin words for salt and for rock. The commercial name covers three distinct nitrates in the text. The first is ordinary saltpetre, or potassium nitrate. The second is Chile saltpetre, or sodium nitrate. The third is wall saltpetre, or calcium nitrate. 

The crusts form by oxidation of nitrogenous matter in place. Alkalies and alkaline earths must be present for that change. Ordinary saltpetre occurs mingled with other nitrates widely. It is found on and in the surface layers of soil. Parts of India, Persia, Arabia, and Spain are named. Deposits in limestone caves of Kentucky and other states are noted. Those cave deposits were probably derived from the soil above. Percolating water gathered them in the caves over time. The entry says they are of no commercial value.
britannica-1911-sapphic-metre:
Sapphic Metre is the subject of a verse entry in the 1911 Britannica. Sapphics are an old form of verse by count of beats. The form is named for the poet Sappho of old Greece. She is thought to have made the form herself. She used it with skill no later poet matched. A sapphic line holds five beats in its span. The middle beat alone holds three sound parts.

A sapphic stanza holds three such lines in a row. A short line called an adonis ends the stanza. Greek verse of the form is shown in the entry. Horace took up the form for Latin verse use. He fixed where the word break should fall in the line. Catullus had used the form in Latin before him. Hymns of the middle ages used the stanza form much. Loose use later spoiled the true shape of the form.
britannica-1911-sapphire:
Sapphire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a blue gem stone. It is a blue transparent variety of corundum, or native alumina. It is much valued as a gem stone by buyers. The colour of the normal sapphire runs across a scale. It varies from the palest blue to deep indigo. The most esteemed tint is that of the blue cornflower.

Many crystals are parti-coloured in their natural state. Blue is spread in patches in a colourless or yellow stone. By skilful cutting, that deep portion can colour the whole gem. Sapphire crystallizes in the hexagonal system of crystals. It is therefore dichroic in its show of colour. In a pale stone that character may not be well marked. In a deep stone the colour splits into two tints. One is ultramarine blue, the other a greenish shade.
britannica-1911-sayre:
Sayre is a borough of Bradford county, Pennsylvania, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It stands on the North Branch of the Susquehanna river, just south of the New York state line. Its people numbered 5,243 in 1900 and 6,426 in 1910.

The borough was served by the Lehigh Valley railway and linked by electric line with Waverly, New York, and with Athens nearby. With Athens, South Waverly, and Waverly it formed in effect one working community. Sayre was the trade centre of a farming and dairying region, with metal works and other factories. Its chief weight came from the locomotive and car shops of the railway. It was settled in 1880, made a borough in 1891, and named for Robert Heysham Sayre, long chief engineer of that line.
britannica-1911-sceptre:
Sceptre is a rod or staff carried as a sign of power, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows the symbol from Greek times onward. Among the early Greeks it was a long staff used by old men, then by judges, war leaders, and priests. Painted vases show it as a tall staff tipped with a metal ornament. The Etruscans made sceptres of great splendour for kings and high priests.

The Roman sceptre likely came from theirs. Under the Roman republic an ivory sceptre marked consular rank, and winning generals carried one too. Emperors used a special form, often ivory tipped with a golden eagle. With Christianity the eagle gave way at times to a cross. In England two sceptres came to be used side by side, one tipped with a cross and one with a dove.
britannica-1911-semaphore:
Semaphore is the name of a device for sending signals to a distance, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. The word joins Greek terms for a sign and for carrying. The device is made of movable arms or blades of wood, worked by levers and fixed to a high post or pole, so that its positions can be read far off.

The most familiar semaphore of the entry's day was the one used in railway signalling on the block system. There, a blade held level means danger, and a blade dropped means safety. With a code, the semaphore was still used in the navy for signalling from ship to ship. Before the electric telegraph came, semaphores carried messages over long distances on land as well. The entry is brief, but it catches a device that served both the railway and the fleet.
britannica-1911-shropshire:
Shropshire, also called Salop, is a western county of England on the border of Wales. The 1911 Britannica article gives its area as 1,343 square miles. The name Salop comes from an early name of its county town, Shrewsbury. To the west the county takes on the hill look of Wales. The Breidden Hills rise in three sharp peaks south of the Severn. Clun Forest spreads its rough, round hills in the south-west.

Four more chains cross the south of the county. They are the Long Mynd, the Caradoc Hills, Wenlock Edge, and the Clee Hills. Brown Clee, at 1,805 feet, is the high point named. The rest of the land rolls in a pleasant, well-farmed way. Near all the county lies in the basin of the Severn. That river flows east to Shrewsbury, then turns south past Ironbridge and Bridgnorth.
britannica-1911-simms-william-gilmore:
William Gilmore Simms, who lived from 1806 to 1870, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American poet, novelist, and historian born at Charleston, South Carolina. His mother died in his infancy, and his grandmother raised him. He clerked in a drug store, then studied law and was admitted to the bar in 1827.

Simms soon left the law for letters, the article relates. He wrote verse from childhood and published poems through the 1820s. His sea poem Atalantis, issued in 1832, made his fame as an author. His tale Martin Faber was warmly received as well. During the Civil War he backed the secession side in a weekly paper. Federal troops entering Charleston damaged his property, and he sat in the state legislature in the 1840s.
britannica-1911-somersetshire:
Somersetshire, a county in the south-west of England, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Bristol Channel bounds it on the north and north-west, with Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Dorsetshire, and Devonshire on its other sides. It covers about 1,630 square miles. In shape it looks like a poorly drawn crescent, broader at its eastern horn than at its western.

The article divides the county into three natural parts. A broad plain of river soil lies between two regions of hills. The Mendip range runs north-west toward the channel and ends in Brean Down, with an island standing as an outpost in the sea. The flat top of the Mendips rises past a thousand feet at Black Down. On the south the hills fall in a steep line cut by glens, among them the famed gorge of Cheddar.
britannica-1911-sphere:
Sphere in geometry is the solid or surface swept by a semicircle turning on its diameter. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives that as the core account from Euclid. Each point on the surface sits at the same distance from the center. That fixed distance is the radius, and any line through the center is a diameter.

All cuts through a sphere yield circles, the entry shows. A cut through the center gives a great circle and a hemisphere. A cut off center gives a small circle and a segment instead. The shortest path between two points follows the great circle arc. Greek study of the sphere in Euclid is traced at the close.
britannica-1911-spire:
Spire is a 1911 Britannica article on a term of church building. The word comes from an Old English term for a blade of grass. So it came to mean anything tapering to a point. In building, a spire is a lofty roof in stone or wood. It is covered with lead or slate and crowns the tower of a cathedral or church.

In their origin, spires were four-sided roofs of slight height. The church of Thaon in Normandy shows that early form. Soon they became features of great importance. They rose as lofty pyramids, generally eight-sided in form. At times they equalled the towers themselves in height. The junction of an eight-sided spire with a square tower posed a distinct problem. Its solutions in English, French, and German spires vary without end. The article follows one roof form from a low cap to a skyline crown.
britannica-1911-squire:
Squire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a shortened form of esquire. At first the word meant an attendant on a knight. In this short form, it has grown special senses. In England it serves in part as a courtesy title. It also describes the chief landed proprietor in a parish. That man is usually the lord of the manor there. Lesser proprietors in the parish are called gentlemen or yeomen.

In some parts the title goes to small freeholders too. Those men belong to the yeoman class of landowners. In Ireland such men are half scornfully called squireens. In the United States the title has also survived. There it is applied to justices of the peace. Local judges and other dignitaries in country districts bear it. The old sense of attendant also lives in the verb. To squire a lady means to wait upon her.
britannica-1911-st-benoit-sur-loire:
St Benoit-sur-Loire is a village of north-central France, in the department of Loiret. It stands on the right bank of the Loire, twenty-two miles east of Orleans by road. Its Latin name was Floriacum. The village holds a huge church, the sole survival of a famed monastery. That house was founded in the seventh century to hold the relics of St Benedict, brought from Monte Cassino.

The house held great weight in the middle ages, in part through its school. It began to fall away in the 1500s. Protestant troops sacked it in 1562, and though Richelieu had the buildings restored, the abbey never won back its old place. The church was built between about 1025 and 1218. It holds the tomb of Philip I and a modern shrine with the remains of St Benedict in the crypt.
britannica-1911-st-maur-sur-loire: Saint Maur sur Loire is a village of western France, in Maine et Loire. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the Loire below Saumur. Saint Maurus founded the first Benedictine house in Gaul there in the sixth century. Normans wrecked that house in the ninth century, the entry says. Before the blow, the saint relics moved to Fossés. What stands now is part of a church from the twelfth and seventeenth centuries. Later halls stand beside it.
britannica-1911-staffordshire:
Staffordshire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a midland county of England. It is bounded by Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Warwickshire, Worcestershire, Shropshire, and Cheshire. Its area is a little over eleven hundred square miles. The county holds the valley of the Trent from its source to the point where the river can bear boats.

The Trent rises in the far north of the county and runs south, then east, then north east through its centre. Its chief side streams run in courses much like its own. The land between three of those rivers is rolling and beautiful, the entry says. Hills rise to some eighteen hundred feet on the Derbyshire border. Dovedale, part of the upper Dove valley, draws many visitors for its scenery.
britannica-1911-ste-anne-de-beaupre:
Sainte Anne de Beaupré is a village in Montmorency county, Quebec, Canada, where the Sainte Anne river meets the Saint Lawrence. The 1911 Britannica article puts it twenty-two miles below the city of Quebec. It stands in rolling farm land, with hills behind it. Near by, falls on the river draw praise, and the fishing is fine. The homes of the village count about 1,500 souls.

For more than two centuries the place has drawn Roman Catholic pilgrims. Cures are still said to come through the prayers of Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin. In the basilica, piles of crutches cast off by the cured keep growing. On the feast of the saint, the twenty-sixth of July, crowds of 30,000 are often seen. The count of pilgrims in 1905 was 170,000. A Scala Santa, built like the Holy Stairs at Rome, stands in the village.
britannica-1911-stirlingshire:
Stirlingshire is a midland county of Scotland, and a survey entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its hills, rivers, and lochs. It covers about 451 square miles, ringed by Perthshire, Lanarkshire, and other counties and by the Firth of Forth. In the north-west a spur of the Grampians tops out at Ben Lomond, 3,192 feet high.

The entry says the chief river is the Forth, which winds along most of the northern border. It follows the Carron, Endrick, Kelvin, and Avon on their courses to the Forth, the Clyde, and Loch Lomond. The lochs include most of the eastern waters of Loch Lomond and a small part of Loch Katrine.
britannica-1911-stone-staffordshire:
Stone is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stone is a market town in Staffordshire, England, on the River Trent. It lies seven miles north of Stafford on the North Staffordshire railway. The entry gives the town's population and its chief remains.

Part of the walls and crypt survive from an old abbey there. The abbey grew from a college of canons founded in 670. The church of St Michael dates from 1750, after the abbey church fell the year before. Alleyne's grammar school was founded in 1558. Shoemaking was the chief trade, with malting, brewing, and tanning beside it. The article also notes old earthworks on the hills nearby, one linked by tradition with the kings of Mercia.
britannica-1911-sture:
Sture, a great house of Sweden, is traced in a family entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. First stands Sten Sture the Elder, born in the year 1440. In 1464 he backed a bishop's fight against Christian of Denmark. His gift was to win peasants and make soldiers of them fast. By 1470 he led the Swedish national cause in open field.

That year Sten beat both a rival lord and the Danish king. On the death of Charles the Eighth he was picked as regent. From 1470 to 1497 he ruled with a statesman's high skill. His win at Brunkebjarg in 1471 set his place firm in Sweden. A hard war with Russia wore his strength down in time. Cast down in 1497, he was picked as regent once more.
britannica-1911-subleyras-pierre:
Pierre Subleyras, who lived from 1699 to 1749, was a French painter in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born at Uzes and left France for Italy in 1728 after winning the grand prix. A large canvas of Christ at the house of Simon made his name there. That work hangs in the Louvre and won him a seat in the Academy of Saint Luke.

A cardinal got him an order for a saint scene to be worked in mosaic for Saint Peter. Pope Benedict the Fourteenth and Roman princes sat for his portraits in those years. Two great canvases for the pope own rooms followed that success. The entry also praises his odd genre scenes and book plates.
britannica-1911-sucre:
Sucre, a city of Bolivia, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is also called Chiquisaca in the text. It is the capital of the department of Chuquisaca. It is the nominal capital of the republic as well. It lies north-east of Potosi. Its people numbered about twenty-three thousand in 1906.

Many of its people are Indians and cholos, the text notes. The city stands in an elevated valley that opens southward. A narrow ravine carries the Cachimayo river out of it. That stream is the chief northern tributary of the Pilcomayo. The elevation of the city gives it a very agreeable climate. Fertile valleys nearby supply its markets with fruit and vegetables. The vineyards of Camargo, in the south of the department, supply wine and spirits. They are of excellent quality, the text says. The city itself is laid out on a regular plan.
britannica-1911-supreme-court-of-judicat:
The Supreme Court of Judicature is the high court system of England, and a legal entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica states how it was formed. It was set up by the Judicature Act of 1873. That act united a set of old courts under one name. The high court of chancery was among them, with the courts of king’s bench, common pleas, and exchequer.

The high court of admiralty joined the union as well. The court of probate and the divorce court came in too. By the same act, the Supreme Court was to have two divisions. One was to be called the high court of justice. The other was the court of appeal, for hearing cases from below. The entry also turns to the Supreme Court of the United States. That court stands at the head of the national judiciary there.
britannica-1911-sutherlandshire:
Sutherlandshire is a far north county of Scotland, mapped in a 1911 Britannica county entry. The Atlantic bounds it on the north and west, Caithness on the east. It ranks fifth in size among Scottish shires by land area in the count. Its west and north shores are cut deep and end in crags and headlands.

High hills give the shire a grand outline against sea and sky on all sides. Ben More in Assynt is the top peak at three thousand two hundred and seventy three feet. Rare plants and beasts mark Ben Hope, from alpine flowers to golden eagles. Lochs, forests, and serrated ridges fill out the wild north landscape survey.
britannica-1911-switzerland-literature:
Switzerland/Literature is a survey article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the writing of a multilingual country. The article opens with a denial: there is no Swiss national literature properly speaking. Instead there are four branches, divided by language. The German branch is by far the most important. The French branch becomes truly Swiss only after 1815.

The German section begins with the documents of the Confederation itself. Later alliances and diet recesses were drawn up in German, not Latin, a sign the league rested on popular consent. The article then turns to the Minnesingers, more than thirty of them in the Swiss districts. The Manesse family gathered their songs into a manuscript that survives in Paris. War songs follow, among them the famous song for the victory of Sempach in 1386.
britannica-1911-tanjore:
Tanjore, a city and district in the Madras presidency of British India, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The city stands on the Cauvery river and is a key rail junction south of Madras. Close to fifty eight thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. It was the last capital of the old Hindu Chola line.

In all ages the city has been a chief centre of rule, letters, and faith in the south. Protestant mission work in India began there at an early date. Mahratta rulers took the city in 1674 and held it in practice until 1799. In that year the district was ceded to the East India Company. The raja kept only the capital and a small tract. Noted sites include a fort palace with a fine library and a great temple with a tall tower.
britannica-1911-theatre:
A theatre is a building made for the staging of plays. The Greek word means a place for seeing. Drama grew out of the chorus dances held in honour of Dionysus. Those dances took place in a round dancing floor in his precinct at the foot of the Acropolis at Athens. The head of the chorus stood on a table by the altar to hold speech with the rest.

As the count of actors grew and speech gained weight, a platform was built at the side of the dance floor. A booth was set up where the players could change dress and masks. Wood stands were put up for the crowd on the slope of the hill. A fall of those stands in 499 BC led to the building of a lasting theatre on the site.
britannica-1911-tidore:
Tidore is an island of the Malay Archipelago, off the west coast of Halmahera and south of Ternate. The 1911 Britannica article calls it near round in shape, with an area of about thirty square miles. Quiet volcanic peaks fill most of the island and rise to 5,700 feet. Woods cover their slopes. The chief town, also named Tidore, stands on the east coast and is walled.

The town is the seat of a sultan who pays tribute to the Dutch, and of a Dutch agent. By a pact of 1879 the sultan holds sway over parts of Halmahera and the Papuan isles. He also rules the west half of New Guinea and the isles of Geelvink Gulf. The people, some 8,000 in count, are Malays of the Muslim faith. They live by farm work and fishing, growing cotton, tobacco, and nutmegs.
britannica-1911-tonnerre:
Tonnerre, a town of north-central France in the department of Yonne, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 52 miles south-east of Sens on the Paris-Lyon railway. Its people numbered 3,974 in 1906. The town sits on a slope of vine-clad hills above the river Armancon. At the foot of the hill rises the spring of Fosse-Dionne, held in a round basin.

Two churches draw the article's notice. St Pierre crowns the hill and has a fine Renaissance side portal. Notre-Dame is mainly Gothic, with a fine Renaissance front. The hospital holds a great timber-roofed hall of the late thirteenth century, now used as a chapel. It holds the tombs of Margaret of Burgundy and of Louvois, war minister of Louis the Fourteenth. The town trades in wine, building stone, and Portland cement.
britannica-1911-tonsure:
Tonsure is explained in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a rite of shaving in two great churches. The word comes from a Latin noun for a shaving. The rite is the cut of part of the hair of the head. It marks a pledge to set work for the church.

In those churches the rite is the first step into holy orders. It gives the rights and the rank of a clerk. A bishop gives it with a set form of acts. A man who seeks it must be firm in the faith and able to read and write. Once marked, he must renew the bare ring on the crown each month. If he fails, he can lose the rights the mark brings. The rite is not of the first age of the church, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-torchere: Torchere is a very short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a candle stand on a tall foot of wood or metal for large rooms. The piece came into use in France near the close of the seventeenth century. At first each stand held a single candle on its top. When stands grew to hold two or three lights, the change felt huge. Such stands lit the great halls and ball rooms of the day.
britannica-1911-tramore:
Tramore, a market village and seaside resort in County Waterford in Ireland, is described in a short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on a bay of the same name, seven miles south of the city of Waterford. A rail line from Waterford ends there. The coast near the village has bold cliffs and fine views.

Readers also get clear warnings about the bay itself. It lies open to the south and can trap ships in fog, when crews may mistake it for Waterford Harbour. Three towers stand on the west cliffs, one with a strange iron figure called the metal man. A sand spit splits the bay, and a stone marks the wreck of the troopship Seahorse in 1816. Dunhill Castle, four miles west, is noted as well.
britannica-1911-travancore:
Travancore, a state of southern India, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stood in political relation with Madras. Its area was just over seven thousand square miles. In 1901 its people numbered close to three million, up by fifteen per cent in ten years.

The state ranked sixteenth among the native states of India in area. In population it ranked third. It runs for more than a hundred and fifty miles along the west coast. It reaches down to Cape Comorin, the south tip of the peninsula. The Western Ghats rise to eight thousand feet, clothed in old forest. Spurs run down toward the coast. A flat belt by the sea is thick with coconut and areca palms. Those palms, the text says, form much of the wealth of the land.
britannica-1911-trouvere:
Trouvere, the name for the medieval poets of northern France, is explained in a literature entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They wrote in the tongue of the north, the langue d oil. The word comes from a French verb that means to find or invent. They thrived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

These poets served at court and sang most of all of refined love. Their art was more a play of thought than a show of feeling. Critics in the entry call them pedants of a fanciful court of love. Their work grew more flat than that of the southern troubadours. Southern poets also sang of satire, faith, humour, and state affairs. The entry tests the old claim that northern song was just a copy of southern song, and finds it wanting.
britannica-1911-vampire:
Vampire is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a word with two linked senses. In eastern Europe it first named a blood sucking ghost, a sense the entry traces to a Serbian word. In later use the same word passed to blood sucking bats found in South America.

The entry explains the folk belief in some detail. A vampire was thought to be a dead person's soul that leaves the grave at night to drink the blood of the living. When the grave was opened, the corpse was said to look fresh and rosy. To stop the attacks, people drove a stake through the body, cut off the head, or burned it. Wizards, witches, and those who died by violence were thought most at risk.
britannica-1911-vellore:
Vellore, a town of British India in the North Arcot district of Madras, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Palar and the South Indian railway, eighty seven miles west of Madras city. The count in 1901 was 43537 people. A strongly built fortress there was famed in the wars of the Carnatic.

Tradition dates that fort to the thirteenth century, but the entry holds the seventeenth more likely. It stands as a fine case of Indian military building, with a temple graced by fine sculptures inside. In 1780 it held out through a two year siege by Hyder Ali. After Seringapatam fell in 1799, the sons of Tippoo Sahib were housed at Vellore. Blame for the sepoy mutiny there in 1806 was laid on their plots. A large grain trade serves the town.
britannica-1911-vendemiaire:
Vendémiaire was the first month of the year in the calendar of the French Revolution. The 1911 Britannica article takes its name from the Latin word for the grape harvest. The month began on the twenty-second, twenty-third, or twenty-fourth of September. It ended on the same dates in October, as the year fell. That span was the grape picking season in the wine lands of north France.

Each day of the new year was tied to a thing of use. In this month one day marked the grape, one the vat, one the pumpkin, and one the wine press. The last day marked the cask. The great event of the month came on its thirteenth day in year four, in October 1795. Royalist rebels rose in Paris that day. The young General Bonaparte put the rising down with cannon fire.
britannica-1911-vere:
Vere is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Macaulay praised the Veres as the longest and most famed line of nobles England has seen. The name seems to come from a small village near Bayeux. The founder, Aubrey de Vere, held a great estate in Essex and nearby counties in 1086. His heir gained the hereditary post of great chamberlain in 1133.

The article traces the line through the earldom of Oxford, gained in 1142. A later earl stood with the barons and helped enforce Magna Carta. The seventh earl fought at Crecy and Poitiers in the wars of Edward the Third. His grandson became the famed favourite of King Richard the Second. The text follows gifts of land and office won by marriage over many generations.
britannica-1911-warwickshire:
Warwickshire is a midland county of England, described in this 1911 Britannica article in terms of its bounds, rivers, and hills. It is bounded by Staffordshire, Leicestershire, Northamptonshire, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire, and Worcestershire, and covers about 902 square miles. The river Avon cuts the county from north-east to south-west into two parts of unequal size.

The north-west part drains to the Trent by streams such as the Cole, Blythe, Rea, and Anker, across land that rises in low swells. The north was once known as the Woodland, for the old forest of Arden, while the south-east was the Feldon, a plain in the Avon valley. Along the south-east edge run the highest hills in the county, near 800 feet, among them Edge Hill.
britannica-1911-watts-dunton-walter-theo:
Walter Theodore Watts Dunton, an English man of letters born in eighteen thirty two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at St Ives in Huntingdon, he bore the name Watts at birth. In eighteen ninety seven he added his mother name of Dunton. He was first trained as a student of nature.

In that youth he saw much of the Gypsy folk of East Anglia. He made close study of their lore and odd beliefs. He then left nature study for the law. He worked at law in London for some years. His spare time went to his true love, which was letters. He wrote for two leading journals for more than two decades. For one of them he was the chief voice on verse.
britannica-1911-wavre: Wavre is a town of Belgium in the province of Brabant, 14 miles south east of Brussels. The short 1911 Britannica note gives its count in 1904 as 8,517 people. The town is famed for the fight there on the day of Waterloo. Grouchy pressed on to Wavre that day and won a vain success over a Prussian corps, while the fate of the whole campaign was settled elsewhere. The Prussians raised a fine monument on the field in 1859.
britannica-1911-wellington-shropshire:
Wellington is a market town in Shropshire, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its rail junction and border past. It lies east of Shrewsbury, with London far to the southeast. Its urban count in 1901 was about sixty-three hundred.

The Wrekin hill rises over thirteen hundred feet near the town. A canal links Wellington with the river Severn. Farm tools and nails are made in its shops. Iron and brass founding and malting add more work. The Roman road Watling Street passes close by the town. Before the Conquest an earl of Mercia held the manor. Kings and great families passed it down across the centuries. Thursday and Saturday markets rest on a charter from the 1690s.
britannica-1911-wigtownshire:
Wigtownshire, a county in the south west of Scotland, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is also called West Galloway. Ayrshire bounds it to the north, and the Irish Sea to the south. Its area is four hundred eighty seven square miles. Two bays cut deep into its coast.

Between Wigtown Bay and Luce Bay lies the Machers, a broad point of land. Luce Bay and Loch Ryan cut the Rinns into a hammer headed shape. The Mull of Galloway, at its tip, is the farthest south point of Scotland. Much of the land looks wild and bleak, with heath and bog. Harbours are poor for large ships, save Loch Ryan at Stranraer. The Cree, the Bladenoch, and the Luce are its chief rivers. Most of its many lochs are small.
britannica-1911-wiltshire:
Wiltshire, a south western county of England, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bounded by Gloucestershire, Berkshire, Hampshire, Dorset and Somerset, and it covers a little under fourteen hundred square miles. A great upland fills two thirds of the county, from the Marlborough Downs in the north east to Salisbury Plain at its heart.

Large tracts of the chalk stand over six hundred feet high, and some peaks reach nine hundred, with Inkpen Beacon the highest of all. Scattered in thousands over the downs lie huge blocks of hard grit called sarsen stones, or grey wethers. The old builders of Stonehenge and Avebury used such stones. Green sand shows in the deeper valleys, such as the vale of Pewsey. The entry praises the county's rich, well wooded valleys as one of its chief charms, and names three ancient forests that still remain.
britannica-1911-wisdom-literature:
Wisdom literature, in the part of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry given here, centres on a book that sets wisdom as the supreme good. Over against the troubles of the righteous, the book declares wisdom the best of all goods. Its moral standard is high, save for bitterness shown toward the wicked.

That word means the enemies of the Jews in this writing, the entry notes. A rare word for conscience occurs in the book, a point the entry marks. The style shows the book was written in Greek, though it holds Hebrew turns of phrase. Its author was in all probability a Jew of Alexandria. Nothing more is known of him. The date is placed late in the first century before Christ. Its lack of a place in the Jewish canon is then addressed.
britannica-1911-worcestershire:
Worcestershire, a midland county of England, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Staffordshire bounds it to the north and Gloucestershire to the south. Its area is seven hundred fifty one square miles. The county holds parts of the rich valleys of the Severn and the Avon.

The Severn runs through the county from north to south, through the Vale of Worcester. The Avon vale, called the Vale of Evesham, is given to orchards and market gardens. The Malvern Hills rise sharp from the flat vale on the west border. Their top peak, the Worcester Beacon, stands near fourteen hundred feet high. The Lickey Hills cross the north east corner of the county. Old forest land survives in part in the Wyre forest. In the Malvern core, very old hard rocks form the highest ground of the district.
britannica-1911-yorkshire:
Yorkshire, a county of England, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies in the north-east of the country. Durham bounds it on the north and the North Sea on the east. The Humber estuary parts it from Lincolnshire. Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire, Cheshire, Lancashire, and Westmorland bound it on the land side.

It is the largest county in England. Its area is just over six thousand square miles. It is more than double the size of Lincolnshire, which ranks next to it. Any account of the county must refer to its three great divisions. They are the North Riding, the East Riding, and the West Riding. The centre of the county is a plain. In the south, about the head of the Humber, that plain resembles the Fens in character. Hills rise to the west, as the article goes on to survey.
britannica-1911-zoological-nomenclature:
Zoological nomenclature, the system for naming animals exactly and conveniently, is explained in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It covers animals that live now or are known to have lived. The article calls it the grammar of classification, and notes that it is international. Popular names of animals differ from country to country.

Linnaeus was the first to adopt a precise system. He explained it in 1751 for plants and extended it to animals in 1758. Its core is the two-name system for species. Each species takes two latinized names: first the genus, then the name peculiar to the species. The article gives the cat family as an example. Cats, lions, tigers, and their kin form the genus Felis. The wild cat, lion, and tiger are set out as separate species within it.
british-airships-past-present-and-future:
George Whale, a late major in the Royal Air Force, surveyed British Airships from the earliest experiments through the machines of the First World War. Chapters divide the subject among private builders, army airships, and the naval airship section. Named types include Parseval and Astra-Torres ships, the coastal and C Star classes, and the great rigids numbered 1, 9, 23, and 33.

Whale gives dimensions, lifting arrangements, and frank judgments, as when the North Sea airship suffers for its badly designed propelling machinery. Written just after the war, the book also looks forward to airships' commercial future. It preserves technical detail and service gossip that official reports left out.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-keeping-s:
Laura Lee Hope wrote a Bunny Brown tale in which the children keep a store. Grosset and Dunlap put out the book at New York. Walter S. Rogers drew the plates. Rain opens the tale, with both children flat-nosed at the pane in a nose-press game.

A grand crash heads the chapter list. Feeding alligators and a thing hid in a desk come next. The corner store gives the book its aim. A new pupil, a busy buzzer, and a barn store fill the mid-run. A fall in a hole marks a late turn. Shop play at full scale — stock, sales, and mishaps — forms the stock here. The frame stays Hope's own: home ground, kind grown help, and small plans grown big for a day. This book's later place in the series shows in its long back list of Brown tales.
calvert-of-strathore:
Carter Goodloe wrote a novel of an American in Paris as France broke, dated 1903. The legation at Paris opens the frame. France of 1789 sets the stage in the second place. A lass with a fine air gives the third its name. Palais Royal scenes come next.

A private secretary's post, old and new friends met, and ice sports fill the early run. Yanks made welcome in Paris and good aims gone wrong turn the tale. Versailles and the king's levee raise the scale. Fourth and Fourteenth of July share one chapter head. Lafayette brings friends to a legation meal. Touraine rides, Christmas Eve, and a bid to forget fill the heart. A duel, a short war spell with Lafayette, and a bold stroke mark the late run. The tenth of August closes the heads.
castle-nowhere:
Castle Nowhere, by Constance Fenimore Woolson, opens on the empty northern curve of Lake Michigan. Woolson describes a shore the school maps leave blank. A hundred miles of shore west of Point St Ignace counts as nothing, by the map makers' account. Jesuit canoes and modern propellers alike cut across and leave it alone. The railroad of the future, she notes dryly, will make British America a garden of roses someday.

Woolson sets her stories in that bypassed wilderness. A castle nowhere is a dwelling built on no route to anywhere. Isolation is her subject and her method. The Great Lakes stories collected here grew from her years on Mackinac Island. She was James Fenimore Cooper's grandniece, and Henry James's friend and rival. Her north is colder than his Europe and as carefully observed. Readers who find the map blank, she promises, are exactly the readers she wants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acre:
Acre, called Saint-Jean-d'Acre, is a Syrian Mediterranean seaport, on a plain with Mount Carmel to the south and the mountains of Galilee to the east. Though choked with sand, it ranks among the best harbours on the Syrian coast. Chanaanite-built and given to Aser's tribe, it was never conquered by them. It passed through Assyrian, Tyrian, Seleucid, and Roman hands, and Claudius granted it municipal rights as Colonia Claudii Caesaris.

Its early Christian community hosted St. Paul. The city was taken by Moslems in 638, by Crusaders in 1104, by Moslems again in 1187, by Crusaders again in 1191, and finally by Moslems in 1291. Napoleon failed before it in 1799, Egypt's viceroy took it in 1832, and the sultan retook it in 1840. Until about 1400 it held a Latin bishop, and it now has a Melchite bishop under Antioch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-in-early:
Adam matters greatly to the Fathers and to apocryphal writers of the first five Christian centuries, as their frequent allusions show. Yet his place in the liturgy is far from prominent. The calendar and one Eastern church hymn carry his name, and he fares little better in the West. The sections referring to him are Holy Saturday's first prophecy and the Genesis readings at Septuagesima time.

In literature, by contrast, Adam is treated generously and becomes hero of several books. They include the Book of the Penance or Combat of Adam and the Struggle of Adam and Eve after the Garden. They also include the Codex Nazaraeus, the Testament of Adam, the Apocalypse of Adam, and the Book of the Daughters of Adam. The Testament survives in fragments of great interest, and the entry follows these works through liturgy and legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aedh-of-kilda:
Aedh of Kildare, Leinster's king and an Irish saint, is commemorated by Colgan under 4 January, though much obscurity attaches to his life and work. The Four Masters' Annals and Ulster's agree on this monarch, who gave up his crown and eventually became Kildare's bishop. Under Aidus, Aedh's latinized form, his name appears in several martyrologies.

Colgan says he resigned Leinster's throne in 591, really 592, entering Kildare's great monastery for forty-eight years' service to God, rising successively to abbot and bishop. His episcopate ran from about 630 to 639, and he died in 639 by the corrected Ulster chronology.
