The method serves studies of superconductors, graphene, and topological insulators.

Wolf's project attacked noisy ARPES data: noisy energy curves can throw off fitted values such as electron temperature. A bad fit can make the excited material look as if it were still at rest. He built a U-net machine learning model with fifteen training layers, following published work, to clean the spectra before fitting. The report mixes the data work with machine learning background and the wider ARPES method.
doe-osti-3007484-detector-response-matri:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31843, by Gregory Bowers and nine co-authors, sets out the mathematics that links a radiation environment to what a detector actually records. Its central object is the detector response matrix, which converts an incoming particle spectrum into counts in the detector's energy channels. Worked equations carry each definition from integral form to matrix form.

Definitions follow ICRU Report 85 for fluence, flux, and radiance, keeping environment counts separate from recorded depositions. The authors then build effective areas for steady sources and flash-effective areas for sudden bursts, written as kernel operators that fold with the incoming spectrum. The framework suits space radiation monitors and any counter that must infer a spectrum from counts.
doe-osti-3007881-independent-analyses-of:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2025/4290, by Zain Karriem, Nicholas Herring, Matthew Jessee, and four co-authors, gives an independent check of Antares Nuclear's R1 Mark-1 heat pipe reactor design. Independent analysis matters because a vendor's own calculations should not be the only evidence behind a new reactor. The scope was split into three coordinated tasks.

The first task built an independent system model and computed steady-state behaviour: the multiplication factor, reactivity coefficients, power distribution, and peak and average fuel temperatures. Oak Ridge calculations were compared line by line with the company's earlier results. Weekly calls and a secure file transfer system coordinated the work between the laboratory and the company.
doe-osti-3007889-parametric-optimization:
Nanostructured alumina-forming austenitic alloys are optimized by Tim Graening, Caleb Massey, Holden Hyer, and six co-authors in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4191, dated September 2025. These steels grow a protective alumina skin at high temperature, and the nanostructure aims to keep them strong under irradiation.

Alloys were produced by laser powder bed fusion, an additive route that prints metal layer by layer. Testing combined microscopy, ion irradiation, and corrosion trials with pre-oxidation and liquid sodium exposure. Tensile specimens were pulled to failure at a strain rate of one thousandth per second after a five-minute thermal soak within five degrees of target. The parameter sweep hunts compositions fit for advanced reactor service.
doe-osti-3011813-land-based-wind-referen:
A reference design for land based wind plant control systems is delivered by Zoe Dormuth, Jon Keller, Venkatesh Venkataramanan, Bryan Richardson, and Keith Schwalm of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The design supports simulation of a wind power plant and its turbines for cyber and operations studies. The code ships in open source repositories.

The combined simulation deploys thirty wind turbines, each talking to a site controller over a SCADA VLAN. The repos hold the plant design, the OT-sim controller modules, and a phenix application for scenario setup. The work gives researchers a repeatable plant model instead of one off test rigs.
doe-osti-3012481-adverse-neurological-ef:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2014578, dated January 2026, sums up a laboratory project on what wildfire smoke does to the brain. Bruce Buchholz led the work, with Dorothy You, Long Nguyen, Esther Ubick, Michael Malfatti, S. Hok, and Heather Enright. Smoke harm to lungs and heart is well documented, while the brain effects rested on thinner population data.

The pages collect the project's journal papers, conference abstracts, and posters. In lab tests, wildfire smoke particles raised IL-8 output and lowered ZO-1, a protein that seals brain blood vessels, in human cells. Animal studies traced smoke products into the brain and measured catechol breakdown products in rat blood after smoke extract was placed in the nose. The results give health researchers early evidence on how smoke may reach and affect the brain.
doe-osti-3014755-high-efficiency-mixing-:
Propane blended with dimethyl ether burned in a mixing-controlled compression ignition engine is the subject of a University of Wisconsin final report under award DE-EE0009879, dated December 30, 2025. The multi-institution program set out to show that the blend can run a high-efficiency engine while cutting the carbon intensity of the fuel.

Work packages covered fuel system development, a propane-DME combustion model, optical engine tests, combustion optimization, and metal engine testing. In single-injection experiments the team swept intake temperature from 120 to 200 degrees Celsius in 20-degree steps at a 0.4 millisecond injection duration, holding in-cylinder density constant. A gas turbine power model and a technology evaluation close out the report's account of the blend's prospects.
doe-osti-3018748-a-cultural-resource-sur:
R Stanley Kerr-Painter of Sandia surveyed 661.5 acres on the Tonopah Test Range for this December 2025 report, SAND2026-16075R. The range sits on Nellis Air Force Base in Nye County, Nevada. Federal projects on such land require a cultural resource inventory first. Kerr-Painter's teams walked the acreage and recorded what they found. Newly recorded resources include road segments tied to military use from World War II through the late Cold War. Each site received a state number, a field number, and an eligibility recommendation.

Sites judged not eligible need no further treatment, and the report says which those are. The survey area's environment and physiography get their own sections, as context for where people lived and traveled. For the Department of Energy's Sandia Field Office, this is compliance work with lasting value. The inventory now stands as the record of what was there before any ground is disturbed.
doe-osti-3022410-environmental-extremes-:
A University of Nevada, Reno final report for DOE award DE-SC0023154, led by Hamed Ebrahimian, Adrian Harpold, and Anne Nolin, documents a partnership-building project with Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. The aim was capacity rather than a single experiment. It brought UNR faculty, students, and postdocs into the Department of Energy's environmental research enterprise in two areas: wildfire and hydrology under environmental extremes.

The report logs the mechanics of partnership. First came a joint virtual lightning-talk session. Then, in November 2022, PNNL's associate laboratory director for earth and biological sciences visited campus. In September 2023 a workshop at Reno brought six PNNL scientists together with 31 UNR faculty and graduate students to develop proposals on wildfire resilience and mountain hydrology. Exposure to the ARM and EMSL user facilities and a student pipeline into laboratory science were explicit goals.
doe-osti-3024749-studies-in-nuclear-and-:
Mohammad W Ahmed of North Carolina Central University reports award DE-SC0005367, which ran February 2021 through January 2024, on nuclear and nucleon structure and neutrino physics. His group works at TUNL, the Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory. One thread uses Compton scattering, bouncing gamma rays off targets, to pin down how easily protons and neutrons deform in electric and magnetic fields, their polarizabilities.

The group led experiments with unpolarized cryogenic liquid targets that added high-precision data to the world set. The group aims to extend the work to the first Compton measurements on helium-3. Listed publications include a Nature Communications paper on stellar helium burning with gamma beams and a time projection chamber. Another paper gives a first measurement of the Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn integrand from the helium-3 gamma reaction.
doe-osti-3025045-scres-energy-quest-work:
Sarah A Troise, Molly E Grear, Noelani R Boise, and colleagues at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report the SCRES Energy Quest workshop in PNNL-39090. The workshop format is a structured community exercise: residents work through energy choices for their own area and rank what matters. Responses were grouped into themes, and the counts show what a community puts first when the trade-offs are made concrete.

Affordability drew 46 mentions, 37 percent of respondents, defined as cutting the residential energy burden through minimal rate increases and lower use. Self-sufficiency followed at 32 percent, about using local energy for necessities and leaning less on outside supply. Reliability, steady power with few disruptions even in unknown circumstances, took 25 mentions, twenty percent.
doe-osti-3025798-bridging-cloud-and-edge:
Struan Clark of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory presented these slides on September 16, 2025, at a DOE Fusion meeting in Santa Fe, report NREL/PR-2C00-97468. The subject is CONNECT, a networking platform meant to bridge cloud computing and edge devices at the lab. Researchers' data needs kept growing, while the first common infrastructure proved too hard to use and networking and security rules blocked data movement.

An earlier fix, a custom ZeroMQ relay built for the ESIF facility, was friendly but hit performance limits, needed constant security patching, and served only a few projects. CONNECT's answer includes graphics processors at the edge: models trained in the cloud deploy outward for low-latency inference, and real-time analytics filter the data on site so only high-value results travel. A named engineer leads the platform's AI service.
doe-osti-3364534-data-for-autonomous-tra:
Report NLR/TP-5400-99520 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, by Stanley E. Young, Joseph Fish, and Faizan Mir, examines the data exchanges that self-driving vehicle services and cities need to share. The final report, prepared for the Federal Highway Administration's Turner-Fairbank Highway Research Center, focuses on three flows: hazard alerts for broad awareness, service performance metrics, and fast-changing regulatory information.

Use cases lean on existing standards, including the WZDx work zone data feeds and vehicle-to-everything traveler information messages defined in SAE J2735. A connected work zone stack runs from field devices through published feeds to warnings inside the vehicle. Accuracy and timeliness of work zone data remain open problems, with no settled method for scoring data quality. The report helps city staff judge what to ask of vehicle operators.
doe-osti-3365066-surveillance-lanl-asmt-: LANL-ASMT got surveillance-procured, and this DOE text reviews NNSS suppliers. The pages detail the 2026 findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The procurement was surveillance. The data were nuclear. The 0059 were 2026. The NNSS were review. The supplier were review.
doe-osti-3365070-scintillator-manufactur: A Los Alamos outline by Tait R. Kuchenbrod, LA-UR-26-23563 (May 2026), plans a paper on making composite scintillators for neutron detection. Helium-3, the standard detection gas, is scarce, so solid scintillators could replace it with faster response. The project makes europium- and sodium-doped LiCaAlF6 particles, a crystal that flashes light when neutrons interact inside it. Planned sections review the scintillation process and earlier LiCAF studies, then present his own crystals, measured by quantum yield and radioluminescence across temperature. The hosted text is the outline, not the finished paper.
doe-osti-3374081-spatio-temporal-dynamic:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0022332, covering September 2020 through August 2023 and filed under Omar Farha, tracks how metal-organic framework sorbents catch and release carbon dioxide over time. The target is direct air capture, pulling carbon dioxide straight from the air. The team wanted design rules for sorbents that stay selective and keep their capacity over many cycles, not just in a first test.

The work watches sorbents during capture and release with in-situ spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography, electron microscopy, and synchrotron methods, backed by computer modeling. A standard aging test baked samples at 80 degrees Celsius in full humidity for seven days, then checked crystal loss. One framework, NbOFFIVE-Ni-1, kept its structure through humid aging far better than the earlier SIFSIX-3-Ni, showing no clear change in its diffraction pattern.
doe-osti-3375076-numerical-simulations-o:
Final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0021151, filed in September 2025, covers computer studies of cold air outbreaks over the sea. Bart Geerts of the University of Wyoming led the project. Branko Kosovic, Lulin Xue, and Timothy Juliano of the National Center for Atmospheric Research were co-investigators. A cold air outbreak sends frigid air off frozen land or ice over warm open water. The clash builds striking cloud streets, yet models still handle the regime poorly.

Field data came from the COMBLE campaign in the Norwegian Sea. An ARM mobile facility sat on the coast of northern Scandinavia at sixty-nine degrees north. A second site ran on Bear Island, at seventy-five degrees north. The campaign lasted from December 2019 to May 2020. Outbreak weather filled about nineteen percent of the time at the main site and twenty-one percent on Bear Island.
doe-osti-3375689-geological-hydrogen-fro:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2025/4924, dated June 26, 2026, is a critical review of geological hydrogen. Eight authors share the byline. Yongkoo Seol leads it as principal investigator. Gabriel Creason is co-investigator. Hydrogen forms in the earth on its own, through water-rock reactions and deep radiation effects. Prospectors now ask if it can be tapped like gas. The review sorts proof from hope across 102 pages.

One case covers ophiolites, slabs of ocean crust pushed onto land. Their rocks drive serpentinization, a reaction that frees hydrogen. Springs at the Cedars gave gas with 15.7 percent hydrogen and 15.8 percent methane, by volume. Nitrogen made up most of the rest. The authors judge the geology sound but the field data thin. Rates and costs stay unproven, they warn, next to better-studied sources such as banded iron formations.
doe-osti-3380402-event-driven-3d-sensing:
Los Alamos National Laboratory technology brief LA-UR-26-25994, issued July 20, 2026 and authored by Dharmesh N. Patel, describes an event-driven 3D sensing architecture for imaging fast events. The disclosure name is Neuromorphic Event-based Light-field Imager, with patent applications pending and a technology readiness level of 3. Some events, the brief argues, happen too quickly to capture twice.

A normal camera commits at capture time to one focus, one exposure, and one depth of sharpness; miss and the detail is gone. This system instead records data that lets the user adjust focus and exposure afterward while rebuilding the scene in three dimensions. Named uses include tracking satellites, monitoring aircraft, observing autonomous systems, and recording high-speed industrial processes, all settings where a second take is not available.
doe-osti-3382676-addendum-to-the-closure: A two-page addendum, DOE/EMNV--0049-ADD, dated June 2026, completes the closure file for Corrective Action Unit 578, Miscellaneous Inactive Sites, at the Nevada National Security Site. The Environmental Management Nevada Program published the closure report in January 2024, before the investigation-derived waste had been disposed of; this addendum supplies the missing disposal documentation. The Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest sits in an appendix, with the lead removed from the unit as a line item and the certified receipt signature recorded. It exists so the closure record shows where the waste went.
doe-osti-3388184-example-alternative-com:
The Example Alternative Compliance Annual Report, part of the EPAct State and Alternative Fuel Provider Fleet Program user guide dated July 2026, shows covered fleets how to write their yearly report. The Department of Energy built a reporting spreadsheet for the purpose. The guide gives two worked examples of a complete report, one using the spreadsheet and one not, both containing every required component.

The example fleet is fictional: Power On, Inc., fleet ID 999000, reporting on model year 2027 under a granted waiver. Its petroleum reduction requirement was 47,400 gasoline gallon equivalents, and its plan aimed at 58,087 through two strategies, compressed natural gas and pure biodiesel. The filled-in tables show planned against actual reductions, with the biodiesel line overshooting its plan widely, 80,539 against 43,925 planned, a model of how to document a good year.
doe-osti-3394088-report-priority-gaps-in:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory interim report LLNL-TR-2020679, by M. Zavarin and dated June 18, 2026, reports priority gaps in high-temperature thermodynamic data for nuclear waste disposal. The milestone sits in the Argillite Host Rock Properties and Processes program. The context is a hot repository concept: waste packages in a deep geological repository that run hotter than the databases were built for.

The gap is concrete. The leading European thermochemical database, Thermochimie, applies only below 80 degrees Celsius. The United States effort therefore extends its SUPCRT-NE database toward the higher temperatures a dual-purpose canister repository design needs, feeding the argillite disposal safety model. The report applies thermodynamic models to the shale generic repository concept and lays out planned fiscal 2027 efforts to close the worst gaps.
doe-osti-3399769-commercial-and-industri:
Commercial and Industrial Energy Procurement in Nigeria: A Consumer's Guidebook, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-7A40-98366 from July 2026, teaches Nigerian businesses to buy their own power wisely. Holly Darrow, Bethany Speer, John Mhyre, and Nana Yaa Asante-Darko are the authors. For a factory or hotel facing an unreliable grid, procuring a private energy system is a major purchase made once, against sellers who make it often.

Two middle sections detail the considerations: the policy landscape, energy system types, procurement options, and what a customer should weigh. A fourth section walks the typical procurement process step by step, naming the stakeholders and the critical questions at each stage, with responsibilities color-coded between consumer, developer, and shared. The guide builds on resources from the Rocky Mountain Institute, GIZ, and the Clean Energy Investment Accelerator.
doe-osti-3427059-beam-description-nomenc:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27294, by John Wesley Lewellen and issued August 13, 2026, sets standard names for describing particle beams. Shared terms keep accelerator teams from talking past each other. The document number in the text is LAMP-ACC-MOA-001.

One section defines the RF bucket, the phase window where particles stay stably accelerated. Particles inside one bucket form a microbunch, or simply a bunch. A bunch lasts much less than one radio-frequency period. A figure shows bucket placement on the waveform. Clear names for beam parts help new staff read machine logs and papers alike.
doe-osti-3520427-evaluation-of-the-fluor:
In August 2026, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/TM-2026/4626, which evaluates neutron resonance parameters for fluorine-19 from thermal energy to 1 MeV. Luiz Leal leads a six-author team. Fluorine appears in molten salts and coolants, so its neutron data matter.

The SAMMY code fit experimental data to set the parameters. Covariance data capture both counting and system uncertainties. Those error data are stored in ENDF format for code users. Work focuses on how parameter errors spread into group cross-section errors. Reactor modelers get fluorine data with honest uncertainty bounds attached to it all.
doe-osti-3648898-technoeconomic-studies-:
Argonne report ANL-26/20, dated August 2026, studies a proposed pumped storage hydro plant at Rorex Creek in Alabama. Stuart M. Cohen, Ningchao Gao, and Thushara De Silva lead the printed author list. The plant would sit near Tennessee River Mile 388 at Pisgah. Guntersville Reservoir would be the lower pool, with a new upper reservoir on Sand Mountain Plateau. An underground powerhouse would hold four variable speed pump-turbine units in the favoured design.

That design rates at twelve hundred megawatts and can run near full output for close to twenty hours. Argonne's valuation tool screened seventy-two future power scenarios. Rockies lab models then ran forty-eight cases through grid and production cost tools. Every screening case gave a positive return. Value rose with high gas prices, high solar build, and high load. It was lowest in the reference and retain-coal cases.
doe-osti-3682676-geochemical-impacts-of-:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2009371, dated February 17, 2026, studies what hydrogen does to reservoir rock in California. Six authors are printed: Gabriela Dávila, Megan M. Smith, and Joshua A. White of Livermore, Guangping Xu of Sandia, Nicolas Huerta of Pacific Northwest, and Wayne Kottkamp of Livermore. The test rock came from a depleted oil and gas field.

Samples reacted at eighty degrees with synthetic brine under set gas pressure. Hydrogen, nitrogen, and methane runs let the team split hydrogen effects from plain water-rock effects. Over two weeks, solution acidity eased from mildly acidic toward neutral in the short runs. Longer runs tracked how major and trace elements in the water shifted with time. One snag is noted plainly: leftover residue from poor vessel cleaning clouded the long-run acidity path. Results give a direct view of non-living hydrogen-rock interplay.
doe-osti-3683765-final-scientific-techni:
Kyoungchul Kong's final report for award DE-SC0024407 covers theory work in particle physics at the University of Kansas. The award ran from June 1, 2023 to May 31, 2026. Kong and his students worked beside experimental teams on collider physics, dark matter, and quantum tools. No hardware or patents came out of the award. Products are journal papers, software, and community reports in public archives.

One study used top quark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider to test quantum entanglement and Bell inequalities at record energies. Dark matter work fills a second section, with models tied to what detectors can see. A third part brings quantum technology into particle physics tasks. One paper compares plain and symmetry-aware graph neural networks, in both classical and quantum forms, for sorting particle jets. Working group reports round out the record. The materials also serve to train students and postdocs at Kansas.
doe-osti-3879372-advanced-mrv-protocols-:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory final report TC-23LB020201, dated April 2026, closes a project on verifying forest carbon storage. Jennifer Holm and Charles Koven are the named leads, with Koven as principal investigator. Carbon markets pay for carbon removal, but weak measurement invites inflated claims. The project built a prototype fusing ground measurements, remote sensing, and machine learning. A vegetation model, FATES, supplies the carbon accounting backbone. Partners included Cultivo, Living Carbon, and the University of California.

Work ran from October 2023 to January 2026 on about 1.7 million federal dollars plus cost share. Year one tested the prototype at real carbon market projects. Year two improved baselines, predicted reversal risk, and ran climate projections at every testbed. Focus stayed on improved forest management and new planting. Lessons were blunt: setup is complex, and each site needs its own calibration data.
doe-osti-3915551-argonne-power-purchase-:
Argonne National Laboratory staff So-Bin Cho, Adarsh Bafana, and Nicolas Stauff wrote the technical manual for APEX, the Argonne Power Purchase Agreement Explorer, in September 2026. The report number is ANL/NSE-26-55. APEX is a tool that works out the price terms of long-term power purchase deals, chiefly for nuclear plants.

Most of the manual shows how the tool builds its finance terms step by step. It derives the cost of capital, the value of tax write-offs over time, and a project finance factor, then folds in the federal investment and production tax credits. A separate part sets default costs for reactor power uprates, with higher caps for boiling water reactors than for pressurized water ones. A short early chapter compares the method with the Annual Technology Baseline approach.
dorothy-dainty-at-glenmore:
Amy Brooks's Dorothy Dainty at Glenmore continues the Dorothy Dainty series for younger readers, illustrated by the author herself. Brooks also wrote the Randy books, and her Dorothy volumes run from Dorothy Dainty and Dorothy's Playmates through school, shore and city to Glenmore.

The Glenmore story opens with a letter from Vera, answered by Dorothy, and follows the girls through school and holiday adventures. Brooks writes in large, clear type for young readers, with her own cover designs and pictures. Children who enjoy wholesome girls' series fiction will find Dorothy Dainty at Glenmore gentle, cheerful and kind.
elsie-dinsmore:
Elsie Dinsmore, by Martha Finley, opens in the schoolroom at Roselands, a pleasant room in the old wing of the house. Finley seats the governess Miss Day with her six pupils. Enna, the youngest, is the spoiled darling of both parents. Her lesson is a trial to teacher and scholar alike. Elsie watches from her desk, the gentle counterweight the first chapter sets in place.

Elsie is eight, motherless, and already famous among readers for her piety. Her trials come from a strict father and a household that misunderstands her conscience. Finley's novel, the first of a long series, defined the Sunday school heroine in America. Elsie weeps, prays, forgives, and converts by example. Critics mocked the books for a century. Girls read them anyway, in the millions. Roselands' schoolroom, with its white muslin and rosewood desks, is where that readership was born.
epilepsy-hysteria-and-neurasthenia-their:
Isaac G. Briggs writes plain help for nervous sufferers in Epilepsy, Hysteria, and Neurasthenia, first published by Methuen in 1921. Twenty-seven chapters sort major and minor epilepsy, rarer types, causes, prevention, and first aid for victims. Neurasthenia and hysteria get their own chapters, then advice to neuropaths and first steps toward health.

Briggs, writing from the University of Birmingham, spends most pages on daily management: digestion, dieting, constipation, hygiene, and sleeplessness. Suggestion treatment gets a chapter; patent medicines get a warning one. Training the nervous child and dangers at puberty follow, with heredity, character, and marriage at the end. His epigraph from Chaucer promises English over Latin terms. The tone is kindly and practical.
essays-in-natural-history-and-agricultur:
Thomas Garnett of Low Moor, Clitheroe, observes his local waters in Essays in Natural History and Agriculture, printed at the Chiswick Press in 1883 after his death. The salmon comes first: facts and observations on its river runs, laws for its preservation, and artificial breeding. Letters on agriculture follow, on wheat grown year after year on the same land, gravelling clay soils, and cotton.

The natural history papers are a bird-watcher's diary: wrens' nests, the long-tailed titmouse, the stoat, the sedge-warbler's mocking powers, and spring arrival dates at Clitheroe in 1832. Fish fill the tail: lampreys, minnow spawning, eels, and ice forming at river bottoms. Garnett argues soil and season from his own fields, humus and quicklime disputed in letters.
essays-on-work-and-culture:
Essays on Work and Culture, by Hamilton Wright Mabie, asks what labor does to the laborer. Mabie's contents open with the question Tool or Man, then The Man in the Work and Work as Self-Expression. A dedication verse to Henry Van Dyke makes a confession. Our dearest thoughts travel out of reach along the slender wires of speech. That suits a book about the inner life of ordinary jobs.

Later essays take up the pain of youth and the year of wandering. Fellowship, work and pessimism, special training against general training, and concentration each get a chapter, closing with the ultimate aim. Mabie writes against the idea of work as mere wages. A trade rightly seen is self expression. A school is a workshop of character. Culture is what a man brings home from his bench besides his pay.
fashions-in-literature:
Charles Dudley Warner's literary essays are gathered here under the title of the best of them, and the volume opens with a long memorial introduction. The introducer recalls Warner as the most undogmatic of idealists, a writer who used the essay as Addison used it, for serious things handled with gayety. Thirty years of reputation, from My Summer in a Garden onward, stand behind the pieces.

The title essay treats literary taste as fashion, subject to seasons like bonnets. Warner asks why schools of writing rise, reign, and become ridiculous, and what in a book lets it outlive its mode. The companion essays apply the same lens to authors, reputations, and the reading public. It is criticism without dogma, from a man the introduction calls the most companionable of teachers.
five-thousand-miles-underground-or-the-m:
Roy Rockwood's Five Thousand Miles Underground, copyrighted in 1908, sails the airship Flying Mermaid into the earth. Professor Amos Henderson calls for his assistant Washington in the machine shed as the tale opens. Mark and Jack, the boy heroes of the Great Marvel series, join the new machine. A mysterious hole in the ocean draws them downward.

Whale attacks, a cyclone, and a mutiny delay the descent. Down into the earth they pass, many miles below, into a strange draught and a new land. Giants, a fish that walked, a snake-tree, and a temple of treasure crowd the underground world. Rockwood wrote boys' series fiction at industrial speed, under a house name. This volume is his hollow-earth entry, cheerful, impossible, and brisk. The Flying Mermaid comes home, as the last chapter promises, with wonders duly witnessed.
folk-lore:
Napier collects the beliefs of his own countryside in Folk Lore, dated 1879. James Napier records the superstitious beliefs of the west of Scotland within his own century. His contents run the course of a life: birth and childhood, marriage, and death. Witchcraft, second sight, charms, and divining fill the middle of the book.

An appendix ties the festivals of the year, Christmas, May Day, St. John's Day, and Hallowe'en, to ancient sun and fire worship. The sampled pages give charms and cures. A boy with the king's evil was cured when his father's dog licked the sores and took them on itself. A pain in the arm was cured with red coral and oak leaves, plugged into the root of an oak. Napier writes as a man of science saving what was fading around him.
for-gold-or-soul-the-story-of-a-great-de:
Sheldon's novel takes the reader inside a great department store, Denton, Day and Company. Pale clerks stand behind the counters while cash girls dart on errands, and hopeful girls crowd the fifth-floor offices for work. Superintendent Duncan Forbes, a junior partner, interviews the earliest applicant with open impatience.

The middle of the book follows suspicion down to the counters. A detective named Hardy watches a haggard, poorly dressed customer while six pairs of hose go missing. He admits he would not tackle a rich suspect, who could make things lively for him. Lurana Sheldon, who wrote from inside knowledge of store work, published the novel in 1900.
french-art-classic-and-contemporary-pain:
Brownell surveys French painting and sculpture as one national school. He begins with the classic painters, from Claude and Poussin onward. Later chapters take up David and Ingres. The romantic section centers on Gericault and Delacroix. The Fontainebleau landscape painters get their own treatment.

Realism follows, with Courbet and Bastien-Lepage. Brownell then treats Manet and Monet and the impressionist break. Sculpture gets three chapters of its own. They run from early masters to Houdon and Rude. The book closes with the new movement in sculpture. Rodin and Dalou stand as its leading names. The whole work weighs schools, not just single artists.
from-a-bench-in-our-square:
Adams tells these linked stories from a bench in a city square. The narrator watches a small neighborhood world go by. Its people include a sidewalk artist, a doctor, and shop girls. The first tale pairs the artist Peter Quick Banta with a sharp young critic. Their chalk drawing contest opens the book's gentle comedy.

Later stories turn on art, money, and small ambitions. Titles point to the range of the square's life. A house of silvery voices and a guardian of a graveyard appear. The Little Red Doctor banters with the outspoken Mayme. Each story stands alone, but the square ties them together. Adams writes urban life with warmth and a light touch.
ginx-s-baby-his-birth-and-other-misfortu:
Edward Jenkins published Ginx's Baby in 1870, a satire on Victorian charity built around one unwanted child of the London poor. Ginx, a laborer with too many children already, tries to give the baby away. The contents divide the joke into what Ginx did with him, and what charity and the churches did with him.

Each denomination and society claims the child, baptizes him, litigates over him, and lets him fall through every crack. Chapters invoke Malthus, magistrates, and the milk of human kindness while the baby grows toward ruin. Jenkins wrote to expose real failures in poor relief, and the book's anger made it a sensation that reformers quoted for years.
glaucus-or-the-wonders-of-the-shore:
Charles Kingsley wrote Glaucus, or The Wonders of the Shore to teach Victorian beginners the pleasures of seashore natural history, first published in 1855 and reprinted for decades. The 1890 edition carries coloured illustrations of sea anemones and other shore creatures. Kingsley addresses the book to a young lady friend and keeps the tone inviting.

He explains dredging, describing the rope lengths, bottles, and patience the work needs, then examines what the dredge brings up under a lens. Tubulipora, anemones, and crabs become wonders rather than specimens. Kingsley, a clergyman-naturalist, saw God's workmanship in every tide pool. His book helped start the aquarium craze and still models how to make science writing warm and exact.
govdocs-archive_org-KlimovGregoryTheTerr:
Gregory Klimov, a Soviet officer who defected to the West, wrote The Terror Machine about the Soviet administration in occupied Germany after the Second World War. Klimov had served in that administration himself. Edward Crankshaw, a British Soviet expert, prefaced the English edition.

He describes arrests, deportations, informers, and the daily brutality of the occupation machine from inside its offices. The account is a defector's testimony, written in the early Cold War as warning and as evidence. Its detail is its value: names, offices, and methods, unvarnished. The book stands among the classic defector accounts that shaped the West's picture of the Soviet system.
govdocs-archive_org-NurembergAndTheOther:
A 1978 booklet from Historical Review Press, Nuremberg and the Other War Crimes Trials, surveys the International Military Tribunal of 1945 and 1946 and the trials that followed it. Historical Review Press was a revisionist publisher, and the booklet argues from that standpoint. It is a pamphlet of advocacy, not an official record.

It describes the scene at Nuremberg, the role of the OSS, and Justice Jackson's opening speech, then lists the defendants and sentences. Appendices take up Katyn, the bombing of civilians, and de-Nazification, pressing the charge that the trials were victors' justice. The booklet is a debated piece of revisionist literature, held complete for researchers of the argument.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Crossfire_Cross: A publisher's flyer promotes Crossfire: The Plot That Killed Kennedy, Jim Marrs' book arguing that President Kennedy died in a plot. The same sheet carries an advertisement for a historical mystery by John Dickson Carr, issued in the same series. Flyers of this kind were trade publicity, printed to sell forthcoming books to shops and reviewers rather than to argue the case itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Hosty-OswaldOne:
An FBI memorandum dated October 1, 1975 went from the Director to the Attorney General of the United States. It reports the Bureau's preliminary inquiry into an allegation concerning Lee Harvey Oswald. Twelve years after the assassination, a claim about Oswald still traveled the full height of the Justice Department.

A preliminary inquiry was the Bureau's first formal step, checking whether an allegation deserved a full investigation. That the Director himself signed off to the Attorney General shows the matter's sensitivity. The memo preserves the opening of that inquiry at the top of the department.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SheridanSquareP: nsia-SheridanSquarePress Sheridan Square Press: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In April 2018 President Donald Trump had nominated Gina Haspel to run the CIA, and the Archive posted her torture file. Declassified documents, it said, showed she personally supervised the torture of a detainee in 2002. That torture included at least three waterboarding sessions.

Haspel subsequently drafted the cable that ordered destruction of the videotapes of the torture. The posting also charged that she served as a senior official while the agency misled presidents, Congress, and the public about whether torture worked. The file assembled the public record against her at the moment the Senate weighed her nomination.
halleck-s-new-english-literature:
Reuben Post Halleck, who also wrote histories of English and of American literature for schools, made this New English Literature as a class text. Its chapters divide the story by ages. The first runs from the year 449 to the Norman Conquest in 1066. Then come the ages from Chaucer's death to Elizabeth, the Puritan age, and the Restoration. A supplementary list of authors and their chief works stands at the end.

Later chapters treat the second forty years of the 1700s, the age of Romanticism from 1780 to 1837, the Victorian age, and the literature of the twentieth century. Portraits and views, from Woden to Exeter Cathedral, fill the picture list. Halleck writes in a clear schoolroom voice, with dates and chief works kept in view. The book shows what an American pupil of its day was taught to know about English letters.
hardscrabble-or-the-fall-of-chicago-a-ta:
John Richardson's Hardscrabble; or, The Fall of Chicago opens in April 1812 at a farmhouse on the Chicago River. Four miles from the fort, a backwoods master lingers by his blazing logs. His hunting-frock, fringed homespun, and sheath knife mark him a denizen of the forest. A grizzled voyageur in a beaded sash serves under him.

Richardson builds his tale of Indian warfare toward the Fort Dearborn massacre of August 1812, when Chicago's garrison and settlers were destroyed evacuating the fort. The farm at Hardscrabble becomes the settlers' refuge and strongpoint. Potawatomi warriors, a half-breed villain, and a kidnapped heroine drive the frontier plot. Richardson had served in the War of 1812 himself, and wrote Canada's first novels. His Chicago is no city yet, only a stockade, a river, and farms waiting for the blow he knew was coming.
herbal-simples-approved-for-modern-uses-:
W T Fernie, a doctor, wrote this guide to healing plants. The hosted copy is the second edition, issued at Philadelphia in 1897. A simple, Fernie explains, is a single herb used as a cure. The book takes up plant after plant in order.

Each entry gives lore, plant facts, and the ills it was used for. Liquorice, for one, is traced as a juice for coughs and sore throats. Fernie mixes old herb lore with the drug trade of his day. Readers can see how home and folk cures stood beside formal medicine then.
here-there-and-everywhere:
Here, There and Everywhere, by Lord Frederic Hamilton, is a diplomat's memoir of people and places, published in London in 1921. Hamilton opens in India, at a tiger shoot in Cooch Behar. The Maharajah's howdahs go down in a long line to the covert side. A probable tiger is reported in the grass jungle ahead. The beat stops. Three hundred yards of jungle front must be covered before the guns are posted.

Hamilton served abroad for years and dined everywhere. His chapters move between courts, camps, and country houses with a raconteur's ease. The tiger shoot sets the pattern: ceremony first, then danger, then the anecdote told at dinner. Empire appears in these pages as a social world before it is a system. Its author knew the princes and the proconsuls personally. He writes of both as characters in a club story that happens to span three continents.
hertfordshire:
Herbert W Tompkins wrote this county guide to Hertfordshire, in England. It first came out in 1903, and the hosted copy is the revised second edition of 1922. Tompkins opens with the county's bounds, hills, climate, and plants. Short chapters add people, roads, trades, history, and old remains.

The bulk of the book lists places in A to Z order. Each entry notes the church, old houses, and points of note. St Albans and its abbey church lead the plates. Walkers and local readers get a compact, fact-filled tour of one shire, town by town.
history-of-american-literature:
History of American Literature, by Reuben Post Halleck, is a school textbook from the author of a widely used English literature history. Halleck explains in his preface that requests from all parts of the United States produced the book. He studied at first hand, he says, far more than a condensed textbook can hold. Judgment and selection need that background. His chapters describe the greatest achievements in American writing from the earliest times to the present.

Halleck warns against dwelling on minor authors. Half is greater than the whole, he quotes, when the half is the essential. Great authors, literary movements, ideals, and animating principles get the attention. American writing is kept in relation to English literature throughout. The book taught several school generations their national canon. Rip Van Winkle's return illustrates the front matter. Irving, the Knickerbockers, and the Hudson valley open the story Halleck's students learned by heart.
history-of-modern-philosophy-from-nicola:
Richard Falckenberg, professor at Erlangen, wrote this history of modern philosophy. A C Armstrong translated it, with the author's leave, for an American edition of 1893. Falckenberg aimed at a manual between the huge histories and the thin sketches. His own teachers included Lotze and Eucken.

The tale runs from Nicolas of Cusa to Falckenberg's own day. Kant gets deep treatment, on concepts, experience, and judgment. Each thinker is placed in a line of growth, not left alone. The tone is clear and teaching-minded throughout. Students get a one-volume map of modern thought, drawn by a working professor of the subject.
hoadly-queries-recommended-to-the-author:
This short pamphlet of queries was printed at London in 1713. Its writer signs himself simply a Christian. The target is the late Discourse of Free-Thinking, by Anthony Collins. The piece sold for four pence and runs as numbered questions.

The first query asks if thought bound by prejudice can be called free. Others ask if bad doctors prove medicine false, and if false coin disproves good. Socrates and his views of God and a future state get close parsing. The method is cross-examination, not essay. Readers see how the free-thinking fight was waged, one sharp question at a time.
holidays-at-roselands-a-sequel-to-elsie-:
Martha Finley wrote this sequel to Elsie Dinsmore, first entered in 1868. Elsie spends her holidays at Roselands, her father's house. Horace Dinsmore, her papa, is tender and stern by turns. Elsie's faith and obedience are tested by his strict rule and her own tender heart.

Morning talks open the tale, with Elsie hiding her trouble from her father. A family friend calls Horace cruel and urges Elsie to stop loving him. Finley answers through Elsie's patient, prayerful stand. Generations of girls read the Elsie books for their mix of tears, duty, and Southern home life.
how-to-fail-in-literature-a-lecture:
Andrew Lang delivered How to Fail in Literature as a lecture at the South Kensington Museum, for a college for working men and women, and printed it in 1890 much enlarged. Lang asks why people take up writing, what success they should want, and why most of them will fail. His answer is a comedy of vocation: many feel the call, few have the gift, and the smallest class of all has both gift and will.

Advice arrives upside down, as counsel on failing well: mistake ambition for talent, scorn pains, and trust the poetic temperament. Lang, who succeeded at nearly every kind of writing, salts the jokes with real wisdom about style, reading, and work. Aspiring authors still quote it.
humorous-masterpieces-from-american-lite:
Edward T Mason edited this anthology of American humor, issued by Putnam's in 1886. The contents read as a roll of the age's wits. Bayard Taylor, Charles Dudley Warner, and Louisa May Alcott stand near the front. Artemus Ward and Mark Twain anchor the comic end.

Stockton gives Our Tavern and A Piece of Red Calico. Alcott's Street Scenes in Washington sit beside her Transcendental Wild Oats. Ward's Tower of London lecture drawls through thumbscrews and the Armada. Mason gathered magazine humor at its flood, before the century turned. Readers get a one-volume survey of how America learned to laugh in print.
in-the-rocky-mountains-a-tale-of-adventu:
W. H. G. Kingston published In the Rocky Mountains, a tale of adventure, in London in 1878. Uncle Jeff comes to a farm called Roaring Water in the first chapter. The household holds sister Clarice, Black Rachel, farm hands, and Lieutenant Broadstreet's troopers. Winnemak, a Native visitor, is wounded and cared for at the spring.

Winnemak warns the farm of enemies in return. Later his people hold Broadstreet prisoner, to the narrator's shock. Clarice and Rachel's fate hangs in doubt. Kingston gives frontier danger, gratitude, and rescue in a boys' tale of the West.
indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-eagle:
Frank Bird Linderman collected Indian Why Stories from Blackfeet elders in Montana, subtitled sparks from War Eagle's lodge-fire. War Eagle tells children why the chipmunk's back is striped, how the ducks got fine feathers, and why the kingfisher wears a war-bonnet. Linderman dedicates the book to artist Charles M Russell and to George Bird Grinnell.

Many tales feature Old-man, the trickster creator, stealing the sun's leggings, outwitting animals, and getting outwitted in turn. Linderman knew his tellers personally and worried that settlement was ending their world. His preface mourns the passing frontier while the stories themselves stay lively, funny, and exact about animal nature as Blackfeet tradition understood it.
initiation-into-literature:
Emile Faguet gave a tour of world literature in Initiation into Literature, rendered from the French by Sir Home Gordon. Chapters begin with ancient India, the Vedas, and Buddhist works. Hebraic literature, Greeks, and Latins follow in order. France in the Middle Ages brings the Song of Roland and the Romance of Renard.

Italy gets close treatment in later chapters. Tassoni won fame by a mock poem on a stolen bucket, Faguet notes. Maffei's tragedy Merope of 1714 earns respect, with Voltaire's witness. The book is a short, opinionated path through the classics for new readers.
kansas-women-in-literature:
Kansas Women in Literature is Nettie Garmer Barker's survey of women writers of Kansas. Its epigraphs boast that the state's children are a nobler pride than its walls of corn. Barker counts Kansas-born and adopted women alike in her galaxy of bright names. The first portrait treats Effie Graham, head of mathematics at Topeka High School.

Graham, Barker says, found romance in arithmetic and showed others the way in her lecture Living Arithmetic. Ex-Governor Hoch called her one of the most gifted women in a state noted for brilliant women. Graham lectured on moving into the king row, other people's children, and the larger service. Barker's sketches mix biography, praise, and quotation. The book preserves a state's pride in its women of letters.
kennedy-square:
Kennedy Square is a novel by F. Hopkinson Smith, set in a Southern square of the late fifties. Smith's preface quotes his own Fortunes of Oliver Horn for the square's portrait: magnolias, glossy box, and Noah's Ark church. Kennedy Square has no church, but it has an archdeacon's house instead. Its atmosphere, he promises, matches the older book's square.

Chapter one opens some sixty years earlier, in the square's great days. Smith builds his story on the square's families, their pride, their money troubles, and their honor. The Civil War era closes around them as the novel proceeds. Smith wrote of old Baltimore society with a painter's eye and a native's affection. Kennedy Square is his tribute to that vanishing world.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance-of-a:
King of the Khyber Rifles: A Romance of Adventure is Talbot Mundy's 1916 novel of India's frontier, here in a combined edition. Its contents list eighteen chapters without titles. Captain Athelstan King of the Indian service is the hero. He works among the tribes of the Khyber Pass country, where Britain watched the road to Afghanistan.

The Khyber Rifles, the famous frontier regiment, give the book its name and setting. Mundy's tale mixes secret missions, tribal councils, and mountain fighting. A hidden valley and a mysterious woman stand at the center of the intrigue, by common report of the novel. Mundy knew India well and wrote its frontier with an insider's love of intrigue. The book made his name in adventure fiction.
kitty-trenire:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote Kitty Trenire, a story for young readers in twenty-one chapters. The opening chapters bring news, a drive, and storms at home and abroad. Kitty's family and friends fill the early scenes.

Later chapters bring Anna's arrival, lessons, alarms, and an exciting night. One chapter is called Missing, and another is called Banished. A girl named Betty has an escapade of her own. The book closes with a chapter titled Good in Everything, hinting at lessons learned through trouble. Home troubles matter as much as outdoor adventures here. Kitty must carry real duties while she is still quite young.
la-grenadiere:
Honoré de Balzac set his tale La Grenadière in a small house by the Loire. Ellen Marriage translated it into English. The house stands about a mile below the bridge of Tours.

Balzac describes white stone houses among gardens and vineyards along the cliffs. The finest fruit ripens there under a southern exposure. Generations of patient work cut terraces into the rock face. Against that calm, rich setting, he places a quiet story of a woman and her sons. Place matters deeply in this tale of a mother and sons. The calm house frames lives marked by loss and duty.
lady-baltimore:
Owen Wister, author of Western fiction, set his novel Lady Baltimore in the South. He dedicated it to S. Weir Mitchell with lifelong affection. A note to readers opens the book on a playful, serious theme.

Wister quotes Burns on seeing ourselves as others see us. He wishes artists could test their work as its audience first. That wish frames a story of manners and memory in an old Southern city. A young visitor meets a proud, fading society there. Romance and gentle comedy carry the clash of old and new ways.
lady-clare:
Alfred Tennyson's poem Lady Clare appears here with twenty-two illustrations. Six artists drew them, including Frederic Schell and F. S. Church. The pictures show lilies, a white doe, and the nurse Alice.

The ballad tells of a lady who seems high born and rich. Her nurse reveals a secret about her true birth. Clare must choose between rank and honest love. She gives up wealth rather than win her lover by a lie. Tennyson's short tale in verse remains a favorite for its clear moral and music. The nurse Alice drives the plot with one spoken truth. Clare's choice, once made, is held with quiet firmness.
landmarks-in-french-literature:
Lytton Strachey published Landmarks in French Literature in London in 1912. Seven chapters carry the reader from the Middle Ages to his own era. A list of authors and a bibliography close the book.

Strachey begins with origins, then treats the Renaissance. The age of Louis XIV gets its own chapter. He moves through the eighteenth century and the Romantic movement. A final chapter covers the age of criticism. His short survey became known for clear judgments and elegant prose about French writing. A chronology at the end helps students place each author. Strachey's brisk verdicts still spark argument among readers.
latin-literature:
J. W. Mackail wrote this survey of Latin literature for a series of manuals. The late Professor William Sellar had first agreed to write it. Mackail, his former pupil, finished the task after Sellar's death.

He offers the book as a tribute to his teacher and friend. Chapters begin with the Roman Republic and its early epic and tragedy. Comedy by Plautus and Terence follows. Mackail traces Roman writing from rough starts to classical polish. Students get a compact map of a vast literature in one volume. Mackail later became known as a critic and anthologist. His survey prizes style as much as bare literary fact.
lazarre:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published her historical romance Lazarre in Indianapolis in 1901. The Bowen-Merrill Company issued it with illustrations by André Castaigne. One caption shows a figure mounting toward the guardians of an imperial court.

That court setting signals the tale's world of rank and intrigue. Catherwood built her reputation on romances set in earlier centuries. French and colonial history often supplied her scenes and characters. Lazarre belongs to that line of richly dressed historical fiction. Readers who enjoy court danger, loyalty, and lost identity will find her manner here.
lectures-on-dramatic-art-and-literature:
August Wilhelm von Schlegel's Lectures on Dramatic Art and Literature shaped Romantic criticism. The book opens with a warm defense of reading itself. A taste for reading, the motto says, shields a person against life's ills.

Schlegel surveys drama from the Greeks to his own century. He champions Shakespeare against French classical rules. His lectures helped Europe rethink what tragedy and comedy could be. Translators carried his ideas into English literary debate. The work remains a landmark of comparative literary history. German Romantic writers reshaped taste through these lectures. English poets and critics borrowed Schlegel's terms for decades.
letters-on-literature:
Andrew Lang's Letters on Literature collect his essays on books and writers. An introductory piece treats modern English poetry. Further letters treat Fielding, Longfellow, and a friend of Keats.

Virgil, Lucretius, and Plotinus represent the ancient world here. Aucassin and Nicolette brings in a medieval French tale. Richardson and Gérard de Nerval receive letters of their own. A dedication thanks a helpful friend Lang never met in person. The book shows Lang's wide, easy learning worn lightly. Lang also wrote on books for young American hunters, he jokes. His range runs from Homer to yesterday's poetry.
lister-s-great-adventure:
Harold Bindloss published this adventure novel in 1920. Part One, called Barbara's Rebellion, opens the contents. Cartwright meddles, and Barbara vanishes in early chapters. A girl on a platform and a trip to Winnipeg Beach follow.

Lister's dissatisfaction grows until a test confronts him. Part Two, The Reckoning, brings Vernon's plot into the open. Barbara returns, and Lister clears the ground for settlement. A dissatisfied shareholder and Cartwright's scruples complicate the ending. Shillito gets away and Barbara plays a part before the reckoning. Vernon's curiosity opens the plot threads of part one.
love-under-fire:
Love under Fire is a Civil War romance by Randall Parrish, dated 1911. Alonzo Kimball painted its five color pictures. The tale opens between the lines, with a despatch-bearer hunted down. A woman, Miss Willifred, soon holds the hero as her prisoner.

Chapters bring night adventures, an overheard talk, and a captured house. The villain Le Gaire forces decisions and fights a duel. The hero even becomes, for a time, a famous swordsman. Love and duty pull the young officer in opposite ways. Parrish writes brisk, old-fashioned war romance. It is full of rides, risks, and a brave heroine.
macleod-of-dare:
Macleod of Dare is a Scottish novel by William Black, printed at New York in 1883. Black had already won readers with A Princess of Thule. The first chapter names the six boys of Dare. It opens at sunset over the lonely western seas by Mull.

Ulva, Lunga, and the Dutchman's Cap darken on the water. In Castle Dare's great hall, candles blaze over a frugal supper. An old lady of proud, fine features sits at the table's head. Faithful Hamish serves the small company in the vast room. Black fills the tale with Highland scenery and sea air. His romance joins old clan pride to modern hearts.
measure-for-measure: William Shakespeare wrote Measure for Measure, and the record holds it under his name alone. The hosted sample for this entry preserves long notes by the head of Project Gutenberg. Those notes treat old spelling in Hamlet and in print shops of the time. No readable scene of Measure for Measure itself appears in the sample. This note stays with the title, the author, and that sample limit for that reason.
meyer-us4826581-controlled-process-for-t:
United States Patent 4,826,581, granted to Stanley A Meyer on May 2, 1989, covers a controlled process for making heat from gases, plus the gear to run it. The method patent is part of his eight-piece water fuel cell family. It widens his claims from engines to heat itself.

The process takes in his fuel gas, burns it under set controls, and draws off the heat for use. The filing spells out each stage, the burners, and the apparatus in claim language. Patents attest that a method was described as new, not that it works. Meyer's fuel claims were found fraudulent by an Ohio court in 1996.
miles-wallingford-sequel-to-afloat-and-a:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea novel as the sequel to Afloat and Ashore. Miles Wallingford himself tells the story in the first person. The opening scene is a rescue: Miles has fought his rival Drewett in the water. Friends haul both men aboard the Wallingford and fight to revive the seemingly lifeless Drewett.

Below deck, Lucy Hardinge waits on her knees, praying for the news she fears. Cooper mixes sea action with the claims of love, honor, and old friendship. Miles narrates with hindsight, judging his younger self as he goes. The novel continues his double life between the merchant sea and home ashore.
monsieur-beaucaire:
Booth Tarkington's romance opens at the card table in Bath, England. The young Frenchman Beaucaire has guessed that a duke will cheat. He plucks the hidden card smilingly from the big Englishman's sleeve. Six silent men step from the entryway, and the duke stands caught, scarlet and white by turns.

Beaucaire promises not murder but disgrace, laughing his clear, light laugh. Behind his manners stands a mystery: Beaucaire is a French prince traveling in disguise, working as a barber. Nash, master of Bath society, dislikes the young Frenchman in the pump room. Tarkington's tale of wit, swordplay, and wooing became a beloved stage and screen romance.
my-buried-treasure:
Richard Harding Davis swears this tale of a treasure hunt is true. Only his partner's name is changed, to Edgar Powell. Powell led the trip and still makes flannels for a living. Davis says his own share is what the story earns.

The two had known each other at college, then lost touch. Powell came back with a plan and a buried hoard in mind. Davis tells what was said and done as best he can. No pact stops him from judging his friend in print. The result is crisp adventure writing, half confession and half yarn, from a master of the short tale.
mysticism-in-english-literature:
Caroline F. E. Spurgeon studies mysticism in great English writers here. Her note, dated April 1913, sets strict bounds at once. She treats only the type that seeks ultimate reality. American letters, though rich in such thought, are left out.

A line from Plato's Phaedo fronts the book on the few true mystics. Contents move from Plato and Plotinus to English thought. Love and beauty mystics include Shelley, Rossetti, and Browning. Keats and Coventry Patmore join that company. Spurgeon quotes Traherne, Jefferies, and Thompson with care. The book maps a quiet, deep stream in English writing.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner gives this whole volume to buried treasure and storied places. Captain Kidd stands first, the most widespread man in history, Skinner jokes. Kidd's pots of gold are said to dot the whole coast. Gardiner's Island, Cape Cod, and the Florida Keys all claim shares.

Hope of something for nothing drove the digging, Skinner notes. Real wealth was wasted hunting doubloons that never showed. Sea-serpents, stone-throwing devils, and lovers' leaps share the book. V1 warns readers to enjoy the tales without trusting the maps. Skinner's dry humor makes this the most playful volume of his great set.
nan-sherwood-at-rose-ranch-or-the-old-me:
Annie Roe Carr opens this Nan Sherwood tale as school reopens. Early chapters bring new girls and a curfew song. Walking the plank and an unpopular Rhoda stir the school plot. A Mexican girl named Juanita enters the tale.

The treasure of Rose Ranch is named by chapter ten. At last the girls reach the ranch and its open spaces. A round-up and an outlaw close the sample contents. V1 says an old Mexican's hidden gold sets off the hunt. Nan and her friends ride and outwit villains out west, in the bright style series readers loved.
nasa-tm-19650020117-fps-16-radar-jimsphe:
James R Scoggins and Michael Susko, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, reported wind data measured at the Eastern Test Range on July 9, 1965. An FPS-16 radar tracked a Jimsphere, a special balloon made to follow small wind changes faithfully. Launch teams at the range need accurate winds high above the pad.

Radar tracking of such a balloon gives a detailed wind profile. Those profiles help decide whether a launch can proceed safely. They also feed studies of how winds vary with height. Scoggins and Susko present the measured data from the range, in a form other launch and weather workers could use directly.
nasa-tm-19650022493-research-within-the-:
Robert E Bourdeau, of the Space Sciences Division at Goddard, surveyed research within the atmosphere, with stress on the ionosphere. That charged layer was once studied only from the ground. Rockets and satellites could now pass through the region itself. Bourdeau says those chances have greatly enriched understanding of how the ionosphere behaves.

He also credits new ground-based experiments for part of the gain. The ionosphere holds charged particles with very small thermal energies. It forms when sunlight ionizes the neutral air high above Earth. Bourdeau's survey shows a field being remade by direct measurement, a theme across space science at that time.
nasa-tm-19650025671-vacancy-formation-in:
Hubert H Grimes at Lewis Research Center measured tiny defects in gold wire under great pressure for this February 1964 article draft. A vacancy is a missing atom in a crystal, an empty site in the metal's regular pattern. Grimes used changes in electrical resistance in gold wires to count such defects. The wires were held under high hydrostatic pressure, squeezed evenly from all sides.

Defect levels affect how a metal conducts and how it ages. Pressure changes the energy needed to form a vacancy. Measuring that change tests basic theories of metals. The work was prepared for a journal of applied physics, a sign that space agency laboratories also did deep basic research.
nasa-tm-19660020100-some-studies-on-the-:
David A Evensen and Robert E Fulton at Langley presented studies in October 1965 on how thin shell structures answer sudden loads. Shells form rocket tanks, fuselage skins, and nose cones. Their response is nonlinear, meaning it does not grow in simple proportion to the load. Topics in the catalog note include flexural vibration of thin circular cylinders under motion.

Buckling of shallow, conical, and spherical shells under sharp pressure is also treated. A shell that survives steady loads can still collapse under a pulse. Dynamic stability was the theme of the conference they addressed. Their studies gave shell designers test-based guidance for a failure mode that steady analysis cannot predict well.
nasa-tm-19660021037-analysis-of-the-moti:
C R Hayleck Jr at Goddard analyzed how a satellite turns when a reaction wheel does the turning, in this December 1965 report. A reaction wheel is a spinning disk inside the satellite. Speeding or slowing the wheel rotates the craft the other way. Hayleck studies the pair as one assembly, tuned for the least weight and power that can do the job.

His case is a slewing maneuver, a planned turn from one aim point to another. The wheel and the satellite trade motion back and forth during the turn. Sizing the wheel too small makes the turn slow or impossible. Sizing it too large wastes mass and power. The analysis gives designers the trade in usable form.
nasa-tm-19660030132-the-relations-betwee:
Robert A. Bruce, of NASA's Langley Research Center, gave this talk at a training program at Wallops Island, Virginia, in August 1966. The audience was learning bio-space technology. Bruce's theme is the two-way pull between a science experiment and the spacecraft built to carry it.

He walks through the steps that connect what an experiment needs with what a spacecraft can provide. To make the links concrete, the talk uses a made-up biological experiment as its example. Each requirement the experiment sets, such as its environment, then shapes a design choice. The lecture notes preserve that lesson for mission planners.
nasa-tm-19670009442-jupiter-s-magnetosph:
J. A. Gledhill wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in February 1967, in its Ionospheric Physics Preprint Series. Gledhill was a senior postdoctoral research associate there. His subject is Jupiter's magnetosphere, the huge bubble of magnetic field around the giant planet. The paper asks what happens to the charged gas trapped inside it.

Jupiter spins fast, completing a full turn roughly every ten hours. If its magnetospheric plasma co-rotates with the planet, centrifugal force flings that plasma outward along the field lines. Near the orbit of the moon Io, the outward force already far exceeds gravity. Gledhill argues there is a maximum plasma density the field can hold in co-rotation at any distance. Beyond it, the plasma breaks away, carrying the field with it. He estimates that maximum density in the equatorial plane by balancing magnetic energy against rotational energy.
nasa-tm-19680018225-transport-properties:
Richard S. Brokaw of Lewis Research Center reviews transport properties of high temperature gases in this 1967 symposium paper. Transport properties include viscosity, diffusion, and thermal conductivity. They govern how gases flow and carry heat in engines and reentry flows.

For cool dilute gases, Chapman-Enskog theory already describes behavior well. Heat conduction is trickier, since rotation and vibration inside molecules add to the heat flux. Work by Mason and Monchick improved that part of the theory, Brokaw notes. At high temperatures, mobile chemical equilibria and free radicals change gas behavior further. Brokaw argues the framework can still predict properties for most practical needs.
nasa-tm-19680024873-an-implantable-multi:
C. M. Winget, J. M. Pope, and colleagues at Ames Research Center describe a tiny radio transmitter built to work inside a living body. Their paper was given at a November 1967 Boston meeting on engineering in medicine and biology. The unit reads four body temperatures at once and sends them out by radio, with no wires through the skin.

Small size and low power use suit the device for long implant tests, the authors note. A ring counter samples a reference resistor and four heat sensors in turn, each shaping the pulse timing of a small oscillator. Such readouts serve studies of daily body rhythms. The animal can be watched closely while nothing outside disturbs it.
nasa-tm-19680025079-the-dry-massive-mode:
Patrick Thaddeus of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies defends a dry, massive model of Venus's atmosphere in this paper. In that model, a deep carbon dioxide atmosphere with no water droplets or dust explains radio observations. Pressure-induced absorption then requires a high ground pressure to fit the data.

Such an atmosphere holds so much heat that nightside cooling stays slight. That creates a problem for the observed microwave phase effect, a small intensity change. Thaddeus argues a model supporter can question whether that effect is real. Measurement errors could fake so small a signal, he notes. He reviews the effect's history at two wavelengths to support the doubt.
nasa-tm-19680025201-the-structure-of-the:
Joseph S. Hogan, of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies and New York University, models the structure of the Martian atmosphere in this study. No spacecraft had yet landed on Mars, so its air had to be built from telescope data and physics. Hogan's model reaches from the surface up into the ionosphere, the charged upper layer observers had detected.

His calculations follow how sunlight is absorbed in carbon dioxide bands and how the gas radiates heat away. A separate chemistry calculation tracks how sunlight breaks carbon dioxide apart and what heating that causes. Weighing mixing against that chemistry, he sets upper and lower limits on particle density in the ionosphere. The scan text is partly garbled, but the model's scope reads clearly.
nasa-tm-19700025450-analysis-of-rendezvo:
Rendezvous radar tracking needs for Mission D are analyzed in this Houston internal note, number MSC-EG-69-6. The radar had to have its angle bias corrected while the two craft flew together. Mission D was Apollo 9, the first crewed flight of the lunar module, tested in Earth orbit.

A data book rule required fifteen minutes of steady radar tracking before any maneuver based on radar updates. The analysis asks whether that much tracking is truly needed to correct the angle bias in the guidance computer. Simulations with only ten minutes of tracking, the summary reports, showed no real fuel penalty. The standing rule, the authors conclude, is a conservative one.
nasa-tm-19700026380-investigation-of-the:
NASA issued this general working paper, number 10,044, on pilot control of gliding parachutes. It investigates what a pilot must see to steer such a parachute well. The goal was landing spacecraft on land rather than at sea, which demanded a far more guided final descent.

The study lays out the mode of operation first, then the test program objectives. Testing ran in three phases, each with its own vehicles and systems described in turn. By comparing phases, the investigators could separate what the pilot saw from what the craft itself did. The aim throughout was a firm list of visual references a pilot needs to land the parachute where intended.
nasa-tm-19710009389-an-evaluation-of-the:
J. W. Montano of NASA's Astronautics Laboratory wrote this evaluation in February 1971, issued as NASA TM X-64569. Its subject is A-286, a stainless alloy strengthened by cold working, meaning it is squeezed or rolled before use to make it harder. Montano set out to measure the alloy's mechanical strength and its resistance to stress corrosion cracking.

The report's contents lay out tensile tests, hardness checks, and low-temperature test work on bar specimens from two makers, Carpenter and Armco. Figures track longitudinal tensile specimens, notched specimens, and hardness across different amounts of cold work. Results and conclusions follow the test sections, giving engineers a compact record of how the worked alloy behaves under load and in cold service.
nasa-tm-19710013626-analysis-of-rotation:
John Zuk and Lawrence P Ludwig of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a May 1971 engineering meeting. It analyzes gas flow across the sealing dam of a noncontacting shaft face seal. Such seals limit leakage along spinning shafts in engines and pumps. Rotation of the seal faces changes the flow in ways simple formulas miss.

The authors treated steady, smooth, subsonic flow at steady temperature. They worked out leakage rates and pressure patterns across the dam. They also gave the conditions where a simpler hydrostatic formula stays valid. The error from using that shortcut is stated. Handy formulas cover leakage, opening force, and the center of pressure.
nasa-tm-19720017690-unipolar-induction-i:
Unipolar Induction in the Magnetosphere presents a new theory of how the solar wind powers Earth's magnetic bubble. Its author names are illegible in the scan. A conductor moving through a magnetic field generates electric currents, an effect called unipolar induction. The paper asks how much of the magnetosphere's activity that effect can explain.

Treating the magnetosheath as a simple ohmic conductor, the theory shows induction can energize several current flows in the magnetosphere. It explains the correlation between the east-west part of the interplanetary magnetic field and polar electric fields and magnetic variations. In the tail region it accounts for effects tied to the field's north-south part. When that field points southward, the theory allows a large energy input into the magnetosphere.
nasa-tm-19720018198-apollo-15-mission-ma:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center issued this anomaly report in December 1971. It is report MSC-05805, anomaly report number one for Apollo 15. During the return to Earth, one of the command module's three main parachutes failed. The crew still splashed down safely, but NASA needed the cause. A failed parachute on a crewed flight demands a full investigation.

Investigators studied several possible failure paths in turn. They examined malfunctions in the forward heat shield area. They studied a broken riser, one of the straps tying canopy to capsule. They also studied fuel expelled from the command module's steering thrusters. The catalog record says a most probable cause was identified. The report runs to thirty two pages.
nature-and-human-nature:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton published Nature and Human Nature in 1855. Its first chapter brings back Sam Slick, his famous clockmaker, at a squire's door. Chapter heads promise clippers and steamers, a woman's heart, and a new way to learn Gaelic.

Later heads turn to a day on the lake, a foggy night, and female colleges. Others name gipsying, a betrothal, a honeymoon, and being lost at sea. Haliburton mixes outdoor sport with sharp talk on manners and love. The Pope lines on the title page set the aim: catch manners living as they rise.
news-from-nowhere:
William Morris, poet, craftsman, and socialist, wrote this tale of a dream England in 1890. It first ran in the Commonweal, the journal of his own league. Morris wrote it in part as a reply to Bellamy's Looking Backward of two years past.

A man wakes in a Thames side England where mills, cash, and slums have all passed away. Folk work at crafts they love, share goods in common, and live in a green, clean land. The book is the chief utopian tale of its decade, and a hymn to work done with joy.
no-13-washington-square:
Leroy Scott published No. 13 Washington Square in 1914, a New York tale named for a house address. Chapter one meets the great Mrs De Peyster. An amiable young gentleman enters next, and the lady stands as mistress of her house. A front picture shows a speaker who never suspected ending in such a little blaze.

A slight predicament and the honor of the name trouble the house next. Behind the blinds, the honeymooners, and the flight move the plot along. The Reverend Mr Pyecroft visits, and an attic room holds a secret. Domestic scenes and a happy family close the contents. Scott plays society manners against house mystery.
no-thoroughfare:
Charles Dickens opens No Thoroughfare with an overture, not a chapter. The date is set with care: November the thirtieth, 1835, by the great clock of Saint Paul's. It is ten at night in London. Lesser church clocks strain their metal throats around the cathedral bell.

One clock lags behind the rest, lower and nearer to the ear. It belongs to the Hospital for Foundling Children. Dickens recalls when foundlings were left, no questions asked, in a cradle at the gate. Now mothers must answer inquiries and give up all claim forever. A veiled lady flutters near the hospital gate. Mystery starts with her.
old-saint-paul-s-a-tale-of-the-plague-an:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this novel of plague and fire. The preface is dated November 30, 1841. The tale centers on Saint Paul's Cathedral in London. Book one opens in April 1665, plague year. A grocer of Wood Street shuts his family indoors.

Ainsworth says he followed a rare narrative by Defoe closely. That account tells how the grocer fed his household safely. Coffin makers, gamesters, and plague nurses fill the scenes. The Great Fire follows the plague in the story. Ainsworth blends fact, legend, and strong melodrama. The novel remains his popular portrait of old London.
on-the-evolution-of-language-first-annua:
John Wesley Powell wrote this study for the Smithsonian Institution. It appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology report for 1879 to 1880. The Government Printing Office issued it in 1881. Powell directed the bureau at that time. He bases the study on American Indian languages.

Powell asks how few words can express many thoughts. A word for every idea would need a vast vocabulary, he says. Language grows by shaping grammar and parts of speech. Sentences join small units into fuller meaning over time. He traces that growth in Native American speech. The paper is an early work of American linguistics.
over-here: Edgar A. Guest published Over Here in Chicago in 1918. He dedicated the poems To the Mothers Over Here. It is a home-front book for the First World War.
